# Scope and replay contract

Status: current. This note is a normative reference. Code comments cite this
document by section number. It lands on main unchanged from revision 23, the
revision in force (branch `request/scope-contract-r15`, `3b3e394f`). Where
the code no longer follows a cited section, the citation check of request
`0270882b` lists it. `docs/scopes.md` is the reader's guide.

Date: 2026-10-04. Design only. Written for request R1. The current
commission of the whole contract is the planner's request `4752a1bc`.

`c69b573d910a2ead7874a8651d022530dc58be85`, and the invitations under

Revision 9 answers the independent review `bfe096fe` of revision 8 at
`a549aac6`, which asked for four corrections, and five requests of the
planner: `a89dcea1`, `687d6524`, `9d55ac57`, `873621d2` and `1f52493c`.
It also disposes of what the I1 deltas note added after revision 8
read it: three groups of repairs and the runtime entries 79 to 95
(sections 15.6c and 15.6d). It keeps everything else of revision 8. It
changes these things:

- Capacity reads nothing that transport acknowledged. The fifth
  dimension counts pending requests, from the history (section 17.1).
- A reservation covers the bytes of the inputs that its settling
  entry newly retains, with a rule for bytes that are stored before
  the entry that names them (section 17.2).
- A handler of class `advisory` declares no sends and no attention
  (sections 6.4 and 7.5).
- A timed entry has a kind, so that a job can name the entry that
  decided it, and a `merge` entry's statement carries that entry for
  each job (sections 6.2 and 6.6, and the companion file).
- An issue that a merge closes names its own deciding entry
  (the companion file; witness 18.17).
- Three statements are made exact: the result of a list guard with an
  unfinished nested guard (section 6.5), the two rules for effects on
  one slot (section 6.6), and this opening.
- Two asks of the proof plan are answered from its text: the subject
  of a replay (section 9.5) and the two kinds of failure (section
  4.2).
- The capacity section says that a flat reserve does not make every
  admitted duty settle, with the planner's case as the witness, and
  what a static rule would have to guarantee as a temporary step
  (sections 17.3a and 17.4).
- Rules that the new I1 entries showed to be unstated are stated: what
  "one input at a time" covers (section 5.2), what an entry that
  records a refusal or a clause retains (section 6.5), and some
  smaller ones (section 15.6d).

Revision 10 answers the independent review `114e2cc5` of revision 9 at
`ba556e96`. That review asked for two corrections. It found the four
finding groups of `bfe096fe` repaired in the design, which is not a
finding about any source. Revision 10 also answers the planner's
capacity follow-through `cc570904`, which names two seams. And it
disposes of what the I1 deltas note added after revision 9 read it:
three repairs of the runtime, two of the rule evaluator, the corrected
entries 81 and 94, and entries 96 to 114, on composition and transport
(sections 15.6c, 15.6e and 15.6f). It keeps everything else of
revision 9. It changes these things:

- Inputs that were fetched before a turn are discarded only when the
  turn writes no entry. An entry that records a refusal keeps what it
  read, and is charged for it in its own transaction, by its kind
  (sections 17.2 and 17.3; witness 18.18).
- A reservation is of a duty's whole closure: the duty, and everything
  that its settling entries can start. Two cases are written out. A
  timed rule may leave its item under another timed rule, so a
  deadline reserves its chain. A request's clause may start a duty,
  such as a timer that is set again, so a request reserves that too. A
  closure that is not finite refuses the definition
  `reserve-unbounded` (section 17.2).
- The reserve of the temporary static rule counts the longest chain of
  timed rules for each item, not one entry for each item (section
  17.3a, with its witness).
- The closing checkpoint has an exact rule: what it reserves, which
  checkpoint uses the reservation, and what arms it again (section
  17.2; the fourth witness of section 17.4).
- A child reads the bytes of its declared definition from its creator,
  by digest, before its genesis turn (section 7.2; witness 18.19).
- Rules that the new I1 entries showed to be unstated are stated: the
  address that an envelope carries (section 4.1); transport's four
  answers, the resolver, and which sends a sender gives up (section
  7.4); what a clause reads (section 6.6); a timed entry that always
  fits (section 6.4); and an accepted key that is answered before any
  fetch (section 5.2).

Revision 10 was reviewed, approved (`98b470c3`) and adopted
(`85c18b66`). Revision 11 is its successor, for the request
`108ea663`, and keeps all of it. It disposes of what the I1
implementation chose after revision 10 read it: entries 115 to 152 of
the deltas note, as the source delivery that was filed for review at
`97518f68` has them (sections 15.6g and 15.6h). It answers what the
authority note asks of this contract in its revision 12, which was a
candidate in review when this revision read it. That note's revision
13 is now adopted (the table below). This revision also carries the
two repairs of the review `74b21dc8` (section 15.3a). It speaks to
five shortfalls that the I1 delivery note lists (section 15.6h). It
changes these things:

- A scope retains, from its genesis, the bytes of every declared
  definition under which it can create a child, and of those that
  these name in turn. A child reads them from its creator, by digest.
  A genesis that cannot have them all is not written (section 7.2;
  witness 18.19).
- A refusal uses a reserved entry only where the owner of the duty
  declares a count of decisions. The form is stated, with its five
  conditions, and the receiver pin of `hold@1` has the count
  `decided` (sections 6.11 and 17.3; witness 18.20).
- A runtime may reserve more than a duty's closure, and never less.
  The budget decides only whether new work is written. Nothing that
  a written entry holds depends on it (sections 17.2 and 17.3;
  witness 18.23).
- A creation does not reserve for its `conflict` clause. After a
  `delivery-unavailable` diagnosis a request is settled only by its
  result. A second diagnosis is never written. Sending the request
  again is transport's bookkeeping, and needs no entry (sections 7.4
  and 17.2; witness 18.21).
- A reply across a transport is an answer only when it is a value of
  its operation's result type. Anything else is no answer, and shows
  nothing about what was recorded (section 9.6; witness 18.22).
- The reads and the checks of an independent verifier are stated as
  the source built them: the history as stored, one retained input,
  a known head, what an anchor covers, and the result for each kind
  of failure (sections 9.1 and 9.3 to 9.5; witness 18.24).
- A fetched entry's definition name is held in the entry that used
  it, as `under` of its `FactUse` (sections 4.1 and 9.3). That
  decides point R1-33.
- Rules that the new I1 entries and the delivery note showed to be
  unstated are stated: the unit of the bound on a member's handle
  (section 6.4); what completes a guard with a `where` (section
  6.5); what "one input at a time" does not promise (section 5.2);
  an item that holds two deadlines (section 17.2); and the value
  that a signer signs (section 2.1).
- The companion file's note N21 names the later answers that are
  history only. It now agrees with its own rows: the first authentic
  answer on a `timed-out` job that no retry superseded decides the
  job.

Revision 11 was reviewed and approved (`52fac973`), and it is adopted.
Revision 12 is its successor, for the commission `d56d7f65`, and keeps

- A name that a definition, an intent or a message chooses is data. No

- A fixed record in a reply has exactly the members of its variant. A

- A transport gives every exchange a deadline, and bounds the bytes of

- An `index` send may carry `if`, and the base of `attribute` for an
  unbound subject is stated (sections 6.6 and 6.7). Both answer the

- The things that a check of a history can rest on are set side by
  side, with what each reads (section 9.4).
- What the later source repaired is marked against the list of section

It changes no other rule of revision 11. Every decision that revision

**Revision 12, amended before review. 2026-10-05.** Revision 12 was
filed for review at `aeda54f7`. No reviewer had claimed it when this
amendment was made. It is still revision 12, and the amendment is two
commits on top of that head: the second corrects the capability rule
of the first, which was worded by the version and not by the forms. It holds two decisions of this note's
author, on questions that the I2 delivery (request `efb4e323`) raised
in its deltas note: entries D3, D4, D21, DJ14 and DK5. That note and
its delivery note were read at `744f2447` on `request/i2-lane-forms`,
with some source files of the I2 base. Section 15.6j says what was
read, and gives each entry its disposition.

- A genesis entry states its act kind. The genesis input has a new
  member, `kind`: the genesis act of the definition that the scope
  pins. A reader of a genesis entry of another scope reads the kind
  from the entry. A replay checks it, and a difference is a
  `mismatch`, `genesis-kind` (sections 4.1, 6.2, 9.3 and 9.4; witness
  18.26). The form of an entry changes, so the source owes one more
  row (section 11.10, row 10).
- A runtime must have code for every capability form that the pinned
  definition uses. When it lacks code for one, it answers
  `unsupported-definition` for the whole scope. A definition that
  lists `hold@1` and uses only its item form runs on a runtime that
  derives the item form. A test may supply a scripted capability as a
  labelled stand-in, and a result that was obtained with one proves
  nothing about the capability (sections 6.1 and 6.11; witness 18.27).

The amendment changes nothing else of revision 12. It adds two open
points at the end of the series, R1-48 and R1-49 (section 13). A
passage that it adds is marked "before its review". Such a passage is
a proposal of revision 12, like every passage that is marked "New in
revision 12".

Revision 12 was adopted at `53f0e183`, the commit on which the first
draft stands. So nothing was to be carried from its review.

It makes these decisions. Section 1 has the same list, as D13-1 to
D13-17.

- A party list that is set whole is recorded with the `list` records
  that exist: one for each member that leaves, and then one for each
  that joins, each group in byte order of member identifier. No record
  form is added (sections 4.1 and 6.6).
- A declared definition's name is a text that is not empty and that does
  not begin with `platform:`. An act kind or a message name does not
  have the form of a step kind, `name@version:step` (sections 6.1 and
  6.2).
- Which entries have a kind is stated exactly. A delivered request that
  no handler received has none. The `where` of a `fact` guard reads a
  field of the named entry (sections 6.2 and 6.5).
- The answer to a refused act carries the path of the failed guard, as
  the member `path`. No entry holds it (section 4.2).
- A replay report carries the name of a named mismatch, as the member
  `name` (sections 9.4 and 9.5).
- Only a `hold` effect changes a hold's holder, epoch or state (section
  6.8).
- `one`, and the `on` of a handler that opens a type which is not
  `many`, select an item only when the type has exactly one. With more,
  the input is refused `no-item` (section 6.4).
- `also` names are resolved by dependency, and not in the order written.
  A chain of `via` names that leads back to itself refuses the
  definition (section 6.4).
- An entry records neither its subjects nor the form that made each
  send. A result clause finds both again from its origin entry, by
  stated rules. The validator refuses a definition in which that could
  find another item or another form (section 6.6).
- A guard whose subject is unbound is read as if it were not written,
  wherever it stands. The base of `attribute` for an unbound subject
  stays as revision 12 has it, and the two rules are set beside each
  other (sections 6.4 to 6.7).
- A notice of a timed rule carries no `if`. The validator counts every
  send that one entry can have (sections 6.6 and 7.5).
- A detached text is one retained input under its digest. A scope keeps
  it with every entry whose input names it. A redaction removes it for
  the whole scope. A scope redacts no text that a pending request of its
  own carries, and makes no send of a text that it does not hold. So a
  delivery that waits for a text always ends (sections 6.2, 6.6 and
  9.2).
- How guards are counted is stated. The example of `propose-manifest` is
  corrected to the pinned row: 24 guards as written, 73 in all, and the
  deepest at level 7 (section 6.1).
- A written effect form that is applied writes its record, also when the
  item already holds that value. Four forms record a difference and
  nothing else. This decides point R1-52, and no entry changes (section
  4.1).
- The depth of a decomposition chain is withdrawn as a bound of this
  contract, because no rule of it reads the number. This decides point
  R1-50 for this contract (section 7.5).
- Each of the 165 source choices has one disposition. 69 points state
  the rules that they needed, each in its own section, under the words
  "Made exact in revision 13" (sections 5.3, 6.1 to 6.8, 6.11, 9.3, 17.2
  and 17.3; section 15.6l).
- Of the thirteen forms that the authority note's revision 15 says this
  contract lacks, two are adopted, nine stay platform code, and two are
  left open, each with its question (section 15.3c).

The counts, each made by a script over this note's tables. Of the 165

Against the I2 source at `744f2447`, no disposition changes the bytes

**Revision 13, corrected after review a7f1c108. 2026-10-05.** Revision
13 was filed for review at `7efb0f7f`. The independent review
`a7f1c108` read it and requested changes: one P2 finding, and five
points of wording. This correction is one commit on that head. It is
still revision 13, and it is a proposal as before.

- *The finding.* Revision 13 made exact that the receiver fetches and
  retains every foreign fact that a declared field names, also one that
  no guard and no part reads (section 6.4, point DH4). The count of the
  foreign entries in a byte reservation still counted only the facts
  that a `fact` guard or a part reads. So a settling form could declare
  a list of facts, read none of them, and reserve nothing for entries
  that its settling entry retains. The count was not a maximum, and the
  guarantee that a settling entry fits its own reservation did not
  follow from it.
- *The correction.* The count is by declaration. A settling form counts
  one foreign entry for each fact that a declared field can name,
  through typed records and lists at their declared maxima, whether or
  not anything reads it; one for each fact that the act's `presents`
  declares; and one, once, for the source entry of a delivery. The sum
  is at most the bound on the foreign entries of one entry. Section
  17.2 states it exactly, and section 17.3 restates the guarantee. No
  mechanism, bound, form or refusal is added.
- *What follows it.* The second witness of section 17.4 gains a
  declared list of facts that nothing reads, and witness 18.9 says so.
  Five rows of the companion file's reservations table have a larger
  number in their last column. One sentence of section 6.4 that
  revision 13 had replaced is marked as replaced.
- *The five points of wording.* Point DH15 says that its list of types
  is an abbreviation, and that a local reference inside a nested typed
  record is a whole fact reference on the wire (section 6.6). Point
  DI21 says which refusals are new work, and names the two exceptions
  (section 17.3). The statements that the later I2 head is not filed
  are corrected: the I2 delivery's second head is filed at `50bba45c`
  and is under review (the opening; sections 11.11 and 15.8). The
  standing of two siblings is corrected: the authority note's revision
  16 at `7bc60cf6` is adopted (act `d6e7e878`), and the recovery
  design's revision 4 at `16777d97` is adopted (act `2621bc2f`). Both
  acts are named as the review cites them.
- *What does not change.* Each of the 165 dispositions, every decision
  D13-1 to D13-17, and every open point is as it was filed. The list of
  what the source must change still has 20 rows, of which 19 are owed:
  the source counts no bytes, and capacity in source beyond entries
  stays with the capacity follow-through `cc570904`. Section 13 still
  names 54 points, and section 18 still has 33 witnesses. Each of those
  numbers was counted again by a script. Every number of a budget or a
  bound stays the proof plan's.
- *What the correction read.* The verdict `a7f1c108`, in full. In this
  note, in full: section 17 from its head to the end of section 17.3a,
  the second witness of section 17.4, and section 17.5; the points DH4,
  DJ11 and DJ12 of section 6.4, and its point "A message's fields"; the
  type listing of section 6.2 and its points D22 and DF1; the table of
  parts and the point D20 of section 6.5; the table of bounds of
  section 7.5; point DH15 of section 6.6; section 11.11; section 15.8;
  and witnesses 18.9, 18.18 and 18.23. The other four witnesses of
  section 17.4 were read in part. In the companion file: its opening,
  the reservations table of its section 1 with the text around it, and
  the fields of the rows of the forms that declare `settles` or that a
  pin reserves. Every other place was found by a
  search for the words of the old count and of each stale label. A
  restatement in other words could have been missed.
- *What it did not read.* The authority note's revision 16, the
  recovery design's revision 4, and the I2 head `50bba45c`. No adoption
  act was checked. What this revision took from the authority note it
  read in revision 15 at `8dfda899`, as the table below says. The
  reading of each later text is owed to this note's next revision.
  Neither adoption closes a debt of source implementation. Nothing was
  run.

A passage that the correction adds or changes is marked "Corrected
after the review `a7f1c108`", or names that review.

**Revision 14. 2026-10-05.** Revision 13, as corrected at `86c6aabd`,
was reviewed and approved (checker verdict `636df0ac`), and the planner
adopted it on 2026-10-05. The commission of this revision states the
adoption. This note does not hold the identifier of the adoption act.
Revision 13 is the contract in force. Revision 14 is its successor, on
that adopted text. It is written for the commission `10e7093d`, which
follows the satisfied commission `c75205df`. The commission is bounded,
and this revision does what it names and nothing more. It keeps all of
revision 13. It is a proposal, and is in force for nobody, until it is
reviewed and adopted.

It makes these decisions. Section 1 has the same list, as D14-1 to
D14-9.

- An entry that is no act may retain an observation. Three inputs may
  hold the member `observed`, a list of `ObservationUse` records: an
  `act`, an `outcome`, and a delivery of a result. An observation may be
  of a key, of a member or of the rules. Each is judged by the guards of
  a grant's observation. This decides point R1-53 (sections 4.1 and
  16.1).
- The observations of one scope follow one another by three rules: reads
  are numbered in a run, runs do not return, and the heads that are
  retained for one subject do not go back. The third is new, with the
  mismatch `observation-older`. A later entry reads an earlier entry's
  observations as history only (section 16.1).
- Bytes beside an intent that are no text travel as `values` in
  `Beside`. A value is matched by its digest in the domain that a stated
  place names, is kept as one retained input, and is never redacted. No
  byte domain of this contract is added. This decides point R1-54
  (sections 6.2, 17.1 and 17.2).
- An entry that is written for an input keeps, in `uses`, every foreign
  entry that was fetched for it, whatever was decided. Witness 18.18
  says that its 116 KiB cases leave the optional `merge` out, and gains
  two cases that count it (sections 6.5, 17.2 and 17.3).
- A reader knows three things of another scope's entry: its bytes, its
  kind and the name of its definition. A field of such an entry is read
  from its bytes, with no declaration of the reader. The mark `{ "self":
  true }` is a record there, and a record with a boolean member `self`
  stays a record everywhere. The wire form of a message does not change
  (sections 6.2, 6.5 and 6.6).
- A number that a part reads in another scope's entry is no item of the
  reader. An effect that would put it in a slot of type `item` is
  refused `bad-field`, and it equals no value of type `item` in a
  comparison (section 6.5).
- The limit on the depth of a traversal counts the chain of foreign
  facts from the target, in the replay and in the settlement of owed
  texts. A limit that is reached in the settlement gives `incomplete`
  (section 9.4).
- Each of the 20 later entries of the I2 deltas note, DP1 to DP5 and DR1
  to DR15, has one disposition. 13 points state the rules that they
  needed, under the words "Made exact in revision 14" (sections 2.1,
  6.2, 6.4 to 6.6, 7.4 and 9.3; section 15.6m). The list of what the
  source must change is counted again at `58465dbf` (section 11.12).
- Six entries of the I3 deltas note are answered. A verifier that lacks
  the rules of a capability step answers `unsupported-definition` at the
  first entry of that step (sections 9.3 and 15.6n).

It makes these decisions. Section 1 has the same list, as D20-1 to
D20-9.

- The data of a platform definition states what an entry observes: rows
  of `observes` on an act, on an outcome's kind and on a clause of a
  result. A row states the kind of observation, where the subjects come
  from, the most of them, the window and the use. An entry retains the
  observations of exactly the subjects that its rows give. This decides
  point R1-67 (sections 6.1 and 16.1).
- An outcome entry has one origin: one earlier entry of its own scope,
  whose `uses` it copies. It fetches nothing (section 6.1; I3 delta
  FC3).
- An item type of platform data may state `holds`: the most operations
  of each kind, the most requests and the most items that are opened or
  sent for one item. The entry that opens the item is new work and takes
  the whole. An `operation` effect states the item that it is `for`. The
  folded state holds what is left. A kind that an item holds is in no
  closure, so the kinds may open each other in a circle (sections 4.1
  and 17.2a; I3 deltas FA3, FA5, FC1 and FC2).
- A request that an outcome's send mark makes is counted with its
  operation (section 17.2; I3 delta FC2).
- A `RulesContent` holds `extents` as a digest, and the bytes are a
  retained value. The bound on `content` is its size by the declared
  types. This decides point R1-61 (section 16.1).
- One more kind of observation: the holders of one action (section
  16.1). The observation of each author is a row of `observes`, and no
  new form.
- A fact reference outside an entry is written as its canonical JSON.
  The digest of a fact is its `hash`, and a ref's name holds the 64
  characters of it. No byte domain is added (section 3).
- A refused deciding entry holds no effect of a platform definition, and
  no place is added for one (section 15.3g).
- Each entry of Part 3 has one disposition (section 15.6t).

What changes in an entry's bytes. Four things, and each is in an entry
only where a platform definition uses the form. An `operation` effect
whose kind an item holds gains the member `for`. An observation of the
rules that was asked as "rules" gains the member `extents`, a digest,
under a rules definition whose data states that slot. An entry may hold
an observation of the kind `holders`. And an outcome entry of a kind
that states `origin` holds a copy of its origin's `uses`, and the
observations that its rows give, where the outcome entries of earlier
sources hold neither. A scope has never run under a definition that uses
any of the four, by the word of the deltas note (its sections 28 to 30).
No entry that uses none of them changes. The
two pinned lane definitions state none of the new members, so neither
changes and neither digest moves: a script read the members of every act
type, handler, item type and send form of both files, at the I3 commit
`44172770`, and found no `observes`, `adds` or `holds`, and no
`outcomes`. A text of a fact and a ref's name are in no entry.

*The rule for every other mention.* It is the rule of revision 20, with
this table in place of that one. The table "The standing in force, for
revision 20", above, is a dated passage from this revision on. No

It makes these decisions. Section 1 has the same list, as D21-1 to
D21-10.

- A held kind reserves, for each kind that its outcomes may open and
  that no item holds, that kind's closure. The amount is in the holder
  from the entry that takes it. It moves to the operation when the
  operation is opened, and to the child's own duty when the child is
  opened. The mark of a kind that no item holds lists no held kind
  (section 17.2a).
- The closure of an operation is counted by outcome entry, and a mark is
  counted by what its `most` allows, wherever it stands: an operation,
  an item with what that item reserves, and changes of state at the
  worst case (section 17.2).
- A row of `observes` states, under `retains`, each value that its
  observation may name, with the most bytes of one. Every form that
  states such a row reserves those bytes: an act that settles, an
  outcome's kind and a clause of a result. A clause's are reserved when
  the entry that sends its request is admitted (sections 16.1 and 17.2).
- A draw past a stated count is a fault. The outcome stays offered, and
  nothing forces an end. That is the planner's answer. The fault is
  shown by a read, which is owed, and the way out is an act that adds to
  the holder, or a revision of the definition (section 17.2a).
- `settles` has a third form, by a mark that the entry sets. This
  decides point R1-68, as the planner decided (sections 6.4, 17.2 and
  17.3).
- A request that is bound to a holder is settled from what the holder
  holds, whatever is decided. Only a request that is not bound is new
  work. That is the planner's answer, and it replaces the conclusion of
  revision 20 on a refused `withdraw` (sections 15.3g and 17.2a).
- A public ref name that stands for a fact holds the 64 lower-case
  hexadecimal characters of the entry hash as one whole component,
  between two fixed parts. That is the planner's answer, made exact
  (section 3).
- In an outcome a subject may rest on an observation of the same entry,
  in a second step and no third. An outcome still fetches nothing. What
  the authority note's section 6.5 must change for that is stated. Point
  R1-69 is decided in part (section 16.1).
- A source of subjects reads no signer and no name that a mark binds.
  Rows that give one subject are whole or absent each for itself, and
  the subject is retained when one whole row gives it (section 16.1).
- A report's `name` may be one of the four names of a broken order of
  observations. The passage on the size of `content` is about the
  compact record only (sections 9.5 and 16.1).

What changes in an entry's bytes. Nothing beyond revision 20. No entry
gains a member. The members `retains` and `second` of a row, `sets` of a
`settles`, `decisions` of a `holds` and `bound` of a handler are members
of a definition's data. The draw of a bound request is derived by the
fold from the entry as it is. A report gains four values of `name`. The
two pinned lane definitions state none of the new members, so neither
changes and neither digest moves. How that was checked: a script read
both files as JSON from the I3 commit `44172770`, and walked every
member at every depth. Neither file has a member `observes`, `holds`,
`adds`, `outcomes` or `bound` anywhere, and each new member of a row or
of a `holds` can stand only inside one of the first three. The 7
`settles` of the two files are 6 of the form `{ of, in }` and 1 of the
form `{ copy }`, and none states `sets`. The words `decisions`, `origin`
and `for` do occur in the files, each as the name of a field or of a
slot, and `step` and `values` as the older members of an act and of an
item type.

**Revision 23. 2026-10-06.** Revision 22, at `a1c709e4`, was reviewed in
the verdict `675776bc`, which asked for changes. It is not adopted.
Revision 19 is still the contract in force. Revision 23 is on revision
22. It keeps all of it, apart from what the passages that are marked
"revision 23" change, and it is a proposal until it is reviewed and
adopted. The verdict has one finding. It credits everything else of
revision 22: a mark as the source of `bound.of`, the marker duties,
check 5 by every edge, and the earlier repairs. This revision changes
none of those rules. It has three parts.

- *Part 1.* The finding. Revision 22 let a binding selector read every
  item of its type, asked for no index, and had a witness that accepts a
  mark with `code`, `row` and `item` only. The planner's answer 3 of the
  act `2d3fa911` requires the opposite: a binding selector names an
  indexed slot, or the validator refuses it. So an implementer had two
  rules of acceptance. The contract now has the planner's. An item type
  declares its indexed slots. A binding selector states the index and
  the field that gives the key. Its rule is given the items that the
  index returns, and no other (sections 6.1 and 17.2a; witness 18.53).
- *Part 2.* The planner's four answers of that act, written as decided
  where the text still asked (sections 1, 6.4, 15.8, 17.2a and 17.3).
- *Part 3.* One sweep, with its table below: each place of revisions 20
  to 22 that leaves an access to the runtime, and each answer of the
  planner's three acts against the text and the witnesses.

*What the verdict says of the scan, kept.* The scan of revision 22 was
finite. Section 17.1 counts live and retained final items against the
budget of items, and the selector read each at most once. So this
revision does not state that no count bounded it. It states that the
owner requires an indexed lookup, and that the contract now requires
it. The finding is one of conformance to that direction. No run showed
a cost.

*The rule for every other mention.* It is the rule of revision 20, with
this table in place of that one. The table "The standing in force, for
revision 22", above, is a dated passage from this revision on. No
sibling's standing changed between the two revisions, as far as the
instruction says. A passage that says "New in revision 22", "Decided in
revision 22" or "Changed in revision 22" is a proposal of revision 22,
which revision 23 carries. Where revision 23 changes such a passage, a
sentence beside it says "revision 23".

It makes these decisions. Section 1 has the same list, as D23-1 to
D23-3.

- An item type of platform data may declare indexed slots, as `indexes`.
  At most 4, each a fixed and required slot of one of seven types. Two
  keys are equal by the equality of section 6.2, which for a fact of
  another scope is the whole fact reference. The index is derived state
  of the fold: written with the opening of each item, complete at every
  head, and rebuilt in a replay (section 17.2a).
- A binding selector states `index` and `key`. Its rule is given the
  items that the index returns for the value of that field, live and
  final, in order of item ID and at most 8, and the fields of the
  message. With none returned it gives none. With 1 to 8 the rule
  chooses one of them, or none. More than 8 is a fault. The validator
  refuses, as `bound-source`, a binding selector with no index, with an
  index that its type does not declare, or with a key of another type
  (sections 6.1 and 17.2a).
- The planner's four answers of the act `2d3fa911` are written as
  decided: the fault of a clause that would open a held kind for a
  final holder stands, as a known limit of liveness; a rule of a form
  that declares `settles` sets no state; a binding selector uses an
  index; and the rows of the branch and of `adopt-head` are the
  authority note's (sections 6.4, 17.2a and 17.3).

What changes in an entry's bytes. Nothing. No entry gains a member. The
data of a platform definition gains two things: the member `indexes` of
an item type, and the members `index` and `key` of a mark at place 2
that is a binding selector. The validator reads each only with its
platform option, and refuses each in a declared definition as it refuses
any member that it does not know. No name of a refusal is new:
`bound-source` is given in four more cases, and
`unsupported-definition` in one more. The two pinned lane definitions
declare no index and no binding, so neither changes and neither digest
moves. How that was checked: a script read both files as JSON from the
I3 commit `44172770`, and walked every member at every depth. Neither
has a member `indexes`, `bound`, `holds`, `outcomes` or `code`, at any
depth. A definition with no `code` has no mark, so it has no binding
selector and no place where `index` or `key` could be read as this
revision reads them. The name `index` does occur, 12 times in
`change.json` and 9 in `issue.json`, each time as the send form `index`
in the `sends` of an act or of a handler (section 6.6). The name `key`
occurs once and twice, each time as the member `key` of a `distinct` or
a `sameSet` guard (section 6.5). Neither is a member of an item type or
of a mark. The new members are read in platform data only, and a lane
definition is a declared definition. So no byte of either file is read
differently.

Seven limits of this reading are stated once, here.

- The source was read to settle the wording of a rule, and to see
  whether an entry describes what was built. That is not a review of the
  source, and it accepts none of it. The I2 base is under its own
  review.
- A second reader's line is a report, and not the writer's own reading.
  Where a disposition rests on one, its row says "a second reader
  found". Some entries of section 15.6l describe an earlier step, and
  a later entry replaced what they say. Their rows say which.
- The witnesses that an I2 entry names are tests of the producer. They
  were not read, beyond their names. Each is cited as the I2 notes
  report it, and none is evidence here.
- A scripted capability and a scripted peer are stand-ins. A result that
  was obtained with one proves nothing about the capability or the peer
  (section 6.11).
- Rows 1 to 3, 5, 6, 8 and 9 of the list of sections 11.9 and 11.10 were
  not read again at `744f2447`.
- The authority note was read at its revision 15, which was then
  proposed. Its revision 16 is now adopted, and this revision did not
  read it. Where this revision adopts a form that revision 15 asks for,
  the form is this contract's own decision. The rules behind it stay
  that note's, and this note's next revision reads them in the adopted
  text.
- Four adopted inputs were not read again, as the table says. No rule of
  this revision changes what revision 12 carries from them: the source
  and removal map of section 11; the connected browser, device and
  workspace outcomes; and the proposal, review, landing and publication

An adopted base is the text in force for its subject. Four things
follow, and all four are limits.

- The adoption of a sibling's base does not adopt this candidate. It
  also adopts no form that this candidate adds, and no form that this
  candidate writes for that sibling, such as the two lane definitions
  of the companion file.
- What a base leaves open stays open with its owner: an interface it
  has not stated, a number, an operational decision, and whatever
  source has still to show.
- Revision 10 was the contract that source followed, until revision 11
  was reviewed and adopted. Since then revision 11 is, until revision
  12 is reviewed and adopted. Revisions 7 and 10 are history.
- A candidate of a sibling is in force for nobody. This revision
  carries no rule of a candidate that is now in review. Where it
  carries a rule of the authority note, it read the rule in that
  note's revision 12, and it says "stated in the authority note's
  adopted revision 13". That is revision 13 at `2709006c`, adopted by
  `d7acffc9`. Such a rule is R3's, and it is taken from an adopted
  note, with whatever label of proposal that note itself keeps on a
  number. The authority note's adoption adopts nothing here. What
  this contract adds for such a rule is a form. The form is a
  proposal of this candidate, and it is adopted only with this
  candidate. If R3 changes the rule, the form is reconciled again.

This note answers decisions D1 and D5 of plan 017 as far as it can, and
names what it leaves to R2, R3 and R4. It defines what a scope is, how
one scope refers to another, what a scope records, how a change takes
effect, what an act means, how state is read, and what a second party
can and cannot check by replay. It keeps no format, identifier or reader
of the earlier model. The type listings are a design, written as
TypeScript for precision. They are not source.

Two words are fixed. A **scope** is an authority scope. A set of paths is
a **resource extent**.

## 1. Decisions

| ID | Decision | Choice | Left to |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1-1 | Scope identity | A scope ID is the digest of a **seed**. A seed names the creator and a **cause**: a digest that identifies the one input that asked for the scope. It contains no hash or sequence number of the entry that creates the scope. | None |
| D1-2 | Incarnation | Minted when a scope's storage is first written. A restore from retained bytes keeps it. A scope created by another scope does nothing until its creator confirms the incarnation. | Refusing a second founding of a lost repository: R3 |
| D1-3 | Placement | One namespace for all scopes. A scope's Durable Object is named by its scope ID and nothing else. Every entry carries `epoch: 0`. | Relocation needs a fence protocol that is not designed. |
| D1-4 | References | Four classes: identity, fact, grant, commitment. A reference to an entry is a view made after the entry is sealed. It is never part of that entry's own bytes. | The grant's freshness proof and the commitment's state machine: R3 |
| D1-5 | History | Each scope keeps one hash-chained history with its own sequence. An entry is one input and the results derived from it. | None |
| D1-6 | What proves a fact | The source scope's history, replayed under its own meaning, or an anchor. Scopes hold no signing keys. | Anchoring: section 9.5, R3 |
| D1-7 | Refusals and retries | An accepted act is recoverable from history for the life of the scope. A refusal of an act is never cached; a retry is judged again. A refused delivery is recorded. | None |
| D1-8 | Retention | A scope keeps its history and the inputs its replay needs. Budgets reserve room for settlement. | Budgets, backpressure, archival: R4 |
| D5-1 | Meaning | A scope pins one definition, with its evaluator profile and capability versions, at creation. Several pinned meanings existing at once is normal history. | Migration of a live scope is not designed. |
| D5-2 | Primitives | Typed **items**; acts that **open**, **transition** or **comment**; handlers that **receive** a message; fixed guard, effect and send forms, as data. | R2 writes the lane forms and reports gaps. Section 6.9 lists forms left to R2 and R3. |
| D5-3 | Application code | Applications supply definitions as data. The platform supplies in code: directory, membership, rules, destination, inbox and task definitions, and the hold capability. The task scope, which holds controls of a hosted agent, is proposed by the R3 draft. | None |
| D5-4 | Admission | Each scope keeps the whole-head rule over its own history. The rule is not narrowed. It is sound only together with the dependency rules of section 5. | Narrowing is a later optimization with its own proof. |
| D5-5 | Cross-scope reads | No guard reads another scope's present state. | None |
| D5-6 | Exclusive resource extents across lanes | Not provided in the first version. A deliberate tradeoff: section 8.5. | R2 shows it is safe for the demonstration. |

Decisions that revision 8 proposed and revisions 9 and 10 keep, as
corrected. The adoption of revision 10 decided each.

| ID | Decision | Choice | Left to |
|---|---|---|---|
| D8-1 | Every point addressed to this contract | Each has one disposition: a form adopted here, a demonstrated mapping onto forms that already exist, or a gap with an owner. Section 15. | The owners named there |
| D8-2 | The forms the lane definitions need | Operand parts, list guards, conditional effects and sends, a fan-out, capability guards and effects, record fields, detached text. No form reads another scope's present state. Sections 6.2 to 6.6 and 6.11. | R2 confirms the instantiations. |
| D8-3 | Bounds on a definition | 16 item types, 64 act kinds, 24 handlers and 8 timed rules, with the other values of section 6.1. Labelled proposals. | R4 measures the validator's cost. |
| D8-4 | Sends from one entry | Bounded by kind: declared forms, one fan-out, the platform's one result or control, and attention. At most 104 in all. The delivery of an advisory sends nothing, by a rule of the grammar. Sections 6.4 and 7.5. | R4 measures the largest entry. |
| D8-5 | An outside effect before an act is admitted | Allowed only as an operation that a sealed `preparation` entry of the owning scope opens. The duty is recorded first. Section 5.5. | R3 owns each capability's steps. |
| D8-6 | A late answer to an attempt | An attempt recorded `unknown` may get one more outcome entry, from its own answer. Earlier entries stay. A selection is derived and is made once. Section 4.3. | R3 owns each effect's evidence. |
| D8-7 | The founder of a repository | A `register` scope is the directory's creator and confirmer. The directory is an ordinary child. Section 7.1. | R3 owns the register's definition. |
| D8-8 | Absence of an act | Stated at a position. Terminal only on a recorded fact that nothing later can undo. Section 9.1. | None |
| D8-9 | Retained judgment inputs | Each has a typed domain, a source, a trust label and restrictions. Retained bytes authorize nothing about mutable foreign state by themselves. Section 16. | R3 owns the windows and the walk. |
| D8-10 | Capacity | Every pending duty reserves, when it is created, what its settlement needs: entries, items, records, pending requests, and bytes for its entry and for the inputs that the entry newly retains. A settlement draws only on its own reservation. A reservation covers the whole closure of its duty: what its settling entries can start. No amount is read from transport's bookkeeping. Section 17. | Every number: R4 |

Decisions that revision 11 proposed. The adoption of revision 11
decided each.

| ID | Decision | Choice | Left to |
|---|---|---|---|
| D11-1 | A definition's named closure | A scope retains, from its genesis, the bytes of every declared definition under which it can create a child, and of those that these name in turn. A child reads them from its creator, by digest. A genesis that cannot have them all is not written. Section 7.2. | The bound on a closure: R4. A platform creator that takes a name from an input: R3. |
| D11-2 | A refusal that uses a reserved entry | Only where the owner of the duty declares a count of decisions, inside five conditions. Every other written refusal is new work. Sections 6.11 and 17.3. | The declarations: R3 |
| D11-3 | What a runtime may reserve | More than a duty's closure, and never less. The budget decides only whether new work is written, and nothing that a written entry holds depends on it. Sections 17.2 and 17.3. | Every number: R4 |
| D11-4 | A `conflict` result, and a diagnosed request | A creation reserves nothing for a `conflict`. After `delivery-unavailable` a request is settled only by its result, no second diagnosis is written, and a new dispatch is bookkeeping. Sections 7.4 and 17.2. | The retry policy: R4. The operator's procedure: R3 and the installation design. |
| D11-5 | An answer across a transport | A reply is an answer only when it is a value of its operation's result type. Anything else is no answer. Section 9.6. | The read values: R2. What authenticates a reader: R3. |
| D11-6 | The definition name of a fetched entry | It is in the entry that used it, as `under` of its `FactUse`. Sections 4.1 and 9.3. | That the definition was activated: R3 (point R1-22) |

| ID | Decision | Choice | Left to |
|---|---|---|---|
| D12-1 | A chosen name | It is data: a member of its own record, compared by its bytes. No name is refused for what it spells. Section 6.1. | The reserved keys of the rule profile: point R1-8 |
| D12-2 | A fixed record in a reply | Exactly the members of its variant, each of its form. A signature and a key ID each have one text form. Sections 2.1 and 9.6. | The forms that I2 and I3 add |
| D12-3 | The reader of a reply | One deadline for an exchange, and a bound on the bytes that are read. After the deadline nothing more is read, kept, joined or parsed. A transport over a binding owes the deadline too. Section 9.6. | Every number: R4. The other party's own buffers: nobody here. |
| D12-4 | Which requests a count of decisions covers | Every bound request, and no other. An owner covers less by a narrower binding. Section 6.11. | Each binding: R3 (point R1-44) |

A replay checks it against the pinned definition, and a difference is a `mismatch`, `genesis-kind`. Sections 4.1 and 6.2. | The genesis act of each platform definition: the authority note's successor (point R1-48) |

When it lacks code for one, it answers `unsupported-definition` for the whole scope. A definition that uses only the item form of `hold@1` runs on a runtime that derives the item form. A scripted capability is a labelled stand-in in tests, and its results prove nothing about the capability. Sections 6.1 and 6.11. | The rules of `hold@1` and `git-read@1`, and confirmation of this choice: the authority note's successor (request `406983fe`; point R1-49) |

Sections 6.1 and 6.2. | That each platform definition's name begins with `platform:`: the authority note's successor (request `406983fe`). The bound on a name: R4 (point R1-37). |

One that was decided `refused`, `unknown-message` has none. The `where` of a `fact` guard reads a field of the named entry. Sections 6.2 and 6.5. | The step kinds of each capability: the authority note's successor |
| D13-4 | The path of a failed guard | The answer to a refused act carries it, as `path`, for `guard-failed` and `capability-refused`. No entry holds it. Section 4.2. | What else a refusal carries: point R1-42 |

| ID | Decision | Choice | Left to |
|---|---|---|---|
| D14-1 | An observation outside a grant | An `act`, an `outcome` and a delivery of a result may hold `observed`, a list of `ObservationUse` records, and no other input may. An observation is of a key, of a member or of the rules. Each is judged by the guards of a grant's observation, and its entry is never clamped. Only the code of a platform definition writes one. Sections 4.1 and 16.1. This decides point R1-53. | Every window, and which entry reads which observation: the authority note's successor (request `f1142e84`). The members of the two further kinds: point R1-55. |
| D14-2 | How one observation follows another | Reads are numbered in a run. Runs do not return. The heads that a scope retains for one subject do not go back: a lower head is read again, and a history that holds one is a `mismatch`, `observation-older`. ## 2. Bytes, identity and placement

### 2.1 Byte domains

Every digest and signature is over a domain tag, a newline, and the RFC
8785 canonical JSON of one value. No value contains its own digest.

| Domain tag | Value | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `artroom-intent-1` | `Intent` | An actor's signature. The intent digest. |
| `artroom-seed-1` | `Seed` | The scope ID. |
| `artroom-entry-1` | `Entry` | The entry hash. |
| `artroom-message-1` | `Message` | The digest of a delivered message. |
| `artroom-delivery-1` | `DeliveryCause` | The cause of a scope that a delivery's handler creates. |
| `artroom-definition-1` | `DeclaredDefinition` | The definition digest. |
| `artroom-text-1` | A text, as one JSON string | The digest by which a detached text field is named (section 6.2). New in revision 8. |
| `artroom-snapshot-1` | A list of `{ ref, target }` pairs, in byte order of `ref` | The digest of a snapshot of staged refs that an ancestry record names (section 16.4). New in revision 8. |
| `artroom-state-1` | The folded state of a scope through one entry | The state digest of a checkpoint (section 9.2). New in revision 8. |

**A domain that an owner declares. New in revision 11.** The table
lists the domains of this contract's own values. A capability version
or a platform definition that keeps a value under a digest declares
the domain tag of that digest, with the value's type (section 17.1,
the last row of the table of bytes). The tag is none of this table's,
and two owners do not share one. R3 asks for a domain for a check's
configuration (stated in the authority note's adopted revision 13;
its section 3.11). The rules definition that retains
those bytes declares it. This contract reads no such bytes, so it
names no tag for them.

```ts
type Digest = `sha256:${string}`;          // 64 lowercase hex characters
type ScopeId = `sc_${string}`;             // 52 base32 characters of a seed digest
type Incarnation = `in_${string}`;         // 26 base32 characters, random
type ScopeKind = "register" | "directory" | "membership" | "rules" | "destination" | "inbox" | "task" | "lane";

interface Intent {
  v: 1;
  to: ScopeRef | null;          // null only when installing a founding register (section 7.1)
  actor: KeyId;
  kind: string;
  on: number | null;            // the item the act is on, by its local ID
  expected: Record<string, number>;   // revision of each item the act names
  fields: Record<string, FieldValue>;
  idempotencyKey: string;
  notAfter: Timestamp;          // proposed: at most 15 minutes after signing
}
interface SignedIntent { intent: Intent; sig: Base64Url }

interface Seed {
  v: 1;
  kind: ScopeKind;
  definition: Digest | PlatformDefinition;
  creator: ScopeRef | null;     // null for a founding register only
  cause: Digest;                // identifies the one input that asked for this scope; section 7.2
  ordinal: number;              // which creation of that input, from 0
}

/** One incoming delivery, exactly. Built by the receiver from the verified envelope. */
interface DeliveryCause {
  v: 1;
  from: FactRef;                // the source fact of the incoming envelope, as verified
  n: number;                    // the ordinal of the incoming send in that source entry
  message: Digest;              // the digest of the delivered message
}
```

- The **intent digest** is over the intent, not the signature.
- **A signer signs bytes that are already fixed. New in revision 11**
  (I1 delta 145). The value is put into its canonical bytes before
  the signer is asked, and the intent that is sent is the value that
  those bytes parse to. A value that has no canonical form is not
  signed. So nothing that changes while a signer waits, such as a
  form that a person is still editing, can make the signed bytes and
  the sent intent differ.
- **A signature and a key ID each have one text form. New in revision
  12** (I1 delta 156). A signature is the unpadded base64url text of
  64 bytes. A key ID is `key_` followed by the unpadded base64url text
  of 32 bytes. Each value has one text: a text with padding, or with
  bits set past its last byte, is not that value. These are forms. A
  text of the right form shows nothing about whether a signature
  holds. Check 1 of section 4.2 decides that, and it comes first.
- A seed's `cause` is a digest in one of three byte domains, by the
  kind of input the creating entry admits: an act's intent digest; a
  delivery's **delivery cause** digest; or, for scopes a directory
  creates at its own founding, the directory's seed digest. A scope
  that an outcome entry creates takes the intent digest of the act
  that opened the operation. Section 7.2 has the table.
- A **delivery cause** names one delivery: the source fact that sent
  the message, the ordinal of that send, and the message digest. The
  source fact is an entry of another history that was sealed before the
  delivery arrived, so its hash already exists, and the receiver has
  verified it (section 7.4). A message digest alone is not a cause: two
  different deliveries can carry the same message bytes.
- A **seed** is stable across retries. The same intent, retried, has
  the same digest. The same delivery, sent again, has the same source
  fact, ordinal and message. Each asks for the same scope. Two different
  deliveries never ask for the same scope, even when their message
  bytes are equal.
- Nothing in a seed is a sequence number or a hash of the entry that
  creates the scope. A delivery cause names the foreign fact that was
  delivered. It does not name the entry that records the delivery,
  which has no sequence number or hash until it is sealed. So no client
  and no scope has to guess a position before an entry is sealed.

**Made exact in revision 14, from the later I2 source choices.** Each
point names the entries of the I2 deltas note that it answers (section
15.6m). Each is a rule of this contract from this revision, for the
reason that the point gives. None changes an entry that the I2 source at
`58465dbf` writes, unless the point says so.

- **DR5.** A value has canonical bytes only when it nests at most 64
  containers, one inside another. A container is a JSON object or a JSON
  array. A deeper value is no value of any domain: it has no digest, no
  entry holds it, and it is no field value. A reader of a reply (section
  9.6) stops its walk of a value at that depth, and a reply that holds a
  deeper value is no answer. A check of a reply that ends in an error of
  the reader, and not in a result, is no answer either. The reason: the
  walk of a value that another party sent must end by a bound that the
  reader holds, and this is the bound under which every entry is
  written. The number is the I2 source's, `MAX_DEPTH` in its bytes
  package. It is a labelled proposal, and R4 owns it with the other
  bounds. How the source counts the level at the bound itself was not
  read.

### 2.2 Incarnation

- A scope mints a random incarnation in the transaction that writes its
  first entry.
- Restoring a scope's storage from retained bytes restores the
  incarnation with it. The scope is the same scope.
- An empty store cannot tell whether it is new or lost. So a scope
  created by another scope starts **provisional**: it has a genesis
  entry and sends its creation result. It admits two things only: the
  confirmation from its creator, and a repeat of its own creation
  request, which it answers from its genesis. Every other input is
  answered `scope-provisional`. It becomes active when its creator
  confirms that incarnation. Section 7.2 says what a provisional scope
  may send. A scope whose genesis was refused admits only a repeat of
  its creation request. Every other message to it is answered
  `not-found` by the resolver of its name (section 7.4).
- A store is **empty** until it holds a genesis entry. An object that
  is reached at a name which holds no scope may create its tables,
  and it answers `not-found`. It mints no incarnation and writes no
  entry. So it is still an empty store, and a later creation that is
  addressed to that name by its seed finds it so. New in revision 10
  (I1 delta 113).
- A creator that already holds a creation result with another
  incarnation records `incarnation-conflict` and never confirms the new
  one. The replacement never becomes a working scope that issues grants
  or effects. An operator act resolves the conflict.
- A founding register has no creator. Its seed has `creator: null`. A
  repository's directory is created by the register and confirmed by
  it, like any child (section 7.1). Every scope a directory creates
  has the directory's `ScopeRef`, with its incarnation, in its seed.
  If a directory's storage is lost after the register holds its
  applied result, a repeated creation makes a provisional directory
  with a new incarnation, the register records `incarnation-conflict`
  and never confirms it. Nothing treats it as the old repository.
  Revision 7 gave the directory no creator; that sentence is replaced.

### 2.3 Placement

One rule: **a scope's Durable Object is the object named by its scope ID
in the one scope namespace.** The kind is inside the seed, so the ID
commits to it. A reference's `kind` is a claim that the scope checks
against its genesis; a wrong kind is answered `not-found`. There is no
second namespace in which the same ID could name another ordering
authority.

At genesis a scope checks that the digest of the seed equals its own
name. No directory lookup is on the path of an ordinary act.

The contract reserves an authority epoch and fixes it at 0. Moving a
scope to another ordering authority needs the former one fenced first.
That protocol is a named gap.

A displayed number such as #42 is a label that the directory allocates.
It is not an identity and no reference uses it.

## 3. References

```ts
/** Identity: this scope, this incarnation. Says nothing about its state. */
interface ScopeRef { scope: ScopeId; inc: Incarnation; kind: ScopeKind }

/** Fact: one sealed entry, exactly. Always built after that entry is sealed. */
interface FactRef { at: ScopeRef; seq: number; hash: Digest }

/** Grant: permission issued by a fact in an authority scope. */
interface Grant {
  issued: FactRef;
  subject: MemberRef;
  key: KeyId;                      // the key that may use it
  principal: MemberRef | null;     // when the key acts for another member
  actions: readonly string[];
  within: ScopeRef | ScopeFilter;
  notAfter: Timestamp | null;
  fresh: FreshnessProof;           // section 16.1; R3 owns the windows
}

/** Commitment: one exact operation its issuer has promised to complete. */
interface Commitment {
  issued: FactRef;
  operation: OperationId;          // stable across attempts
  subject: FactRef;
  cancelBy: unknown;               // R3: the point of no return
  result: FactRef | null;
}

interface MemberRef { membership: ScopeRef; member: MemberId }
```

1. An identity reference supports navigation. It proves nothing.
2. A fact reference names an entry with its content and its meaning at
   that time. It does not say anything is true now.
3. A decision that needs a present condition uses a grant or a
   commitment, never a fact and never a link.
4. A link grants no authority.
5. **Views.** A fact reference, a duty ID and a receipt are views. They
   are derived after an entry is sealed and travel beside it. An entry
   may contain fact references to earlier entries of any scope. It
   never contains a reference to itself. Inside its own scope an entry
   names itself, where an effect needs that, by the word `self`, which
   the fold reads as its own `seq`.
6. A fact reference commits to all history before it, through `prev`.
   Because an entry can only contain hashes that already exist, two
   facts cannot depend on each other.

**A fact reference as text, and the digest of a fact. New in revision
20** (the authority note's adopted revision 26, its section 12.1.5, "The
founding commit, and the receipt"; I3 delta ER9). A platform definition
may write a fact reference outside an entry: in a line of a commit
message, and in the name of a ref. No text said which bytes those are.

- *The text.* The text of a fact reference is the RFC 8785 canonical
  JSON of the `FactRef`, as UTF-8, and nothing before or after it. The
  members stand in this order, which is the order of that standard:
  `at`, with `inc`, `kind` and `scope` inside it; then `hash`; then
  `seq`. No space and no line feed is inside it.

  ```
  {"at":{"inc":"in_...","kind":"lane","scope":"sc_..."},"hash":"sha256:...","seq":41}
  ```

- *Its bytes, exactly.* `inc` is `in_` and 26 characters. `scope` is
  `sc_` and 52 characters. `kind` is one of the eight scope kinds. `hash`
  is `sha256:` and 64 lower-case hexadecimal characters. `seq` is the
  position as decimal digits, with no sign, no leading zero, no fraction
  and no exponent. A position has at most 16 digits (section 3.1). That
  standard writes a whole number as its digits when a JSON number
  carries it exactly, which holds for every position up to
  9,007,199,254,740,991. Every byte is a printable ASCII character. The
  text is at most 237 bytes, with the kind `destination` and that
  position. A script built that value and counted it.
- *In a commit message.* A line holds a word, one space, the text and
  one line feed, as the authority note's rows state the word. The text
  holds no line feed, so it never ends the line early.
- *Why not a URI.* A fact URI of section 3.1 names a host. A reference
  does not, and a commit that names a host would have another ID at
  another host. So a commit holds the reference.
- *The digest of a fact.* A fact has no digest of its own. Where a text
  asks for "the digest of a fact", it is the fact's member `hash`: the
  entry hash, in the byte domain `artroom-entry-1` (section 2.1). No
  byte domain is added. The reason: an entry's bytes hold its `at` and
  its `seq`, so the entry hash already names the scope, the incarnation,
  the kind and the position. A second digest over the three members of
  the reference would name the same entry and add nothing.
- *In a ref's name.* The part of the name that stands for a fact is the
  64 hexadecimal characters of its `hash`, in lower case, without the
  prefix `sha256:`. The prefix is left out because a ref's name may hold
  no colon, by the rules of Git as the writer knows them: no Git command
  was run for this revision. So `refs/artroom/receipts/` and the 64
  characters is a name of 86 bytes.
- *The name, exactly. Made exact in revision 21*, as the planner
  confirmed (act `1f8aba72`). A public ref name that stands for a fact
  is three parts in this order: a fixed part, the 64 characters, and a
  second fixed part, which may be empty.
  - The 64 characters are the hexadecimal digits of the entry hash, each
    `0` to `9` or `a` to `f`, in lower case. Nothing stands before them
    or after them in their component: no `sha256:`, no tag and no
    length.
  - Each fixed part is a constant of the platform definition's version.
    It holds only the letters `a` to `z`, the digits, `-` and `/`. The
    first begins with `refs/` and ends with `/`. The second is empty, or
    begins with `/` and does not end with one. Neither holds `//`, and
    no component of either begins with `-`.
  - So the 64 characters are one whole component of the name. A reader
    finds them by splitting the name at `/`. One name holds the
    characters of one fact, once.
  - *The rules of Git that this relies on. Attributed, and not
    executed.* They are the rules of the manual page of `git
    check-ref-format`, as the writer knows them. A name is components
    that `/` separates. No component begins with a dot or ends with
    `.lock`. A name holds no two dots in a row, no ASCII control
    character, no space, and none of `~`, `^`, `:`, `?`, `*`, `[` and a
    backslash. It does not begin or end with `/`, hold `//`, end with a
    dot or hold `@{`, and it is not the one character `@`. A name of the
    form above holds only `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `-` and `/`, has no
    empty component, and so meets each of those rules. No Git command
    was run for this revision. The builder of row I3-46 runs `git
    check-ref-format` on each name that a version states, and that check
    is owed with the row.
  - `refs/artroom/receipts/` and the 64 characters, with an empty second
    part, is such a name, of 86 bytes.
- *Whose fact.* A rule builds such a name, and such a line, only from a
  fact that the scope holds as verified: a reference to an entry of its
  own history, or to an entry that an entry of the scope names in
  `uses`. A reference that was never verified could state another `at`
  beside a true hash. The name would be the same and the line would not
  be, and the commit's ID covers the line.
- *What a reader can check.* The last part of the ref's name equals the
  64 characters of `hash` in the line of the commit that the ref names.
  That needs no entry and no host.
- *What does not change.* No entry holds this text or this name, so no
  entry's bytes change. A fact inside a JSON file, such as a receipt, is
  a member of that file's value, written by the canonical form of the
  whole value: that is the same bytes as the text above.

### 3.1 A URI for a scope, a fact and an item

New in revision 17, for the commission `9626787f`. The owner's
direction: every thing with an attached scope is addressed by its
scope's URI, and that URI resolves. A reference of this section names a
scope, or an entry of one. It does not say where to ask. A URI adds
that: a host. It is a way to write a reference for a person, a page, a
tool or another system. It is no fifth class of reference.

**The grammar.** ABNF, in the notation of RFC 5234. `host` and `port`
are those of RFC 3986. Every literal is in lower case, and the grammar
is case-sensitive.

```abnf
artroom-uri = "artroom://" host [ ":" port ] "/" scope [ fact-tail / item-tail ]
scope       = scope-id [ "@" incarnation ]
scope-id    = %s"sc_" 52b32             ; section 2.1: the seed's digest
incarnation = %s"in_" 26b32             ; section 2.2
b32         = %x61-7A / %x32-37         ; a to z, and 2 to 7
fact-tail   = "/" position "/" hash
item-tail   = %s"/items/" item-type "/" position
position    = "0" / ( %x31-39 *15DIGIT ) ; no sign, no leading zero, at most 16 digits
hash        = %s"sha256:" 64hexdig
hexdig      = DIGIT / %x61-66           ; 0 to 9, and a to f
item-type   = %s"~." / %s"~.." / plain-type   ; revision 18: one component, below
plain-type  = 1*( literal / pct )        ; and not "." and not ".."
literal     = ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" / "_" / "."
pct         = "%" 2HEXUP                 ; never the code of a literal
HEXUP       = DIGIT / %x41-46            ; 0 to 9, and A to F
```

- It has no user information, no query and no fragment. A text with one
  of them is no artroom URI.
- The scope ID and the incarnation are the texts of section 2.1, with
  their trailing bits zero, as their guards check. A text that fits the
  grammar and is no scope ID is no artroom URI.
- A `position` in a fact tail is the entry's `seq`. In an item tail it
  is the item's local ID, which is the `seq` of the entry that opened
  it. The word `items` cannot be a position, so the two tails are never
  confused.
- An item type is a chosen name, and it may be any text that is not
  empty (section 6.1). "The item type, as one component", below, says
  how it is written. Corrected in revision 18: revision 17 gave three
  rules for it that did not agree, in the grammar, in this list and in
  the normal form.
- In the scope part and in a fact tail, a `:` and an `@` stand as
  themselves. Both are allowed in a path by RFC 3986. Neither stands as
  itself in an item type.

**The item type, as one component. Decided in revision 18** (the
verdict `8645c22b`, its first finding). A chosen name may hold any
byte: `x:y`, `x@y`, `a/b`, a space, a `%`, a name that is `.` or `..`,
and text that is not ASCII. One rule writes every name as one part of a
path, and reads it back.

1. *To write a name.* Take its UTF-8 bytes. A byte that is an ASCII
   letter, a digit, `-`, `_` or `.` is written as itself. Every other
   byte is written as `%` and two upper-case hexadecimal digits. There
   is no exception: a `:`, an `@`, a `/`, a `%`, a space and a `~` are
   each encoded.
2. *The two names of dots.* If the result is exactly `.`, write `~.`.
   If it is exactly `..`, write `~..`. A `~` appears in a component in
   those two cases only, because step 1 encodes every `~` of a name.
3. *To read a name.* Split the path at `/` first. Then, for the
   component of the item type: `~.` is the name `.`, and `~..` is the
   name `..`. Any other component with a `~`, and a component that is
   exactly `.` or `..`, is no item type. Otherwise decode each `%` and
   its two digits to a byte, and read the bytes as UTF-8. Bytes that are
   not UTF-8 are no name.
4. *The normal form of a component.* It is what step 1 and step 2
   write. A text that encodes a byte which step 1 writes as itself, as
   `%2D` for `-`, is brought to the normal form by decoding that one
   byte. If the component is then `.` or `..`, it is written `~.` or
   `~..`. No other encoded byte is ever decoded in the normal form: `%3A`
   stays `%3A`, and `%2F` stays `%2F`. Lower-case digits of an encoding
   are made upper-case.
5. *The request.* The component is carried into the `https` path as it
   is, byte for byte. The route reads it by step 3. It does not read it
   by a general decoding of percent-encodings alone, which would not
   know `~.`.

- *Why `~.` and not `%2E`.* The standard that browsers and the serving
  platform's URL parser follow treats a path part that is `%2E` or
  `%2e` as `.`, and `%2E%2E` and its mixed forms as `..`, and removes
  them as dot segments. So an encoded dot cannot carry the name `.`
  through such a parser. `~.` is no dot segment for any parser. No
  parser was run for this revision: this is the writer's knowledge of
  that standard, and row I3-19 owes a check of it.
- *Why no byte of a name stands as `~`.* So that `~.` can only mean the
  name `.`. The name that is the two characters `~.` is written `%7E.`.
- *One name, one component.* Step 1 is a function of the name's bytes.
  Steps 3 and 4 accept one canonical component for each name. Corrected
  in revision 19: this said "one text". A reader accepts more than one
  text for a name, such as `%2D` for `-`, and step 4 brings each to the
  normal form before anything is compared. So two names never share
  a component, and a formatter and a parser give each other's input
  back.
- *An empty name.* No definition has one: the validator refuses an empty
  name, and this contract accepts that (section 6.1). So a component is
  never empty, and an empty one is no item type.
- *What a part between two hosts may do.* A server or a proxy that
  decodes `%2F` to `/` before it routes breaks the path of a name that
  holds a `/`. The reader is then answered `not-found`, or another
  item's view on that host's word. It is never given a proof, because an
  item URI gives none. A name with a `/` is always addressable by the
  fact of the entry that opened its item.
- *Length.* A name has no bound of its own. The bound on a URI holds
  (below), and a name that does not fit has no item URI.

| It names | The form | An example, with the IDs cut short |
|---|---|---|
| A scope, as a host holds it | `artroom://host/scope-id` | `artroom://example.org/sc_abc…` |
| A scope in one incarnation | `artroom://host/scope-id@incarnation` | `artroom://example.org/sc_abc…@in_def…` |
| A fact: one sealed entry | Either of those, with `/seq/hash` | `artroom://example.org/sc_abc…/42/sha256:0f3…` |
| An item | Either of those, with `/items/type/n` | `artroom://example.org/sc_abc…/items/report/17` |

**The normal form.** Every artroom URI has one normal form, and it is
compared by its bytes.

1. The scheme and the host are in lower case. A host that is a name is
   written as a name of the DNS in its ASCII form: a label that is not
   ASCII is written as its A-label, which begins `xn--`. A host with a
   trailing dot loses it. An IPv4 or IPv6 literal is written as RFC 5952
   and RFC 3986 write it.
2. The port is left out when it is 443, which is the port of the
   mapping below, and when it is empty.
3. Corrected in revision 18. In the scope part and in a fact tail, a
   percent-encoded letter, digit, `-`, `_`, `:` or `@` is decoded, and
   any other percent-encoding there is no artroom URI. In the item type,
   the normal form is that of "The item type, as one component", above,
   and no `:` and no `@` is decoded. Then the text must fit the grammar.
4. One trailing `/` is removed. No dot segment and no empty segment is
   allowed, and none is removed: a text with one is no artroom URI. The
   names `.` and `..` of an item type are no dot segments: they are
   written `~.` and `~..`.
5. Nothing of a scope ID, an incarnation or a hash is changed. A text
   with an upper-case letter in one of them is no artroom URI. It is not
   folded to lower case, because the guard of an ID refuses it.

**What "the same" means.** Four relations since revision 18, where
revision 17 had three. The host is in none but the first.

| Relation | Holds when | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| Identical | The normal forms are the same bytes. | The same text. Nothing more. |
| The same scope ID | The scope IDs are equal. Hosts and incarnations may differ. | Both name a scope with one seed (section 2.1): one kind, one definition, one creator and one cause. They name the same scope whatever the host. A host does not make a scope: it holds a copy of one, or it does not. |
| The same selector. New in revision 18. | For two item URIs: the scope IDs, the item types and the positions are equal, and at least one of the two states no incarnation. | Both ask for the item of that type and number in a scope with that seed. They may name two different items: each host answers from the life of the scope that it holds, and two lives have two opening entries. It serves discovery, and the comparison of what two hosts hold under one seed. It is never the same reference. |
| The same reference | For two scope URIs: the scope IDs are equal, both state an incarnation, and the incarnations are equal. For two fact URIs: the scope IDs, the positions and the hashes are equal. For two item URIs, corrected in revision 18: the scope IDs, the item types and the positions are equal, both state an incarnation, and the incarnations are equal. Or, after both are resolved: the two answers state the same incarnation and the same opening fact. | For scopes: one `ScopeRef`, apart from its `kind`, which the seed fixes. For facts: one `FactRef`, because the hash commits to the entry's bytes, which hold its scope with its incarnation. For items: one item of one life of the scope. |

- *Why two item URIs with no incarnation are not the same reference.
  Corrected in revision 18* (the verdict's second finding). Revision 17
  called them the same reference when both left the incarnation out. A
  host answers such a URI from the life that it holds. A host that does
  not hold the scope can hold a replacement under the same seed, with
  another incarnation (below). So `artroom://a/S/items/t/0` and
  `artroom://b/S/items/t/0` can be answered from `S@I` and from `S@J`,
  with two opening entries. An item tail holds no hash, so nothing in
  the two texts tells them apart. They are the same selector, and no
  more.
- *How an item is compared for identity.* By URIs that both state the
  incarnation. Or by resolving both: the answer to an item URI states
  the scope's reference, with its incarnation, and the fact of the entry
  that opened the item. Two answers with the same opening fact are one
  item. A URI with no incarnation still resolves, and still serves to
  find a scope and to compare two hosts.
- *Two incarnations of one scope ID are not the same reference.* At most
  one of them is the scope that its creator confirmed (section 2.2). The
  other is a replacement that never became a working scope. Two URIs
  that differ in the incarnation name the same scope ID, and a reader
  must not treat them as one working scope.
- *An absent incarnation* names the scope as the host holds it. It is
  enough to find the scope. It is not a `ScopeRef`. A reader that needs
  one reads the incarnation and the kind from the answer, and then holds
  them on that host's word, or on what it verified.
- *A fact URI is self-verifying, whatever the host.* A reader that holds
  the URI holds the hash. Any host that returns bytes with that hash has
  returned that entry. An incarnation in a fact URI adds nothing, and
  must equal the one in the entry.
- *Two different scopes never share a normal form.* The scope ID is the
  digest of the seed, and no two seeds are known to share one. The item
  type has one encoding. The grammar has one reading.

**Resolution.** The URI maps to an `https` request by a fixed rule: the
scheme becomes `https`, the host and the port stay, and the path is
`/v1/scopes/` and what the table gives. A reader's credential, where a
read needs one, travels in the request and never in the URI.

| The URI | The request | What it answers | What the reader does with it |
|---|---|---|---|
| A scope | `GET https://host/v1/scopes/<scope>`, where `<scope>` is the URI's scope part, with its incarnation if it has one | The summary of section 9.1: the scope's reference, with its incarnation and its kind, its definition, its head, and its live items | It checks that the scope ID in the answer is the one that it asked for. The head and the definition are the host's word, until the reader verifies them: below. |
| A fact | `GET https://host/v1/scopes/<scope>/entries/<seq>` | One entry by its position | It computes the entry's hash, in the entry's byte domain (section 2.1), from the entry that came back, and compares it with the hash of the URI. A difference means that the host did not return that entry, and the reader uses none of it. It checks that the entry's `at` and `seq` are the ones that it asked for. |
| An item | `GET https://host/v1/scopes/<scope>/items/<type>/<n>` | The item's present view, at the head that the answer states: its type, its state and its slots. From revision 18 the answer also states the scope's reference, with its incarnation, and the fact of the entry that opened the item. | It is a view at a position, on the host's word. It proves nothing (section 3, point 1). A reader that needs proof reads the entry that opened the item, as a fact. |

- *The incarnation in a request.* A request whose scope part states an
  incarnation is answered only by a scope in that incarnation. A host
  that holds the scope in another answers `wrong-incarnation` (section
  9.1). A request with none is answered by the scope as the host holds
  it.
- *A host that holds no copy answers `not-found`.* So does a name that
  holds a refused genesis, and a reference with a wrong kind (sections
  2.2 and 2.3). `not-found` from one host says nothing about another
  host, and nothing about whether the scope exists.
- *Every other answer of a read stands.* A reader may be answered
  `forbidden`, `scope-provisional`, `unsupported-definition`,
  `too-large` or `unavailable` (section 9.1). "The URI resolves" means
  that a host answers one of these, or the value. It does not mean that
  every reader may read every scope.
- *What a reader verifies.* For a fact: the hash, always. For a scope,
  when it must not rest on the host: that entry 0 holds a seed whose
