  `from` is compared with a name and with nothing else. So a declared
  definition under such a name would pass, by its name, for a platform
  definition that it is not. This is a rule on one member of a
  definition, like the rule on `timed:` (section 6.2). It refuses a
  definition before any scope pins it. The owner of the platform
  definitions (request `406983fe`) is asked to confirm the other half:
  that every platform definition's name begins with `platform:`, as the
  type above writes it. The name has no bound of its own. The unit of a
  bound is the bytes of the name's UTF-8 form, and the number is R4's
  (point R1-37). Until R4 sets one, the bound on the definition's bytes
  is the only limit on it.
- **`timed`.** The timed rules of section 5.2 are declared here. Section
  6.4 gives the form and its validation.
- **`rules`.** Each key is the name of one expression, and each value is
  its text in the language of the pinned profile. A `rule` guard names a
  key. Section 6.5 gives the validation and the replay rule. Nothing of
  a definition lies outside its digest: the digest is over the whole
  value, with its rule texts.
- **A chosen name is data. New in revision 12** (I1 delta 153). The
  keys of `items`, `acts`, `receives`, `timed` and `rules`, the names
  of states, slots and fields, an act's kind and a message's name are
  chosen by whoever writes a definition, an intent or a message. Each
  is a text. The rules on it are the ones that this contract states:
  an act kind or a message name does not begin with `timed:` (section
  6.2), and one item type does not use one name for two slots (section
  6.3). I1's validator also refuses an empty name, and that is
  accepted. A name is a member of a record only when the record's own
  bytes hold it, and it is compared by its bytes. No name has a
  meaning that the language of a runtime gives it. No name is refused,
  and none is read as present, because of what it spells. I1 found
  that a field named `__proto__` lost its value, and that an item type
  of that name reserved nothing for its timed rules. Its repair
  refuses no name. One limit stays. The rule profile `restricted@1`
  reserves three keys of a rule's input, so a `rule` guard that reads
  a field of one of those names is false. That is a refusal by the
  profile (section 6.5), and it is part of point R1-8.
- **A name that has the form of a step kind. New in revision 13** (I2
  delta DJ17). One more rule on a chosen name is stated, in section 6.2:
  an act kind or a message name does not have the form
  `name@version:step`. The reason is the reason for the prefix `timed:`.
  Such a name could be taken for the kind of an entry that only a
  capability writes. The rule above stands: a name is refused only by a
  rule that this contract states, and this is one.

**Bounds on a definition. Proposals.** Each value is a labelled
proposal. None is measured. R4 measures the validator's cost at these
values before they are accepted (R4 section 8.6).

| Bound | Revision 7 | Revision 8 | Needed by |

| Act kinds | 48 | 64 | `issue` has 50 and `change` 52 |
| Receive handlers | 24 | 24 | `issue` has 7 and `change` 4 |
| Timed rules | Not stated | 8 | `issue` has 1 and `change` 2 |
| Rules | Not stated | 16 | Neither lane definition declares one |

The lane counts are those of
`notes/2026-10-04-scope-and-replay-contract/lane-instantiations.md`,
counted by script from one data value at revision 8. Revision 9's
changes to that file alter none of them: the companion file says which
counts were checked again by hand. They differ from R2's in one
place: R2 counts 13 item types for `issue`, and its `change` item is
written here as the relationship copy that section 7.3 keeps, so
`issue` declares 12.

**The bound on the elements of a list. Decided in revision 19** (the
authority note's adopted revision 24, its section 3.2; the I3 delta
EM6). The row "Elements of a list field or slot" said 32. It says 64
from this revision. That note asks for the number. The decision is also
what kind of number it is.

- *What is decided.* Each list type states its own `max`, as the form of
  section 6.2 has it. This contract states one maximum for that `max`.
  It is the same for every list field and every list value slot of every
  definition. It is 64, as a labelled proposal that R4 measures, like
  every value of this table. A definition in which a list type states a
  larger `max` does not validate.
- *Why one maximum, and not a number in this contract for each kind of
  list.* A definition already states the number for each of its lists,
  and that is the number which is enforced: a value longer than its
  type's `max` is refused. A table of numbers here, by what a list
  holds, would state the same fact a second time, and it would put the
  lists of particular definitions into the common grammar. One maximum
  bounds the work of the validator and of the commit on any one list,
  which is what the row is for.
- *Why 64.* The lists that need it state `max: 64`, each of texts of at
  most 64 bytes (that note's section 3.2). The first value of the
  longest of them has 34 elements. 34 is the length of one value. It is
  no bound of this contract, of a definition or of a runtime, and
  nothing reads it. 64 is also the bound on the members of a party list,
  so a list value and a party list have one number.
- *The configured bound.* A runtime holds the bound as a configured
  value. A definition in which a list states a `max` above the bound
  that a runtime is configured with does not validate there, and a scope
  under it is not founded or created there: `unsupported-definition`
  (section 4.2), as for any definition past a bound of the runtime.
- *What each count reads.* No count reads the length of a value that a
  list happens to hold. The validator checks each list type's `max`
  against the configured bound. The static size of an entry form counts
  a list value at its type's `max`, each element at the largest that its
  own type allows: point D10, above, whose words "or at the bound on the
  elements of a list, whichever is less" stand, with the bound now 64.
  The guard `every` reads at most the list's `max` elements (section
  6.5). The `kind` list of a `fact` type holds at most the bound
  (section 6.2, point D16). Section 17.1 says what the five dimensions
  of capacity count of a list.
- *What does not move.* The bound of 32 on the items of one fan-out, and
  the bound of 32 on the fields of one send, are rows of their own and
  keep their numbers (sections 6.6 and 7.5). The bound on the foreign
  entries of one entry stays 128: an input that names more is refused
  `entry-too-large` before any is fetched (section 17.2), so a longer
  list of facts fetches no more than before. A `collect` list is bound
  by the `max` of its item type, and not by this row, as before. Each
  list type of the two pinned lane definitions states a `max` of at most
  32, so neither definition changes, and no static size of either
  changes.
- *Sizes, as sums by the types. None is measured.* One list of 64 texts
  of 64 bytes is 4,289 bytes of canonical JSON when every byte is
  printable ASCII, and 24,769 when every byte is a control character,
  which canonical JSON writes as 6 bytes. Five such lists in one entry
  are 123,845 bytes at that worst, which is inside the entry size of
  section 7.5. A key's observation holds one list of actions (section
  16.1). Its largest size with 64 actions was not counted again, and is
  R4's.

**How guards are counted, and the example of `propose-manifest`. New in
revision 13** (I2 deltas DG1 and DJ21). The two rows of the table on
guards cite the pinned row since this revision. Every other lane count
of the table is still the companion file's.

- *The count.* Every guard of the written list is counted, and every
  guard that is nested in an `each`, a `has` or an `anyOf`, at any
  depth. So the count "counting those nested" includes the guards as
  written. A clause of a `where` or of a `match` is not a guard and is
  not counted. The guards of an `each` or of a `has`, and each
  alternative of an `anyOf`, are a list of at most 24. Each condition of
  an effect, a send or a notice is a list of its own, with the same
  three bounds.
- *The level.* A guard as written is at level 1. A guard that is nested
  in a list form is one level below that form. "Nested at most 8 deep"
  means that no guard stands below level 8.
- *The pinned row.* The row `propose-manifest` of the pinned `change`
  definition was counted for this revision by a script, with exactly the
  rule above, over `packages/lanes/definitions/change.json` in the I2
  source at `744f2447`. The file is the same bytes at `40bf1e33`, where
  the first draft counted it, and a second reader counted it again. It has 24 guards as written, and 73 in all: 24,
  26, 7, 9, 3, 2 and 2 at the levels 1 to 7. Its deepest guard is at
  level 7. The lane design's adopted revision 14 states the same three
  numbers for its own row (its sections 5.3 and 13.4). So the row is at
  the bound of 24, inside the bound of 96, and one level inside the
  bound of 8. It also has 16 effects, which is that bound.
- *Why this note said 23, 70 and 7.* Those are counts of the companion
  file's row, made by its script at revision 8 from the lane design's
  revision 12. The companion file is not brought up to the adopted
  revision 14, and it says so. The first two numbers differ because the
  rows differ, and not because the counting does. The I2 note reports
  that the rule above gives 70 and 7 over the companion file's row (its
  entry DG1). That was not counted again here.
- *Why the I2 note says 8.* Its pin test records the least depth bound
  at which the validator passes the row, and that is 8. The validator at
  `744f2447` refuses a list form that stands at the level of the bound,
  also when the form nests no guard. The two deepest guards of the row
  are `has` forms at level 7 that have a `where` and no nested guard. So
  the row is refused at a bound of 7, although no guard stands below
  level 7. That is a difference of counting, by one, for a list form
  that nests nothing. The rule here is the rule on guards, and the
  source owes the difference: section 11.11, row 16. Under the rule here
  the row sits at two bounds exactly, the 24 guards as written and the
  16 effects, as the lane design says. It does not sit at a third.

**Why raise the numbers and not split a definition.** This decides
point R1-13. The bounds exist for three reasons: the validator's work
when a definition is activated; the size of a scope summary, which
holds one count for each type and state (section 9.1); and the bytes
that every scope pinning the definition retains. A summary at 16 types
of 16 states holds at most 256 counts. Act kinds affect only the
validator and the bytes, and the new bound on bytes limits both. A
split of `change` would put its integration work in a separate scope,
with a new definition and a creation exchange for every pull request
(R3 point U7). That is more entries and more deliveries to save two
item types. So the values are raised, and one structural bound, the
definition's bytes, is added.

- A platform definition's version has one fixed meaning, stated in the
  specification. A changed meaning is a new version. A runtime or
  verifier that does not implement a version answers
  `unsupported-definition` and admits nothing to that scope. A runtime
  whose temporary capacity rule does not support a declared definition
  answers the same, when a scope would be founded or created under it
  (sections 17.2 and 17.3a). So does a runtime that cannot hold or
  pin a definition's named closure (section 7.2).
- **A capability form with no code. Added to revision 12 before its
  review** (I2 deltas D3 and DJ14, which report the I2 plan's question
  Q1). The rule above, for a version that a runtime does not
  implement, is made exact for a capability. It is a rule on the forms
  that a definition uses, and not on the name of a version alone.
  - *The rule.* A runtime must have code for every capability form
    that the pinned definition uses: each guard, each effect, each
    record that a form reads or writes, each kind of an entry that
    only the capability writes, such as `hold@1:check`, and each
    `carried` part. When the definition uses a form that the runtime
    does not derive, the runtime answers `unsupported-definition` for
    the whole scope. It founds no scope under that definition, and it
    creates none: section 7.2 gives the answer in each case. It admits
    nothing to a scope that exists under that definition: no act, no
    delivery and no timed entry. A verifier that lacks the code
    answers the same, at the genesis (section 9.4).
  - *The item form of `hold@1`.* A definition may list `hold@1` and
    use only its item form: the hold type and the `hold` effect of
    section 6.8. It runs on a runtime that derives the item form, and
    it needs no other code of the capability. This is what section 6.8
    says, what section 11.8 records of I1, and what I1's source and
    the I2 base do.
  - *The test.* The validator reads every capability form of a
    definition and checks it against the tables that section 6.11
    declares: the capability's name and version, the name of a guard
    or an effect, its arguments, the record kind of a `carried` part,
    and the step in a kind. It derives none of them. A valid
    definition lists each form that the runtime cannot derive. That
    list is exactly the test: it is empty, or the scope is refused. So
    a definition can be valid in a runtime that cannot run it. A
    listed version of which the runtime derives no form at all is
    itself on the list. The I2 base treats `git-read@1` so.
  - *Why the whole scope.* A runtime could run the rows that use no
    such form, and stop at the others. It does not. Part of the
    definition's meaning would then be absent from the scope: an act
    that the definition admits would have no answer there, and a duty
    that needs such a form could never settle. A scope runs every turn
    under its whole pinned definition, or none.
  - *Tests.* Section 6.11, "A scripted capability is a stand-in", says
    what a test may supply in place of the code, and what its result
    shows.
  - *The owner.* The real rules of `hold@1` and `git-read@1` belong to
    the authority note's successor (request `406983fe`). That request
    is named here as the I2 notes give it, and it was not read. This
    note decides only the contract's side: what a runtime answers when
    it lacks code for a form, and what a result with a stand-in may be
    cited for. That owner is asked to confirm both. Nothing here says
    that it has. One question about the item form stays with that
    owner: point R1-49.
- A scope that exists runs every turn under its pinned definition. A
  repeated founding or creation that names another definition changes
  nothing: the definition that a founding or a creation asks for is
  used only while the scope has no genesis (I1 delta 85).
- A scope's meaning never changes. Who may act today is a separate,
  present question: roles, keys and grants are current, and are never
  read from a pinned party slot.
- **Several meanings at once.** Scopes created under different
  definitions live side by side. That is history inside one
  architecture, not a second architecture.
- **First-version policy.** A new definition applies to scopes created
  after it. A runtime upgrade keeps every definition, profile and
  capability version that a retained scope pins, until that scope is
  exported or the deployment is reset after settlement. Migration of a
  live scope to another definition is not designed.
- The lifecycle design N2 is an input. Its rules do not carry over by
  themselves. Each one that is kept is a form below.
- Keeping the existing restricted evaluator profile is a proposal
  (point R1-8). Its source was not read through for this note.

**Made exact in revision 13, from the I2 source choices.** Each point
names the entries of the I2 deltas note that it answers (section 15.6l).
Each is a rule of this contract from this revision, for the reason that
the point gives. None changes an entry that the I2 source at `744f2447`
writes, unless the point says so.

- **D9.** The bound on the bytes of one definition counts the UTF-8
  bytes of the definition's canonical JSON. The domain tag and the
  newline of its digest are not counted. The validator checks this bound
  first, and reports that one problem and no other. The reason: the
  bound limits the validator's own work, so it is checked before that
  work.
- **D10.** A party list that states no `max` holds at most the bound on
  the members of a party list. An effect that would pass the list's own
  `max`, or that bound, refuses the input `slot-full`. The static size
  of a timed entry counts a party list at its `max`, and a list value at
  its `max` or at the bound on the elements of a list, whichever is
  less. The reason: a size that the validator counts is sound only when
  the commit enforces the same number (section 6.4).
- **D15.** A scope answers a read of one of its entries with the name of
  its definition: the `name` that its pinned declaration states, or, for
  a platform definition, the platform name without its version. A scope
  that cannot read its own declaration gives no name. The read fails,
  and the reader's input is not judged now. The reason: a name that a
  scope guessed would let another scope's judgment rest on it. Where the
  name is kept is section 4.1: in the `FactUse`. The source keeps it
  beside the retained copy, which is row 4 of section 11.10.

**Platform code: a mark, and its rule. New in revision 15** (I3 deltas
EC6, EC4, EA6 to EA8 and E10; section 15.3e). Sections 15.3c and 15.3d
say that nine of the forms P13 to P25 "stay platform code", and that a
verifier derives an entry of such code "again with the same code". No
text said how that code joins the data of its row. This passage says it.
It is one rule: **a mark stands in the data where a form of the same
kind would stand, and its rule is run where that form would be
derived.**

- *The two parts of a platform definition.* One version of a platform
  definition is its **data** and its **rules**, under one name and
  version. The data is a value in the forms of this section, with the
  marks below. The rules are a table of pure functions, one for each
  name that a mark of the data states. **Platform code** means those
  rules, and nothing else of a runtime. A runtime or a verifier has both
  parts of a version, or it does not implement the version. The
  specification of a version states both: the data as its tables, and
  for each rule its place, what it reads, what it returns and the
  refusals that it names. For the seven platform definitions that is the
  authority note's section 12.1.
- *A mark.* A mark is a record of two texts. `code` names one rule of
  the definition's version. `row` names the gap that the specification
  lists for it, such as `P13`, so that a reader knows why the place is
  code. Neither is empty.

```ts
/** A mark: in the data of a platform definition, and nowhere else. */
interface Mark { code: string; row: string;
                 refusals?: readonly string[];   // revision 17: the names that the rule may refuse with; at places 1 and 4
                 most?: { effects: number; operations?: readonly string[]; opens?: string };   // revision 17: at places 5 and 7
                 clock?: true;                   // revision 17: the rule reads the commit's reading
                 always?: true }                 // revision 19: on a send mark of a written list: the rule returns exactly one request

/** The data of a platform definition: the declared forms, and seven places where a mark may stand. */
interface PlatformData extends DeclaredDefinition {
  outcomes: Record<string, Mark & { attempts: number;                    // revision 17: the most attempts of the kind
                                    send?: Mark & { result: ResultClauses; once?: true };   // revision 17: at most one request. `once`: revision 20
                                    origin?: "opening" | "rule";         // revision 20: the entry whose `uses` an outcome copies (below)
                                    observes?: readonly Observe[] }>;    // revision 20: section 16.1
                                    // place 7: by the kind of each operation that this definition owns (section 4.3)
}
// Places 1 to 6 are in the forms of sections 6.2 to 6.6. Each is read so in platform data only:
//   1  the `grant` of an act                 string | (Mark & { grant?: string })
//   2  a name of `also`                      AlsoRule | (Mark & { item: string })
//      revision 23: a mark at place 2 that is a binding selector also states `index: string; key: string` (section 17.2a)
//   3  the type of a field, or of a slot     FieldType | (Mark & { type: "code" })
//   4  a guard of a written list             Guard | Mark
//   5  an effect of a written list           EffectForm | Mark
//   6  a send of a written list              SendForm | (Mark & { result: ResultClauses })
```

| # | The place | Where the rule is run | What the rule returns | When it does not hold |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The member `grant` of an act | Check 9 of section 4.2, in place of the grant check. Not run when the mark states a `grant` and a current grant of that action is held. | That the signing key may act. From revision 17 it passes with no member: the act then has no signer, as a handler has none. | Refused `unauthorized`, with the rule's name if it states one |
| 2 | A name of `also`, of an act or a handler | Check 8, where the name is resolved | One local item of the type that the mark states, or none | It never refuses. With none the name is unbound. |
| 3 | The type of a field of an act or a handler; the type of a slot of an item type | For a field, check 7. For a slot, check 11, for each effect that sets it. | Whether the value is of the type | Refused `bad-field` |
| 4 | A guard of the written list of an act or a handler. Not inside a list form, and not in an `if` or an `unless`. | Check 10, at its position in the list | That it holds, that it does not, or that it is not completed | Refused `guard-failed`, with the rule's name and the path of its position. Where the specification states it: `unsupported-definition` or `bad-field`. Not completed: Unavailable `guard-incomplete` or `dependency-unavailable`. |
| 5 | An effect of the written list of an act, a handler or a result clause. It has no `of`, `if` or `unless`. | Check 11, at its position in the list. In a clause, when the clause runs. | Effects: none, one or several | It never refuses. The checks on effects refuse. |
| 6 | A send of the written list of an act or a handler | Check 12, at its position in the list | No request, or one: a `create`, a `tell` or a `relate` | It never refuses. The checks on sends refuse. |
| 7 | `outcomes`, by operation kind | The judgment of each outcome entry of an operation of that kind, at each thing that section 4.3 leaves to the owner | Whether the kind selects; the owner's local guard; whether another attempt is allowed; whether the evidence is well formed; and the entry's effects and sends, as places 5 and 6 | An outcome that does not follow is `bad-input` (section 4.2) |

- *What a rule is given.* Six things, and no other. A runtime and a
  verifier give a rule the same.
  1. The folded state before the entry: items, records, operations, the
     scope's own requests and the index of accepted keys.
  2. The entry's input, whole: an act's signed intent with its `actor`,
     which is the signing key; the grant; `observed`; a delivery's
     `from` and message; an outcome's evidence.
  3. The commit's one clock reading, which is the entry's time.
  4. The entry's retained inputs: each entry in `uses`, by its bytes;
     each value beside the intent (section 6.2); and each definition's
     bytes that the entry retains.
  5. The scope's own earlier entries, by position, as a local fact is
     read (section 6.2), and as section 16.1 lets a later entry read the
     observations of an earlier one.
  6. What the judge resolved before the rule's place: the fields as
     read, the subjects that are bound, the signer, and the bounds that
     the judge was given. Each is a function of the five above and of
     the rules before it in the order. Confirmed in revision 17 (I3
     delta EJ7): also the scope's own reference, and the position of
     the entry that is being written. The input of item 2 may be a
     diagnosis, whose entry runs the clause `undelivered`. A rule uses
     the position to compute, as for the ID of an operation that the
     entry opens. An effect in an entry still names the item that its
     own entry opens as `"self"` (section 4.1). Corrected in revision
     18: revision 17 said that an effect which holds the entry's own
     position as an item is a fault of the rule. That did not fit the
     source, whose check of a rule's opening asks that the rule name
     the item by that position (`effects.ts`, line 191, at `3d06620b`).
     The two are kept apart. What a rule returns is the judge's own
     interface: a rule may name the opened item by the position that it
     was given, or as `"self"`. What the entry records is this
     contract's: the judge writes `"self"`, and no entry holds its own
     position in an effect. Whether the source's judge writes `"self"`
     after that check was not read: row I3-27.
- *What a rule is not given.* The bytes of a detached text: a rule reads
  a text's digest only, because the bytes may be redacted (section 6.6).
  Storage. The network. Any clock but that one reading. A random value.
  The order in which inputs arrived. Transport's acknowledgments. The
  present state of another scope. The result of a read that the entry
  does not retain. So a rule reads nothing that a replay does not hold.
- *A binding selector is given less. New in revision 22* (the verdict
  `dc1da38a`, its first finding). A mark at place 2 may bind the name
  that the `bound.of` of a handler names (section 17.2a, "The source of
  `bound.of`"). Its rule is then a **binding selector**, and it is given
  two things in place of the six: items of the type that the mark
  states, as the folded state before the entry holds them, and the
  fields of the message as they were read. It is given no clock reading,
  no retained input, no earlier entry and nothing else of the state.
  Every other mark at place 2 is given the six, as before.
  Changed in revision 23 (the verdict `675776bc`; the planner's act
  `2d3fa911`). Revision 22 gave the rule every item of the type. It is
  given fewer now. The mark states `index`, a slot that its type
  declares as indexed, and `key`, a field of the message. The first of
  the two things is the items that the index returns for the value of
  that field: live and final, in order of item ID, and at most 8. The
  rule is given no other item of the type. Section 17.2a has the index,
  and the rule for no item, for several and for more than 8.
- *What a rule returns is in this contract's forms.* Each effect is a
  member of `Effect` of section 4.1, and one of these: `open`, `state`,
  `party`, `list`, `ref`, `value`, `operation` and `attempt`. Each
  request is a `Send` of section 4.1. A refusal is a `Reason` of section
  4.2. An entry gains no member, and nothing in an entry says that a
  rule ran: the data and the rules of the pinned version say it. So "an
  entry that platform code writes has only this contract's forms" is a
  property of the type of a rule's result.
- *The written forms keep their meaning.* In a row with marks, each
  written form is validated and derived as it is in any definition. A
  rule replaces no written form, removes none and changes the result of
  none. The data of such a row does not give the row's behaviour alone,
  and the mark is how the data says so: a reader of the data sees each
  place that is code, and which gap it answers.
- *The joined lists are checked as one.* The effects of an entry are the
  opening, the written effects and each rule's effects at its mark's
  position, the capability's own, and attention, in the order of section
  4.1. An entry opens at most one item, whatever opens it. No two
  effects of the list set one slot, or the state, of one item, apart
  from successive changes of one party list (section 6.6). Every value
  is checked against its slot's type. The bounds of section 7.5 and the
  capacity of section 17 count the whole entry. The bound on the written
  effects of a row counts a mark as one form. The specification states
  the most effects and sends that each rule returns, and the static size
  of the row counts that most (section 17.2; point R1-59). Revision 16
  decides the rule: "A declared maximum for everything that derives",
  below.
- *A fault of a rule is no judgment.* A rule that returns something
  outside its place's type, an effect that is no member of the list
  above, an item of another type, a refusal name that its specification
  does not state, or effects that conflict with a written effect, has a
  fault. The input is not judged: an act is answered `unavailable`, a
  delivery is retried, and nothing is written. This is the rule of
  section 6.11 for a capability's rules (point "D11, DJ19").
- *A rule that reads the clock.* The specification says of each rule
  whether it reads the commit's reading. An entry of a row with such a
  rule judges time, and is never written clamped (section 5.3).
- *What the validator does at a mark.* With its platform option, it
  checks that the mark is well formed and stands at one of the seven
  places. It reads through it and derives nothing. It makes no static
  check that would need the rule's result: a required slot may be set by
  an effect mark of the row; an effect mark conflicts with no written
  effect; a value of a type that is a mark is assignable to that type
  only. It refuses a mark in a timed rule, as `timed-partial`: a timed
  rule's effects are total (section 6.4), and no rule is shown to be
  total (point R1-58). It lists every mark with its place. That list is
  the test of the next point. It does not read the table of rules, so a
  definition can be valid in a runtime that cannot run it, as for a
  capability form.
- *A mark with no rule: the whole scope.* A runtime must have, for every
  mark that the pinned data lists, a rule of that name whose kind is the
  kind of the mark's place. When one is missing, the runtime answers
  `unsupported-definition` for the whole scope, exactly as for a
  capability form with no code, above. It founds no scope under the
  definition and creates none. A scope that exists under it admits
  nothing: no act, no delivery, no timed entry and no outcome. So no
  entry of a row is ever written with part of its meaning absent. This
  confirms the I3 builder's decision EC4. The earlier reading, that such
  a scope runs the rows that are data (I3 delta EA6), is not adopted.
- *The order of rules.* The rules of one entry are run in the order of
  the checks of section 4.2, and inside one written list in the order of
  the list. That order is in the data. No rule's position depends on the
  table of rules, or on the order in which a runtime holds them.
- *A slot or a field typed by code.* Section 15.3c says that a slot
  which must hold an entry of either lane definition "is typed by that
  definition's code". This is place 3. The data writes the type as a
  mark, and so states no shape for the value. The value is still a
  `FieldValue` of section 4.1: an entry's bytes hold it, and an operand
  copies or compares it whole. The commit's type check of section 6.6,
  "A slot never holds a value outside its type", is made by the mark's
  rule: it is asked for each effect that would set the slot, with the
  value and the entry's retained inputs, and the effect is refused
  `bad-field` when the rule says no. For a field the same check is made
  at check 7. A slot whose type the forms can write is not typed by
  code, also when only a rule can build its value: the type is then
  data, the commit checks it as data, and the rule's effect is checked
  like a written one. The notice's `source` of the inbox is that case
  (section 15.6o, entry E10).
- *An operation that a rule opens.* An effect rule may open an operation
  whose owner is its own definition, of a kind that `outcomes` lists. An
  operation of a kind that it does not list is a fault of the rule. So
  the data names every kind of outcome entry that a scope under it can
  hold.
- *A declared definition holds no mark.* The validator refuses each of
  the seven forms unless its platform option is set, as it refuses any
  form that it does not know: the top level of a declared definition has
  no `outcomes`, and none of its lists holds a record with the member
  `code`. The option is reachable from no input (section 15.6n, entry
  E9): a definition that a founding, a creation, an `activate` or a
  value beside an intent names is validated without it. So no declared
  definition names a rule, and no input chooses which rule is run. A
  declared definition reaches a platform scope only as every scope does:
  by a request, or by reading one of its sealed entries.
- *A stand-in rule.* A test may supply a rule from its own table, as it
  may supply a scripted capability, under the same four conditions
  (section 6.11): it comes only through test support, it is labelled a
  stand-in wherever it appears, a result with it shows what the row's
  written forms do around the rule and proves nothing about the rule,
  and an entry that was written with it is test data.
- *What changes in bytes.* No entry that a source writes today changes.
  The canonical bytes of a declared definition do not change, so no
  pinned lane digest moves. A platform definition is pinned by its name
  and version, and no digest names its data (the authority note's
  section 12.1). Whether a version should also be named by a digest of
  its data and of its rules is point R1-60.

**A declared maximum for everything that derives. New in revision 16**
(I3 deltas EF7 and EH10; point R1-59). The bounds of this section and of
section 7.5 count what a definition writes. Since revision 12 code
derives part of an entry as well: a capability's effects and steps, an
owner's rules for an outcome, a hold's workspace, and from revision 15 a
platform rule. Nothing bounded what such code returns in one entry but
the entry's size. One rule of the task definition voids up to 62 items,
and the end of a hold revokes every live token of it.

- *What declares a maximum.* Each of these, in the tables of its
  version: a platform rule at places 5, 6 and 7 (above); a capability
  effect; a step; the rule of an operation's outcome; and the code of a
  hold's workspace. It declares three numbers: the most effects, the
  most requests and the most operations that it returns in one entry.
- *The form of a number.* A constant of the version. Or a constant times
  a **state bound**: a number that the version states as the most of
  some thing that the scope holds at once, such as the tokens of one
  hold that are `minting` or `live`, or the controls of a task that are
  `queued`.
- *What the validator counts.* For each row, the most that its entry
  holds: its written forms at their bounds, and the declared maximum of
  each mark and of each capability form in it. For an entry that no row
  writes, such as an outcome and the end of a hold, the declared maximum
  of its code. The sum must fit three bounds of section 7.5: the sends
  of one entry, the entry's size, and one that is new, the derived
  effects of one entry. Its number is R4's, and none is proposed. A
  definition, or a capability version beside it, whose count does not
  fit is not pinned: `unsupported-definition`.
- *In the commit.* Code that returns more than it declared has a fault,
  and the input is not judged (above). An entry of an act, of a
  preparation or of a request that would still pass a bound is refused
  `entry-too-large`, with the bound's name. Nothing is cut short.
- *An entry that cannot be refused.* A timed entry, the end of a hold
  with what it is under, an outcome, a result and a confirmation are
  written whatever they hold. So the count of such an entry must hold
  before it is derived. Where its code's maximum is a constant, the
  validator's count is enough. Where it is a constant times a state
  bound, the version names the **opening**: the one kind of entry that
  raises that state. That entry can be refused, and it is refused when
  it would raise the state past the bound. So the state never passes its
  bound, and the entry that cannot be refused fits. A version with such
  code and no stated bound, or with a bound that no refusable opening
  holds, is not valid.
- *The two cases that exist.* The end of a hold: the state bound is the
  tokens of one hold, and the opening is the step `token`, which the
  authority note's revision 21 refuses `tokens-full`. The outcome of a
  stop: the state bound is the queued controls, and the opening is a
  control, which the task definition refuses `controls-full` at 62.
- *What a verifier does.* It makes the same count from the pinned
  definition and the bounds that it is given, and a history that holds
  an entry past a bound is a `mismatch`, as section 9.3's fourth check
  has it for the entry's size.
- *What is not decided.* Every number: the bound on the derived effects
  of one entry, each state bound, and each rule's maximum. They are
  R4's, with the capacity work under `cc570904` and the owner of each
  rule. The other four dimensions of capacity are section 17's and are
  not changed.

**Marks, made exact from the source that built them. New in revision
17** (I3 deltas EJ1 to EJ15; section 15.6r has one row for each). The
source built the seven places from revision 15 and found them silent or
unbuildable in these points. Each is a rule of this contract from this
revision.

- *A mark states three things as data.* `refusals`: the names with
  which the rule may refuse, at places 1 and 4. `most`: the most that
  the rule returns, at places 5 and 7. `clock`: that the rule reads the
  commit's reading. Revision 15 left them to "the specification", and
  revision 16 to "the tables of its version". They are members of the
  mark, so that the validator counts from the data alone, and a reader
  of the data sees them. A rule that refuses with another name, returns
  more than `most`, or reads the clock without `clock`, has a fault.
- *What `most` holds.* `effects`: the most effects of the eight forms.
  `operations`: the kinds of the operations that the rule may open, each
  a key of `outcomes`, at most one of each in one entry. `opens`: the
  item type that the rule may open, when it may open one. A send mark
  returns no request or one, and states no `most`.
- *What the validator now counts* (EJ6). For a row with marks: `effects`
  into the bound on the derived effects of one entry (above). One item
  of the type `opens` into the rule of one new item for an entry, and
  into that type's `max`. For each kind in `operations`: what that
  kind's row in `outcomes` reserves, which is its `attempts`, two
  entries for each, and the same count of its own `most`. A send mark as
  one request. An entry of an act or a handler with marks has no static
  size in bytes: it can be refused `entry-too-large`. An outcome entry
  cannot be refused, so its size is counted: `effects` times the largest
  effect that the definition's slots allow. That last count, and the
  other four dimensions of capacity, are owed with the capacity work
  under `cc570904`.
- *A request of an outcome's rule, and its clauses* (EJ1). An outcome's
  mark may hold one member `send`: a send mark, with its clauses as
  data. An outcome has no subject and no field. So its row writes no
  send, and each effect of such a clause is an effect mark, whose rule
  names its items by their IDs. The rule of the send returns no request
  or one, and it may return a `create`.
- *The cause of a scope that an outcome entry creates* (EJ1). It is the
  fourth row of section 7.2's table, which revision 8 added for the
  register: the digest of the intent of the act that opened the
  outcome's operation. The deltas note says that no such cause exists.
  It does. An operation that no act opened gives no cause, so a `create`
  from its outcome is a fault of the rule, until a row needs another
  cause.
- *A clause runs no selection rule* (EJ3). A name of `also` that a mark
  selects was bound by a rule, from the input and the state of the entry
  that made the send. A clause runs later, on another state. It does not
  run that rule again, and such a name is unbound in a clause. The
  validator refuses a clause that names one, or a name that is reached
  through one. A clause that must change such an item holds an effect
  mark, whose rule finds the item. This is as the source has it.
- *A written list of sends holds at most one mark* (EJ4). A result names
  its request by ordinal, and a send that is not made takes none. A
  rule's request states no type and no name in the data. So in a list
  with a mark, every written send is one that is always made, exactly
  once: no `if`, no fan-out, no subject that may be unbound, and no
  `index` send. The form of each recorded send is then found by
  counting, and the mark's request is the one that is left. Any other
  list with a mark is refused. This is as the source has it. No entry's
  bytes change. A row that needs two requests from rules is point R1-63.
  Changed in revision 19: a list may hold several marks when at most
  one of them does not state `always` ("More than one send mark",
  below).
- *Where a mark may be a type* (EJ5). It is the type of a field of an
  act or of a handler, or of a reference slot or a value slot. It is not
  the type of an element of a list or of a member of a record. A field
  whose type is a mark has no `default`. No constant and no source of a
  written type is assignable to it. A timed rule does not copy such a
  slot, because the type states no bound on its bytes. As the source has
  it.
- *Which failed checks on a rule's output refuse, and which are faults*
  (EJ10). A rule's effect is refused as a written effect would be: a
  value outside its slot's type, a party list that is full, an item that
  was final before the entry, a required slot that is unset, and a type
  at its `max`. Everything that no written effect could do is a fault:
  an effect outside the eight forms, an effect on no item, a slot or a
  state that the type does not declare, a second opening, an opening in
  another state than the initial one, a value for a detached text, an
  operation that the definition does not own, an attempt that is not the
  first of an operation of this entry, a conflict with another effect,
  and, added here, an effect that sets a `fixed` slot of an item that
  existed before the entry. The validator refuses a written effect of
  that last kind, and no validator reads a rule.
- *An outcome's rule* (EJ11). An outcome entry is never refused. So an
  effect of its rule that a check would refuse is a fault, and nothing
  is written: the outcome stays offered, and the fault is reported to
  operators, as `bad-input` is. Whether the source states an opened
  operation beside the effects or among them is its own choice: the
  entry holds the same `operation` and `attempt` effects.
- *A founding that the rule does not pass* (EJ13). It is refused
  `unauthorized`, and nothing is written. No refused genesis is recorded
  for it.

**Marks and rules, from the later I3 source. New in revision 19** (I3
deltas EN2 to EN8, EP5, EP6, ER5 and ER6; section 15.6s). Each point is
a rule of this contract from this revision. Where a point says "as
built", the I3 source at `4f771d90` has it by the word of its deltas
note. Nothing of that source is accepted.

- *More than one send mark. Decided in revision 19* (EP6). This decides
  point R1-63. A send mark in a written list may state `always: true`.
  Its rule then returns exactly one request in every entry of its row,
  and a rule that returns none there has a fault. A written list of
  sends may hold several marks when at most one of them does not state
  `always`. The reason is the counting of the point on EJ4, above, which
  still holds. Every written send of a list with a mark is made exactly
  once. So for a list of k forms, an entry of the row records k sends of
  the list, or k less 1. With k, each form made its send at its own
  position. With k less 1, the one mark that does not state `always`
  made none, and the send of each later form is one ordinal earlier. So
  the form of each recorded send, and the clause of each result, is
  found by counting. The validator refuses a list in which two marks do
  not state `always`. No send gains a member, and no entry's bytes
  change. An outcome's mark still holds at most one `send`.
- *A sibling's scope ID in a `create`, and whether a slot is set* (EP6).
  No operand is added for either. Each is a value of a field of the
  request that a send mark's rule returns, and the rule derives it from
  what it is given. A genesis input holds the scope's own seed. In a
  list whose marks all state `always`, the ordinal of each creation is
  the position of its form, counted after the result that a child's
  genesis sends first. The specification of the rule states the
  derivation. The reason for no operand: the rows that need one each
  hold a send mark under this point, so a form would say again what a
  rule already gives.
- *A signed intent is no field value* (EP5). No field type holds a
  signed intent, and none is added. A creation that needs a founder's
  intent names, by a fact, the entry that holds it, and its rows read
  what they need from that entry by the parts `scope` and `set` (section
  6.5). As built. A row of a specification that gives a `create` a field
  for a signed intent is its owner's to amend.
- *A rule that decides a further attempt is given the state* (ER5). The
  rule of place 7 that says whether another attempt is allowed is a rule
  like every other. It is given the six things above, with the folded
  state before the outcome entry. The source gives it the result and the
  operation only.
- *What an operation is for* (ER6). An `operation` effect gains no
  member. An outcome's rule may read the entry that opened its
  operation: it is the scope's own entry at the position that the
  operation's ID states, and item 5, above, gives it. That entry's input
  and its effects say what it acted on. A platform definition may
  instead keep a slot that names its operations. Which it does is its
  specification's.
  Changed in revision 20: under a definition that states `holds`, an
  `operation` effect of a kind that an item holds gains the member
  `for` (section 17.2a). Under any other definition it gains none, as
  here.
- *Four faults of a rule. Confirmed in revision 19, as built* (EN2, EN3,
  EN6 and EN8). Each is something that no written form could do, so it
  is a fault, and the input is not judged. First, an effect on a `fixed`
  slot of an item that existed before the entry, also one that empties
  the slot. The item that the entry opens is the one exception. A result
  clause runs in a later entry, so its rule sets no fixed slot of the
  item that the request's entry opened. Second, a `state` effect on a
  hold, an effect on a hold's `holder`, `epoch` or end, and the opening
  of a hold type: only a `hold` record changes those (section 6.8), and
  a rule returns none. Third, a `relate` that names `"self"` in an entry
  that opens no item. Fourth, in an outcome entry: an opening past its
  type's `max`, and more requests than the bound on the sends of one
  entry (section 7.5). A rule of a result clause that would open an item
  past `max` changes nothing, and the result is recorded, as for any
  clause whose effects cannot apply (section 7.4).
- *A list change that changes nothing* (EN4). A rule's `list` effect
  that adds a member whom the list holds, or removes one whom it does
  not hold, is not recorded, as for a written form (section 4.1). As
  built.
- *The fields of a rule's message* (the table of checks in section 13 of
  the deltas note). The bound on the fields of one send holds for a
  request that a rule returns. A message with more is a fault: the
  validator refuses a written send with more, so no written form could
  make one. The source does not make this check.

**What platform data states for the turn, and for capacity. New in
revision 20** (I3 deltas EY4 to EY6, FA3 to FA7 and FC1 to FC6; sections
15.3g and 15.6t). Five members are added to the data of a platform
definition. Each is data and no code. None is a mark, so the places
where a mark may stand are still seven. The validator reads each of the
five only with its platform option, and refuses each in a declared
definition as it refuses any member that it does not know. So no
declared definition changes, and no pinned lane digest moves.

```ts
// Revision 20, in platform data only. The listing of `PlatformData`, above, holds the two members of a kind.
interface ActType     { observes?: readonly Observe[];                 // section 16.1
                        adds?: Held }                                  // section 17.2a: to the item that the act is on
// A `create`, a `tell` and a `relate`, beside `result`:
//                      observes?: Partial<Record<"applied" | "refused" | "superseded" | "conflict", readonly Observe[]>>
interface ItemType    { holds?: Held }                                 // section 17.2a
interface Held        { operations?: Record<string, number>;           // by kind of `outcomes`: the most that are opened for one item
                        requests?: number;                             // the most requests that are sent for one item
                        items?: number }                               // the most items that are opened for one item
// An outcome's kind:   origin?: "opening" | "rule"                    // the one entry whose `uses` an outcome of the kind copies
//                      observes?: readonly Observe[]
// An outcome's `send`: once?: true                                    // at most one outcome entry of one operation makes the request
// Revision 21, in platform data only, each inside a member above or on a handler:
//   a row of `observes`:  retains?: readonly { domain: string; max: number }[]   // with `of: "rules"` (section 16.1)
//                         second?: true                                         // in an outcome, with `from: "rule"` (section 16.1)
//   Held:                 decisions?: Record<string, number>                    // by message name (section 17.2a)
//   a `tell` handler:     bound?: { of: Subject; where: readonly Where[] }      // section 17.2a
// And in every definition: `Settles` has a third form, `{ of, sets, in }` (section 6.4).
// Revision 23, in platform data only:
//   ItemType:             indexes?: readonly string[]                           // its indexed slots, at most 4 (section 17.2a)
//   a mark at place 2:    index?: string; key?: string                          // on a binding selector, and on no other mark (section 17.2a)
```

| Member | Where it stands | What it states | Its rules |
|---|---|---|---|
| `observes` | An act; a kind of `outcomes`; a `create`, a `tell` or a `relate`, by clause | What the scope reads before the turn of an entry of that form | Section 16.1, "The subjects that an entry observes" |
| `origin` | A kind of `outcomes` | Which one earlier entry of the scope gives an outcome its `uses` | "The origin of an outcome", below |
| `holds` | An item type | What an item reserves for the operations, the requests and the items that are opened or sent for it | Section 17.2a |
| `adds` | An act | What an act adds to the reservation of the item that it is on | Section 17.2a |
| `once` | The `send` of a kind of `outcomes` | That one operation makes the request at most once | Section 17.2, "A request that an outcome sends" |

Added in revision 21. Four more members of platform data, each inside
one of the five or on a handler, and none a mark. The validator reads
each only with its platform option. A fifth thing is not platform data:
the third form of `settles`, which any definition may state (section
6.4).

| Member | Where it stands | What it states | Its rules |
|---|---|---|---|
| `retains` | A row of `observes` with `of: "rules"` | The byte domains of the values that the row's observation may name, with the most bytes of one | Section 16.1, "A value that a row may retain"; section 17.2, "A value that an observation names" |
| `second` | A row of `observes` of a kind of `outcomes`, with `from: "rule"` | That the subjects are named after the other rows are read, from their observations | Section 16.1, "A second step, in an outcome" |
| `decisions` | A `holds`, and an `adds` | By message name, the most bound requests that are decided for one item | Section 17.2a, "A request that is bound to a holder" |
| `bound` | A `tell` handler | The item that a delivery is bound to, and the conditions of the binding | The same |

Added in revision 23 (the verdict `675776bc`; the planner's act
`2d3fa911`). Two more things of platform data, and neither is a mark.
The validator reads each only with its platform option, and refuses
`indexes` in a declared definition as it refuses any member that it does
not know.

| Member | Where it stands | What it states | Its rules |
|---|---|---|---|
| `indexes` | An item type | The slots of the type by whose value its items are found: its indexed slots | Section 17.2a, "An index that an item type declares" |
| `index`, `key` | A mark at place 2 that is a binding selector | The indexed slot that the selector uses, and the field of the message that gives the key | Section 17.2a, "The source of `bound.of`" |

- *The origin of an outcome. Decided in revision 20* (I3 delta FC3).
  Section 17.2 says that an outcome retains what its owner declares,
  and no form let an owner declare a foreign entry. An outcome has no
  field, so nothing in its input names one. This is the form. An
  outcome entry has at most one **origin**: one earlier entry of its own
  scope. With `origin: "opening"` it is the entry that opened the
  outcome's operation, at the position that the operation's ID states.
  With `origin: "rule"` the rule of the kind names it by its position,
  or names none. With no member `origin` the outcome has none.
  - *What the entry holds.* Its `uses` is a copy of the `uses` of its
    origin, each `FactUse` whole and in that order, and nothing else.
    With no origin its `uses` is empty. This is the rule of a result
    clause, whose entry copies the uses of the entry that sent the
    request (sections 4.1 and 6.6).
  - *Nothing is fetched.* The scope retained each of those entries when
    it wrote the origin. So an outcome reads no other scope before its
    turn, adds no bytes for them, and can never name more foreign
    entries than the bound of section 7.5: its origin was held to that
    bound when it was written.
  - *What a rule is given.* Each entry in the outcome's `uses`, by its
    bytes, as item 4 of what a rule is given. A rule reads no foreign
    entry that the outcome's `uses` does not name.
  - *The answer to the question of entry FC3.* An outcome's `uses` does
    not hold the entries that its rules read, and it does not hold
    whatever a caller gave the judge. It holds the entries that its
    origin retained, read or not. That is how an act's `uses` holds
    every fact that a declared field names, read or not (section 6.4,
    point DH4).
  - *What the validator checks.* That `origin` is one of the two words.
    With `"opening"`, nothing more.
  - *What the rule may name.* A position below the entry that is being
    written. A position that is no entry of the scope is a fault of the
    rule. The rule is given what the next point lists.
  - *Replay.* The verifier finds the origin again, by the operation's
    ID or by the rule, and compares the `uses`. A difference is a
    `mismatch`.
  - *What an entry of another scope must be to be at hand.* A fact that
    a declared field of the origin's own input names, by a written type
    of section 6.2: a `fact`, or a list or a record that holds one. A
    field whose type is a mark states no shape, counts no fact (section
    17.2) and fetches none. So a specification that has an outcome read
    entries of a lane gives the message that the origin recorded a
    written type for them. Which message and which fields is its
    owner's.
- *Place 7, completed.* The row of place 7 in the table above lists
  what the rule of a kind decides. Later revisions and the I3 source
  added to it, and this is the whole list. The rule of a kind is a
  table of functions under one name.

  | The function | It is given | It returns | Stated in |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Whether the kind selects, and the owner's guard | The six things | A truth value | Section 4.3 |
  | Whether another attempt is allowed | The six things | A truth value | The point on ER5, above |
  | Whether the evidence is well formed | The six things. Confirmed in revision 20 (I3 delta EY4): the evidence check is a rule like every other, and it reads the state. | A truth value. False: the outcome is `bad-input`. | Section 4.3 |
  | The body of an outcome that is `unknown` | The folded state, the operation and its attempt, and the scope's own earlier entries | A body, where the specification states one for `unknown`. Otherwise none, and the body is `null`. | "The body of an outcome that is not known", below |
  | The origin, with `origin: "rule"` | The folded state; the outcome as it is offered, without `observed`; and the scope's own earlier entries | One position, or none | "The origin of an outcome", above |
  | The subjects of a row of `observes`, with `from: "rule"` | The same three, and each entry in the outcome's `uses`, by its bytes | A list of key IDs, or of member IDs | Section 16.1 |
  | The effects | The six things | Effects, to its `most` | Place 5 |
  | The request of its `send` | The six things | No request, or one | Place 6 |

  The last two rows are what the table's row calls "the entry's effects
  and sends". Since revision 17 an outcome's mark holds at most one
  request, in its `send`, and the row's words "and sends" mean that one
  (I3 delta EY2). The functions of the fifth and the sixth row read no
  clock and no observation: they say what is to be read.
  Changed in revision 21: for a row that states `second`, the function
  of the sixth row is also given the observations of the rows of its
  form that do not state it (section 16.1, "A second step, in an
  outcome"). It still reads no clock, and the function of the fifth row
  reads no observation.
- *What the judge resolved, for an outcome. Decided in revision 20* (I3
  delta EY6). Item 6 of what a rule is given is "what the judge
  resolved before the rule's place". For an outcome that includes two
  things that the ledger derives before the owner's effects: whether
  this outcome is `selected`, and whether the entry opens a further
  attempt. The rule of the effects and the rule of the `send` are given
  both. The reason: a rule that derives `selected` again, from the same
  state, can come to differ from the ledger, and the entry would then
  hold a request that its own `attempt` effect does not explain. The I3
  source derives it again in each send rule: row I3-47.
- *The body of an outcome that is not known. Confirmed in revision 20,
  as built* (I3 deltas EY4 and FA7). An outcome that is `unknown` has
  the basis `none` (section 4.3). That says that no answer of the
  attempt, and no decisive read, stands behind the result. It does not
  say that the body is empty. Where a specification states a body for
  `unknown`, the body has one of two sources. The rule of the kind
  derives it from the folded state and the scope's own entries, so that
  a runtime with no answer can still offer the outcome. Or the outside
  port gives it, where the specification puts in it something that was
  seen beside the answer, such as a read back. Either way the body is
  recorded input (section 4.1), and the evidence check judges it as it
  judges every body. How a driver carries an answer that is not known
  and still holds a body is the builder's.
- *A creation that no child could verify. Confirmed in revision 20, as
  built* (I3 delta EY5). The rule of an outcome's `send` may return a
  `create` (the point on EJ1, above). The sending scope makes, on its
  own history, the four checks that the child makes of the opening
  entry (section 7.2). A `create` that fails one is a fault of the
  rule: the outcome is not judged and nothing is written. The reason is
  the general one: no written form could make such a request. The same
  holds for a `create` from the outcome of an operation that no act
  opened.
- *A reference to the item that the entry opens. Confirmed in revision
  20, as built* (I3 delta FA4). A rule's effect may set a reference slot
  of the type `{ type: "item", of: T }` to the item that its own entry
  opens, when that item is of the type T. The check that the value
  names an item of the type is made on the state with the entry's
  opening applied, as it is for a written effect that names `"self"`.
  The entry records `"self"`, and never its own position (item 6,
  above, and row I3-27).
- *A rule may read what an item still holds, and may not treat it as
  leave.* The counts of section 17.2a are in the folded state, so a
  rule is given them with the rest of the state. A rule may read them
  to stay inside them, as a rule that opens one read and no second. A
  count that is not used up permits nothing: whether an operation is
  opened is decided by the rows of the specification, and never because
  room is left. This is not the budget, which no rule reads (section
  17.3, "The budget decides only whether").

### 6.2 Fields

```ts
type FieldType =
  | { type: "text"; max: number }            // at most 64 KiB
  | { type: "int"; min: number; max: number }
  | { type: "bool" } | { type: "time" }
  | { type: "enum"; of: readonly string[] }
  | { type: "member" }                        // a MemberRef
  | { type: "item"; of: string }              // a local item of that type
  | { type: "fact"; kind: readonly string[]; under: string }   // an entry of one of those kinds, under a definition of that name
  | { type: "scope"; kind: ScopeKind }
  | { type: "digest" } | { type: "commit" } | { type: "tree" }
  | { type: "record"; of: Record<string, FieldType & { required: boolean }> }   // new in revision 8
  | { type: "list"; of: FieldType; max: number };   // at most 64 elements from revision 19; revisions 7 to 18 said 32 (section 6.1)
// Revision 19, in platform data only: `{ type: "digest"; value: { domain: string; max: number } }`
// is the type of a field that names a value beside the intent ("A value beside an intent", below).
```

`text` may carry `detached: true`. Revision 7 wrote `kind: string` for a
fact; a list is the same form with more than one kind allowed.

Each field in an act is `required` or optional. An optional field may
have a `default`. An unknown field is refused.

**Values.** The shapes are those of the I1 deltas 21 and 22. A `time`
is `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ`, or the same with exactly three fraction
digits when they are not all zero, so one instant has one text. A
`member`, a `scope` and a `fact` are a `MemberRef`, a `ScopeRef` of the
stated kind and a `FactRef`. An `item` is a local ID and must name an
existing item of that type, or the input is refused `no-item`. A
`commit` and a `tree` are 40 or 64 lowercase hex characters. A `text`
is bounded in UTF-8 bytes.

**No value.** An absent optional field, an empty slot, an empty list
and a part that an entry does not have are all the one value **none**.

**Equality.** Two values are equal when their canonical JSON is equal,
after local facts are put in normal form (below). None equals none and
nothing else. A definition that must not let two empty values match
adds a `set` guard.

**The kind of an entry.** A `fact` type's `kind` is compared with the
act kind of an act or a genesis entry, which a genesis entry holds as
the member `kind` of its input (below), with the handler's message name
for a delivery of a request, and with the capability and step for a
preparation entry or its outcome entries, written `hold@1:check`. For
a timed entry it is compared with the key of the entry's rule, written
after the prefix `timed:`, as in `timed:job-deadline`. That last case
is new in revision 9: without it no slot could name the entry that
timed a job out. The validator refuses an act kind or a message name
that begins with `timed:`, so the two cannot be confused.

**The kind of a genesis entry is in the entry. Added to revision 12
before its review.** Revision 12 as it was filed compared a `kind`
with "the act kind of an act or a genesis entry", and a genesis entry
held its seed and not its act kind. Only the definition that the seed
names by digest held it. So a reader could learn the kind of a genesis
only when it pinned that same definition.

- *What that cost.* The I2 delivery found it, and its deltas note
  reports the case from a scenario on real storage (entries D21 and
  DK5; the scenario T3, which was not read here). A `change` lane pins
  `change`. The `file` entry of an `issue` lane is that lane's
  genesis. A manifest whose `goal` named that entry was refused
  `guard-failed`, and the same manifest with a `revise` entry as its
  goal was accepted. A goal that is an issue's `file` entry is the
  common case of the lane forms (R2 revision 14, sections 5.1 and
  5.2).
- *The rule.* The kind of a genesis entry is the member `kind` of its
  input (section 4.1). Every reader reads it there: the scope itself,
  for a local fact; another scope, for an entry that it fetched; and a
  verifier. No reader derives it from a definition that it holds.
- *What the value rests on.* The same as any other member of a fetched
  entry. The entry is verified whole against the hash in the fact
  reference, before any part of it is read (section 6.5). At run time,
  that the source admitted the entry rests on the trust of section 7.4
  in the object that answered. In replay it rests on the source's own
  history, in which the source's genesis is checked against the
  definition that it pins, or on an anchor (sections 9.3 and 9.4).
- *What it does not prove.* A reader that does not hold the foreign
  definition cannot itself check that the recorded kind is that
  definition's genesis act. It relies on the foreign scope's judge, as
  it does for every other entry of that scope: it does not judge the
  guards of a fetched act entry again either. The slot's `under` still
  names the definition, and the `under` check does not change: the
  name is the one that the source answered, and the using entry
  records it (section 4.1). The kind and the name are two checks, and
  one does not excuse the other. Neither shows that a repository
  activated the definition (point R1-22).
- *Two other ways, not taken.* The reader could retain the foreign
  declaration and derive the kind from it. That is more retained bytes
  in every scope that names such a fact, and a fetch of a declaration
  for every check of a kind. The source could state the kind beside
  the definition's name, in the fact reference or in its answer. That
  would be the claim of the sender, where the member is the entry's
  own, under the entry's hash and under its scope's own judgment.
- *So the common case holds.* A lane under one definition accepts a
  fact that names the genesis of a lane under another definition, when
  the slot's kinds include that genesis act and its `under` is that
  definition's name. It refuses the same fact when the kinds do not
  include it. Witness 18.26.

**Which entries have a kind, exactly. New in revision 13** (I2 deltas
D21, DI12 and DJ17; revision 12 answered D21 for a genesis). A kind is
read from the entry's own bytes, and every reader reads it in the same
way: the scope itself, another scope that fetched the entry, and a
verifier.

| Entry | Its kind |
|---|---|
| An act | The `kind` of its signed intent. |
| A genesis | The member `kind` of its input (above). |
| A timed entry | `timed:` and the key of its rule. |
| A delivery of a `tell` that a handler received, whatever was decided | The message's name: the member `message` of the request's body. |
| A delivery of a relationship update that a handler received, whatever was decided | The relationship's name: the member `name` of the request's body. |
| A delivery of a request that was decided `refused`, `unknown-message` | None. |
| A delivery of a request whose body states no name. It is decided `refused`, `bad-field`. | None. |
| A delivery of a result, a control or an advisory; a diagnosis; a settlement; a checkpoint | None. |
| A preparation entry | The capability and the step, from the members `capability` and `step` of its input, as in `hold@1:stage`. Only the capability's code writes such an entry (section 6.1). |
| An outcome entry. Made exact in revision 16. | The owner and the kind of its operation, from the members `owner` and `kind` of its input, joined by a `:`, as in `hold@1:check`. Revision 13 said "each outcome entry of its operation" has the kind of the preparation entry, and no bytes of an outcome held it. Whatever the result. |

- *Why a refused request may have no kind.* The name in a request is the
  sender's choice. A request that no handler of the receiver's
  definition receives could carry any name: an act kind of that
  definition, or `timed:` and the key of one of its rules. If the entry
  had that name as its kind, a sender could make a scope record an entry
  of a kind of the sender's choosing, and a `fact` slot of a third scope
  could then name it. The decision `refused`, `unknown-message` is in
  the entry's bytes, so a reader that does not hold the receiver's
  definition reads it too. A request that a handler received and then
  refused keeps its kind: the definition declares that message.
- *The kind of an outcome entry, and what a `fact` guard may check of
  it. New in revision 16.* For an operation that a step opens and that
  has the step's name, the kind is the one that revision 13 gave:
  `hold@1:check` is the outcome of the operation `check`, whichever
  entry opened it. For an operation of another name it is that name: the
  outcome of a mint is `hold@1:mint`, where revision 13's words gave it
  the step `token`. No `fact` type of a pinned definition names such a
  kind. A `fact` guard over an outcome entry checks its kind and its
  definition's name, like any fact. Of its parts it reads `ref`,
  `scope`, `seq`, `kind` and `carried`, and no other: an outcome has no
  intent, no field and no primary item. The kind says nothing of the
  result. An outcome that is `refused` or `unknown` has the same kind,
  and carries no record. So a row that needs a completed check reads the
  carried record, as the guard `ancestry` reads the `check` record and
  its state (section 6.11).
- *An outcome's kind cannot be chosen by a sender or by a definition.*
  The validator's rule on the form of a step kind, below, keeps an act
  and a message from the kinds of a capability's operations. One rule is
  added for the kinds of a platform definition's operations: an act
  kind, a handler's message, the message of a `tell` and the name of a
  `relate` do not begin with `platform:`. No pinned row does.
- *An entry with no kind* satisfies no `fact` guard, and no `fact` slot
  can hold it. Its part `kind` is none.
- *The form of a step kind.* A text has the form of a step kind when it
  is made of these parts, in order: a text that is not empty and holds
  no `:` and no `@`; the character `@`; a second text of the same sort;
  the character `:`; and any text. The validator refuses an act kind, a
  handler's message, the message of a `tell` and the name of a `relate`
  that has this form. Those are the places where it refuses the prefix
  `timed:`. Without the rule an act could be named `hold@1:check`, and
  its entries would pass, by their kind, for entries that only the
  capability writes. In a `fact` type and in `presents`, a kind of this
  form must name a step that a listed capability version declares, and
  it is then a form that needs the capability's code (section 6.1). The
  I2 source makes the second check and not the first: section 11.11, row
  14.

**A local fact. This answers R2's point R2-21.** A `fact` value whose
`at` is this scope and incarnation is a **local fact**. In the commit
the scope checks that its own entry at that `seq` has that hash. If it
does not, the input is refused `fact-mismatch`. If it does, the value
is put in normal form: a **local entry reference**, which is the
`seq`. A local fact is not fetched and is not in `uses`. Its kind and
definition are this scope's own.

- A reference slot whose type is `fact` holds either a foreign fact
  reference or a local entry reference.
- An effect may fill such a slot from `self` when the slot's kinds
  include the kind of the entry being written. The effect records
  `"self"`, and the fold holds the entry's `seq`.
- So a slot that was set from `self` and a field that names the same
  entry by its fact reference are equal, and a guard may compare them.
  The comparison reads this scope's own history, which the head check
  covers.
- No guard can compare the entry being written with a fact, because no
  fact reference to it exists before it is sealed. The validator
  refuses an operand that is `self`.
- When a local entry reference is sent in a message, it is sent as that
  entry's fact reference (section 6.4).

**A record.** A record has named members, each with a type, required or
not. A record may be a field, an element of a list, or the type of a
value slot. A member is named after its field with a dot:
`source.lane`. An unknown member is refused. This answers gap G14.

**Detached text. This answers gap G2.** A `text` field with
`detached: true` is held beside the signed intent and named in it by
digest.

- In the intent, in every entry and in every effect, the value of the
  field is the digest of the text, in the domain `artroom-text-1`. The
  signature covers the digest. The bytes are never part of an entry.
- The scope receives the bytes with the intent, checks them against
  the digest and the field's `max`, and keeps them as a retained input
  under that digest. A mismatch is refused `bad-field`.
- When a send carries a detached text, the message carries the digest
  and the bytes travel beside the message. The receiver checks and
  keeps them the same way.
- The validator refuses, as `redactable-read`, a definition in which a
  guard, a rule, an `attribute` effect, an attention form, a send to a
  scope of another kind than `lane`, or an `index` send reads a
  detached value.
- Section 6.6 gives the `redact` effect, and section 9.3 what replay
  says of a redacted text.

**Detached text, made exact. New in revision 13** (I2 deltas DJ3, DJ5
and DJ7).

- *One retained input for each digest.* A text is kept as one retained
  input of the kind `text`: the text as one JSON string in canonical
  form, under its digest in the domain `artroom-text-1`. Within one
  scope a digest names one input, however many fields, slots and entries
  name it (section 9.2).
- *Which entries keep a text.* A scope keeps a text with every entry
  that it writes whose input names the text in a detached field that the
  definition declares. That is: an act, in a field of its act type; a
  genesis, in a field of the genesis act, read from the founding intent
  or from the creation request; and a delivery of a request or of an
  advisory that a handler received, in a field of that handler, whether
  the delivery was applied or refused. A message that no handler
  receives has no declared field, so it names no text. Which digests an
  input names is a function of the pinned definition and the input
  alone, and the runtime and a verifier use the same function.
- *Held.* A scope **holds** a text from the entry that keeps it until an
  entry whose `redact` effect lists its digest (section 6.6). A later
  entry that keeps the same text holds it again. So whether a text is
  held at a position is a function of the history, and a verifier
  derives it without the bytes.
- *A text that a delivery names.* The receiver has the bytes before its
  turn. It reads them from its own retained inputs when it holds the
  text. Otherwise it reads them from the scope that sent the message,
  which answers only for a text that a send of the named entry carries,
  and it checks them against the digest. While the bytes are not at
  hand, the delivery is not decided: transport answers `retry`, with the
  reason `dependency-unavailable`, and the sender keeps the duty
  (section 7.4). That holds when the sender cannot be read now, when it
  answers that it holds no such text, and when what it serves is not the
  text that the digest names. Nothing is recorded on bytes that were not
  checked. So the sentence above, that the receiver checks the bytes
  "the same way", holds for the check and not for the answer. An act
  whose text does not match its digest is refused `bad-field`. A
  delivery waits, and it is decided `refused`, `bad-field`, only for a
  text that is at hand and is longer than its field's `max`. The
  receiver does not refuse the message for bytes that it cannot have: a
  refusal would rest on what the sender holds now, which is another
  scope's present state (section 5.1). Section 6.6, "A text that a
  request carries", says why this wait ends. Who may ask a scope for a
  text that it sent is for the authority note's successor (request
  `406983fe`).
- *What "reads a detached value" means.* The refusal `redactable-read`,
  above, is made exact as the I2 source builds it. An operand whose
  stated type is a detached text is refused wherever it is written, with
  two exceptions: the source of an effect, and a field of a message to a
  lane. A message goes to a lane when it is a `create` of kind `lane`,
  or a `tell` or a `relate` whose `to` has a type that states the kind
  `lane`. So a guard, a condition, the `where` of any range, a bound of
  a `count`, a `collect` in a message to a scope that is no lane, and a
  field of an `index` send are all refused one. A `rule` guard is
  refused in an act or a handler one of whose fields, or one of whose
  subjects' slots, is a detached text, because a rule reads every field
  and every subject whole (section 6.5). A `set` or an `unset` guard on
  such a slot is allowed: it reads whether the slot holds a value, and
  not the value. The rule is wider than replay needs, since a guard that
  read only the digest could be derived again after a redaction. It is
  kept as it is written. One rule is simpler than two, and both pinned
  definitions pass it.

**Made exact in revision 13, from the I2 source choices.** Each point
names the entries of the I2 deltas note that it answers (section 15.6l).
