Each is a rule of this contract from this revision, for the reason that
the point gives. None changes an entry that the I2 source at `744f2447`
writes, unless the point says so.

- **D16.** The `kind` of a `fact` type is a list of texts. Each is not
  empty, no two are equal, and the list has at least one and at most the
  bound on the elements of a list. A single text is not a `kind`. A fact
  may be copied into a `fact` slot when each kind of its type is a kind
  of the slot's type and both state one `under`. The reason: a type with
  no kind would name no entry, and a copy may narrow what a slot can
  hold and may not widen it.
- **D22.** A fact is **local** when its scope ID and its incarnation are
  this scope's. A judge is given a reader of this scope's own sealed
  entries, by position. The runtime gives it from its stored history,
  inside the commit. A verifier gives it from the entries that it has
  checked. The reader is no part of the folded state, and no digest
  covers it. A local fact is refused `fact-mismatch` when it names
  another scope kind, when the scope has no entry at that position, or
  when that entry has another hash. The check is made with the fields,
  in byte order of the field names, before authority. After it the fact
  is held as its `seq`, in normal form, and an effect that copies it
  records the `seq`. With no reader the input is not judged. A runtime
  fetches no local fact. A genesis that names its own scope is a refused
  genesis, `fact-mismatch`. The reason: the head check of section 5.2
  covers the scope's own history, so a local fact needs no fetch, and a
  judge stays a function of what it is given.
- **D25.** Equality puts a fact in normal form at the comparison,
  whatever read the value. A fact reference to this scope whose hash is
  the hash of this scope's entry at that position is that position. One
  with another hash is compared as it is, so it equals no local
  reference. No guard refuses `fact-mismatch`: only the reading of a
  field does. The reason: a guard has three results, and none of them is
  a refusal of the input's bytes.
- **DF4.** The normal form holds at any depth. A local fact that is a
  member of a record, or an element of a list, is put in normal form
  before the comparison, whether the value came from a field or from a
  part of a fetched entry. The reason: whether two values are equal must
  not depend on the route by which one of them was read. The I2 source
  does this for a record that is a field. Its comparison does not look
  inside a record that a part read, so such a record equals no record
  that holds the same local fact in normal form. That fails closed, and
  it is not this rule: section 11.11, row 18.
- **DF1.** A `record` type has at least one member. A member states a
  type and whether it is required, and nothing else: it has no default.
  A member's name holds no dot, because a member is named after its
  field with a dot. A member may be of any field type, also a record or
  a list. The number of members has no bound of its own; the bound on a
  definition's bytes limits it. A value of a record is a JSON object
  that has every required member and no member that the record does not
  declare. The static size of a record is the sum of its members, each
  at its most. A record may be copied into a record slot when each of
  its members is a member of the slot's record that can hold it, and the
  slot's record requires no member that the source may lack. The reason
  for each: a dot inside a name would give one name two readings; a
  record that could hold an undeclared member would have no static size;
  and a copy may narrow and may not widen.
- **DF5, DI3.** The validator refuses the prefix `timed:` in four
  places: an act kind, the `message` of a handler of any class, the
  message of a `tell`, and the name of a `relate`. A message's name is
  read as it is written. No class is written in front of it, because a
  handler states its class (section 6.4). The reason is the reason of
  revision 8: a timed entry has the kind `timed:` and the key of its
  rule, and no other entry may pass for one.
- **DJ4.** A detached text may be written in three places: a field of an
  act, a field of a handler's message, and the type of a value slot. The
  validator refuses it as an element of a list, as a member of a record,
  and in a reference slot. `detached` is `true` or is left out. A
  detached field, and a slot for a detached text, take no default. Such
  a slot is set only from a detached field or from another such slot, or
  is emptied with `null`. A constant, a plain text and a value whose
  type only the commit knows are refused as its source. A detached text
  is not a value of a plain text type, and a plain text is not a value
  of a detached one. The reason: a scope keeps the bytes of a text for
  the input that carried it, and removes them by the slot that held it.
  A digest that arrived as an element, a default, a constant or a part
  of another scope's entry would name bytes that this scope never
  received. Nothing could be read under it, and nothing redacted.
- **DJ6.** The value of a detached field is a digest. Any other value is
  refused `bad-field`, like any value that is not of its field's type. A
  judge is given a reader of texts, which gives one of three answers for
  a digest. *At hand*, with a length: the bytes hash to that digest, and
  have that many UTF-8 bytes. A text longer than its field's `max` is
  then `bad-field`. *No such text*: nothing came under that digest, and
  the field is `bad-field`. *Not at hand, and not asked for*: nothing
  about the bytes is checked. A runtime never gives the third answer. A
  verifier gives it for a text whose bytes it does not find, and then
  requires a tombstone (section 9.3). With no reader of texts, an input
  that names a detached text is not judged. For an act the refusal is an
  answer, and nothing is written. For a delivery only the `max` can
  refuse, because a text that is not at hand leaves the delivery
  undecided (above). The entry that records that refusal keeps the
  bytes, so a verifier derives the same refusal. The reason: the check
  needs bytes that are no part of an entry. Three answers keep the judge
  a function of what it is given, and let a verifier derive every entry
  again whether or not a text was later removed.
- **DJ1.** What travels beside a signed intent has one form, the
  argument `Beside` of the operations that take an act and a founding:
  `{ texts?, presented? }`. `texts` is a list of texts with no names.
  The scope computes the digest of each, and so learns which field names
  it. It reads at most as many texts as the act has detached fields, and
  none that is longer than a text may be. A text that no field names is
  not kept. `presented` holds the presented facts, by the names that the
  act declares in `presents` (section 6.4). Neither member is signed, so
  neither is part of the intent. A retry sends the same intent with the
  same `Beside`. A founding takes `texts` only. The reason for texts
  without names: a name that came beside the bytes could disagree with
  the digest in the signed intent, and the digest already says which
  field a text belongs to. The route over HTTP is the source's, as
  section 15.6e, entry 111, says. Revision 14 adds a third member,
  `values`: "A value beside an intent", below.

**A value beside an intent. New in revision 14.** This decides point
R1-54. Two acts of the rules scope need bytes that are no text:
`activate`, for the bytes of a definition and of its named closure, and
`keep-configuration`, for the bytes of a check's configuration (the
authority note's revision 16, section 12.1.4, rows marked P21). A text
cannot carry them. A text is at most 64 KiB, a redaction may remove it,
and no judgment reads it. A definition may be larger, it must stay, and
the act's judgment reads it.

- *What a value is.* One JSON value, in one byte domain of section 2.1.
  Its bytes are its canonical JSON. Its digest is over the domain tag, a
  newline and those bytes, like every digest of this contract. No second
  domain of this contract is added. A definition is in
  `artroom-definition-1`, which exists. A check's configuration is in
  `artroom-check-configuration-1`, which the rules definition declares,
  by the rule "A domain that an owner declares" of section 2.1.
  `artroom-text-1` is for texts only.
- *How it travels.* `Beside` is `{ texts?, presented?, values? }`.
  `values` is a list of values, each as its canonical bytes, with no
  names and no domain tags. Nothing in `Beside` is signed. A founding
  still takes `texts` only.
- *What names a value.* A place of the act that the platform
  definition's specification states, with the one domain of that place.
  There are two kinds of place. One is a field of type `digest` of the
  act. The other is a digest that a definition which the same input
  makes the scope retain names as a child's definition: its named
  closure (section 7.2). The scope computes the digest of each value in
  each domain that the act's places state, and so learns which place
  names it. The reason for no tag beside the bytes is the reason of
  point DJ1: a tag that came beside the bytes could disagree with the
  place, and the place already states the domain.
- *What is read.* At most as many values as the act's places can name,
  and none that is longer than the bound of its domain. The values are
  checked with the fields of the act, after its signature and after
  every check that section 4.2 puts before the fields. A value that no
  place names is not kept. An act of a declared definition has no such
  place, so a scope under a declared definition reads no value and keeps
  none.
- *The checks, in the commit.* A place that requires a value and has
  none at hand is refused `bad-field`. That is so when no value came
  under its digest, when the bytes that came are not the canonical form
  of a JSON value, and when the value is longer than the bound of its
  domain. The check that a value has the type of its domain, and every
  further check, is the platform definition's: that a definition
  validates and states the name that was given, and that a
  configuration's `image` is a content digest, are the authority note's.
- *Retention.* The scope keeps each named value as one retained input,
  under its domain and its digest, with the entry that names it (section
  9.2). One domain and one digest are one input, however many entries
  name it.
- *No redaction.* A value is never removed. No `redact` form names one,
  and no tombstone answers for one. The reason is the difference from a
  text: a judgment reads a value, and a child pins a definition by its
  digest, so a replay without the bytes is `incomplete` (section 9.3). A
  member must not put text that may have to be removed into a value.
  Bytes that a person wrote, and that a redaction must be able to reach,
  travel as a detached text.
- *The bound.* Each domain has a bound on one value, in bytes. A
  definition has the bound of section 6.1, and a closure the bound of
  section 7.2. The owner that declares a domain states that it has a
  bound. Every number is R4's (point R1-28). A platform definition whose
  act can retain a value with no stated bound is outside this contract,
  as a form that may retain an unbounded input is (section 17.2).
- *How a version states a place. Decided in revision 19* (I3 delta EM1).
  In the data of a platform definition, the type of a field that names a
  value is written `{ type: "digest", value: { domain, max } }`.
  `domain` is the byte domain of the place. `max` is the bound on one
  value of that domain, in canonical bytes. Two fields of one definition
  that state one domain state one `max`, or the data does not validate.
  The second kind of place needs no member. Where a field's domain is
  `artroom-definition-1`, the definitions of that value's named closure
  are places as before: at most the bound on a closure, each inside the
  bound on a definition. The validator reads the member only with its
  platform option. Without the option it is refused, as any unknown
  member is, so no act of a declared definition has a place.
- *What the member bounds, before the turn.* The scope reads the places
  of an act from the pinned data. That gives the most values that the
  act's places can name: one for each field that states `value`, and for
  a definition its closure. The scope computes the digest of a value
  only in the domains that those fields state, and it reads no value
  past the largest `max` among them. The static size of the act's entry
  form counts each place at its `max` (section 17.2). A rule states no
  domain and no bound of its own. It reads the value that a field names,
  which the judge matched: item 4 of what a rule is given (section 6.1).
  Which fields state the member is the specification's. Until its rows
  state it, a rule that holds the domain and the bound in its code is a
  stand-in, and the judge has no bound on the values at hand.
- *The code of each case. Confirmed in revision 19* (I3 delta EQ1). The
  three cases of "The checks, in the commit", above, are refused
  `bad-field`. A check of a value's content is a guard of the platform
  definition, and a guard that does not hold refuses `guard-failed`
  (section 4.2). One rule at place 4 may refuse with both codes and
  state one name for them, as the source does for a configuration. The
  name is the specification's, and each code is as this point says.
- *Who may fetch one.* A retained value is read by its domain and its
  digest, as any one retained input is (section 9.1), and the reader
  checks the bytes against the digest. The holder answers only for a
  value that an entry of its history names. Three readers are known: a
  reader that a read session admits to the scope's retained inputs; a
  scope that needs the value for a judgment of its own, as a child reads
  its definition from its creator (section 7.2) and as the directory
  reads an activated definition from the rules scope; and the checker
  service, for a configuration. Who is admitted to each read is the
  authority note's.
- *Capacity.* Sections 17.1 and 17.2 count a value as they count a text:
  once for each domain and digest, at its real size when the entry that
  names it is new work, and at the bound of its domain in a reservation.
- *No value beside a message.* No row needs one. A scope that must read
  a value which a message names by digest reads it from the scope that
  holds it, before its turn, and checks it against the digest. While it
  cannot be read, the delivery is not decided, and transport answers
  `retry`, `dependency-unavailable`. That is the rule of section 7.2 for
  a child's definition, and nothing is added to it.
- *What does not change.* No entry's bytes. An entry holds the digest in
  an ordinary field of its intent, as before.

Three things that the authority note lists under P21 need no new form.
The directory's `open-issue` and `open-pr` read a definition from the
rules scope by its digest, before the turn: sections 17.1 and 17.2
already count "a definition that an input names", and where the bytes
are read is that note's (its gap G16). The founding intent inside the
directory's `create` is a field of the creation message, so it is inside
the creating entry's bytes. The private bytes of a checkpoint are no
retained input of any scope (section 15.9).

**What a reader knows of another scope's entry. New in revision 14.** A
scope that fetched an entry of another scope, and a verifier that reads
the retained copy, know three things about it.

- *Its bytes.* The hash in the fact reference covers them, and the
  reader checks that before it reads anything (section 6.5).
- *Its kind.* From the bytes, by the table "Which entries have a kind,
  exactly", above.
- *The name of its definition.* The `under` that the source answered,
  and that the using entry records (section 4.1).

The reader does not hold the other scope's definition. So it knows the
type of no field, of no slot and of no member of that entry. A
declaration of the reader's own that has the same name, a handler or a
genesis act, says nothing about the other scope's entry. From this
follow the rules of section 6.5 for a part: a field of another scope's
entry is the value that its bytes hold, with no type applied; the mark
`{ "self": true }` in such a field is a record; and a number in such an
entry is a number, and no item of the reader.

A reader never reads a value of another scope's entry as a fact
reference unless the bytes hold a whole one: `at`, `seq` and `hash`.
Where a guard would need more than the bytes give, the guard does not
hold. No reader fills the gap from its own declarations.

**Made exact in revision 14, from the later I2 source choices.** Each
point names the entries of the I2 deltas note that it answers (section
15.6m). Each is a rule of this contract from this revision, for the
reason that the point gives. None changes an entry that the I2 source at
`58465dbf` writes, unless the point says so.

- **DR6.** The mark `{ "self": true }` is read as the envelope's `from`
  in one place only: a field of a message, or of a creation request,
  that the receiver's own definition declares as a fact or as a list of
  facts, at any depth of lists. The reader is then the scope that the
  message was sent to, and the declaration is that of the handler which
  received it, or of its genesis act. In a field of any other declared
  type the value is read as it is. So a record type with a boolean
  member named `self` holds `{ "self": true }` as a record, and a field
  of that type is applied. A field that the handler does not declare
  reads no mark, and is refused as an unknown field. The mark is never
  read inside a record: a sender writes none there (section 6.6). The
  fixed member `item` of a relationship update is read as before: the
  mark there is the owner's entry. The reason: the mark stands for a
  fact, and only the receiver's declared type tells it from a record.
  The destination reads the `operation` of a `reserve` in this way: it
  is the receiver, its field is a fact, and the mark is the `merge`
  entry that sent the message.
- **DR12.** Point DF4 is built: the comparison puts a local fact in
  normal form inside a record and inside a list, at any depth, whichever
  side holds the whole reference. The sentence of that point about the
  I2 source describes the snapshot `744f2447`. At `58465dbf` the
  function `equal` follows records and lists (section 11.12, row 18).

### 6.3 Items

```ts
interface ItemType {
  many: boolean;
  max: number;                               // most live items of this type; not a bound on retained final items
  states: Record<string, { final: boolean }>;        // at most 16
  initial: string;
  parties: Record<string, SlotRule & { list: boolean; max?: number;
                                       author: boolean }>;   // at most 8
  refs: Record<string, SlotRule & { to: FieldType }>;        // at most 12
  values: Record<string, SlotRule & { of: FieldType; default?: FieldValue }>;  // at most 12
}
interface SlotRule { fixed: boolean; required: boolean }
```

- A type that is not `many` has `max` 1. Nothing else is read from
  `many`. An opening that would make more than `max` live items is
  refused `type-full`.
- One item type may not use one name for two slots, of the same kind
  or of different kinds. An operand names a slot without a kind.
- A party list's `max` is at most 64. Adding a member who is already in
  a list, or removing one who is not, records no effect. A change that
  would pass `max` is refused `slot-full`. A derived list is never cut
  short.
- Only an effect of the entry that opens an item may set one of its
  `fixed` slots. A result clause and a timed rule may not.

- An item has a state, slots and a **revision** that counts the acts
  and handlers that changed it.
- A `fixed` slot is set by the act that opens the item and never again.
  That is how accepted terms stay what was accepted.
- A `required` slot must be set by the opening act. The validator
  refuses a definition whose opening act does not set one.
- An item in a final state refuses every transition. Comments are still
  allowed.
- **Live and retained items.** An item is **live** while its state is
  not final. An item in a final state is a **retained final item**. It
  is kept for as long as the history is kept, because guards,
  attribution, duties and replay read it. `max` bounds the live items
  of a type: an opening that would exceed it is refused. `max` does not
  bound retained final items. A type whose items open and reach a final
  state again and again stays within `max` while its retained final
  items grow. A numeric bound on the retained final items of a scope is
  owed to the proof plan, R4. This note sets none. No retained item,
  duty or provenance record is evicted or deleted to meet a bound.
- **Opening, exactly.** When an entry opens an item: the item is
  created in its `initial` state; each slot takes its `default`, or is
  empty; then the opening effects apply in the order written. After
  them every `required` slot must hold a value, or the input is refused
  `required-unset`. The validator refuses a definition in which an
  opening leaves a required slot with no effect that sets it.
- **No guard on a nascent item.** In an `open` act a guard may not name
  the new item's state or slots as its subject. It may name the act's
  fields, the signer, other items in `also`, and the scope's items.
- **No conflicting effects.** The validator refuses an act or handler
  in which two effects set the same slot of the same subject, or two
  set its state.
- **Revisions.** A new item has revision 1. An existing item that one
  entry changes rises by one, once, however many of that entry's
  effects touch it. An item that is only read does not rise.
- A party slot marked `author` counts toward attribution (section 6.7).

**Made exact in revision 13, from the I2 source choices.** Each point
names the entries of the I2 deltas note that it answers (section 15.6l).
Each is a rule of this contract from this revision, for the reason that
the point gives. None changes an entry that the I2 source at `744f2447`
writes, unless the point says so.

- **DG22.** Whether an opening sets every required slot is checked
  twice. The validator counts an effect as setting its slot also when
  the effect is under a condition, or when its source may be absent. It
  does not count an effect whose source is `null`. The commit then
  refuses `required-unset` for every case that the validator could not
  show. The reason: the validator cannot know which conditions hold, and
  two effects whose conditions exclude each other together always set a
  slot that neither sets alone.

### 6.4 Acts and handlers

```ts
interface ActType {
  step: "open" | "transition" | "comment";
  on: string | null;                       // item type of the primary item
  also: Record<string, AlsoRule>;          // at most 4 other local items
  fields: Record<string, FieldType & { required: boolean; default?: FieldValue }>;
  presents?: Record<string, { kind: readonly string[]; under: string; required: boolean }>;   // at most 4
  grant: string;                           // the action a current grant must cover; always required
  settles?: Settles;                       // section 17
  guards: readonly Guard[];                // at most 24 as written
  effects: readonly EffectForm[];          // at most 16
  sends: readonly SendForm[];              // at most 8
  attention: readonly Notify[];            // at most 8
}
interface ReceiveType {
  message: string;                         // a `tell` message's name, or a relationship's name
  class: "tell" | "relate" | "advisory";   // for an advisory, `message` is its type: `index` or `notify`
  from: { kind: ScopeKind; under?: string };
  fields: Record<string, FieldType & { required: boolean }>;   // the message's fields, or a relationship update's detail
  opens: string | null;                    // the item type this handler opens, if any
  copies?: number;                         // `relate` only: the most keys this scope keeps a copy for
  also: Record<string, AlsoRule>;
  settles?: Settles;
  guards: readonly Guard[];
  effects: readonly EffectForm[];
  sends: readonly SendForm[];              // empty when `class` is `advisory`
  attention: readonly Notify[];            // empty when `class` is `advisory`
}
/** How an act or handler selects one other local item. */
type AlsoRule =
  | { item: string; by: string }                             // named by a field of type `item`, or by a local fact whose entry opened it
  | { item: string; via: { slot: string; of: Subject } }     // the item that a reference slot of another subject names
  | { item: string; one: true };                             // the one item of a type that is not `many`
type Subject = "on" | `also.${string}` | "scope";
type Settles = { of: Subject; in: readonly string[] } | { copy: readonly string[] };
// Revision 21: a third form, `{ of: Subject; sets: string; in: readonly string[] }`: by a mark that the entry sets (point DI17, below).
interface TimedRule {
  on: string;                              // the item type; this makes it a timed item type
  states: readonly string[];               // live states in which the rule applies
  deadline: string;                        // a value slot of type `time`
  effects: readonly EffectForm[];
  attention: readonly Notify[];
}
```

Revision 8 adds `presents`, `settles`, `AlsoRule`, `TimedRule`, and the
members `class`, `fields`, `opens` and `copies` of a handler. Revision 7
gave a handler no declared fields and no way to open the one item that
section 4.1 allows it (I1 delta 42).

- **Timed rules.** A live item of type `on`, in one of `states`, whose
  `deadline` slot holds a time, holds that deadline under the rule.
  The validator refuses a rule unless all of these hold: `on` is an
  item type; each of `states` is a state of it that is not final;
  `deadline` is a value slot of type `time`; every effect has the
  rule's own item as its subject; no effect reads a field or the
  signer, because a timed entry has neither; no effect sets a fixed
  slot; and one effect takes the item out of `states`, by a `state`
  effect or by `hold: end`. So a transition that is applied is not due
  again under the same rule. It may be due under another: a rule may
  leave its item in a state of another timed rule. Section 17.2
  reserves for that chain, and refuses rules that lead to one another
  in a cycle. **A timed rule's effects are total.**
  The validator refuses, as `timed-partial`, a rule with an effect
  that the fold could refuse in the commit: an `add` to a party list,
  an `attribute`, a copy that is not statically assignable, a value
  set from the commit time, whose derived time could pass the last
  timestamp (section 6.6), or a capability effect that its capability
  does not declare total. **A timed entry always fits. New in
  revision 10** (the I1 deltas note, section 15). For each timed rule
  the validator computes an upper bound on the canonical bytes of the
  entry that the rule can write, whatever its item holds. The bound
  adds the entry without its effects, each effect record, each value
  that an effect copies at the most that its slot's type allows, and,
  for each attention form, every member that its slot can hold. A
  party list that an effect copies is counted the same way: at every
  member that the list can hold. That is its `max`, or, when it
  declares none, the bound that the runtime enforces on such a list
  (I1 delta 137). I1 uses its bound on the elements of a list there,
  which is 32, and refuses a larger `max`. Section 6.1 proposes 64
  for a party list. Either is sound, when the fold enforces the bound
  that the validator counted. The
  validator refuses the definition when that bound passes the entry
  size of section 7.5. The name of that refusal is I1's. The bound
  needs a bound on one member's handle. **The unit of that bound is
  the bytes of the handle's UTF-8 form. New in revision 11.** Quoting
  and escaping are not part of that length. They are part of the
  entry. So the static bound on a timed entry counts each handle at
  the most bytes that its canonical JSON form can take: at most six
  bytes for each byte of the handle, because RFC 8785 writes a
  control character as an escape of six bytes, and two more for the
  quotes. An effect that would put a longer handle in a party slot is
  refused `bad-field`, so a slot never holds a member that the bound
  did not count. The number is R3's to state and R4's to set. 256 is
  stated in the authority note's adopted revision 13, which keeps it
  a proposal that R4 owns, and it is the value that I1 holds as
  temporary. Which characters a
  handle may hold is R3's too. A
  timed entry is a settling input and is never refused for capacity
  (section 17). So a selected transition that passes its three checks
  of section 5.2 always commits, and the drain makes progress. Nothing
  skips a due item, moves its time on without its entry, or records it
  as settled. A fault can still leave a timed draft that cannot be an
  entry, as when a deployment lowers the entry size under a scope
  that was validated at a larger one. Then the drain stops, the turn
  ends `unavailable`, nothing is written and the transition stays
  due. That is a fault of the host (section 4.2). It is not a rule
  for passing over a due item. A timed rule's effect may set a
  reference slot of its
  item from `self`. The validator accepts that only when the slot's
  kinds include this rule's own kind, `timed:` and its key (section
  6.2). It is then total, like a `state` effect. A timed rule declares
  no sends. Its attention is advisory. The `timed` input of section 4.1 names the
  rule by its key here, and the order of section 5.2 uses that key as
  the rule's name.
- **`presents`.** An act may declare facts that are presented beside
  the intent. They are not signed, because some cannot be: an entry
  that was recorded for this intent names the intent's digest, so the
  intent cannot name that entry. A presented fact is fetched before
  the turn like a fact field, is checked for its kind and definition
  by a `fact` guard, and is retained in `uses`. What binds it to the
  intent is a guard that the definition writes, such as "the entry
  names this intent's digest". The entry records which facts were
  presented.
- **Three ways to name another item.** `by` is revision 7's form. A
  `by` field may also be a local fact: it selects the item that the
  named entry opened. `via` selects the item that a reference slot of
  another subject names. `one` selects the one item of a type that is
  not `many`. Revision 13 replaces the sentence that stood here, on
  the order of the names: the next point.
- **The order of the names. New in revision 13** (I2 delta DH8).
  Revisions 8 to 12 said here: "The names are resolved in the order
  written, and a `via` may name only an earlier one." `also` is a
  record. The canonical bytes of a definition put the names of a record
  in the order of RFC 8785, and keep no other order (section 2.1). So
  "the order written" is not in the bytes that a scope pins, and it
  cannot be a rule. The rule is by dependency.
  - A name with `by` or with `one` depends on no other name. A name with
    `via` depends on the subject whose slot it reads: `on`, or another
    `also` name.
  - A `via` name is resolved after the subject that it reads, whatever
    the names are. When that subject is unbound, or its slot is empty,
    the name is unbound.
  - A `via` may read `on` only in a transition. The item that an `open`
    act or a handler opens has no slots before the entry.
  - A **cycle** is a chain of `via` names in which each reads a slot of
    the next, and the last reads a slot of the first. A name that reads
    a slot of itself is a cycle of one. The validator refuses a
    definition that has a cycle in the `also` of one act or handler. An
    act names at most 4 other items, so the check is small.
  - The result does not depend on the order in which a runtime visits
    the names. Each name selects an item, or none, as a function of the
    fields, the state before the entry, and the names that it depends
    on.
  - Both pinned definitions need this. In `propose-manifest`,
    `commitment` reads a slot of `hold`, and in the byte order of the
    names `commitment` comes first. In the `publication` handler,
    `manifest` reads a slot of `merge`, and comes first too.
- **An unbound name.** An `also` name is **unbound** when its `by` field
  is absent, when its `via` slot is empty, or when a `one` type has no
  item yet. A guard whose subject is unbound is not evaluated, and the
  input does not rest on it. An effect or a send whose subject is
  unbound, or whose `if` reads an unbound subject, is not applied. An
  operand that reads an unbound subject is none. So an optional item is
  written once, and a definition that must have it adds a guard that
  fails on none.
- **An unbound subject inside a list form and in a condition. New in
  revision 13** (I2 delta DI6). The point above is made exact for the
  places that it does not name.
  - A guard whose subject is unbound is read as if it were not written,
    wherever it stands: in the written list, nested in an `each`, a
    `has` or an `anyOf`, or in a condition. It makes no list false, and
    it leaves no list not completed. A nested guard has the subject of
    the guard that holds it, unless it names its own (section 6.5). So a
    list form whose own subject is unbound is not evaluated at all.
  - So a list whose every guard has an unbound subject holds, as a list
    with no guard holds. An alternative of `anyOf` whose every guard is
    unbound holds, and the `anyOf` holds with it. A definition that must
    not pass in that way adds a guard that fails on none, as the point
    above says.
  - An operand that reads an unbound subject is none, also inside a
    guard whose own subject is bound.
  - An effect, a send or a notice whose `if` reads an unbound subject is
    not applied. "Reads" means one of two things: a guard of the list,
    at any depth, has that subject as its `of`; or an operand of the
    list names it, as the `of` of a slot or as an `item`.
  - An `unless` has no rule of its own. It is judged as it is written,
    by the first three rules. So an `unless` whose every guard has an
    unbound subject holds as a list, and its form is not applied. An
    `unless` whose guard only reads an operand of an unbound subject
    compares none.
  - A `where`, a `match` and an `except` keep the rules that they have:
    an operand of an unbound subject is none, and an unbound subject in
    `except` leaves nothing out (section 6.5).
  - The `of` inside an `attribute` effect is not the subject of a guard,
    and it is not the subject of its effect. Section 6.7 has its rule,
    and the two rules do not meet: an `attribute` whose own subject is
    bound is applied, also when the subject whose attribution it takes
    is unbound.
  - In the two pinned definitions, no guard that is nested in a list
    form of an act's or a handler's own guards names an `also` subject
    of its own. Three nested guards do so inside an `if`, in the
    `closes` handler of `issue`, and there the fourth rule decides: the
    effect is not applied. Neither of the two `unless` lists has a guard
    with an `also` subject. That was counted by script. So no pinned row
    turns today on the second rule, or on the first half of the fifth.
- **Expected revisions, exactly.** The keys of `expected` are `on` for
  a transition, and one key for each `also` name that is bound,
  however it was selected. An `open` act and a `comment` have no `on`
  key. Any other key is refused `bad-intent`. An `also` entry may not
  be named `on`.
- **A handler's subjects.** A handler has no signer. It names local
  items in `also`, with fields of the message. When `opens` names a
  type that is `many`, each applied delivery opens one item of it, and
  `on` is that item. When `opens` names a type that is not `many`, the
  handler opens it only if the scope has none, and otherwise `on` is
  the one that exists. A handler with `opens: null` has no `on`.
- **A type that is not `many`, with more than one item. New in revision
  13** (I2 deltas DH6 and DH10). A type that is not `many` has at most
  one live item, and it may also hold retained final items (section
  6.3). So "the one item" is not always one.
  - `one` selects by the number of items of the type, live and final
    together. With none, the name is unbound. With exactly one, it
    selects that item, live or final. With more than one, the input is
    refused `no-item`.
  - A handler whose `opens` names such a type follows the same count.
    With none, the delivery opens one, and that is `on`. With exactly
    one, that item is `on`, live or final. With more than one, the
    delivery is decided `refused`, `no-item`.
  - Nothing chooses among several. A rule that took the live one, or the
    newest, would be a rule that no definition asked for. A definition
    that must go on after an item of such a type has reached a final
    state declares the type `many`.
  - `on` may then be an item that the entry did not open. So the
    validator holds such a handler to the rules for an item that exists:
    no guard reads `on`; an effect on a fixed slot of `on` is refused;
    and a `state` effect on `on` is refused when the type has a final
    state. An effect on an `on` that is final refuses the delivery
    `final`, in the commit (section 6.6).
  - A handler opens no hold: section 6.8.
  - The two pinned definitions use `one` for three types: `intent`,
    `proposal` and `rules`, by script. The I2 note reports that nothing
    opens one of them twice (its entry DH10).
- **A message's fields.** A `tell` handler declares the fields of its
  message, and a `relate` handler the fields of the update's detail.
  An unknown or ill-typed field is decided `refused`, `bad-field`. A
  field of type `fact` is fetched when a `fact` guard or a part reads
  it (section 6.5). Revision 13 replaces that sentence: every foreign
  fact that a declared field names is fetched, read or not (point DH4,
  below). While it cannot be fetched, the delivery is not
  decided and is retried (section 7.4).
- **`copies`.** A `relate` handler states how many keys the scope keeps
  a copy for (section 7.3). A first update for a new key beyond that is
  decided `refused`, `type-full`.
- **An advisory handler ends the exchange. New in revision 9.** A
  handler of class `advisory` declares no sends and no attention. The
  validator refuses, as `advisory-sends`, a definition in which one
  declares either. Such a handler may have guards and effects, and may
  open its one item. Revision 8 gave this class the same forms as the
  others, while section 7.5 counted no sends for the delivery of an
  advisory. The rule here makes that count a bound on the grammar.
  - *Why.* An advisory has no result (section 7.4). A send that an
    advisory caused would have no request behind it and no result to
    end it, and two scopes could tell each other without end. A
    request, its result and a control end by section 7.4. An advisory
    ends because its handler sends nothing.
  - *Nothing declared is dropped.* A definition that declares such a
    send or notice is refused before any scope pins it. No runtime
    meets one and leaves it out.
  - *What a member is told is unchanged.* The scope whose act or
    handler changes something declares the `notify`, and that send
    goes to the member's inbox. The inbox's `notify` handler records
    the notice by its own effects, as an item that the member reads.
    The directory's `index` handler records its row the same way.
    Neither needs a send of its own.
  - A platform definition's code owes the same rule.
- **`settles`.** An act or handler may declare that it settles an item
  in stated states, or a relationship copy in stated states. Section 17
  says what that reserves.
  From revision 21 it may also declare that it settles an item by a mark
  that the entry sets: "`settles` by a mark", below.
- **A comment, exactly.** A `comment` step has no guards, no effects,
  no sends and no `also`. It may have attention. Neither lane
  definition uses it: there a comment is an item (gap G12).

- **Subjects.** A guard or effect names its subject: `on`, the primary
  item; `also.<name>`, another local item the act names by a field; or
  `scope`. So an act that opens a report can require that its signer is
  the performer of the commitment it names.
- **Opening.** `open` creates the primary item in its `initial` state
  and sets its fixed slots by its effects.
- **Selecting items.** A `transition` names its primary item in the
  intent's `on`, by local ID. Each `also` entry names a field of type
  `item`; the field's value selects the item, and its type must match.
  An `open` act has no `on`: its primary item is the one it creates,
  of the type the act's `on` states.
- **Expected revisions.** The intent's `expected` has one key for the
  primary item of a transition, `on`, and one for each `also` name. A
  mismatch is refused `revision-moved`. An `open` act has no `on` key.
- **No aliases.** In the commit, `on` and each `also` name are resolved
  to local items before any guard or effect. If two names resolve to
  the same item, the input is refused `alias`. So each subject is one
  distinct item, its expected revision is checked once, and it rises
  once. This is separate from the lawful case of one act changing
  several different items, which stays atomic. The validator's static
  check for two effects on one slot of one subject still applies.
- **`self`.** Inside a scope, `self` is a local reference to the entry
  being written, and so to the item it opens. Its type is a local
  item reference, never a fact reference. In a message, `self` is not
  expanded by the sender: the receiver reads it as the envelope's
  `from`. A send field filled from a slot that holds a local reference
  to an earlier entry is sent as that entry's fact reference, whose
  hash already exists.
- **Atomic.** All effects of one input, on the primary item and on each
  `also` item, take effect in the one commit. Each changed item's
  revision rises by one.
- **Authority and party, both.** Every act needs a current grant for
  its `grant` action. A `signer` guard is checked as well, never
  instead. There is no form that lets any signer act with no grant.
- **One relate send for each key.** A relationship key is the target
  scope, the owner's item and the relationship name. In the commit,
  after the subjects are resolved, each `relate` send of the entry is
  resolved to its key: the target by its scope ID, the item by its
  local ID, the name as written. If two sends of one entry resolve to
  the same key, the input is refused `duplicate-relation`: an act gets
  the answer Refused, and a delivery gets a deciding entry `refused`
  with that reason. This holds however the two were named: by two
  fields, by a field and a slot, by two slots, or by `self` and a
  reference to the item that the entry opens. The validator also
  refuses a definition in which two `relate` sends of one act or
  handler are written with the same `to`, `item` and `name`. One entry
  may still send updates for several different keys. In this grammar
  only acts and handlers declare sends; a form added later that sends
  owes the same check.
- A comment changes no item and meets no guard.
- A handler runs when a delivery of that message type arrives from a
  scope of that kind. It has guards and effects like an act and no
  signer.
- **A genesis is not an act kind.** The genesis kind, sent as an act,
  is refused `unknown-act`. Only a genesis entry runs it.
- **A genesis opens no timed item.** The validator refuses, with
  `genesis-timed`, a definition whose genesis act has a timed item type
  (section 5.2) as its `on`, or has a `hold` effect. Such a definition
  is never activated, so no scope pins it. A genesis entry opens one
  item and no other item exists yet. So after any genesis no item holds
  a deadline, and none can until an act of the active scope opens a
  timed item. The rule covers every genesis: a child's and a
  directory's. A platform definition's code owes the same rule.
- **Time values set by a genesis.** A genesis may still set a value
  slot from the commit time plus a constant duration. The commit time
  is the time of the genesis entry, not of the confirmation. Such a
  value is not a deadline: no timed rule reads it, because the item's
  type is not timed. A `before` or `after` guard of a later act may
  read it. That act is admitted only when the scope is active, and it
  is judged on its own commit clock.

*Definitions refused and passed by the genesis rule.* X1 and X2 are
made up for this table.

| Definition | Genesis act | It opens | Timed rule that names that type | Validation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| X1 | `start` | `hold`, the type of `hold@1` | The hold's end | Refused `genesis-timed`. |
| X2 | `start` | `job`, with a `deadline` slot | The job's deadline | Refused `genesis-timed`. |
| `issue`, in the R2 draft | `file` | `intent` | None | Passes this check. |
| `change`, in the R2 draft | `open` | `proposal` | None | Passes this check. |

What was found in R2 revision 6 at `abc9c365`: the two definitions have
two timed rules. A hold's end is on the `hold` item, which the act
`take-hold` opens. A job's deadline is on the `job` item, which the act
`request-check` opens. Neither act is a genesis. So no lane form needs
a deadline at genesis, and the exclusion costs the lane definitions
nothing.

**Made exact in revision 13, from the I2 source choices.** Each point
names the entries of the I2 deltas note that it answers (section 15.6l).
Each is a rule of this contract from this revision, for the reason that
the point gives. None changes an entry that the I2 source at `744f2447`
writes, unless the point says so.

- **DH1.** A handler states its `class`, its `message`, `from`,
  `fields`, `opens`, `also` and its forms. A `relate` handler states
  `copies`. A handler may state `settles`. The validator refuses two
  handlers for one class, one message and one sender kind. The message
  of an advisory handler is `index` or `notify`. A `tell` may have any
  name that sections 6.1 and 6.2 allow. The reason: the class is part of
  what finds a handler (section 7.4), so a `tell` and a relationship of
  one name are two messages, and no name needs a prefix that says its
  class.
- **DH2.** A relationship update for which the definition has no
  handler, for its name, the sender's kind and the sender's definition,
  is decided `refused`, `unknown-message`, and the scope keeps no copy.
  The reason: a scope keeps a copy for a relationship that it declares a
  handler for, and the handler's `copies` bounds the keys. With no
  handler nothing bounds them, and any sender of the right kind could
  make a scope keep copies.
- **DH3.** A `relate` handler states `copies`, an integer of at least 1.
  No other handler states it. The count is of the keys that this scope
  holds for that relationship name whose owner is a scope of the
  handler's `from.kind`. A key is counted for as long as the scope holds
  its copy, in whatever state. The check is made last, after the
  handler's guards, effects and sends, as the check of a type's `max` is
  for an act. A first update for a new key at or past the number is
  decided `refused`, `type-full`, with no effect and no copy. The
  reason: a handler is found by name and kind, so that is what its bound
  counts, and section 4.2 puts bounds last. This contract states no most
  for `copies`. The number is R4's, with the other bounds.
- **DH4, DI4.** The fields of a message are read as the fields of an act
  are. A field that the handler does not declare, a required field that
  is missing, and a value that is not of its field's type are each
  decided `refused`, `bad-field`, before any guard is judged. A field of
  a message has no default. For a `relate`, the fields are the update's
  detail and nothing else: the `update` operand reads its state, its
  item and its revision (section 6.5). Every foreign fact that a
  declared field of an act or of a handler names is fetched before the
  turn and recorded in `uses`, whether or not a guard or a part reads
  it. That replaces the narrower sentence of revision 8, which fetched a
  fact "when a `fact` guard or a part reads it". The reason: the kind
  and the `under` of a fact are bounds of its type, and they can be
  checked only with the entry at hand. So a fact that is only copied
  into a slot needs its entry too, and one rule serves an act and a
  handler. The source entry of a delivery counts toward the bound on
  foreign entries. A message that names more facts than the rest of that
  bound is decided `refused`, `bad-field`, and none is fetched. A
  deciding entry that refuses, and the entry of an advisory whose
  handler refused, record what was read (section 17.2).
- **DH5.** A field of type `item` in a message takes two values. The
  first is a fact of this scope, with the hash of this scope's entry at
  that position, when that entry opened an item: it is read as the
  item's local ID. The second is a bare local ID. Any other value is
  `bad-field`. A value that names an item of another type than the field
  states is `no-item`. A local ID that arrives from another scope
  selects an item and proves nothing about it. The handler's guards say
  who may name it, as the guard `not-the-parent` of the lane rows does.
  The reason for taking a bare ID: a child sends back the position that
  its parent gave it, as a number, and the adopted lane rows select the
  parent's item by it.
- **DH9.** The validator checks each way of naming another item. `by`
  names a field of type `item`, of the named type; or a field of type
  `fact` under this definition's name, each of whose kinds opens the
  named type, by an `open` act on it or by the message of a handler that
  opens it. `via` names a slot of `on` or of another `also` name, of one
  of those two types. `one` names a type that is not `many`. A name has
  exactly one of the three. The reason: a name that could never select
  an item of its type would always be unbound or `no-item`, and that is
  a mistake the validator can show.
- **DH11.** A name is **unbound** when its `by` field is absent, when
  its `via` slot is empty or the subject of that slot is unbound, and
  when its `one` type has no item. A value that is present and selects
  no item of the type is not unbound: the input is refused `no-item`.
  `expected` has a key for each bound name and for no other. A key for
  an unbound name is refused `bad-intent`. The reason: the signer states
  the revision of each item that the act will read, and an act that
  states a revision for an item it does not select was signed for
  another state than the one it is judged on.
- **DJ11, DJ12.** The `act` input of an entry has the member `presented`
  always. It is an empty record when nothing was presented. Each
  presented fact is read as a fact field of the type that `presents`
  states. A name that the act does not declare, a value that is no fact
  reference, and a required fact that is absent are each refused
  `bad-field`. A foreign one is fetched before the turn, is recorded in
  `uses`, and counts toward the bound on foreign entries. One that names
  this scope is checked against the scope's own history, and is refused
  `fact-mismatch` like a local fact in a field (section 6.2). The guards
  read it in normal form, and the entry records the whole reference as
  it arrived. `presents` declares at most the bound, 4 as proposed. The
  validator refuses `presents` on the genesis act, and a `presented`
  operand that names no declared fact. A result clause reads the facts
  that were presented to its origin entry, from that entry's input. A
  founding may carry detached texts, and is presented no fact. The
  reason for the last: nothing travels beside a creation, so a genesis
  act that needed a presented fact could never be created by another
  scope.
- **DI17.** `settles` has two forms. `{ of, in }`: `of` is `on` or an
  `also` name, and is not the item that the entry opens. `in` is a list
  of states of that subject's type, and is not empty. `{ copy }`: in a
  `relate` handler only. It is a list of states of the relationship,
  each a text that is not empty, and the copy is the one that the
  handler's update is for. The reasons: an item that an entry opens was
  in no state before it, so it awaits nothing; and a relationship's
  states are the sender's words, which the validator cannot check
  against a type. A final state may be listed in `in`. Whether one
  should be is the lane design's question (point R1-45).
- **`settles` by a mark. New in revision 21.** This decides point R1-68
  by its smaller option, as the planner decided (act `1f8aba72`): the
  first notice that a key behind a publication is compromised must be
  recordable at a destination with no free room, and that entry sets a
  mark and changes no state. `settles` has a third form: `{ of, sets, in
  }`.
  - *The grammar.* `of` is `on` or an `also` name, and is not the item
    that the entry opens. `sets` names a value slot of that subject's
    type. The slot has the type `bool`, is required, states `default:
    false`, and is not `fixed`. It is the **mark**. `in` is a list of
    states of the type. It is not empty, and it lists no final state.
  - *What it means.* An item of the type **awaits** this settlement
    while its state is one of `in` and its mark is `false`. An entry of
    the form settles it when the entry finds the item so, and its
    effects leave the mark `true`. The entry need change no state.
  - *The mark is set once.* No effect may set the mark to `false`, or
    empty it. The validator refuses a written effect on the slot that is
    not a `value` effect of the constant `true`. A rule's effect that
    sets it otherwise is a fault. So an item whose mark is `true` never
    awaits this settlement again, and the duty cannot be created twice
    for one item by its mark.
  - *Why no final state.* An item that is final cannot be changed
    (section 6.6). An item that awaited a mark in a final state could
    never be settled, and its reservation would never be released. For
    the form `{ of, in }` whether a final state should be listed stays
    the lane design's question (point R1-45).
  - *What the validator checks.* The three members, as the grammar says.
    That the slot is as stated. That no written effect of the definition
    sets the slot but to `true`. As before, a form states one `settles`,
    and where several forms settle one item the largest reservation
    counts.
    Changed in revision 22: the last sentence is replaced. The largest
    counts among the forms that settle one duty, and a duty is one state
    of an item, for the first form, or one mark of an item, for the
    third. Two marks of one item are two duties, and each is reserved
    ("Several marks on one item", below).
  - *What the judge does.* It derives whether the entry is settling, as
    point DI21 of section 17.3 says for a state: before the entry the
    subject's state was one of `in` and its mark was `false`, and after
    the entry's effects the mark is `true`. An entry of the form that
    finds the mark `true` already, or the state outside `in`, is new
    work. So is a refusal, which sets nothing.
  - *What it reserves.* Row 3 of section 17.2: for the settling act or
    handler, 1 entry, the records it changes, 1 pending request for each
    request among its sends, and what its effects and its marks can
    start, with the bytes of all of that. It is reserved from the entry
    that puts the item in a state of `in` with the mark `false`, which
    is new work or is counted in the closure of the duty that its entry
    settles. It is released when the mark is set, or when the item
    leaves the states of `in`.
    Made exact in revision 22: this is the amount of one marker duty.
    Section 17.2, "A marker duty", states it whole: when the duty
    begins, what it is summed with, and why a mark that is `true` is in
    no later count.
  - *Replay.* The verifier derives the same word from the folded state
    before the entry and from the entry's effects. No entry records it.
    A verifier needs it only to check that new work fitted (section
    17.3).
  - *In which definitions.* In any. It is a form of `settles`, and it
    needs no code. No pinned lane definition states it, and a definition
    that does has other bytes and another digest.

Revision 20 left the form out because several rules read `settles`. This
is each of them, and how it reads the third form.

| The rule that reads `settles` | Where | How it reads `{ of, sets, in }` |
|---|---|---|
| The listing of `Settles`, and the point "`settles`" | Section 6.4 | A third member of the union, by a comment under the listing. The point names it. |
| Point DI17: `settles` has two forms | Section 6.4 | It has three. `of` follows the rule of the first form. `in` lists no final state, where the first form may list one. |
| Row 3 of the table of duties: "the item is in a state that a `settles` declaration lists" | Section 17.2 | The item awaits a settlement: by a state, as before, or by a mark, as above. The row reserves the same things for either. An item may await both, and then reserves both. |
| "A request's clauses": a duty of row 3, "when an effect can set a state that a `settles` lists" | Section 17.2 | Also when an effect can set a state of `in`, or opens an item whose initial state is one of `in`. The mark is taken as `false`. That counts more than is needed when the mark is `true`, and never less. |
| Point DI18: what a list of effects can start, and the state that the form's own `settles` lists | Section 17.2 | "What an item in that state reserves for its settlement" includes a settlement by a mark, for each state of `in`. For the settled subject the form's own mark is not counted: the entry leaves it `true`. The subject's states are counted as for any other subject, because the entry need not leave them. |
| Point DI19: a timed rule that leads to a state which awaits a settlement | Section 17.2 | A state of `in` awaits one, with the mark taken as `false`. The item reserves it already. |
| The table of the two kinds, the row "Settling": "when its subject is in a listed state at the commit and the entry takes it out of the listed states" | Section 17.3 | Or when its subject awaits a settlement by a mark at the commit and the entry sets the mark. "Changed in revision 21", under the table. |
| Point DI21: the judge says whether an entry is settling | Section 17.3 | As "What the judge does", above. Every refusal by such a form is new work, as the point says. |
| "An entry that records a refusal": a refusal takes no item out of a pending state | Section 17.3 | It sets no mark either. Unchanged. |
| The static rule, condition 2: "the sum of `max` over the item types that a `settles` names"; and "a definition that declares no send, no `settles`" | Section 17.3a | The sum reads the same for either form: at most `max` live items of the type await at once. A definition that states the third form declares a `settles`, and is outside the rule for timed rules only. |
| "What this form does not cover": an act or a delivery on a holder is new work unless its form declares `settles` | Section 17.2a | With the third form the first notice sets a mark, is settling, and has its entry from row 3. "Changed in revision 21", beside the text. |
| The third reason of "No effect of a refused deciding entry": an applied `withdraw` is reserved by `settles` on the state `queued` | Section 15.3g | Unchanged: that is the first form. |
| The witnesses of section 17.4, and the `settles` of `check` and of `check-error` | Sections 17.4 and 6.10 | Unchanged: each is the first form. |

**Several marks on one item, and a rule of a settling form. New in
revision 22** (the verdict `dc1da38a`, its second finding). Revision 21
let one item have several marks, each with its own forms. Three of its
sentences on what such an item reserves did not agree. "What the
validator checks", above, took the largest reservation over the forms
that settle one item. Point DI18 of section 17.2 took the largest over
the forms that settle one state. And the fifth row of the table above
left out the form's own mark, and counted the subject's states with
every other mark taken as `false`. Take an item with the marks a and b,
and two acts that each set one of them. The first sentence can give the
two settlements one reservation. The third can count from a to b and
back to a, without end. One rule replaces the three. Section 17.2, "A
marker duty", has it whole, with the amounts. This is what it says of
the form.

- *One duty for each mark of each item.* A **marker duty** is an item
  and one of its marks, written (item, slot). It is pending while the
  slot is `false` and the item's state is in the `in` of a form that
  settles that slot.
- *From the opening.* A mark is `false` from the entry that opens its
  item. So the duty begins with the entry that leaves the item in a
  listed state: the opening entry, where the initial state is listed.
  That entry reserves it, once.
- *Alternatives.* The forms that settle one mark of one type are
  alternatives of one duty, and the largest of them counts. A form that
  settles another mark, or that settles by state, is no alternative of
  it.
- *A sum.* An item reserves each of its pending marker duties, and its
  state duty and its deadline beside them. Several marks on one item
  work as before: each is settled by its own entry, in any order, and
  each entry has its room.
- *Set once, counted once.* A mark only becomes `true`. A marker duty
  that is completed is never pending again, and no later count holds it.
  That is why the count of an item with several marks ends.
- *A rule of a form that declares `settles` sets no state. New in
  revision 22.* Found by the sweep of this revision (the opening, "The
  sweep of revision 22"). Revision 21 counts a change of state by a rule
  at the worst case: for each effect of the mark's `most`, one more item
  in the state of the definition that reserves most (section 17.2, "What
  a mark may start"). In a form that declares `settles`, that worst case
  holds the form's own duty, on another item: the state that its
  `settles` lists, or the mark that it names, taken as `false`. So such
  a form with an effect mark reached its own duty by type, its closure
  was not finite, and the definition was refused `reserve-unbounded`.
  The case that the third form exists for is such a form: the authority
  note's first notice sets its mark by the rule of an effect mark. The
  rule from this revision: in an entry of a form that declares
  `settles`, of any of the three forms, an effect that a rule returns is
  no `state` effect, and sets no slot that a timed rule names as its
  `deadline`. A rule that returns one has a fault, and nothing is
  written (section 6.1, "A fault of a rule is no judgment"). So the
  validator counts, for an effect mark of such a form, the operations of
  `most.operations` and the item of `most.opens`, and no change of
  state. A written effect of the form may set a state as before, and is
  counted from the data. What was checked: by a search of the authority
  note's adopted revision 26 for `settles`, one row of its platform
  definitions declares it today, `decide-recovery` of the task, and that
  row holds no mark. The two pinned lane definitions hold no mark at
  all. So the rule changes no row that exists.
  Confirmed in revision 23: the planner answered that this is the
  wanted rule (act `2d3fa911`, answer 2). The entry's own `settles`
  decides. A mark that names the states that its rule may set stays a
  later optimization, as the act `39749e26` said.
- *Four rows of the table above, read with this.* The third: an item may
  await several marks and a state, and reserves each. The fourth and the
  sixth: "the mark is taken as `false`" holds for an item that the count
  does not name, and for a mark of the settled item that is not
  completed. The fifth is replaced by rule 7 of "A marker duty": the
  form's own mark and every mark of the item that is `true` are
  completed, and a state of the settled item is counted only where a
  written effect of the form sets it.

Witness 18.54.
Witness 18.51.

**Made exact in revision 14, from the later I2 source choices.** Each
point names the entries of the I2 deltas note that it answers (section
15.6m). Each is a rule of this contract from this revision, for the
reason that the point gives. None changes an entry that the I2 source at
`58465dbf` writes, unless the point says so.

- **DR8.** Point DH5 holds at any depth. Where a handler's declared type
  is `item`, in a field, in an element of a list or in a member of a
  record, a fact of this scope whose hash is the hash of the entry that
  opened an item at that position is read as that item's local ID. A
  fact that names no such entry is left as it is, and is then no value
  of the type: `bad-field`. An item of another type than the declared
  one is `no-item`. The reason: a sender writes a local reference as a
  whole fact reference wherever the message holds one (section 6.6), so
  the receiver reads it back wherever its type says `item`.
- **DR14.** A handler that states `from.under` receives a message only
  from a sender whose pinned definition has that name. The name is the
  one that the receiver read with the source entry (section 7.4). A
  message from a sender under another definition is received by no
  handler: it is decided `refused`, `unknown-message`, as point DH2
  says. So it names no fact and no text. The receiver fetches nothing
  for it beside its source entry, keeps no text for it, and its decision
  waits on no dependency. A verifier takes the name from the `under` of
  the source entry's use, and asks for the same texts. The reason: a
  decision that reads no dependency must not wait on one, and a sender
  must not make a scope fetch or keep bytes for a message that no
  handler receives.

### 6.5 Guard forms

Every guard has an optional `of` naming its subject; the default is `on`.
A guard that names a field may carry `ifPresent`.

| Form | Holds when |
|---|---|
| `state: [..]` | The subject's state is one of these. |
| `signer: [slot..]` | The signer's member is in one of these party slots of the subject. |
| `notIn: [slot..]` | The signer's member, and its principal if it has one, are in none of these slots. |
| `set: slot`, `unset: slot` | A slot holds a value, or none. |
| `equals: { a, b }`, `differs: { a, b }` | Two operands are equal, or not. An operand is a field, a slot, the signer or a constant. |
| `some: { type, states, where? }` | At least one local item of that type is in one of those states. `where` is a list of `equals` over its slots. |
| `none: { type, states, where? }` | No local item of that type is. |
| `count: { type, states, where?, min?, max? }` | The number of such items is within the bounds. |
| `every: { list, states }` | Every item named by a list field or slot is in one of those states. |
| `fact: { field, where? }` | The foreign entry named by the field was fetched; it is of the act kind and definition name the field's type states; `where` is a list of `equals` over its input fields and effects. |
| `before: { slot }`, `after: { slot }` | The commit clock is before or after a time in a value slot. |
| `rule: name` | A named expression in the profile is true. Its input is exactly: the subjects' records, the act's kind and fields, the signer's member, and the content of each fetched fact. It has no clock and no other item. |

**Forms added in revision 8.** The table above is revision 7's and
stands. These forms are added. Each reads only what section 5.1 allows:
the act's or the message's own bytes, this scope's state, and entries
that were fetched by hash before the turn. None reads another scope's
present state.

```ts
type Operand =
  | { field: string; part?: Part }                 // a field of the act, or of the message in a handler
  | { presented: string; part?: Part }             // a fact presented beside the intent (section 6.4)
  | { slot: string; of?: Subject | "each"; part?: Part }
  | { element: string; part?: Part }               // the element that an enclosing `each`, `has`, `distinct` or `sameSet` binds
  | { item: Subject | "each" }                     // a local reference to that subject's item
  | { signer: true }                               // acts only
  | { sender: true }                               // handlers and result clauses: the envelope's source scope
  | { source: EntryPart }                          // handlers only: a part of the verified source entry
  | { update: "state" | "item" | "revision" }      // `relate` handlers only: the update being applied
  | { result: "reason" }                           // result clauses only: the name in the result's reason
  | { scope: true }                                // this scope's own reference
  | { intent: true }                               // the digest of the intent being judged
  | { none: true }
  | { const: FieldValue };
type Part = EntryPart | { of: EntryPart; then: "scope" | "seq" };
type EntryPart =
  | "ref" | "scope" | "seq"                        // read from the reference; nothing is fetched
  | "kind" | "intent" | "on"
  | { field: string }
  | { opened: string }
  | { set: { item: Operand; slot: string } }
  | { carried: string };

type Where = { equals: { a: Operand; b: Operand } } | { differs: { a: Operand; b: Operand } };
interface Range { type: string; states: readonly string[]; where?: readonly Where[];
                  except?: readonly Subject[] }
type CapabilityArg = Operand | { each: Operand; as: string; value: Operand } | { items: Range; slot: string };

/** Added to the guard forms. Every guard may also carry `reason?: string`. */
type AddedGuard =
  | { count: Range & { min?: number | Operand; max?: number | Operand } }
  | { fact: { field: string } | { presented: string } | { element: string } }
  | { each: { list: Operand; as: string; where?: readonly Where[]; guards: readonly Guard[] } }
  | { has: { list: Operand; as: string; where: readonly Where[]; guards?: readonly Guard[] } }
  | { anyOf: readonly (readonly Guard[])[] }
  | { distinct: { list: Operand; as: string; key: Operand } }
  | { sameSet: { list: Operand; as: string; key: Operand; items: Range;
                 match?: readonly Where[]; ordered?: boolean } }
  | { capability: { name: "hold" | "git-read"; guard: string; with: Record<string, CapabilityArg> } };
```

*Operands.*

| Operand | Reads | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `field`, `presented` | The act's signed fields, or the facts presented with it. In a handler, `field` is a field of the message. | A member of a record is named with a dot. |
| `slot` | A slot of a subject. The default subject is the guard's own. In the `where` of a range, and in the `match` of `sameSet`, a slot with no `of` is a slot of each item the range covers. | The validator derives, for each range, the slots an index must cover. `of: "each"` is the item of a fan-out (section 6.6). |
| `element` | The element bound by the nearest enclosing form with that `as` name. | A member of a record element is named with a dot. |
| `item` | A local reference to the subject's own item. | It compares with an `item` slot, and with a number read from a part. |
| `sender` | The source scope of the envelope, with its incarnation, as verified (section 7.4). | Answers gap G11. |
| `source` | A part of the source entry that the receiver read and checked before recording anything (section 7.4). | The source entry is then retained in `uses`. Answers part of gap G17. |
| `update` | The state, the owner's item or the revision of the relationship update being applied. | |
| `result` | The `name` of the reason on the result being recorded. | For a clause that depends on why a request was refused. |
| `intent` | The intent digest of the act being judged. | So that a presented entry can be tied to this intent. |

*Parts. This answers gaps G1 and G7.* A part reads inside an entry that
a fact reference names: a fact field, a presented fact, a fact held in
a slot, a fact that is an element of a list, or the source entry.

| Part | Is | Needs the entry's bytes |
|---|---|---|
| `ref` | The fact reference itself. | No |
| `scope`, `seq` | The entry's scope with its incarnation, and its position. | No |
| `kind` | The kind of the entry, as section 6.2 defines it. | Yes |
| `intent` | The intent digest of an act, genesis or preparation entry. | Yes |
| `on` | The local ID, in the entry's own scope, of the entry's primary item. For an entry that opens an item it is the entry's own `seq`. | Yes |
| `{ field }` | A field of the entry's intent, or of the message it delivered. | Yes |
| `{ opened }` | `"state"`, or a slot: what the entry's own effects left on the item it opened. A party list is the list of its members, in the order of the effects. | Yes |
| `{ set }` | `"state"`, or a slot, of the item with that local ID in the entry's scope: the value that this entry's own effects gave it. None when no effect of this entry set it. | Yes |
| `{ carried }` | A member of a capability record that this entry's effects hold, written `kind.member`. None when the entry holds no record of that kind, or more than one. | Yes |
| `{ of, then }` | When the part named by `of` is itself a fact reference: its `scope` or its `seq`. | As `of` |

- **Each operand is validated by itself.** The validator checks both
  operands of an `equals` or a `differs`, and every operand of any
  other form: its shape, its type, and the rule that no guard reads a
  slot of a nascent item (section 6.3). A valid first operand excuses
  nothing about the second. A bare `null` is not an operand; none is
  written `{ none: true }`.
- **A fact reference is verified whole.** Before any part of a fetched
  entry is read, the entry's own scope, incarnation and position must
  equal the reference's `at` and `seq`, and its bytes must hash to the
  reference's `hash`. A reference that fails is refused
  `fact-mismatch`, whether the fact is local or foreign. Two
  references with one hash and different scopes or positions are two
  references, and each is verified. Fetches and `uses` are deduplicated
  only after that, by the whole reference.
- An entry is fetched when a `fact` guard names it or when a part that
  needs its bytes reads it. It is fetched by its hash, before the turn
  (section 5.2, step 1), and listed in `uses`. A reference that is only
  copied, compared whole, or read for `scope` or `seq` is not fetched.
  `uses` lists each fetched entry once, in byte order of scope ID and
  then by `seq`. Revision 13 replaced the first and the third sentence
  of this point (section 6.4, point DH4): every foreign fact that a
  declared field names, and every foreign presented fact, is fetched,
  whether or not a guard or a part reads it. Revision 14 marks them
  here as replaced. The order of `uses` stands.
- **An entry records what its judgment read. New in revision 9**
  (the I1 deltas note, section 12, with the branch that it repaired
  after event `fb6f8e03`: a refused genesis that had read a fact
  before the field that refused it). An entry that records a refusal
  holds, in `uses`, every foreign entry that was read before the
  refusal, and, in `prepared`, every rule result that was read. That
  covers a refused genesis, the deciding entry of a refused request,
  and the entry of an advisory whose handler refused. An entry that
  runs a result clause with effects, which is a delivery of a result
  or a diagnosis, holds in `uses` each fact that the clause reads,
  after the source entry and once each. A clause with no effects
  reads none, and no clause fetches anything (section 6.6). A refused
  act writes no entry and records nothing. So no written judgment
  rests on bytes that only another entry, or another scope, retains.
  Sections 17.2 and 17.3 say how the bytes that such an entry keeps
  are charged.
- **A written entry records every entry that was fetched for its
  input. New in revision 14.** The point above says "every foreign
  entry that was read before the refusal". Since point DH4 of section
  6.4, every foreign fact that the input names is fetched before the
  turn, so "read" had two meanings: fetched, or reached by the judge.
  The rule is the first. The foreign entries that an input **names**
  are the source entry of a delivery or of a created genesis, every
  foreign fact in a declared field, and every foreign presented fact.
  They are a function of the pinned definition and the input alone, as
  the texts that an input names are (section 6.2). An entry that is
  written for the input holds every one of them in `uses`, whatever
  was decided, and whichever field or guard refused it. A fact that
  was fetched is never left out of a written entry because the
  refusal came before a guard read it, or before the judge reached its
  field. Three inputs name no fact beside the source entry, and
  nothing more is fetched for them: a message that no handler
  receives; a message whose fields are not values of their declared
  types; and a message that names more facts than the bound allows.
  The reason: the fetch and the record then follow one function, a
  verifier derives `uses` without knowing where a judgment stopped,
  and no fetched byte is dropped by a scope that goes on to write.
  The I2 source records, for a refusal by the reading of a field, only
  the facts of the fields before it: section 11.12, row 23.
- A part never causes a second fetch. `{ of, then }` reads the
  reference that a part yields. It does not read the entry behind that
  reference. To read inside another entry, the act names that entry
  too, as a field or a presented fact. That is why this contract adds
  no `follow` option: an act that needs the report behind an
  acceptance names both facts, and a guard checks that the report's
  `scope` and `seq` are the acceptance's scope and its `on`. Every
  entry that a judgment reads is then named by hash in the input.
- A part of an entry whose definition the reader does not hold is read
  from the entry's bytes: its fields and its recorded effects. A part
  that is not there is none. A part is never an error.
- A part of a local fact, or of a slot that holds a local entry
  reference, is read from this scope's own history.

*List guards, and the others.*

| Form | Holds when |
|---|---|
| `count` with an operand as `min` or `max` | As `count`, with the bound read from a slot or a field. Answers gap G5. |
| `fact` over a presented fact or an element | As `fact` over a field. |
| `each: { list, as, where?, guards }` | For every element of the list for which every `where` holds, every guard holds with the element bound. An empty list holds. Answers gaps G6 and G8. |
