| `has: { list, as, where, guards? }` | Some element of the list satisfies every `where` and every guard. An empty list fails. |
| `anyOf: [[..], [..]]` | At least one alternative holds. An alternative holds when each of its guards does. |
| `distinct: { list, as, key }` | No two elements have equal keys, and no key is none. |
| `sameSet: { list, as, key, items, match?, ordered? }` | The keys are distinct. The set of keys is exactly the set of local IDs of the items that the range covers. For each element, every `match` holds between the element and its item. With `ordered`, the keys ascend. Answers gap G10, with `each` and `has`. |
| `except` in a range | The items of those subjects are left out. An unbound subject leaves nothing out. |
| `capability` | The named guard of a declared capability holds for those arguments. Section 6.11. Answers gaps G17 and G19. |

- `list` is an operand whose value is a list: a list field, a list
  slot, or a list read by a part from a fetched entry.
- A guard nested in `each`, `has` or `anyOf` takes the enclosing
  guard's subject unless it names its own.
- `ifPresent` skips a guard when a field or a presented fact that it
  names is absent.
- A `where` may now hold `differs` as well as `equals`.
- `reason` names the refusal (section 4.2). It changes no judgment.
- **A `reason` on a nested guard names nothing. New in revision 13** (I2
  deltas DG9 and DI14). The name of a refusal is the `reason` of the
  failed guard of the written list, and its path is that guard's
  (section 4.2). When a nested guard fails, the guard of the written
  list that failed is the list form which holds it. A `reason` on a
  nested guard, or on a guard of a condition, is accepted by the
  validator and names no refusal: one refusal has one name. Neither
  pinned definition writes one, by script.
- **The `where` of a `fact` guard. New in revision 13** (I2 delta D21).
  Revision 7's table says that this `where` is a list of `equals` over
  the entry's "input fields and effects". Exactly: only a `fact` guard
  over a field has a `where`. Each clause is an `equals`. Its `a` is `{
  field: name }`, and it is read as the part `{ field }` of the named
  entry: a field of its intent, or of the message that it delivered. Its
  `b` is any operand of the act. The validator refuses any other clause,
  and it refuses a `where` on a `fact` guard over a presented fact or an
  element. No `where` reads an effect. An ordinary `equals` guard reads
  what an entry's effects set, by the parts `opened` and `set`.
- No form is added for "the author, or anyone with a wider grant". It
  is two act kinds, each with its own grant (gap G9). `anyOf` joins
  guards. It never joins grants: an act has one `grant`.

*Three results.* A guard is true, false, or not completed (see
"Complete evaluation", below). A list of guards is false when one is
false on a completed evaluation; otherwise it is not completed when
one is not; otherwise it is true. `anyOf` and `has` are true when one
alternative or element is true; otherwise not completed when one is
not; otherwise false. `each` follows the rule for a list. `sameSet`
needs complete evidence for the range it reads: it is an exact set.
`distinct` reads no range and is always completed. The enumeration of
the list that an `each` or a `has` reads is always complete, because
that list is a field, a slot or a part of a fetched entry. That does
not complete the form. Its result follows the rules above, so it is
not completed when a nested guard that it needs is not. Case 3 of
witness 18.2 is such an `each`. Revision 8 said that the list forms
over fields are always completed, which was true of the enumeration
only.

*`rule`, exactly.* The guard names a key of the definition's `rules`.

| | Rule |
|---|---|
| Declaration | `rules` maps a name to the text of one expression in the language of the pinned profile. |
| Validation | The validator refuses a definition, as `rule-undeclared`, when a `rule` guard names no key; and as `rule-invalid`, when a text does not parse under the pinned profile, reads a name outside the inputs below, or exceeds the profile's static limits. |
| Inputs | Exactly those of the table above: the subjects' records, the act's kind and fields, the signer's member, and the content of each fetched fact. No clock and no other item. |
| Evaluation | In preparation (section 5.2, step 5). The entry records `{ rule, input, result }`, where `input` is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of those inputs. The commit reuses the result only when the digest it computes is equal. When it is not, as when the signer's standing changed between the two readings, the prepared result does not fit: the input is not judged, and an act is answered `unavailable` (I1 delta 90). |
| Replay | The verifier evaluates the text, read from the pinned definition's bytes, over the retained inputs, and compares both the digest and the result. A missing input is `incomplete`. |
| A rule that does not evaluate | A rule holds only when its expression gives `true`. Any other value, and any deterministic refusal by the profile, is false. A fault of the evaluator prepares nothing, and the input is not judged. |
| A profile with no evaluator | A runtime or verifier whose profile cannot evaluate answers `unsupported-definition` for a definition whose `rules` is not empty. I1 reports that it reviewed and kept the earlier restricted evaluator as `restricted@1` (delta 77). This note has not read that review, and point R1-8 stays open until I1's independent review. Neither lane definition declares a rule. |

**What the range guards cover.** `some`, `none` and `count` read only
this scope's items, which the head check covers. Each covers every item
of the named type whose present state is in its `states` list, live or
retained final, exactly as that list says. `every` reads the items that
one list names, at most 32. From revision 19: at most the list's `max`,
which is at most 64 (section 6.1).

- If no listed state is final, the guard covers live items only. The
  type's `max` bounds their number.
- If a listed state is final, the guard also covers retained final
  items. `max` does not bound them (section 6.3).

**Complete evaluation.** A range guard's evaluation is **completed**
when its result can no longer change, whatever the rest of the
enumeration would find. A guard is judged on a completed evaluation or
it is not judged.

- The index is ordered. Within each type and state the items are kept
  in order of item ID, and live timed items are also kept in the order
  of section 5.2. So a page of a read, a range guard's scan and the
  search for the next due transition cost the items they return, and
  not the items the scope retains. A scope that opens and ends holds
  for ever does the same work for each act. This is a rule about the
  index. It is not a bound on retained items, and nothing is evicted.
  I1 finds the next due transition by reading one page of live items
  for each timed rule. A type's `max` bounds that page, so its cost
  does not grow with what the scope retains. That meets the purpose of
  this rule and is accepted for I1. The order of section 5.2 kept in
  the index stays the rule, and R4 measures the difference.
- The scope keeps an index of its items by type and state, with an
  exact count for each pair. The index is written in the same
  transaction as each entry, so it is local state under the head check.
- A guard with no `where` is answered from those counts.
- A guard with a `where` is answered from an index on the slots that
  the `where` names, which the validator derives from the definition;
  or by reading every page of the indexed set inside the commit.
- **Complete evidence** is an exact count from the index, or every
  page of the indexed set read in the commit. It completes every guard.
- A **witness** is a matching item read in the commit, in the state
  that the head check covers. Enough witnesses complete an evaluation
  when no further item could change the result, even though the scan
  has not finished. The table says which results those are.
- A scan that stops early, at a work limit or between pages, with
  neither complete evidence nor enough witnesses, completes nothing.

| Guard | Completed by witnesses, with the scan unfinished | Needs complete evidence |
|---|---|---|
| `some` | It holds, by one matching item. | That it fails. That is an absence. |
| `none` | It fails, by one matching item. | That it holds. That is an absence. |
| `count` with a `min` | The `min` is met, by `min` matching items. | That the `min` is not met. |
| `count` with a `max` | The `max` is broken, by `max` + 1 matching items. | That the count is within `max`. That is an upper bound. |
| An exact count, in a guard or a read | Never. | Always. |

- A `count` with both bounds holds only when its `min` is met and its
  count is within `max`. So it holds only on complete evidence.
- A result completed by witnesses is a completed Boolean evaluation.
  The input is judged on it: passed, or refused with the guard's
  reason. It is the result that the whole enumeration would give. A
  verifier derives the guard over every item in the folded state
  (section 9.3) and gets the same result.
- The strict rule is unchanged. An absence, an upper bound that holds
  and an exact count are never established by a partial scan.
- An input with a guard whose evaluation is not completed is not
  judged. An act is answered `guard-incomplete`, which is in the
  Unavailable class of section 4.2. A delivery is not decided and is
  retried.

**What completes a guard with a `where`. New in revision 11** (I1
delta 88; the I1 delivery note, section 7). I1 writes an index on the
slots that a `where` names, and no guard reads it yet: a guard with a
`where` reads pages. Three kinds of evidence may complete such a
guard, and no other.

1. *Every page.* Each page of the items of that type in the listed
   states is read in the commit, and each item is tested against the
   whole `where`. This is complete evidence for every result. It is
   what I1 does. Its cost grows with the items in those states. The
   work limit R4-B2 may stop it, and it then completes nothing.
2. *An index on the slots.* It is complete evidence only when all of
   these hold.
   - It is written in the same transaction as every entry that opens
     an item of the type, changes its state or changes one of the
     indexed slots. So it is local state under the head check.
   - It is complete for the type. Every item of the type has its rows
     from the entry that opened it. An index that is added to a scope
     which already holds items is evidence for nothing until every
     item's rows are written.
   - Two values have one key exactly when section 6.2 calls them
     equal, after a local fact is put in normal form.
   - It answers only an `equals` between a slot of each item and an
     operand that has one value for the whole evaluation: a field, a
     constant, the signer, or a slot of another subject. A `differs`,
     and an `equals` between two slots of one item, are tested on
     each item that the index returns, and every page of that
     narrower set is read.
3. *A witness.* An item that was read in the commit and passes the
   whole `where`, tested on the item itself. The table above says
   which results a witness completes.

An exact count comes from the first kind, or from the second when
every clause of the `where` is one that the index answers. An index
is derived storage. It is in no dimension of section 17.1, and a
verifier never reads it: a verifier derives the guard over the folded
state (section 9.3). An index that is written and never read is
unused storage. No judgment rests on it, so it makes no judgment
wrong.

Until R4 gives the bound on retained final items and on the work of one
guard, this contract does not claim that a guard over final states
always completes. It claims only that no guard passes, and none
refuses, on evidence that the rest of the enumeration could overturn.

**Made exact in revision 13, from the I2 source choices.** Each point
names the entries of the I2 deltas note that it answers (section 15.6l).
Each is a rule of this contract from this revision, for the reason that
the point gives. None changes an entry that the I2 source at `744f2447`
writes, unless the point says so.

- **D18.** A `reason` is a text that is not empty. Only a failed guard
  gives a refusal its name. A refusal by an effect, by a send or by a
  bound has no name. A capability guard that does not hold gives the
  name that the capability declares, and a `reason` that the definition
  wrote on that guard names nothing (section 6.11).
- **D19.** The validator refuses an operand that its place does not
  have. `signer` and `intent` are operands of an act. `sender` is an
  operand of a handler and of a result clause. `source` is an operand of
  a handler. `update` is an operand of a `relate` handler. `result` is
  an operand of a result clause. `of` is written on a slot only. `part`
  is written on a field, a presented fact, a slot and an element. A
  guard that reads the item that its act opens, or a slot of it, is
  refused `nascent-guard`. The reason: an operand that its place does
  not have would always read none, and that is a mistake the validator
  can show.
- **D20.** What each part reads, exactly. `on`: the entry's own `seq`
  when the entry opens an item; otherwise the `on` of an act's intent,
  or the item of a timed entry; otherwise none. `intent`: the digest of
  the intent of an act, and of the founding intent of a founded genesis;
  a created genesis has none. `{ field }`: a field of an act's intent;
  for a genesis, a field of the founding intent or of the creation
  request, with `self` read as the creator's entry; for a delivered
  `tell`, a field of the message; for a delivered update, a member of
  its detail. `{ opened }` and `{ set }` read the entry's recorded
  effects and nothing else, so a slot that holds only its type's default
  is none. A party list is read as the members that the entry's `add`
  and `remove` records left, in order. `{ of, then }` reads a whole fact
  reference only: a bare position that a foreign entry recorded for its
  own scope is not one, and gives none. A part that needs an entry's
  bytes reads them only for an entry that the input named, by a fact
  field, a presented fact or the source entry, and for this scope's own
  entries. For a fact that a slot holds, such a part is none. Where the
  definition states the type of a part's value, the validator requires
  that it is a fact. The reason for the limit on bytes: no part causes a
  fetch, so what a part reads is fixed by the input and by the scope's
  own history.
- **D26.** The `update` operand reads three things. `state` is the
  update's state. `item` is the fact reference of the entry that opened
  the owner's item, as the message carries it. `revision` is the `seq`
  of the owner's entry that sent the update, as section 7.3 defines a
  revision.
- **DG2, DI5.** The guards of an act, of a handler, of a nested list, of
  an alternative and of a condition are each one list with three
  results. A guard that is neither true nor false is **not completed**:
  an unfinished scan, a clock that is behind, a rule with no prepared
  result, a fact that is not at hand. A list is false when one of its
  guards is false, also when another is not completed, and the refusal
  names the false guard. A list with no false guard and one that is not
  completed is not judged, with the reason of the first such guard. An
  act is then answered `unavailable`. A delivery is not decided. A
  result whose clause has a condition that is not completed is not
  recorded now, and is offered again. The reason is witness 18.2, case
  4: an unfinished read cannot change a result that another guard has
  made false, and a refusal writes nothing that rests on the guard that
  was not judged.
- **DG3.** A list operand that reads none is the empty list: an absent
  field, an empty slot, an unbound subject. So `each` holds and `has`
  fails. A value that is not a list fails every list form. Only a value
  to which the definition gives no type can be one: a part of a fetched
  entry. The reason: a form with nothing to enumerate must not hold over
  a value that it cannot read.
- **DG4.** A `count` guard fails when a bound that is written as an
  operand reads anything but an integer of at least 0. The validator
  refuses an operand whose stated type is not `int`. The reason: an
  absent bound would turn `min` into no bound at all.
- **DG5.** `except`, exactly. With no `where`, the guard is answered
  from the exact counts, less each `except` subject that is of the
  range's type and in a listed state, once each. With a `where`, the
  scan passes over those items. The validator refuses an `except`
  subject of another type, and the item that the act opens. A range
  names at most 5 subjects: `on`, and the 4 `also` names.
- **DG6.** `sameSet` is judged in this order. A value that is no list
  fails. The range is read from every page, and an unfinished scan
  leaves the guard not completed, also when the keys alone would fail
  it. Then: no key is none; no two keys are equal; there are as many
  keys as items; and each key equals the local ID of an item, by the
  equality of section 6.2. Each `match` clause is judged with the
  element bound, and a slot with no `of` is a slot of that element's
  item. `ordered`: the item IDs rise strictly in the order of the list.
  The range is read once for the form, so the validator refuses, in the
  range's `where`, the element that the form binds. The reason for
  reading the range first: `sameSet` is an exact set, and it needs
  complete evidence whatever the keys are.
- **DG7, DF3, DI1.** `as` is a text that is not empty and holds no dot.
  An inner form may bind a name again, and the nearest binding is read.
  `{ element: "k.name" }` reads the member `name` of the record that `k`
  binds, and `k.a.b` goes on through a member that is a record. Where
  the definition states the element's type, it is a record with that
  member, or the validator refuses the operand. Where only the commit
  knows the type, as for a list that a part reads from a fetched entry,
  any member may be named, and a member that is not there is none. The
  reason: a part is never an error, and what it reads has no declared
  type.
- **DF3, DF14, DI11.** A member of a record field or of a record slot is
  named with a dot, as section 6.2 says, and a `field` or a `slot`
  operand may name one. `ifPresent` then asks of the value that the
  operand reads: the guard is passed over when that value is none, which
  is when the field is absent or its record holds no such member. The I2
  source does not read a member of a field or of a slot. Its validator
  answers that the name is no field or slot, so it refuses a definition
  that this contract allows. That fails closed. No pinned row names such
  a member. The form is owed with the forms of section 11.8, by the
  builder, when a row needs it, and it is no row of section 11.11.
- **DG8.** A `fact` guard over an element needs an element whose type
  the definition states, and that type is `fact`. The validator refuses
  any other. The guard compares the entry's kind and the name of its
  definition with that type. A `fact` guard over a presented fact reads
  its type from the act's `presents`, and `ifPresent` passes over a
  guard whose presented fact is absent. The reason: without a stated
  type there is no kind to compare, and a `fact` guard that held for an
  entry of any kind would prove nothing.
- **DG10.** The validator refuses an `anyOf` with no alternative: it
  could never hold. `ifPresent` is written on a guard that itself names
  a field or a presented fact in an operand: `equals`, `differs`,
  `every` and `fact`. On a list form it is refused, and each nested
  guard may carry its own.
- **DI16.** A position has a type and no stated most: the `seq` of an
  entry, and the revision of an update. The validator asks only that the
  slot which takes one is an integer. The commit checks the value
  against the slot, and refuses `bad-field`. A timed rule copies no
  position, because its effects are total. The reason: this contract
  states no most for a position, and where the validator cannot know a
  value the commit checks it (section 6.6).
- **DJ16.** The part `{ carried }` is written `kind.member`. The kind is
  a record kind of exactly one listed capability. The member is any
  name, and its type is the commit's to know. The part reads the entry's
  own `record` effects: the member of the one record of that kind. It is
  none when the entry holds no such record, or more than one, or the
  record has no such member. It reads a sealed entry's bytes and no rule
  of a capability. A definition that writes it still uses a capability
  form (section 6.1), because only a capability's code writes a `record`
  effect. The names of a record's members are the authority note's.

**Made exact in revision 14, from the later I2 source choices.** Each
point names the entries of the I2 deltas note that it answers (section
15.6m). Each is a rule of this contract from this revision, for the
reason that the point gives. None changes an entry that the I2 source at
`58465dbf` writes, unless the point says so.

- **DR9.** What the part `{ field }` reads, by the entry and by who
  reads it. The rule: a field of an entry is read as the scope that
  wrote the entry holds it, and never through a declaration of another
  scope (section 6.2, "What a reader knows of another scope's entry").
  This replaces the words of point D20 for a genesis and for a delivery,
  and the words "with `self` read as the creator's entry" now hold for
  the scope's own genesis only.

| The entry | Read by the scope that wrote it | Read by another scope, or by a verifier of that scope's use |
|---|---|---|
| An act | The field of the signed intent, as the intent holds it. A default that the definition gives an absent field is not read: the part is none. | The same. |
| A founded genesis | The field of the founding intent, in the same way. | The same. |
| A created genesis | The field of the creation request, read by the types of the genesis act of the scope's own definition. The mark, in a field of type `fact` or in a list of facts, is the creator's entry: the `source` of the genesis input. | The member of that name in the `fields` of the creation request, as the bytes hold it. The mark is the record `{ "self": true }`. |
| A delivery of a `tell` that a handler received, whatever was decided | The field of the message, read by the types of that handler. The mark, in a field of type `fact` or in a list of facts, is the delivery's `from`. A field that the handler does not declare is read as the bytes hold it. | The member of that name in the `fields` of the message, as the bytes hold it. The mark is the record. |
| A delivery of a relationship update that a handler received, whatever was decided | The member of the update's `detail`, read in the same way. | The member of that name in `detail`, as the bytes hold it. |
| A delivery of a request that no handler received: decided `refused`, `unknown-message`, or one whose body states no name | As the bytes hold it: no declaration of the scope admitted its fields, as none gave it a kind. | As the bytes hold it. |
| A delivery of a result, a control or an advisory; a timed entry; a diagnosis; an outcome; a preparation; a settlement; a checkpoint | None. | None. |

The other parts read the same value for every reader. `ref`, `scope` and
`seq` read the reference. `kind`, `intent`, `on`, `{ opened }`, `{ set
}` and `{ carried }` read the entry's bytes with no declaration: its
input and its recorded effects, as point D20 says. A part reads no fixed
member of a message's body: `message`, `name`, `item`, `state`,
`directory` and `membership` are not fields.

Three things follow from the table.

1. *A record stays a record.* A scope may declare a record type with a
   boolean member `self`. Its value `{ "self": true }` is read as that
   record by the scope that declared it, and by every other reader.
2. *No reader resolves the mark in another scope's entry.* In the bytes,
   the mark and such a record are one value. Only the receiver's
   declared type tells them apart, and another reader does not hold it.
   So the value is a record there, and it equals no fact reference. `{
   of, then }` over it gives none.
3. *One comparison cannot be made.* A guard cannot compare a field that
   was sent as the mark, in a delivery or in a created genesis that
   another scope recorded, with the sender's entry. It is false, where
   the I2 base let it pass when the reader happened to declare a handler
   of the same name. A reference to an earlier entry is whole in the
   bytes, and is compared as before.

The sender's entry of such a delivery is in the entry's bytes all the
same, as the `from` of its input, and for a created genesis as `source`.
No part reads it today, and none is added: a script of the I2 worker
found that every `{ field }` part of the two pinned definitions reads an
act, and no row needs it. If a row does, the form is a part that reads
that member, and not a change of what a message holds (section 6.6, "Why
the mark stays").

The I2 source at `58465dbf` reads a field in this way, in `fieldOf` of
its `operand.ts`, with one difference: an own request whose body states
no name reads none there. That fails closed: section 11.12, row 22.

- **DR15.** A number that a part reads in another scope's entry is that
  scope's own: a position, a local ID of one of its items, or a count.
  It is an integer, and it is no item of the reader. This covers `seq`,
  `on`, a field that the other scope types as `item`, and what `{ opened
  }`, `{ set }` and `{ carried }` read, in a fetched entry and in the
  source entry.
  - *Into a slot.* An effect whose source is such a number does not fill
    a slot of type `item`, or an `item` inside a list or a record of a
    slot, at any depth. The commit refuses the input `bad-field`, as it
    refuses any value that is outside its slot's type (section 6.6). The
    number may fill a slot of type `int`. The reader's own item is named
    by a declared field of type `item`, by a slot of type `item`, by the
    operand `item`, or by a part of an entry of the reader's own
    history.
  - *Why refused, and not carried as a reference.* An item is named
    outside its scope by the fact of the entry that opened it (section
    4.1). A number gives no hash, and a part causes no fetch, so no
    whole reference can be made from it. A slot that needs another
    scope's item takes that fact, in a slot of type `fact`.
  - *In a comparison.* Such a number never equals a value whose type is
    `item` in the reader: the operand `item`, a field or an element that
    the definition declares as `item`, and a slot of type `item`. An
    `equals` of the two is false, and a `differs` is true. A key of
    `sameSet` that is such a number equals no local ID. Two numbers that
    parts read are compared as numbers, so a guard that compares two
    numbers of one other scope is sound, as the `unpin` handler of the
    companion file does. The reason: the IDs of two scopes would
    otherwise be equal by coincidence, and a party that chooses which
    entry to present could choose the coincidence. The pinned `closes`
    handler of `issue` compares a plan's `scope` with `{ scope: true }`
    before it compares the plan's `on` with the goal's `currentPlan`.
    Under this rule the second comparison is false by itself for a plan
    of another lane, and the handler decides as before.
  - *No pinned row changes.* A script over the two pinned files at
    `58465dbf` found no effect that copies a part of an entry into a
    slot which holds an item. It found one comparison of a value of type
    `item` with a part, in three effects of that `closes` handler, and
    each stands beside the comparison of the scopes.
  - *The message field of point DH5 is another thing.* A bare number in
    a field that the receiver's handler declares as `item` is the
    sender's word for an item of the receiver, and the handler's guards
    say who may name it.
  - *The second reading of entry DR15.* `{ of, then }` gives none for a
    bare position, also in the reader's own entry. That is point D20,
    and it fails closed.
  - *The source.* The I2 source takes the number as a local ID of the
    reader: section 11.12, row 21.

### 6.6 Effect, send and attention forms

| Effect form | Does |
|---|---|
| `state: name` | Sets the subject's state. |
| `party: { slot, from }` | Sets a party slot from the signer, a field, a field of a fetched fact, another slot, or none. For a list slot: `add` or `remove`. |
| `ref: { slot, from }` | Sets a reference slot from `self`, a field, another slot, or none. |
| `value: { slot, from }` | Sets a value slot from a field, a constant, or the commit time plus a constant duration. |
| `attribute: { slot, of }` | Fills a party list with the attribution of the named subject (section 6.7). |
| `hold: { open \| renew \| end, extent }` | Uses the hold capability. Platform code. |

| Send form | Class | Sends |
|---|---|---|
| `create: { kind, definition, fields, result }` | Request | A creation message with a seed for a child scope. |
| `tell: { to, message, fields, result }` | Request | A declared message to the scope a reference slot names. |
| `relate: { to, name, item, state, detail, result }` | Request | A relationship update owned by this scope, for one key: the target, the owner's item and the name. An entry sends at most one for each key (section 6.4). |
| `index: { fields }` | Advisory | A projection row to the directory. |

Besides these, the platform itself sends two kinds of message that no
definition declares: a **result**, the terminal answer to a request
(section 7.4); and a **control**, the creator's confirmation of a
child's incarnation (section 7.2).

| Attention form | Tells |
|---|---|
| `notify: { slot, of, when: "before" \| "after", reason }` | The members in that party slot as it was before the effects, or as it is after. So a party who is being replaced is told, and so is the one replacing them. |

**Forms added in revision 8.**

```ts
type Source = Operand | null;                       // null empties the slot
type Condition = { if?: readonly Guard[]; unless?: readonly Guard[] };
type EffectForm = { of?: Subject } & Condition & (
  | { state: string }
  | { party: { slot: string; from: Source | readonly Operand[]; list?: "add" | "remove" } }
  | { ref: { slot: string; from: "self" | Source } }
  | { value: { slot: string; from: Source | { time: { plusSeconds: number } } } }
  | { attribute: { slot: string; of: Subject; with?: readonly AuthorSource[] } }      // section 6.7
  | { hold: { do: "open" | "renew" | "end"; extent?: Operand } }                      // section 6.8
  | { redact: { slot: string } }
  | { capability: { name: "hold" | "git-read"; do: string; with: Record<string, Operand> } }   // section 6.11
);
type SendSource = "self" | Operand | { collect: { items: Range; fields: Record<string, string> } };
type SendForm =
  | { create: { kind: ScopeKind; definition: Digest | PlatformDefinition | "self";
                fields: Record<string, SendSource>; result: ResultClauses } }
  | { tell: { to: { slot: string; of?: Subject }; message: string; if?: readonly Guard[];
              fields: Record<string, SendSource>; result: ResultClauses } }
  | { relate: { each?: Range; to: SendSource; name: string; item: SendSource; state: string;
                if?: readonly Guard[]; detail: Record<string, SendSource>; result: ResultClauses } }
  | { index: { if?: readonly Guard[]; fields: Record<string, SendSource> } };   // `if`: new in revision 12
type ResultClauses = Partial<Record<"applied" | "refused" | "superseded" | "undelivered" | "conflict",
                                    readonly EffectForm[]>>;   // `conflict` on a creation only
interface Notify { notify: { slot: string; of: Subject; when: "before" | "after"; reason: string;
                             if?: readonly Guard[] } }
```

- **A source is an operand.** A party, a reference and a value are each
  set from an operand of section 6.5: a field, a slot of any subject, a
  part of a fetched fact, the signer or a constant. `null` empties the
  slot. A value may also be the commit time plus a constant number of
  seconds. The validator refuses a number of seconds longer than the
  span that a timestamp can name, the years 0000 to 9999, and the fold
  refuses `bad-field` a derived time past the end of the year 9999. So
  no time arithmetic fails inside a commit (the I1 deltas note,
  section 13). A list slot may be set whole, from a list operand or
  from a list of member operands. Revision 7 let a value come from a field or
  a constant only, so an act could not copy a goal's conditions into a
  commitment.
- **A slot never holds a value outside its type.** An effect that
  copies a value into a slot needs a source that is assignable to the
  destination: the same type, with bounds inside the destination's. A
  text's `max`, an integer's range, a list's `max` and its elements,
  an enum's values and a reference's kind are all bounds. The
  validator refuses a copy that it can show is not assignable. Where
  it cannot know, as for a part of a fetched fact, the fold checks the
  actual value against the destination in the commit and refuses
  `bad-field`. Comparing two values needs only comparable types and
  has no such rule. The operand `{ source: "ref" }` is a fact under
  the definition that the handler's `from.under` names, of a kind that
  the validator cannot know. So the validator refuses a copy of it
  into a slot whose `under` is another name, and the fold checks its
  kind in the commit. When `from` has no `under`, the fold checks
  both. Revision 8's `closes` handler copied a source entry of
  `change` into a slot for entries of `issue`. This rule refuses that
  definition, and the companion file now writes the slot from `self`
  (witness 18.17).
- **A copy preserves its source.** A slot operand reads the slot of
  that name on its subject, whatever kind of slot it is: a name is
  used once in an item type (section 6.3). So a reference may be
  copied from a value slot that holds one, and the reverse. A source
  that is present is copied as it is. It is never read as none because
  the reader looked in another kind of slot.
- **No effect changes an item that was final before the entry.** This
  is section 6.3's rule for every kind of effect: a state, a party, a
  reference, a value, an `attribute`, a `redact`. The fold judges it
  on the state before the entry. An effect of an act or a handler on
  such an item refuses the input `final`; an effect of a result clause
  on such an item is not applied. A final item may still be read, and
  named in `also` for that. An entry that takes a live item to a final
  state may carry its other effects on that item in the same entry.
  The rule covers every effect that is applied, also one that would
  record no change, such as an `add` of a member who is already in the
  list (I1's repair 6). An effect is applied when its subject is
  bound, its source is present and its `if` or `unless` lets it
  through. An effect that is not applied is not judged by this rule.
- **An absent source.** An effect whose source is an absent optional
  field, or reads an unbound subject, is not applied. To empty a slot,
  a definition writes `null`. Stated in revision 13 (I2 delta DG26):
  the `of` inside an `attribute` effect is not a source in this sense.
  When that subject is unbound the effect is still applied, with the
  base of section 6.7.
- **`if` and `unless`. This answers gap G3.** An effect, a send or an
  attention form with `if` is applied only when every guard of the
  list holds in the commit. With `unless` it is applied only when not
  every guard holds. The guards are judged on the state before the
  entry's effects, with the same rules as the act's own guards. A
  guard in `if` or `unless` that is not completed leaves the input not
  judged. A clause's condition is judged in the commit that records
  the result. Section 6.4 says how a condition reads an unbound
  subject (revision 13).
- **No conflicting effects, restated.** Any two effects of one list
  that name one slot, or the state, of one subject are refused by the
  validator as `effect-conflict`. Each result clause is its own list.
  Two rules allow a pair. They are different in kind, and revision 8
  was wrong to say of both that at most one effect applies.
  - *Conditions that exclude each other.* An `if` and an `unless` with
    the same guards. Or two effects whose `if` lists hold an `equals`
    of the same operand with two different constants, or a `state`
    guard on the same subject with two lists that share no state. At
    most one of the two can apply, so they never meet.
  - *Successive changes of one party list.* Two effects that each
    `add` to, or `remove` from, one party list. Both may apply. They
    apply in the order written, the second to the list that the first
    left, so the result depends on nothing but that order. `assign`
    in the companion file adds one member and removes another in one
    entry. An effect that sets a list whole, beside one that changes
    it, is still a conflict.
- **A state effect needs a live subject.** A `state` effect on an
  existing subject needs a `state` guard on that subject, among the
  act's guards or in the effect's own `if`, that lists no final state.
  A result clause and a timed rule cannot be checked that way before
  they run, so the fold checks them: a `state` effect on an item in a
  final state is refused `final`, and a clause's effect on such an
  item is not applied.
- **`redact`. This answers gap G2.** The subject's slot is a detached
  text. The effect removes, from the scope's retained inputs, the
  bytes of every text that the slot has held: its present digest and
  each earlier one that the item's history shows. It records those
  digests. The entry that holds the effect is the **tombstone**: who
  removed the text, when, and under which grant. The slot keeps its
  digest. A scope never removes text that an unsettled operation's
  evidence names.
- **A redaction, made exact. New in revision 13** (I2 deltas DJ8 and
  DJ9).
  - A `redact` effect is an effect of an act. The validator refuses it
    in a handler, a timed rule and a result clause: only an act's entry
    has a signer and a grant, and the tombstone states both. The slot is
    a value slot that holds a detached text. It may be a fixed slot,
    because the effect sets nothing.
  - The folded state holds, for each slot that holds a detached text,
    the digests that the slot has held and that no entry has redacted,
    in the order in which the slot first held them. A `value` effect on
    such a slot adds its digest. A `redact` effect lists exactly those,
    with a digest that an earlier effect of the same entry put in the
    slot, and the fold then empties the list. An effect with nothing to
    list is not recorded. A checkpoint's state digest covers the lists
    (section 9.2).
  - A redaction is by digest, and for the whole scope. A text is one
    retained input under its digest (section 6.2). So the effect removes
    the bytes for every slot and every entry of the scope that names
    that digest, and not only for the slot that it names. Another slot
    that holds the same digest keeps the digest, and keeps its own list.
    A later `redact` of that slot lists the digest again and removes
    nothing.
  - Nothing counts the holders of a text. A count would be a second
    state to keep beside the retained inputs. And a redaction that left
    the bytes in place, because another slot named them, would not be a
    removal.
  - A later input that carries the same text is kept again, and the
    scope then holds the text again (section 6.2). The earlier tombstone
    answers nothing for it.
  - The bytes are removed in the commit that seals the tombstone.
- **A text that a request carries. New in revision 13** (I2 delta DJ3).
  A delivery that names a detached text waits until its receiver has the
  bytes (section 6.2). Two rules make that wait end. Both are rules on
  the sender, and both read only the sender's own history.
  - *No redaction while a request carries the text.* A request
    **carries** a text when the body of its message has, at any depth, a
    string value that equals the text's digest. An act whose `redact`
    effect would list a text that a pending request of this scope
    carries is refused `text-in-use`. A request is pending until its
    result, or an `undelivered` diagnosis, is an entry (section 17.1).
    The same act is admitted once that request has settled. A value of
    another type that happens to equal the digest makes the redaction
    wait too. That errs toward keeping bytes.
  - *No send of a text that is not held.* A send carries a detached text
    in each field, and each member of a `collect`, whose source the
    definition types as a detached text. A send that would carry one
    which the scope does not hold at that commit is refused
    `send-unresolved`. A slot keeps its digest after a redaction, so
    without this rule a later send could carry a digest that names no
    bytes anywhere. The text of the input that is being judged is held:
    its entry keeps it.
  - *Why the wait ends.* By the two rules, every request that carries a
    text was sent while its sender held the text, and the sender still
    holds it while the request is pending. So the receiver's read fails
    only while the sender cannot be read. That is the case of any
    delivery whose source entry cannot be read, and section 7.4 ends it:
    by the request's result, or by a diagnosis. A request that stands at
    `delivery-unavailable` stays pending, and its texts stay held, until
    its result is recorded. The rule of revision 8 stands beside these
    two: a scope removes no text that an unsettled operation's evidence
    names.
  - *What it costs.* A refused act writes nothing and reserves nothing.
    The first check reads the pending requests of the scope, which the
    fifth dimension bounds (section 17.1), and the origin entry of each,
    from the scope's own history. An index over them is derived storage
    (section 6.5). R4 measures the cost.
  - *Replay.* Both rules are judged in the commit, from the folded state
    and the scope's own history. So a verifier derives them again. A
    tombstone that lists a text which a pending request carried at that
    position is a `mismatch`. So is an entry with a send of a text that
    was not held.
  - *The way not taken.* The receiver could decide such a request
    `refused` when the sender answers that it holds no such text. That
    decision would rest on the sender's present state, and nothing that
    the receiver retains would show it (section 5.1). The sender's
    tombstone entry could be fetched and retained as that evidence. That
    would be a new read and a new reason, and no row needs it while the
    two rules hold.
  - The I2 source at `744f2447` has neither rule: section 11.11, row 15.
    Neither pinned definition sends a text from a slot. The one send
    that carries a text is the `create` of `add-concern`, and it carries
    a field of its own act.
- **`capability`.** A declared capability's own effect, on its own
  records (section 6.11). `hold` is the hold capability's effect on
  the hold item and is kept as revision 7 wrote it.
- **`definition: "self"`.** A `create` may name the creating scope's
  own pinned definition. A definition cannot hold its own digest
  (section 2.1), so a goal that creates a concern of the same form
  needs the word.
- **A `tell` is addressed by a reference slot. This answers R2's point
  R2-15.** The slot may be a slot of any subject, and of the item the
  entry opens, read after the entry's effects. A field is not an
  address: it is a value of one entry, and a slot is state that the
  next send can read again. So `manifest` gets a fixed slot for the
  lane that staged its commit, as R2 proposes.
- **A conditional send. This answers gap G16.** A send with `if` is
  made only when its guards hold. A send that is not made is not in
  the entry and takes no ordinal. A send with no `if` whose target is
  none is refused `send-unresolved`.
  **An `index` send may carry `if`. New in revision 12.** This answers
  the lane design's gap G20. Revision 8 gave `if` to `tell` and to
  `relate`, and not to `index`. An `index` send with `if` is made only
  when its guards hold, by the same rule, and one that is not made
  takes no ordinal. A `create` still has no `if`, and nobody has asked
  for one.
- **A fan-out. This answers gap G15.** A `relate` with `each` makes one
  send for each item that the range covers, in ascending order of item
  ID. In that form `of: "each"` and `item: "each"` name the item of
  that send. Each send has its own key, so the rule of section 6.4
  holds for each: two that resolve to one key refuse the input
  `duplicate-relation`. The validator refuses, as `fan-out-unbounded`,
  a fan-out whose range lists a final state or whose type's `max` is
  over 32, and a form list with more than one fan-out. So a fan-out
  makes at most 32 sends, from complete evidence: the range reads live
  items only, and the index gives them exactly.
- **`collect`.** A send field may hold a list of records, one for each
  item that a range covers, in ascending order of item ID. Each record
  has the named members: `"item"` is the item's fact reference,
  `"state"` its state, and any other name a slot. A slot that holds a
  local item or a local entry reference is sent as a fact reference,
  as section 6.4 says. A member whose slot is empty is left out of its
  record, as any absent value is. The validator
  requires a range with no final state. The list has at most the
  type's `max` records, and section 6.2's bound of 32 elements does
  not apply to it. From revision 19 that bound is 64 (section 6.1), and
  it still does not apply. The range needs complete evidence. This is how a
  `merge` entry carries its complete eligibility statement, with the
  entry that decided each job (the companion file's `merge`; witness
  18.16).
- **The order of an entry's sends.** Ordinals run from 0. A child's
  genesis sends its result at ordinal 0, as section 7.2 shows, and
  then its written send forms. Every other entry sends its written
  send forms in order, a fan-out's sends in its own order, and then
  the platform's one result or control. Attention sends come last in
  every entry, in the order of the forms and, inside one form, in byte
  order of the member's identifier.
- **The body of each message.** `create`: `{ fields, directory,
  membership }`; `membership` is new in revision 13 (below).
  `tell`: `{ message, fields }`. `relate`: `{ name, item, state,
  detail }`. `index`: `{ fields }`. An absent value is left out. A
  local item reference is sent as the fact reference of the entry that
  opened the item, and as the mark `{ "self": true }` when that is the
  entry being written. The mark is not a value of any field type. A
  message has at most 32 fields.
- **Where an `index` send goes.** To the scope's directory. A lane
  records its directory at genesis: its creator, when that is a
  directory; otherwise the directory that its creator recorded, which
  the platform puts in every `create` of a lane. The I1 delta 38 sent
  it to the creator, which for a concern is its parent lane; that is
  changed. A scope with no directory has no `index` send.
- **Attention is bounded by the definition.** Each `notify` makes one
  advisory send for each member it tells. The validator adds, over the
  attention forms of one act, handler or timed rule, 1 for a single
  slot and the slot's `max` for a list, and refuses a sum over 64 as
  `attention-unbounded`. So no entry has to drop a notice. A `notify`
  with `if` is made only when its guards hold. A handler of class
  `advisory` declares none (section 6.4).
- **A notice of a timed rule has no `if`. New in revision 13** (I2 delta
  DH20). A timed entry is always written (section 6.4). A condition that
  was not completed would leave it not judged, and nothing says what
  would follow. So the validator refuses an `if` on a notice of a timed
  rule, as it refuses a condition on an effect of such a rule. In an act
  or a handler, the `if` of a notice is judged on the state before the
  entry's effects, and a notice whose `if` reads an unbound subject is
  not made (section 6.4).
- **A result clause's subjects** are those of the entry that made the
  send, as that entry resolved them, and `each` for a fan-out send. A
  clause may read `sender` and `result`.
- **A clause fetches nothing. New in revision 10** (I1 delta 102). The
  entry that runs a clause is a delivery of a result or a diagnosis.
  It reads the origin entry from this scope's own history. It reads a
  foreign entry only from the origin entry's `uses`, which this scope
  retains. A part that needs the bytes of an entry that the origin
  entry did not use is none (section 6.5). So the entry that settles
  a request never waits on a fetch for its clause. And it retains no
  foreign entry that the scope did not hold already, apart from the
  result's own source entry (section 7.4).
- **How a clause finds its form and its subjects. New in revision 13**
  (I2 deltas DH12, DH19 and DI10). A clause runs in a later entry than
  the one that made its send. An entry records its sends. It records
  neither which form made each send, nor which items its names selected.
  This revision does not add those records, so no entry's bytes change.
  The entry that records a result or a diagnosis reads its **origin
  entry**, the entry of this scope that made the send, from the scope's
  own history, and derives both again. These are the rules, and a
  verifier uses the same ones.
  - *The form.* The send forms of the origin's act or handler, and the
    origin's recorded sends that are requests or `index` rows, are in
    one order (above). Each recorded send, in the order of its ordinal,
    is matched to the first form, at or after the last form matched,
    that **makes** it. A `create` form makes a `create` whose seed has
    the form's kind and its definition, with `self` read as the scope's
    own pinned digest. A `tell` form makes a `tell` with its message
    name. A `relate` form makes a `relate` with its name and its state.
    An `index` form makes an `index` row. A fan-out may have made the
    next send as well, so the match stays on it. After any other form
    the match moves on. The clause of a request is the clause of the
    form that its send is matched to.
  - *Where that is not enough.* Two forms of one list **say the same**
    when they make messages of one type and name: two `create` forms of
    one kind and definition, two `tell` forms of one message, or two
    `relate` forms of one name and state. A form is **always made once**
    when it is a `create`; or a `tell` with no `if` whose `to` reads no
    `also` name; or a `relate` with no `if` and no `each`, whose `to`
    and `item` read no `also` name. The validator refuses a list in
    which two forms say the same, unless both are always made once, or
    neither has a result clause with an effect. In every list that
    passes, the match finds the form that made the send, or the clauses
    that it could confuse have no effect.
  - *The subjects.* `on` is the item that the origin opened. For a
    transition it is the item that the origin's intent names. For a
    handler that found the one item of its type, it is that item: the
    one item of the type among those that existed before the origin. A
    `by` name selects by the origin's field, as the origin did. A `one`
    name selects among the items that existed before the origin entry,
    so an item that was opened since is not selected. A `via` name reads
    its slot as the slot is now. Each subject is then read as it is now.
    A name that the origin left unbound stays unbound.
  - *Where that is not enough.* A slot that is not fixed may hold
    another item by the time the clause runs. So the validator lets a
    clause name no `also` name whose selection passes through a slot
    that is not fixed: a `via` whose slot is not fixed, or a `via` that
    reads a slot of such a name. A fixed slot is set by the entry that
    opens its item and never again (section 6.3). So a chain of fixed
    slots selects the same item again.
  - *`each`.* A clause of a fan-out send may read `each` only where the
    update's `item` is written `{ item: "each" }`. The recorded send
    then names that item, and the clause finds it from the send. Where
    the update is for another item, the entry records nothing of the
    item of that send, and the validator refuses a clause that reads
    `each`.
  - *The signer, the fields and the presented facts* are the origin's:
    the member who signed it, with no principal (section 6.7); its
    fields; and the facts that were presented beside its intent.
  - *What recording them would cost.* More members in every entry that
    names an `also` item or sends a request, and a second source for
    what the definition and the history already fix. Where the two
    differed, a verifier would need a rule for which one to believe. The
    cost of not recording is the rows that the validator refuses: a
    clause on an item that is selected through a slot which can change,
    and two request forms that say the same where one is not always made
    and one has a clause. Neither pinned definition has such a row. The
    I2 note reports that, and a script over the two pinned files agrees:
    no row with a `via` name has a clause with an effect, and the two
    rows with more than one send form make messages of different names.

- A **request** has a `result` clause with effects for each terminal
  outcome: `applied`, `refused`, `superseded`, `undelivered`, and
  `conflict` on a creation. An outcome with no effects written changes
  nothing. `undelivered` means shown never received, on a stated
  trust in the sender's attempt log; section 7.4 says what that proof
  is and what it rests on. The receiver's decision returns as a result message and
  takes effect in the sender as an entry (section 7.4).
- A **result** and a **control** never have a result of their own. That
  is what ends the exchange.
- An **advisory** send has no result. Transport acknowledges it. No
  guard in the sender reads whether it arrived, and no capacity amount
  counts whether it did (section 17.1). Its receiver's handler sends
  nothing (section 6.4).
- Attention goes to inbox scopes inside the application. It is
  advisory. A send outside the application is not a form in the first
  version; R2 and R3 own its successor, with the corrections recorded in
  `7318cd52`.

**Made exact in revision 13, from the I2 source choices.** Each point
names the entries of the I2 deltas note that it answers (section 15.6l).
Each is a rule of this contract from this revision, for the reason that
the point gives. None changes an entry that the I2 source at `744f2447`
writes, unless the point says so.

- **DG12.** An effect whose source operand reads none is not applied,
  whatever the reason: an absent field, an unbound subject, an empty
  slot, a part that the entry does not have. It records nothing, and no
  rule judges it. `null` is written to empty a slot, and the validator
  refuses `{ none: true }` as a source. In a list of member operands, an
  operand that reads none gives no member, and the list is still set.
  The reason: an operand has one way to read nothing, so there is one
  rule. This changes I1's source, which recorded a `null` for an absent
  field and copied an empty slot as empty.
- **DG13.** A source reads each subject as the effects that are written
  before it, in the same entry, left it. It reads the item that the
  entry opens as `on`. So `{ item: "on" }` in an `open` act is the new
  item, and a slot that an earlier effect set can be copied. A
  condition, and the range of an attribution source, read the state
  before the entry. The reason: the order written is then the only thing
  that the result depends on, as section 6.7 already says of
  `attribute`.
- **DG14, DI8.** Where the definition states the type of a source, the
  validator shows that the slot can hold it: the same type, with bounds
  inside the slot's. For any other source the commit checks the value: a
  part that is read from an entry's bytes, a constant, `sender`,
  `scope`, `result`, `source` and `update`. A list is within its `max`,
  and each element is checked. An item is a local item of the slot's
  type, named by its ID or by the fact of the entry of this scope that
  opened it. A fact is a fact reference whose entry is at hand: this
  scope's own entry with that hash, the source entry of the delivery, or
  an entry that was fetched for the input. Its kind is one that the slot
  states, and its definition's name is the slot's `under`. A fact to
  this scope is held in normal form. A bare number is no fact. The
  validator refuses a copy of the source entry into a `fact` slot whose
  `under` is not the name that the handler's `from.under` states. When
  `from` states no `under`, the commit checks the kind and the name. The
  reason: a slot never holds a value outside its type, a kind is a bound
  of the type, and a kind cannot be read without the entry's bytes. So a
  fact whose entry is not at hand fails closed. One limit is stated: a
  number that a part reads from a foreign entry may name a local item of
  the slot's type, and is then taken for it, as a bare local ID in a
  message is (section 6.4).
- **DG15.** The rule for an item that was final before the entry is
  judged after the subject, the condition and the source. An effect on
  such an item whose subject is unbound, whose condition fails or whose
  source is absent is not applied, and does not refuse the input.
- **DG16, DI5.** A guard in a condition has the default subject `on`, as
  a guard of an act has. It does not have the subject of its effect.
  With both `if` and `unless`, the form is applied when every `if` guard
  holds and not every `unless` guard does. A condition is a list with
  the three results of section 6.5. The input is not judged when one
  condition is not completed and the other does not already decide that
  the form is not applied. The reason for the default: one default for
  every guard, so a guard reads the same wherever it is written.
- **DG18.** In an `open` act, a condition may not read the item that the
  act opens: `nascent-guard`. The state before the entry has no such
  item. In a result clause it may, because the item exists by then, and
  it may read `result` and `sender`. An effect of a timed rule takes no
  condition: `timed-partial`.
- **DG19.** "Conditions that exclude each other" is read narrowly. Two
  effects on one slot, or on the state, of one subject are allowed in
  two cases. (a) The `if` of one and the `unless` of the other are the
  same list, by canonical JSON. (b) Each has an `if`, and the two lists
  each hold one guard of a pair that cannot both hold: two `equals` with
  one side of the same canonical JSON and the other sides two different
  constants, or two `state` guards whose lists share no state. In (b)
  the two guards have the same subject, are written at the top of their
  lists, and neither carries `ifPresent`. Anything else is a conflict,
  also when a reader can see that the conditions exclude each other. The
  reason: the validator must be sure, `ifPresent` lets both guards pass
  when a field is absent, and a definition can always be written in one
  of these forms.
- **DG21.** The `state` guard that a `state` effect needs counts when it
  is written at the top of the act's guards, or at the top of the
  effect's own `if`. One in an `unless`, and one that is nested in a
  list form, does not count. The reason: an `unless` lets its form
  through when its guards do not hold, and a nested list shows nothing
  about every path.
- **DG27.** In a timed rule the validator refuses, as `timed-partial`: a
  condition; a party list that is set whole from a source; and a source
  whose type the definition does not state, apart from a constant into a
  value slot. A slot of the rule's own item, a constant and `null` stay.
  The static size of a timed entry counts a value that is copied from a
  slot at the most that the slot can hold. The reason: a value that the
  commit must check can be refused there, and a list that is set whole
  writes a number of records that the static size does not count.
- **D23, DF6, DH7.** Which entries may set a `fact` slot from `self`. An
  act of any step may, when the slot's kinds include the act's own kind
  and the slot's `under` is this definition's name. A timed rule may,
  when the slot's kinds include `timed:` and the rule's key. A handler
  of class `tell` or `relate` may, when the slot's kinds include its
  message's name. The handler of an advisory may not, because its entry
  has no kind (section 6.2). A result clause may not. The reason: the
  entry that is being written has exactly the kind that section 6.2
  gives it, and the slot's type must be able to hold an entry of that
  kind. The record is section 4.1's. The I1 and I2 sources record the
  entry's own position where section 4.1 writes `"self"`. That is an
  existing row of section 11.8, and it is not counted again.
- **DH13, DI9.** A scope's directory is a function of its genesis entry:
  the creator that the seed names, when that is a directory; otherwise
  the `directory` member of the creation message's body, when it is a
  reference to a directory; otherwise none. It is no member of the
  folded state, so the state that a checkpoint digests does not hold it.
  An entry that needs it reads the genesis entry from the scope's own
  history, and with no history to read the input is not judged. A
  `create` of a lane carries `directory`: the creating scope itself,
  when it is a directory; otherwise the one that it records; and the
  member is left out when it has none. A scope with no directory makes
  no `index` send, and the form takes no ordinal. The reason: the
  runtime and a verifier then read one entry in the same way, and
  nothing is kept twice.
- **DH15.** A send reads every operand on the subjects as the entry's
  effects left them, with the item that the entry opens as `on`. A slot
  with no `of` is a slot of the primary item. A value whose type the
  definition states as `item` or `fact`, or as a list of them, is sent
  as section 6.4 says: a local reference as a fact reference, and the
  entry being written as the mark. What a part reads inside an entry is
  sent as it is, and the part `ref` is the reference. The `to` of a
  `tell` names a slot of type `scope`. The `to` and the `item` of a
  `relate` are checked by type where the definition states one, and by
  value in the commit, which refuses `send-unresolved`.
  *Corrected after the review `a7f1c108`.* The words "as `item` or
  `fact`, or as a list of them" are an abbreviation, and not a limit.
  The rule is that of sections 6.2 and 6.4, and it is for every local
  reference that a message carries. A local reference that is a member
  of a typed record, or an element of a list inside one, at any depth,
  is sent as a whole fact reference too. This point discharges nothing
  of that rule. The I2 delivery owns the repair of its source for
  nested typed records, and that repair is owed to review at the
  delivery's next head. This revision read no such repair and accepts
  none.
- **DH16.** When a send is made. The subject of a send is what its
  address reads: the `of` of the slot of a `tell`, and each `also` name
  that the `to` or the `item` of a `relate` reads. A send whose address
  reads an unbound name is not made. A send whose `if` reads an unbound
  name is not made (section 6.4). The `if` is judged on the state before
  the entry's effects, and a guard of it that is not completed leaves
  the input not judged. A send that is made and whose target is none is
  refused `send-unresolved`, with an `if` or without one. That replaces
  the words "with no `if`" of revision 8: an `if` that held does not
  excuse a target that is none. A field that reads an unbound name is
  none, and is left out.
- **DH17, DI10.** A fan-out, and a `collect`, read their range as a
  guard reads one: every page up to the work limit, with `where` and
  `except`. A scan that stops completes nothing, and the input is not
  judged. The range covers the items as they were before the entry. In
  its `where`, a slot of the item that the range covers is read as it
  was before the entry, and an operand that names another subject is
  read as the operands of a send are, after the entry's effects. The
  `if` of a fan-out is judged for each item, with `each` bound. Its
  `item` and `to` are operands, which may read `each`. The validator
  requires a range that lists no final state, over a type whose `max` is
  at most the bound on a fan-out, and at most one fan-out in a list.
- **DH18.** A `collect` gives a list of records, one for each item that
  its range covers, in ascending order of item ID. `item` is the item's
  fact reference and `state` its state, also when the type has a slot of
  that name. Any other member is a slot, sent as a send's field is, and
  left out when it is empty. The validator refuses a range that lists a
  final state, and a member that names no slot. A `collect` is a field
  of a send, and never an address.

**Made exact in revision 14, from the later I2 source choices.** Each
point names the entries of the I2 deltas note that it answers (section
15.6m). Each is a rule of this contract from this revision, for the
reason that the point gives. None changes an entry that the I2 source at
`58465dbf` writes, unless the point says so.

- **DR2, DR13.** The passage of point DH15 that was corrected after the
  review `a7f1c108` is the rule, and it is now read in the source. A
  send puts a value on the wire by the type that the definition states
  for it, through records and lists to any depth. A local item reference
  is sent as the fact of the entry that opened the item. A local entry
  reference is sent as that entry's fact reference. A fact that is
  presented beside the intent is a fact for this rule, so one that names
  this scope is sent whole and never as a number. A fact of another
  scope is sent as it is. The `to`, the `item` and every field follow
  the one rule. The reason: the type that puts a value in normal form on
  the way in restores it on the way out, so a receiver that declares the
  same type reads the same value.
- **DR11.** "A slot never holds a value outside its type" holds at any
  depth. Where the definition states no type for a source, the commit
  checks the value against the slot, and it checks a member of a record
  and an element of a list by their declared types: no unknown member,
  every required member, an item that exists and is of its type, and a
  fact whose entry is at hand and is of a kind and a definition that the
  type states. The reason: the same value must pass or fail whether it
  is the slot's value, an element or a member. Point DR15 of section 6.5
  narrows one case: a number from another scope's entry is no item.

**Why the mark stays. New in revision 14.** A message names the entry
that sends it by the mark `{ "self": true }`, and not by a fact
reference. The I2 repairs ask whether the sender could write the whole
reference instead, so that a reader of the receiver's entry could
compare it (point DR9 of section 6.5). It cannot.

- A message is part of the entry that sends it: it is
  `sends[n].message`, inside the entry's bytes.
- A fact reference to that entry holds its `seq` and its `hash`. The
  `seq` is allocated in the commit, and the hash is over the entry's
  bytes (section 4.1).
- So a message that held the reference would hold the digest of bytes
  that include the message. No value contains its own digest (section
  2.1), and an entry never contains a reference to itself (section 3,
  point 5).
- A reference without its hash is no fact reference. A scope and a
  position alone would name whatever entry a history shows there, and
  would prove nothing.

So the wire form does not change, and no point is opened for it: no row
of either pinned definition reads such a field in another scope's entry.
The mark is written in these places only: the value of a whole field or
of an element of a list whose type is `item` or `fact`, the `item` of a
relationship update, and no member of a record. The validator refuses a
send source that holds `self` inside a record.

**The address of an attention send. New in revision 13.** The
authority note asks where an attention send goes (its revision 15, at
`8dfda899`, section 12.1.8, row P23; that revision was proposed when it
was read). The I2
deltas note has the same gap from the other side (its entry DN6). This
contract's part is decided here.

- An attention send is addressed to a member, and not to a scope: `to: {
  member }`, with the member reference that the notice tells. The type
  `Send` of section 4.1 has that third form of `to`, for a `notify` and
  for nothing else.
- The sending scope cannot name the member's inbox. An inbox's scope ID
  is the digest of a seed, and the seed's cause is an input of the
  membership scope that the sender does not hold. Which inbox a member
  has now is membership's present state, and no judgment reads that
  (section 5.1).
- So the entry records what its own judgment fixed: the member. The
  entry stays a function of the definition, the input and the state,
  and a verifier derives the same send.
- The platform finds the inbox when it dispatches the send. That read is
  outside every judgment. It is allowed because the send is advisory: it
  has no result, no guard reads whether it arrived, and no capacity
  amount counts it (sections 7.4 and 17.1).
- The envelope that the inbox receives names the inbox as its `to`. For
  this one class, that is not the send's own `to`. The inbox reads the
  source entry, as every receiver does, and finds the send by its
  ordinal.
- Not this note's: how the platform finds the inbox, what follows when
  the member has none, and what the inbox's handler checks of the
  member in the send. They belong to the authority note's successor
  (request `406983fe`), with the inbox definition. The lane forms own
  what a notice says.
- No source makes an attention send. I1 records one `attention` effect
  for each `notify` (its delta 36), and the I2 source builds nothing
  more (its entry DN6). The send comes with the inbox definition, in
  I3. It is no row of section 11.11.

**`membership` in a `create`. New in revision 13.** Section 16.1 reads a
grant from "the membership scope named in the observing scope's
genesis". No form said where a genesis names it. The authority note
asks (its revision 15, section 12.1.8, row P20).

- The body of a `create` is `{ fields, directory, membership }`.
  `membership` is the reference of the membership scope that the
  creating scope records. The platform puts it in every `create`, as it
  puts `directory` in a `create` of a lane. A membership scope itself,
  and the register, are created without it.
- Confirmed in revision 19 (I3 delta EM17). A membership scope records
  itself as its membership scope, with its incarnation. It is created
  without the member, and for a scope of the kind `membership` the
  function of the genesis entry gives the scope's own reference. So a
  `create` that a membership scope sends holds its own reference, and
  guard 1 of section 16.1 reads an observation of the scope's own
  standing as `of` itself. As built.
- A scope records its membership scope as it records its directory
  (above): it is a function of the genesis entry, and no member of the
  folded state.
- It is a member that the platform sets, and not a field. A field is
  declared by the definition and filled by a form. A declared definition
  must not choose which membership judges its grants, or leave it out.
- Not this note's: which scope the member names for a scope that is
  created in the same entry as its membership scope, where only the
  scope ID can be known; when the incarnation is then fixed; and every
  rule of an observation. They are the authority note's (its row P20
  holds them as code).
- No source reads a membership scope yet: the authority of I1 and I2 is
  a test stand-in. The member is owed with the authority port, in I3.
  It changes the bytes of every creation message and of every genesis
  that follows one. It is no row of section 11.11.

### 6.7 Attribution

Review independence needs to know whose work is in a contribution. That
is more than who reported it.

- The **attribution** of an item is: every member who was ever in one
  of its `author` party slots; every member who was ever the holder of
  a hold whose `under` reference names it, whether or not they wrote
  anything; the signer of the act being judged; and, for each of those
  who acted under another member's authority, that principal as well. Counting every holder may name
  someone who wrote nothing. That errs toward fewer eligible reviewers,
  and it needs no record of who pushed what.
- The `attribute` effect names the item whose attribution it takes. A
  report takes the attribution of the commitment it reports on, not of
  the report item, which is new and has no history. So a former
  performer and a former holder under that commitment are in it. The
  set is derived from this scope's own history, and a verifier derives
  it again.
- A manifest's authors are the union of the attribution lists of every
  fact it selects, plus the attribution of the manifest itself, which
  covers the integrator and any conflict resolution.
- **How the history is kept.** Each item's record holds the members
  ever put in one of its `author` slots. A member made the holder of a
  hold joins the history of the hold, and of the item that the hold's
  `under` names; that item's revision does not rise for it. So the
  base attribution of an item is local state that the fold keeps with
  each entry, and needs no scan.
- **When a principal is counted.** When the member put in a slot is
  the signer of that entry, the grant's principal joins with it. A
  member whom another signer puts in a slot brings no principal then,
  because no grant of theirs was judged. Later, whenever a member who
  is in the item's attribution signs an entry that changes the item,
  or a hold under it, the principal of the grant judged for that
  entry joins the item's attribution. That is what "acted under
  another member's authority" means in the first bullet.
- **A clause brings no principal.** A grant is judged for the entry
  that it is presented with. An entry that records a result or a
  diagnosis judges no grant. So a result clause that reads the signer
  reads the member who signed the origin entry, and no principal, also
  when that member signed the origin under one. Derivation and the
  fold then agree (the I1 deltas note, section 13).
- **Within one entry.** An `attribute` effect takes the history as it
  stands after the effects written before it in the same entry. If an
  earlier effect of the entry makes a member the holder of a hold
  under the subject, that member is in the list. A cache that is
  brought up to date only after the entry does not satisfy this.
- **More sources. This answers gaps G8, G13 and G18.** `attribute` may
  carry `with`, a list of further sources. The result is the set union
  of the base attribution and every source, with duplicates removed,
  in byte order of member identifier.

  ```ts
  type AuthorSource =
    | { items: Range; slot: string }                   // a party list of each local item the range covers
    | { subject: Subject; slot: string }               // a party list of another subject of the act
    | { each: Operand; as: string; list: Operand }     // a list read, by a part, from each fetched fact of a list
    | { list: Operand };                               // a list read from one fetched or presented fact
  ```

  A report takes in the `authors` of each input item whose `for` is
  its commitment, in any state. A manifest takes in the `authors` of
  each selected report, read from the report's entry; the `authors` of
  the manifest it supersedes; and the attribution list that a
  presented entry of another lane carries (section 16.3).
- **Completeness.** A range in a source needs complete evidence: the
  result is an exact set. If it is not completed, the input is not
  judged, as for a guard. A source that reads an unbound subject or an
  absent fact adds nothing.
- **An unbound subject. New in revision 12.** This answers the lane
  design's gap G27. When the subject that `attribute` names is unbound
  (section 6.4), there is no item whose history can be taken. The base
  is then the part of the first bullet that reads no item: the signer
  of the act being judged, and the principal of the grant that was
  judged for it. Every source in `with` is still taken. The effect is
  applied, because its own subject is the item whose slot it fills,
  and that item is bound. In a result clause the base is the member
  who signed the origin entry, with no principal, as above. In an
  entry that has no signer it is empty. This is how the lane design's
  revision 14 reads it (its section 5.4). Revision 13 changes nothing
  in this rule. The I2 source at `744f2447` does not apply the effect
  when that subject is unbound, so an opening whose author list is
  required is refused `required-unset` (its delta DG26). That fails
  closed, and it is not this rule: section 11.11, row 11.
- **No truncation.** A result longer than the slot's `max` refuses the
  input `slot-full`.
- A Git author line is text. It is not attribution and not authority.
- Which key belongs to which member, and which member acts for which
  principal, are authenticated by grants. R3 defines that contract. The
  owner-of-agent review choice kept from plan 005 is a policy value
  that the rules scope discloses; R3 places it.

**Made exact in revision 13, from the I2 source choices.** Each point
names the entries of the I2 deltas note that it answers (section 15.6l).
Each is a rule of this contract from this revision, for the reason that
the point gives. None changes an entry that the I2 source at `744f2447`
writes, unless the point says so.

- **DG24.** An `attribute` effect records one `list` record with
  `change: "add"` for each member of its result that the slot does not
  hold yet, in byte order of member identifier. So the slot of a new
  item is in byte order, and a list that already held members keeps them
  first. The attribution history that each item keeps is in the order in
  which members joined it. No entry's bytes show that order, and no rule
  reads it: a derived list is put in byte order before it is recorded.
- **DG25.** `with` holds at most the bound on a list of effects, 16 as
  proposed. The number is R4's. `items` reads a party slot, single or
