  list, of each item that its range covers, from the state before the
  entry and from every page; an unfinished scan leaves the input not
  judged. `subject` reads a party slot of that subject, as the effects
  so far left it. `each` reads a list from each element of a list, with
  the element bound. `list` reads a list from one operand. A source that
  reads none adds nothing. A value that `each` or `list` reads is a list
  of member references, each within the bound of a handle, or the input
  is refused `bad-field`. The validator refuses a source whose stated
  type is not a list of members, or whose slot is no party slot. The
  reason for the refusal: a value that is no member must not enter a
  party list, and leaving it out would hide a mistake of the definition.

### 6.8 The hold capability

A hold names a resource extent, a holder and an end time. It has an
**epoch** that rises each time the hold is opened, renewed by another
holder, or ended. Workspace writes are fenced by scope, hold and epoch.

A hold ending is a `timed` entry that changes the hold item only. It
fences the former holder's writes. It changes no commitment and no
party slot, because no effect of its rule names one. A former holder
may still settle what it owes.

A hold fences its own holder and epoch. It gives no exclusivity against
other lanes (section 8.5).

**The item form of `hold@1`. New in revision 8.** A definition that
lists `hold@1` may use the `hold` effect. The **hold type** is the item
type that an act with `hold: { do: "open" }` opens. The validator
requires all of these of a definition that has one.

| Part | Required |
|---|---|
| States | One state that is not final, the type's `initial`, and one that is final. |
| `holder` | A party slot that holds one member, not fixed. |
| `under` | A reference slot to a local item, fixed and required. Attribution reads it (section 6.7). |
| `epoch` | A value slot of type `int`, required. Only the `hold` effect sets it. |
| The end time | A value slot of type `time`, required. The opening act sets it with an ordinary `value` effect, from the commit time plus a constant. A renewal sets it the same way. |
| The timed rule | One rule whose `on` is the hold type, whose `states` is the state that is not final, whose `deadline` is the end-time slot and whose effects include `hold: { do: "end" }`. |
| The opening act | It is an `open` act of the active scope, never the genesis (section 6.4). Exactly one `grant` is used by the acts that have `hold: open`. |

| Effect | Derived |
|---|---|
| `hold: { do: "open" }` | On the item the entry opens: `holder` from the signer, `epoch` 1. Recorded as `hold`, `open`, with the epoch. |
| `hold: { do: "renew" }` | `holder` from the signer. The epoch rises by one when the holder after the entry's effects differs from the holder before them. Recorded with the epoch. |
| `hold: { do: "end" }` | The state becomes the final state. The epoch rises by one. It counts as the `state` effect that a timed rule needs. It is total: on a hold that is not final it cannot be refused. |
| No form: a hold ends with what it is under | When an entry's effects take an item to a final state, the capability ends, in the same entry, every hold in the state that is not final whose `under` names that item. Each is recorded as `hold`, `end`. The capability finds them by an index on `under`, which gives complete evidence. |

`extent` is an operand that the validator checks. It is recorded only
when the definition also writes an ordinary `value` effect for a slot
of that name.

The slot names `holder`, `under` and `epoch` are fixed by the
capability. The I1 delta 4 kept the epoch outside the declared slots;
here it is a declared slot, so a read and a replay see it as state
like any other. The last row of the second table is new. R2 states it
as the capability's rule (R2 section 3.3) and both lane definitions
rely on it.

**A renewal by the member who already holds. Stated in revision 12.**
The second row of the second table decides it. The holder does not
change, so the epoch does not rise. The end time moves by the act's
own `value` effect, and the hold's deadline is then the new end time,
under the same timed rule. So the hold still reserves 1 entry for its
end (section 17.2), and the renewal itself is new work. The capability
reads the hold and nothing else. Whether a hold may still be renewed
after something else has happened in its lane, such as a merge, is a
guard that a definition writes, or does not write. The capability has
no such rule of its own (section 15.10, seam 8).

**Only the `hold` effect changes a hold. New in revision 13** (I2 delta
DF8). The second table above says that the `hold` effect sets the
holder, from the signer, the epoch and the final state. It did not say
that nothing else may. The epoch fences the holder's writes. A holder
that a `party` effect set, or an end that a `state` effect made, would
change who holds, or end the hold, with no rise of the epoch. So the
validator refuses three effects on any subject whose type is a hold
type: a `party` effect on `holder`, a `value` effect on `epoch`, and a
`state` effect. It refuses two `hold` effects on one subject in one
list. An act that opens a hold type has `hold: { do: "open" }`. No
handler opens a hold type, and none has a `hold` effect that opens: a
hold is opened by an `open` act, which has a signer. `holder` and
`epoch` count as set by the opening, so both may be required, and
`epoch` takes no default. The end time is still set by an ordinary
`value` effect, as the first table says. Both pinned definitions pass
these rules.

**Both lane definitions declare it. This answers R3's point O7.** A
capability version has one meaning, and any definition of kind `lane`
may list it. `issue` and `change` both list `hold@1`, with the same
hold type, the same guards and their own grants. Nothing is built
twice, and no check is lowered. A hold's token, fork, environment and
export, and the records behind them, are section 6.11 and R3.

**Made exact in revision 13, from the I2 source choices.** Each point
names the entries of the I2 deltas note that it answers (section 15.6l).
Each is a rule of this contract from this revision, for the reason that
the point gives. None changes an entry that the I2 source at `744f2447`
writes, unless the point says so.

- **DF7.** The first table is read as requirements, each exactly. The
  hold type has two states: its `initial`, which is not final, and one
  final state. `holder` is a party slot of one member, and is not fixed.
  `under` is a reference slot to a local item, fixed and required.
  `epoch` is a value slot of type `int`, required, with no default. One
  timed rule on the type has `hold: { do: "end" }` among its effects;
  its deadline is a value slot of type `time`, required, and that slot
  is the hold's end. A `value` effect on that slot, in any act, handler,
  timed rule or clause, is from the commit time plus a constant. An act
  that renews a hold sets that slot. A definition may have more than one
  hold type, and all its acts with `hold: open` still use one grant.
  `hold: end` counts as the `state` effect that a timed rule needs. The
  reason for reading "a renewal sets it the same way" as a requirement:
  a renewal that left the end where it was would be an act that changes
  the holder and not the time for which the hold is held.
- **DF9.** A hold's change is one record: `hold`, the item, the change
  and the epoch. The fold derives the rest from it. For `open` and
  `renew` the holder is the member of the grant that the entry was
  judged on. For `end` the state is the hold type's final state. The
  epoch goes into the slot `epoch`, which is a value like any other in a
  read. The judges apply the record to their working copy with the
  function that the fold uses. One thing follows that the I2 source does
  not do. The parts `{ opened }` and `{ set }` read what an entry's
  effects set (section 6.5), and a `hold` record sets the holder, the
  epoch and, for an end, the state. So those parts read them. The source
  reads `party`, `ref`, `value`, `list` and `state` records there, and
  gives none for what a `hold` record set. That fails closed, and it is
  not this rule: section 11.11, row 19.
- **DF10.** The slot `epoch` can hold 1 and 2, or the validator refuses
  the type. A renewal by another member is refused `bad-field` when the
  epoch after it could not rise once more. A renewal by the holder does
  not raise the epoch, and is never refused for it. The reason: `hold:
  end` is total, so every end, written, timed or with what the hold is
  under, must have room to raise the epoch. The code is the one that a
  derived value outside its type has.
- **DF11.** Where a `hold` effect may be written. `open`: in an `open`
  act only, on its primary item. `renew`: in an act, on a hold that the
  act does not open. Not in a timed rule, a handler or a result clause,
  because none of those entries has a signer, and the holder is taken
  from the signer. `end`: anywhere. In an act and in a handler it needs
  a `state` guard on its subject that lists no final state, as a `state`
  effect does, and is refused `final` without one. In a result clause
  the fold checks it when the clause runs.
- **DF12.** A hold ends with what it is under, exactly. The ends are
  derived after the entry's written effects and the records of its
  capability effects, and before attention (section 4.1). The items:
  each subject of the entry that was not final before it and is final
  after its written effects, in an act, a handler, a timed rule and a
  result clause. The holds: every hold that was live before the entry,
  or that the entry opens, that is still live after the written effects
  and whose `under` is such an item. A hold that the entry ends by a
  written `hold: end` is not ended again. The order: by the name of the
  hold type, and then by the hold's ID. Each end raises the epoch by
  one, and tells nobody. The validator refuses a hold type whose `under`
  names a hold type: this contract states no chain of holds. The static
  size of a timed entry counts, for a rule that takes its item to a
  final state, one end record for every hold that could be under it: the
  `max` of each hold type whose `under` names the rule's type. How the
  holds are found is the storage's choice, as long as the evidence is
  complete. The I2 source reads one page of the live items of each hold
  type, at the type's `max`, where the table above says "an index on
  `under`". Both are complete, and no entry differs.
- **DF13.** `extent` is any operand that its place has, checked like
  every operand. The rule against a guard that reads the item which its
  act opens does not apply to it. Nothing is derived from it, and
  nothing is recorded for it.
- **DI2.** A handler that opens a hold type, or that has `hold: { do:
  "open" }`, is one mistake, and the validator reports it once. Which
  problem name it reports is the source's.

### 6.9 Where application code stops, and forms not yet defined

An application writes a definition and pages. It writes no guard code.
A need that these forms cannot express is a finding for the platform.

| Not defined here | Owner |
|---|---|
| The exact issue, work and pull request definitions. The forms they need are now in sections 6.2 to 6.6 and 6.11, and the definitions are written in them in the companion file. | R2 |
| The `git-read` capability: the walk, its bounds and what it reads from the host. Its guard form, its record and its replay row are here (sections 6.11, 16.4 and 9.3). | R3 |
| The hold capability's token, fork, environment and export rules, and the rules behind each record of section 6.11. The forms that touch those records are here. | R3 |
| Grant, revocation and commitment messages, and their handlers in every scope | R3 |
| The register, destination, membership, rules, directory, inbox and task platform definitions, in full | R3, with R2 for the directory's index and the inbox |
| The founding rule: who may found, the first admin, membership before any ordinary act | R3 |
| A secret that scopes use to check read sessions, which is not a scope signing a fact | R3 |
| Attention outside the application | R2, R3 |
| Numeric bounds, as measured budgets | R4 |
| The bound on a scope's retained final items, and on the work of one guard or read that covers them | R4, in the proof plan |

D5 is answered here for the shape of meaning and its pinning. It is not
answered for those rows.

### 6.10 Forms the lane definitions ask for

Revision 7 listed twelve gaps, G1 to G12, as proposed and outside the
grammar. R2 revision 12 lists nineteen. Revision 8 gives each a
disposition. The forms are in sections 6.2 to 6.6 and 6.11, and
section 15.2 has the table with the mapping for each. In short:

| Gaps | Disposition |
|---|---|
| G1, G7, G11 | Operand parts and the operands `sender` and `source` (section 6.5). No `follow` option. |
| G2 | Detached text and `redact` (sections 6.2 and 6.6). |
| G3, G16 | `if` and `unless` on effects, sends and attention (section 6.6). |
| G4, G9, G12 | Already expressible. Section 15.2 shows the mapping. |
| G5, G6, G8, G10 | `count` bounds from operands, `each`, `has`, `anyOf`, `distinct` and `sameSet` (section 6.5). |
| G13, G18 | Sources for `attribute` (section 6.7), and a presented entry as a retained input (section 16.3). |
| G14 | The `record` field type (section 6.2). |
| G15 | The fan-out, and sends bounded by kind (sections 6.6 and 7.5). |
| G17, G19 | Capability guards, effects and records (section 6.11). |

Four things in R2 were said in revision 7 to need more than an operand.
They stand as follows.

- **Redaction.** The result classes are here: a text with a tombstone
  is reported as redacted, and a text missing without one is
  `incomplete` (section 9.3). Who may redact is the act's grant, which
  R3's role table places. How long bytes are kept before a redaction
  is allowed, and what a backup or an export still holds, are R4's.
- **Provenance of a selected report.** A manifest names, for each
  selection, the acceptance and the report it accepts. Both are
  fetched and both are in `uses`. The terms fact and the conditions
  fact are read from them as references. Whether that closure is
  always enough is for R2's review of the instantiated guards.
- **Named check attempts.** A retry is a new job item. That the
  checker is qualified is a guard over the lane's copy of the rules;
  that a result is authentic is the act's signature and grant. New in
  revision 9: a job holds `decidedBy`, the entry whose effects gave it
  its present state, and a `merge` entry's statement carries it for
  each live job (the companion file; witness 18.16). What the
  destination checks of that entry at reservation is R3's (R3 sections
  3.11 and 6.5; point R1-30).
  **What replaces the entry that decided a job, exactly. New in
  revision 12.** The rule is R3's (its section 6.3, "Which entry
  decides"), and the rows are R2's, as its adopted revision 14 has
  them (its section 7.2). Nothing here changes either. This says what
  the forms give, because the commission asks for it exactly.
  - `decidedBy` is a reference slot that is not fixed, and an ordinary
    `ref` effect sets it from `self`. So "replaces" means that the
    slot holds the later entry from that commit on. The item does not
    keep the earlier value. The history does: the timed entry is still
    an entry, and its own effects still show that it set the job
    `timed-out`.
  - A job has at most one replacement. The effect has an `if` that
    lists `requested` and `timed-out`, and the timed rule applies in
    `requested` only. So the slot is set at most twice: by the timed
    entry, and then by the first answer that is admitted while the job
    is `timed-out`. No effect sets it on a job that is `passed`,
    `failed`, `errored` or `superseded`.
  - The late answer is a settling entry. `timed-out` is in the
    `settles` of `check` and of `check-error`, and the entry takes the
    job out of the listed states. It draws on the entry and the item
    that the job reserved for its first answer (section 17.4).
  - No statement is written again. A `merge` entry that listed the job
    as `timed-out`, with the timed entry as its `decidedBy`, keeps
    those bytes whatever is decided later.
  - While a merge is in progress the answer is refused
    `merge-in-progress`, by a guard of the row. It is an act, so the
    refusal is an answer and writes nothing. The job stays `timed-out`
    and keeps its reservation. The same signed answer may be sent
    again until its `notAfter`.
  - One thing neither owner states: what ends the pending state of a
    `timed-out` job that nobody answers and nobody retries. Until
    something does, the job holds 1 entry and 1 item, and its lane
    does not reach a closing checkpoint with nothing pending. That is
    finite, because a lane holds at most 64 live jobs. Owner: R2
    (point R1-45).
- **The frozen source.** It is R3's protocol. Its forms are a `tell`
  with `collect`, a `relate` handler and a `state` guard, all in
  section 6.

### 6.11 Capabilities

A **capability** is platform code with a name and a version. A
definition lists the versions it uses, and its scopes pin them. Revision
7 gave a capability one effect, `hold`. Revision 8 gives every
capability the same four kinds of declared form, so that a definition
can use platform state without holding it as items, and so that a
replay can derive what the platform did. This answers gaps G17 and
G19, and R3's points O3, O8 and O9.

| A capability version declares | What it is | Used by a definition as |
|---|---|---|
| **Records** | Kinds of local state that are not items. Each kind has a key, states, and values. | Never directly. A definition reaches a record only through the guards and effects below. |
| **Guards** | Named conditions over its records, the arguments and local state. Each has named refusals. | `capability: { name, guard, with }` (section 6.5) |
| **Effects** | Named changes to its records. | `capability: { name, do, with }` (section 6.6) |
| **Steps** | Preparation it performs before an act (section 5.5), with the operations each opens. | Not written in a definition. A step is asked for with a signed intent. |

**Code for the forms that a definition uses. Added to revision 12
before its review.** A runtime needs the capability's code for each
form of these four kinds that a pinned definition uses, and for
nothing that it does not use. Section 6.1 gives the rule and the
answer when code is missing: `unsupported-definition`, for the whole
scope. A definition that uses only the item form of `hold@1` (section
6.8) uses none of the records, guards, effects and steps below, and
runs without them. The tables of this section are also what a
validator checks a definition's capability forms against. It can do
that without the capability's code, and it derives nothing by doing
it.

**A bound request that no handler receives. New in revision 16** (I3
delta EH4). "Bound means covered", below, says that every first decision
of a bound request moves the count, whatever is decided. One refusal
comes before any handler: `unknown-message`, for a sender that pins
another definition than the handler's `from` names. It is covered too.
The binding reads the verified envelope, the message's own fields and
the record, and no handler. So a request can be bound although no
handler receives it. Its deciding entry is a settling entry with the one
`record` effect that sets the count. It has no kind (section 6.2), and
its fields are read as the bytes hold them (section 6.5). Which
capability a judge asks for the binding: each listed version whose table
of reserved requests declares a `tell` of that message name. For the
license requests of a receiver pin the case is narrow: the binding
requires that the sender is the task scope that the pin names. The
authority note owns which refusals its table lists.

**Platform code is no capability. New in revision 15.** A rule of a
platform definition (section 6.1, "Platform code: a mark, and its rule")
follows this section's model in four things. A runtime needs the code of
every one that the pinned definition uses, or it answers
`unsupported-definition` for the whole scope. The commit and a replay
derive it the same way, from the same inputs. A fault of the code is no
judgment. A test's stand-in is evidence for nothing about the code. It
differs in three things, each for a reason. A capability is listed by
any definition, and a rule belongs to one version of one platform
definition: a declared definition must not reach platform code. A
capability form writes its arguments as operands, and a mark writes
none: a rule reads the entry's input itself, because what it needs has
no operand. A capability effect changes only the capability's records,
and a rule's effects change items and open operations: the platform
definitions hold their state as items.

**A scripted capability is a stand-in. A rule about evidence. Added to
revision 12 before its review** (I2 delta DJ14). This is a rule about
what a test result shows. It is not a rule of the runtime, and it adds
no form.

- A test may supply a **scripted capability**: code that answers a
  capability guard, and gives the records of a capability effect, from
  a table that the test itself writes. It stands where the
  capability's code would stand.
- It comes only through test support that the production entry does
  not import. So no deployed runtime can hold one, and the rule of
  section 6.1 stays whole for every runtime that is not a test.
- It is labelled a stand-in wherever it appears: in the name or the
  first comment of each test that uses it, and in every note, guide or
  report that cites a result which was obtained with it.
- A result that was obtained with it shows what a definition's rows do
  after a capability has answered: which guard refuses, which effects
  and sends follow, and what an entry then holds. It proves nothing
  about the capability. It proves nothing about a real hold, a Git
  read, a pin, a license or a provider.
- So such a result is evidence for no row of the tables below, and for
  no witness of section 18 that states a capability's own rule. An
  entry that was written with a scripted capability is test data. It
  is not an entry of `hold@1` or of `git-read@1`, and a replay that is
  given the same script shows only that the script agrees with itself.
- The authority note's successor (request `406983fe`) owns the real
  rules of `hold@1` and `git-read@1`. This note decides only the
  contract's side, and asks that owner to confirm it. If that owner
  refuses a scripted capability, this rule is removed and the rule of
  section 6.1 stands unchanged.
- The I2 base has one, and its deltas note says where (entry DJ14:
  `packages/scope/src/testing.ts`). That file was not read for this
  note, apart from finding the function's name in it.

**Records.**

- A record is local state of the scope. It changes only by a `record`
  effect of a sealed entry. The head check covers it. The scope indexes
  records by kind and state, with exact counts, as it indexes items.
- A record is not an item. It has no revision in `expected`. It does
  not count toward "one new item for each entry": an entry may open
  one item and also change records. Each record counts in the capacity
  accounting of section 17.
- A record's key is a list of values that the capability defines, such
  as a number from the capability's own counter, or a scope reference
  with an intent digest. A key is never reused.
- A record in a final state is retained like a retained final item.
- An operand reads a record of another scope only as `carried`: from
  the `record` effect of a fetched entry (section 6.5). So what is
  read is what one sealed entry recorded, not the record's present
  state.

**Guards.** A capability guard is derived in the commit like any guard,
from its arguments, local state and the entries in `uses`. It reads no
clock except through a time slot, and nothing outside the scope. When
it fails, the refusal is `capability-refused` with the name the
capability declares. A capability guard whose evidence is a range needs
complete evidence, as section 6.5 says.

**Effects.** A capability effect is derived in the commit and recorded
as `record` effects. A verifier derives them again from the
capability's stated rule.

**Reserved requests, and a count of decisions. New in revision 11.**
This answers R3's gap G15. It is the form behind the first repair of
the review `74b21dc8`. A capability version may declare that a
record, while it is in a pending state, reserves one entry for each
of a bounded number of numbered requests (section 17.2, row 6). It
then declares all of this.

| Declared | What it is |
|---|---|
| The request | The class and the name of the message, and the field that carries its number. |
| The bound | The highest number that a request may carry. It is a constant of the capability version. |
| The count | One value of the record: the highest number that this scope has decided for the record. |
| The binding | When a delivery is **bound** to the record. It reads the verified envelope, the message's own fields and the record, and nothing else. It requires a number that is higher than the count and not higher than the bound. |

The rules are the same for every such declaration. Section 17.3
gives the five conditions that make them sound.

- The deciding entry of a bound request is a settling entry, whatever
  it decides: `applied`, or `refused` for any reason. It draws on the
  entry that the record reserved for that number.
- That entry holds one `record` effect of the capability, which sets
  the count to the request's number. When the request is applied,
  the capability's written effect carries it. When the request is
  refused, the capability derives it, and it is the entry's only
  effect: a refused request applies no effect of its handler. The
  record's state, its key and its other values do not change.
- The count never falls. A request that is not bound, and is applied
  from free room, raises the count when its number is higher and
  leaves it otherwise. So no request can make a record reserve
  again what it has already used.
- The record then reserves one entry for each number above the count,
  up to the bound. The entry for the number that was decided is used.
  One for a lower number that never came is released.
- A repeat of an envelope writes nothing, and is answered with its
  first deciding entry (section 7.4). A request that is not bound
  draws on nothing. Its deciding entry is new work, whatever it would
  decide.
- Before the record exists, nothing is reserved. The request that
  makes the record is new work.

The count is a value, and it changes by an effect that the entry
records. So both amounts of section 17.1 stay functions of the folded
state, and a verifier derives the binding, the effect and the
reservation from the history alone. R3's other option was no value,
with the number derived from the earlier deciding entries. Each
commit would then have to find those entries, and a reader that
starts at a checkpoint would not have the number in the state that
the checkpoint digests (section 9.2). It is not taken.

**Bound means covered. New in revision 12.** The commission asks how
this general form stands beside R3's two declarations, which name
particular refusals. The answer is one rule and one owned question.

- *The rule.* A request is covered by a count of decisions exactly
  when it is bound. Every first decision of a bound request moves the
  count and uses the reserved entry, whatever is decided. A request
  that is not bound is new work, whatever is decided. There is no
  third case, of a bound request whose refusal leaves the count where
  it was. So the binding alone says which kind an entry is, for the
  scope and for a verifier.
- *How an owner covers less.* By its binding. A binding reads the
  verified envelope, the message's own fields and the record
  (condition 4 of section 17.3). It may ask more of the message than
  the fields that find the record. An owner that wants only
  well-formed requests covered declares that a request is bound only
  when every field of its message is present and of its type. A
  malformed message is then not bound, and its refusal is new work.
- *R3's `withdraw`.* R3 says that a `withdraw` which is `not-owner` or
  `malformed` is not covered (its section 5.8). In these terms neither
  is bound. The outcome is the one that R3 states: the deciding entry
  is new work. Nothing of R3's decision changes, and R3's next
  revision is asked to confirm the reading.
- *R3's license request.* Revision 11 restated the binding as two
  fields that are read by themselves. So it covered a refusal that
  comes before the handler's guards, as `bad-field` or `no-item`. R3's
  text names three refusals, all of the handler's guards. It also says
  that the first decision of a bound request uses the entry "whatever
  it decides". It does not speak of a request that is bound and is
  malformed in another field. So one question is open, and it is R3's:
  is a license request bound by its source, its `export` and its `k`
  alone, or only when the whole message is a well-formed
  `export-license`? That is point R1-44. The table says what does not
  depend on the answer.

| A license request at a standing pin | Under either answer | Depends on R3's answer |
|---|---|---|
| Bound, and applied | Settling. The license entry. `decided` and `k` are its number. The result is `applied`. | Nothing |
| Bound, and refused by a guard of the handler: `export-not-authorized`, `target-not-held` or `target-fixed` | Settling. The result is `refused`, with that reason. The entry's one effect is the `record` effect that sets `decided`. | Nothing |
| From the pin's task scope, for its export, with a number above `decided` and at most 3; and another field of the message is absent or ill-typed, or its `hold` names no item | A correct task scope sends none. Whichever way it is decided, at most the reserved entries are used, and nothing is released. | Whether it is bound. If it is: settling, `refused` with `bad-field` or `no-item`, and `decided` moves. If it is not: new work, with no effect, and at a full lane it is not decided. |
| From another scope or incarnation, or for another export, or with a number that is not above `decided` or is above 3 | New work, whatever it would decide | Nothing |
| A repeat of an envelope | Nothing is written. It is answered with the first deciding entry. | Nothing |

The two answers give the entry of the third row different bytes. So
that row is not to be built as decided. The form of this section
stands as revision 11 has it, with the wider binding, until R3's next
revision answers. The other four rows are the same under both answers.

**What `hold@1` declares.** The rules behind these are R3's proposals
(R3 revision 9, sections 4.2, 5 and 6.2) and are restated only as far
as the forms and a replay need them. R3 is the authority for them. The
forms are this contract's.

| Record kind | Key | States (final in bold) | Values |
|---|---|---|---|
| `root` | A root number from the capability's counter | `creating`, `live`, `retiring`, **`retired`** | The commit; the hold and instance it was staged from; the commitment that hold is under |
| `pin` | The consumer's scope reference with its incarnation, and the digest of the intent it was prepared for. For a report, or a manifest staged by its own lane, the consumer is this scope. | `provisional`, `held`, **`released`** | The root; the commit; the consumer's entry that admitted the act, once known; how it was released, `unpinned` or `never-admitted`; the entry that showed it |
| `check` | The intent digest and the root number | **`recorded`**, **`too-large`** | The intent digest; the commit; the consumer; the lane, hold and instance of the source; the root; the attribution list of the source commitment; the ancestry record (section 16.4) |
| `receiver-pin` | The `export` item | `standing`, **`released`** | The checkpoint's digest; the receiving hold and its instance; the holder; the task scope's reference; the number of the latest license request applied; and `decided`, the highest license number that this lane has decided, applied or refused. `decided` is new in revision 11; the rule that needs it is stated in the authority note's adopted revision 13. |

Other records of the capability, such as tokens, forks, instances and
fork seeds, are R3's to list in the same form. No guard of a lane
definition reads them.

| Guard | Arguments | Holds when | Refusals |
|---|---|---|---|
| `staged` | `commit`; `under`; `pin` | With no presented `pin`: this scope holds a `live` root for the commit, staged under that commitment, with a `provisional` pin whose key is this scope and this intent, and a `check` record for this intent and that root. With a presented `pin`: nothing local is required; the definition's own guards tie the presented entry to the intent. | `not-staged` |
| `pin` | `consumer`; `intent`; `commit` | A `pin` with that key exists and names that commit, and it was not released as `never-admitted`. | `no-pin`, `pin-mismatch`, `never-admitted`. The last is new in revision 11. |
| `license` | `export`; `from`; `checkpoint`; `hold`; `instance` | `from` is the task scope that the ended hold of the export records. That hold is the checkpoint's. `instance` is the receiving hold's present instance. No `receiver-pin` exists for the export, or the one that exists is `standing` and names this hold and instance. | `export-not-authorized`, `target-not-held`, `target-fixed` |
| `settled` | `export`; `from`; `final`; `by` | `from` is the task scope that the `receiver-pin` names; or no pin exists, `final` is `withheld`, and `from` is the task scope that the ended hold records. And the source entry `by`, as fetched, is the entry of that task scope whose own effects make the release of this export final in that state. | `export-not-authorized`, `not-final` |

| Effect | Arguments | Changes |
|---|---|---|
| `pin-hold` | `commit`; or `consumer`, `intent` and `manifest` | The pin becomes `held`, with the admitting entry. On a pin that is `held` or `released`, the confirmation is recorded and the state stays. |
| `pin-release` | `commit`; or `consumer`, `intent`, `manifest` and `by` | A `provisional` or `held` pin becomes `released`, `unpinned`, with the entry that showed it. |
| `license` | As the guard, and `k` | The `receiver-pin` becomes `standing`, or stays standing, with `k`. Since revision 11, for R3's rule, stated in the authority note's adopted revision 13: `decided` is raised to `k` when `k` is higher, and it is never lowered. The entry that holds this effect is the license entry. |
| No form: the first decision on a bound license request, when it is a refusal. New in revision 11. | None | `decided` becomes the request's number. Nothing else of the pin changes: not its state, its target or its `k`. "The license requests of a receiver pin", below. |
| `settle` | `export`; `by` | The `receiver-pin` becomes `released`. |

| Step | May be `foreign` | Action judged | Derives |
|---|---|---|---|
| `stage` | Yes: the intent may be addressed to a change lane while the hold is in this lane | The grant of the act that opens the hold type, on a ten-second observation (section 16.1), and the capability's guards on the hold | A `root`, `creating`. The operation `stage`, whose attempts create the ref. Its outcome `confirmed`, on a read that shows the ref, makes the root `live`, records the `provisional` pin and opens the operation `check`. |
| `check` | Yes | The act's own grant, in its ordinary window. A `live` root for the commit must exist. | The `provisional` pin, if there is none. The operation `check`: one read of the canonical repository. Its outcome entry is the **check entry**. Its evidence is the ancestry record. It records the `check` record, `recorded`, or `too-large` when the walk passed a bound. |

The check entry is what R2 and R3 call the pin entry, when the consumer
is another lane. It is presented beside the `propose-manifest` intent
and retained by the change lane (section 16.3).

**The license requests of a receiver pin. New in revision 11.** The
rule is R3's. It is stated in the authority note's adopted
revision 13 (its section 4.2, "A reserved license
decision"). It is restated here as far as the form and a replay need
it. `hold@1` declares the form of "Reserved requests", above, for
the record `receiver-pin` while it is `standing`.

| Declared | For `receiver-pin` |
|---|---|
| The request | The `tell` request `export-license`. Its number is the field `k`. |
| The bound | 3. It is R3's proposal (its point U15). |
| The count | `decided`. |
| The binding | The envelope's source scope, with its incarnation, is the task scope that the pin names. The field `export` names the `export` item that is the pin's key. `k` is higher than `decided` and at most 3. The two fields are read by themselves: a message in which either is absent or ill-typed is not bound. |

So a standing pin reserves 3 less `decided` entries: 2 once request 1
has made it, 1 after a decision on request 2, and none after request
3. Request 1 arrives when no pin stands, so its deciding entry is new
work, also when it is a refusal. A bound request may be refused by
the handler's guards, as `export-not-authorized`, `target-not-held`
or `target-fixed`, or by a check that comes before them, as
`bad-field` or `no-item`. Each such entry sets `decided` and nothing
else. R3's text names the three reasons. The form covers every first
decision, which is how the review `74b21dc8` words the repair. That
wider cover is this note's addition, and R3 is asked to confirm it.
Revision 12 keeps it, and says exactly what is asked: "Bound means
covered", above. The confirmation is owed to R3's next revision. The
adoption of R3's revision 13 did not give it, and this note does not
claim it. Witness 18.20.

**Two answers that are incidents. New in revision 11.** R3's adopted
base decides two deliveries `refused` and calls each an incident (R3
revision 9, section 6.2, "Other answers"): a `pin-confirm` for which
the lane holds no pin, and an `unpin` for a pin that settlement
released as `never-admitted`. Both are refusals of the guard `pin`.
The first is `no-pin`, which revision 8 has. The second is
`never-admitted`, which is added to the guard's row. Each deciding
entry is written `refused` with that name. It is new work, and it
changes no record. The guard is one guard for both handlers, so a
`pin-confirm` for a pin that was released as `never-admitted` is
refused the same way: the lane's own settlement entry recorded that
no entry could follow. How an incident is kept and shown is R3's (its
gap G13).

**How R3's order of steps maps onto entries.** R3 section 6.2 gives
seven steps in the staging lane S.

| R3's step | Entry of S |
|---|---|
| 1. The checks before dispatch | The judgment of the `preparation` entry, step `stage`. A failure is an answer and no entry. Nothing was caused. |
| 2. S records the staging operation, with the root `creating` | That `preparation` entry. |
| 3. The ref is created, and a read shows it | The outcome entries of the operation `stage`. `confirmed`, on the read, makes the root `live`. |
| 4. S records the read's token duty, then reads | The operation `check` is opened by the entry of step 3, or by a `preparation` entry, step `check`, for a reuse. |
| 5 and 6. The walk, the record, and the snapshot stored | Before the outcome entry of `check` is written. The snapshot's bytes are stored first, by their digest. |
| 7. The record is retained | The outcome entry of `check`: the check entry. |

For a reuse, R3's order starts at step 4, and here at a `preparation`
entry of step `check`.

**What `git-read@1` declares.** One guard. The walk and its bounds are
R3's (R3 section 6.2).

| Guard | Arguments | Holds when | Refusals |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ancestry` | `commit`; `row`, which is `report` or `manifest`; `pin`, a presented check entry or none; `selected` and `earlier`, the commits that a manifest names | A `check` record for this intent and commit exists: local, or carried by `pin`. Its state is `recorded`. Its ancestry record names `commit`. When the record is local, R3's guards 2 to 6 hold against this scope's records and items at this commit. And the list F of the record passes the row: for `report`, F is empty; for `manifest`, each commit of F is in `selected` or `earlier`, or is carried through a stop at such a commit. | `ancestry-too-large` when the record's state is `too-large`. `ancestry-stale` when the commit differs or one of guards 2 to 6 fails. `unnamed-work`, with the commit, when the row fails. |

When the record is carried by another lane's entry, guards 2 to 6 read
that lane's records. That lane judged them in the commit of its check
entry, and they are not judged again here. Section 16.4 gives the
record, and section 9.3 what a replay derives.

**Made exact in revision 13, from the I2 source choices.** Each point
names the entries of the I2 deltas note that it answers (section 15.6l).
Each is a rule of this contract from this revision, for the reason that
the point gives. None changes an entry that the I2 source at `744f2447`
writes, unless the point says so.

- **DJ15.** How the validator reads a capability form. A definition
  lists each capability at most once, in a version that this section's
  tables have. A form names a listed capability, a guard or an effect
  that its version declares, and arguments that the table names for it.
  A guard may write any of its arguments. The arguments of an effect are
  all of one of the sets that its table allows, and may be a part of
  that set. An argument of a guard is an operand, or `{ each, as, value
  }`, or `{ items, slot }`. An argument of an effect is an operand. A
  capability effect names no subject unless it writes `of`. It sets no
  slot, and it conflicts with no other effect. A timed rule has none:
  `timed-partial`. Which arguments are required, and what a missing one
  means, are the capability's rules, which the authority note's
  successor owns (request `406983fe`).
- **DJ18.** When a capability guard of an act's or a handler's own list
  does not hold, the refusal is `capability-refused`, with the name that
  the capability declares for it. A `reason` that the definition wrote
  on that guard names nothing. A capability guard that is nested in a
  list form fails that form, which is then refused as any guard is. The
  records of each written capability effect are recorded after every
  written effect of the entry, in the order of their forms (section
  4.1). The arguments of each are read where its form is written.
- **D11, DJ19.** What this section's tables state is all that a
  validator checks of a capability: the states of each record kind and
  which are final; the arguments and the named refusals of each guard;
  the sets of arguments of each effect; whether a step may be `foreign`;
  and the reserved requests of a pin. A judge is given a capability's
  rules as an input, like the reader of its own history. A guard's
  answer that its version does not declare, and a record of a kind or a
  state that it does not declare, are faults of the rules, and are not
  judgments. With no rules, a capability form is not judged. No runtime
  reaches that case, because it pins no definition whose forms it cannot
  derive (section 6.1).

## 7. Composition

### 7.1 Founding a repository, in order

Revision 7 gave a repository's directory no creator, and had its genesis
send its three creations at once. R3 proposes a founding register that
claims the founding, creates the repository at the Git host and
confirms the directory (R3 section 3.8, point O5). Revision 8 adopts
the register as a scope kind and as the directory's creator. This
section gives the order as far as this contract defines it. The
register's definition, `platform:register@1`, is R3's.

**The register.** A deployment has one founding register. It is the
only scope with no creator.

1. An installer builds an intent with `to: null`, kind `install`, and
   a random idempotency key, and signs it.
2. The service computes the intent digest and the seed
   `{ kind: "register", definition, creator: null, cause: intent digest, ordinal: 0 }`.
   The scope ID is the seed's digest.
3. The object with that name checks that its store has never been
   written, mints an incarnation, and writes the genesis entry. That
   entry contains the seed, the incarnation, the kind of its genesis
   act (section 4.1) and the signed intent. Its
   hash is computed last, over bytes that do not contain it. A scope
   with no creator is active from its genesis.

These three steps are revision 7's steps 1 to 3 for a directory, moved
to the register. Who may install a register, and that a deployment
addresses only the register it was installed with, are R3's and the
installation design's. A register store that is empty, or that holds
another incarnation than the configured one, founds nothing (R3
section 3.8).

**A repository.**

| Step | Scope | Entry | Sends |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Register | An act: the founder's signed intent, kind `found`, addressed to the register. It records a claim, and opens the operation that creates the repository at the Git host. The directory's seed is fixed here: `{ kind: "directory", definition, creator: the register, cause: that intent's digest, ordinal: 0 }`. | Nothing. |
| 2 | Register | The outcome entries of that operation's attempts (section 4.3). The operation selects: the first `confirmed` outcome recorded while the claim has no repository selects that one. | On the selecting outcome only: a request, `create`, with that seed, the claim's fact, the founder's signed intent and the repository. |
| 3 | Directory | Genesis, provisional: the seed, a new incarnation, the kind of its genesis act, the source and the creation message. Its creations of membership, rules and destination are sealed in this entry as duties and are held (section 7.2). | One message: the result of the creation. |
| 4 | Register | The delivery of that result. The claim becomes active. | A control: `confirm`, naming that genesis. |
| 5 | Directory | The delivery of the confirmation. The directory is active. | The held creations. Each child is provisional until the directory confirms it. |

- **The directory is an ordinary child.** Every rule of section 7.2
  applies to it: what it checks at genesis, what a provisional scope
  admits and sends, a refused child, a conflict, and a repeated
  creation after its storage is lost. Nothing is special to it. Its
  three children take the directory's seed digest as their cause, as
  before.
- **The cause.** The entry that sends the creation is an outcome
  entry. The seed's cause is the digest of the founder's intent, which
  the act of step 1 admitted and which opened that operation. Section
  7.2's table has this case.
- **What the founder signed.** An intent to the register, which
  exists. The directory's scope ID is derived from that signed intent
  and from the register's reference. Nobody signs for a scope that
  does not exist yet.
- **Whose incarnation.** The service mints the directory's incarnation
  when it first writes that store. The register records the first
  applied result and confirms that incarnation. A second one is an
  `incarnation-conflict` and is never confirmed (section 2.2).
- **A second founding from the same intent** is the same act: the
  register answers it with the first receipt (section 4.2).
- **A late answer.** A creation attempt recorded `unknown` may be
  answered later. Its outcome entry settles that attempt, records the
  repository as not selected when the claim already has one, and
  changes neither the claim nor the directory (section 4.3).

The rule "every act needs a current grant" cannot admit the founding
itself. The founding rule is part of the register's definition: who
may found, how the founder becomes the first admin, and what a
directory may admit before its membership scope is active. R3 states
it. R3 must make sure that no ordinary lane becomes active before the
membership that grants its first parties.

### 7.2 Creating a child, in order

Issue #42 is the example. Four entries in two scopes; then the exchange
is over.

| Step | Scope | Entry | Contains | Sends |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Directory | D.17, an act | The requester's signed intent, kind `open-issue`, addressed to the directory. The grant the directory judged. Effects: #42 allocated. | Ordinal 0, a request: `create`, with the seed `{ lane, definition, creator: directory, cause: that intent's digest, ordinal: 0 }`, the opener's `MemberRef` as the directory judged it, and the fields the lane's genesis act needs. |
| 2 | Issue lane | I.0, genesis | The seed, a new incarnation, the kind of its genesis act (section 4.1), the source D.17 and ordinal 0, and the creation message. The genesis act opens one item, `intent`, with `requester` from the opener. Decision `applied`. Provisional. | Ordinal 0, a result: `of` D.17 ordinal 0, `applied`. |
| 3 | Directory | D.18, a delivery | From I.0, ordinal 0: the result. The `create` send's `applied` clause runs: #42 is created and holds the child's `ScopeRef`. | Ordinal 0, a control: `confirm`, naming I.0. |
| 4 | Issue lane | I.1, a delivery | From D.18, ordinal 0: the confirmation. The scope becomes active. | None. |

- **What the child checks at step 2.** Its own name equals the seed's
  digest. The source entry D.17, read as section 7.4 says, contains a
  `create` at ordinal 0 with that seed and that message digest. The
  seed's cause matches D.17 by the kind of its input, as the table of
  causes below says: here D.17 is an act, and the cause is its intent's
  digest.
- **Where the child's definition comes from. New in revision 10** (I1
  delta 101), **and restated in revision 11** (I1 deltas 115 to 118).
  A seed names a declared definition by its digest, and
  the child needs the bytes to judge its genesis. It reads them from
  its creator, the scope that its seed names, by that digest, before
  its genesis turn. They are an immutable input (section 5.1). The
  child checks them against the digest in the domain
  `artroom-definition-1`, validates them, pins them and retains them
  (section 9.2). Their content rests on the digest, and on no trust
  in the creator. So the creator's incarnation is not checked again
  for this read. The read of the source entry, just before it,
  checked the incarnation, and the digest is the whole proof of the
  bytes. A platform definition is code, and nothing is read for it.
  - *The named closure.* A declared definition names, in its `create`
    send forms, the definitions under which its scopes can create a
    child: `self`, a platform name, or a digest. Its **named
    closure** is the set of declared definitions that are reached
    from it by following those digests, in any number of steps. The
    closure is finite and has no cycle, because a definition cannot
    hold its own digest, or the digest of a definition that holds its
    digest (section 2.1). A deployment bounds how many definitions
    one closure may have (section 6.1; point R1-37).
  - *A scope holds its closure from its genesis.* Revision 10 had a
    creator retain a named definition with the first entry that names
    it, and left open where that entry reads the bytes. For a
    declared definition the names are known from the definition
    itself. So a scope retains every definition of its named closure
    with its genesis entry, each under its digest, checked against
    that digest and validated. They are written in the transaction of
    the genesis, and the bytes dimension counts each once (section
    17.1). A child's closure is part of its creator's closure,
    because the child's definition is in it. So a creator can always
    serve what its children need, and what their children need in
    turn, for as long as its history is retained. No entry after the
    genesis newly retains a definition.
  - *Where each scope reads its closure.* A child reads it from its
    creator, by digest, after it has read its own definition and
    before its genesis turn. A scope with no creator has no scope to
    read from. In this contract that scope is the founding register,
    which is a platform definition. I1's founding of a directory
    under a declared definition stands in for it (section 15.6c,
    entries 83 and 84). It takes the declarations as a list beside the signed
    intent (I1 delta 116), as a detached text travels beside its
    intent (section 6.2).
  - *A genesis that cannot have its whole closure is not written.*
    This is the part of I1's delta 116 that changes. I1 accepts a
    founding that lacks a named declaration. A creation under that
    definition then waits without end: it is retried, it is never
    diagnosed, and nothing can supply the bytes later. That is a duty
    that can never settle. So the rule is this. When a declaration of
    the closure is not supplied to a founding, the founding is
    answered `dependency-unavailable`, nothing is written, and the
    same signed intent may be sent again with the declarations. When
    one is supplied and does not validate, when the closure is larger
    than its bound, or when a `create` send of the closure names a
    platform version that the runtime does not implement, the
    founding is refused `unsupported-definition`. A declaration that
    is supplied, and that the closure does not name, is ignored and
    is not retained.
  - *When the child's read fails.* The creator may be out of reach,
    may not answer within the fetch time limit, may answer that it
    holds no bytes under a digest, or may serve bytes that do not
    hash to the digest. In each case the creation is not decided:
    nothing is written, transport answers `retry` with the reason
    `dependency-unavailable`, and the creator keeps the duty (section
    7.4). The same holds, with the reason `unsupported-definition`,
    when the bytes hash to the digest and do not validate in the
    child's runtime, and when the seed names a platform version that
    the child's runtime does not implement. The creator validated its
    closure at its own genesis, and it holds it. So each of these is
    a creator that is only slow, or a fault of the host: lost
    storage, or a difference of configuration between two runtimes
    (section 4.2). No answer is not a refusal, and it shows nothing
    about the definition. None of these answers is a routing refusal.
    So such a creation is never diagnosed `undelivered`. It stays
    pending, and it is shown as outstanding (section 9.1).
  - *A platform scope that takes a name from an input.* A platform
    definition is code. Its code may create a scope under a
    definition that an input names, as a directory creates a lane.
    For that case revision 10's rule stands: the bytes, and now their
    named closure, are an immutable input of the first entry that
    names them. They are read before that entry's turn, checked,
    validated and written with it. An input whose bytes cannot be
    read is not written: an act is answered `dependency-unavailable`,
    and a delivery is not decided. One whose bytes do not validate is
    refused `unsupported-definition`: an act gets that answer, and a
    request a deciding entry `refused` with that reason. Where such a
    scope reads the bytes is R3's: point R1-35.
  - So no creation is sent under a definition that its child could
    not pin, and no child lacks a declaration that its own children
    need.
  - I1 first asked a definitions port, which a deployment does not
    supply (its delta 101, as first written). At `97518f68` it reads
    from the creator, as this section says (its delta 115). The
    creator is the one scope that every child can name, and it
    already answers the read of the source entry.

**Four facts about a definition, kept apart. New in revision 12.** The
commission asks about a definition's bytes, its name and its
activation in the source, and about the closure of a creator's
declarations. They are four facts, with four different grounds.
Nothing new is decided here. The table says where each stands.

| Fact | What it is | What it rests on at run time | What a replay checks | Open, and whose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Its bytes | The declaration, which a seed names by its digest | The digest. No trust in the scope that served the bytes. | The retained bytes against the digest, and validation under the bounds given | The bound on a declaration's bytes and on a closure: R4 (point R1-37) |
| Its name | The member `name` of those bytes, which `under` is compared with (section 6.1) | For a scope's own definition: its pinned bytes. For a fetched entry: the source's answer, which the using entry records as `under` of its `FactUse` (section 4.1). | The `under` against the definition that the source's genesis pins. With an anchor, the name is reported under `anchor`. | The bound on a name: R4 (point R1-37) |
| Its activation | That a repository's rules scope chose it for new lanes | Nothing in this contract. No scope reads it. | Nothing | R3 (point R1-22; its gap G7). Until it is decided, a fact from a lane of another repository, under a definition of the same name, passes a `fact` guard. |
| Its named closure | The declarations that a creator must hold, so that its children can be created | For a declared creator: its own genesis, which is not written without them. For a platform creator that takes a name from an input: the first entry that names it. | That the scope retains every definition of its closure, each under its digest | Where a platform creator reads the bytes: R3 (point R1-35; its gap G16) |

- A name is the claim of whoever wrote the bytes. It is not an
  activation. A digest is not one either: it shows which bytes, and
  not who chose them.
- R3 treats its gaps G7 and G16 as one question. It proposes an answer
  and does not decide it: the directory admits a lane's creation only
  for a definition that the rules scope has activated, on an
  observation of the rules that its entry retains; and a lane is of a
  repository when its seed's creator is that repository's directory.
  This contract decides neither part. Its forms already give such an
  answer three things. An observation of the rules is a retained
  judgment input with a form (section 16.1). The bytes are read before
  the turn, by digest (section 5.2, step 1). A seed's creator is in
  the scope's own genesis, which a replay of the source reads.
- One thing such an answer would need, and the forms do not have. A
  `fact` guard reads the fetched entry and its `under`. It does not
  read the source's seed. So "a lane of this repository" cannot be a
  guard today. If R3 decides that it must be, the form is one more
  member beside `under`, recorded in the same way, and it is this
  contract's to add then. It is not added now.
- The source at `a3e5a77e` takes a founding's declarations beside the
  signed intent, and still accepts a founding that lacks a named one
  (section 11.10, row 1). It founds a directory under a declared
  definition, as its stand-in for a register. Its set of platform
  names has no register, and it has no activation at all. Those are
  I1's stated omissions. I3 owns the platform definitions.

- **Whose intent.** The requester signed an intent to the directory.
  The child does not treat it as an intent to itself. The child's
  genesis takes its first parties from the opener that the creator
  judged and recorded, and it can show the signed intent by naming
  D.17. Nobody signs for a scope that does not exist yet.
- **Grants.** The opener being in a party slot gives no authority.
  Every later act in the child needs its own current grant.
- **What a provisional child admits.** A repeat of its own creation
  request, which it answers from its genesis; and the confirmation.
  Nothing else. A confirmation is admitted only when all of these hold:
  its envelope's source scope and incarnation are the creator named in
  the seed; the source entry, read as section 7.4 says, is a delivery of
  a result whose `of` is the creation request and whose `from` is this
  scope's genesis; and the control names this genesis. The entry that
  records it activates the scope. Any other confirmation is answered
  `source-unverified`, records nothing and activates nothing.
- **What a provisional child sends.** One message: the result of its
  creation request, from its genesis, sent again until transport
  acknowledges it. Nothing else leaves a provisional scope. It decides
  no other request, so it sends no other result; it sends no request,
  no control and no advisory. If its genesis act declares other sends
  or an outside effect, they are sealed in the genesis entry as duties
  and are held: none is dispatched and no attempt starts before the
  entry that records the confirmation. A provisional scope writes no
  timed entry, and none is ever owed: its genesis opened no timed item
  (section 6.4) and it admits no act, so no item holds a deadline
  before the confirmation. The entry that records the confirmation is
  therefore never written ahead of a due transition, and the rule of
  section 5.2 holds for it unchanged. The drain first finds something
  due only after an act of the active scope has opened a timed item.
  So a provisional scope that is never confirmed has issued no grant,
  taken
  no hold, changed no other scope and started no outside effect. R3's
  ownership and founding fences must agree with this rule. Where they
  need more, R3 states it.
- **What a refused child admits and sends.** A repeat of its creation
  request, answered from its genesis. Nothing else, ever. It sends its
  `refused` result and nothing else.
- **Repeats.** A repeated creation message is answered with I.0's fact
  and adds nothing. A repeated confirmation is answered with I.1's fact
  and adds nothing. A confirmation that names another genesis is
  answered `source-unverified` and adds nothing.
- **A refused child.** If the genesis act's guards refuse, the child
  writes I.0 with decision `refused` and sends the result `refused`.
  That scope is terminal: it admits nothing but a repeat of its
  creation request, ever, and exists to retain the decision. The directory's D.18 runs the `refused` clause. No
  confirmation is sent.
- **A conflict.** If the directory already holds an applied result with
  another incarnation for that seed, D.18 runs the `conflict` clause
  and sends no confirmation. The second child stays provisional for
  good.
- **A repeated creation after the child's storage is lost.** A creation
  is addressed by a seed and names no incarnation. Two cases.
  - *Before the creator holds an applied result.* The repeat reaches an
    empty store, which writes a new provisional genesis with a new
    incarnation. Its result is the first that the creator records, and
    the creator confirms that incarnation. The lost one was provisional
    and was never confirmed, so by the rule above it had sent nothing
    but its result. A late result from the lost incarnation cannot be
    verified, because its history cannot be read. It is answered
    `source-unverified` and records nothing.
  - *After the creator holds an applied result, or has confirmed.* The
    creator sends no creation again. If a creation is delivered all the
    same, the new provisional scope's result carries another
    incarnation, the creator records `conflict`, and nothing is
    confirmed.

  No request invents an incarnation. No replacement of a confirmed lost
  incarnation becomes active by this path. The ownership fences are
  R3's.
- **Restart on either side.** Every message is a send of a sealed
  entry, so it is delivered again until transport acknowledges it. Each
  receiver answers a repeat from its history.

A child has no right to change its creator or its siblings.

**The kinds of cause.** A seed's `cause` is a digest in one of
three byte domains, by what kind of entry asked for the scope:

| The creating entry is | `cause` is | What the child and a verifier check |
|---|---|---|
| An act | The digest of that act's intent, in `artroom-intent-1` | The source entry's input is an act whose intent has that digest, and its sends contain this seed at this ordinal. |
| A delivery, whose handler creates a scope | The digest, in `artroom-delivery-1`, of the delivery cause: the incoming source fact, the incoming send's ordinal and the message digest | The source entry's input is a delivery. The delivery cause built from that input's `from`, `n` and the digest of its `message` has that digest. Its sends contain this seed at this ordinal. |
| A genesis, as when a directory creates its membership, rules and destination scopes | The digest of the creating scope's own seed, in `artroom-seed-1` | The source entry is that scope's genesis, the digest of its seed is the cause, and its sends contain this seed at this ordinal. |
| An outcome, as when a register creates a directory. New in revision 8. | The digest, in `artroom-intent-1`, of the intent of the act that opened the outcome's operation | The source entry's input is an outcome. Its operation was opened by an earlier entry of that scope whose input is an act with that intent digest. The source entry's sends contain this seed at this ordinal. |

Three byte domains still serve: the fourth row uses the first row's
domain. In each case the proof is the send in the source entry. A matching
digest alone admits nothing, and no signature is invented for a scope
that a genesis creates.

**How the child reads the entry that opened the operation. Decided in
revision 19** (I3 delta EP1). The fourth row asks the child to check an
earlier entry of the creator, and no text said how the child comes to
hold it. It holds it as a fetched fact. A `create` that an outcome entry
sends names the opening entry by a fact among its fields. The child
fetches it before its genesis turn, as it fetches every fact that a
creation's fields name. The child and a verifier check four things of
that entry. It is of the creating scope. Its position is the one that
the ID of the outcome's operation states, and is before the source
entry. Its input is an act whose intent has the digest that is the
seed's `cause`. And it holds the `operation` effect of that ordinal. A
creation with no such fact among its fields is answered
`source-unverified`, and nothing is written. The genesis retains the
entry in its `uses`, so a replay holds it. This is as the I3 source has
it, by its deltas note.

- *Why a field, and no new member.* The source entry seals the message,
  and so the fact's hash. A fetched entry is checked against the hash of
  its fact. The read, its bound, its retention and its place in a replay
  are those of every fetched fact (sections 6.5 and 17.2). A member of
  the seed or of the message would change the bytes of every creation.
- *Which field.* The check finds the fact by its scope and its position,
  and not by a name. The child's definition declares the field, as it
  declares any field of its genesis.
- *What it proves.* What a fetched fact proves, and no more: that the
  bytes are an entry with that hash. That the creator's history holds
  the entry rests on the creator's source entry, as the creation itself
  does (section 9.4).

**Why a delivery cause is not the message digest.** The creator builds
the delivery cause from the envelope it verified, before it writes the
entry that records the delivery. Every part already exists: the source
fact is sealed in the sender's history. The creating entry's own hash
and sequence number are not in it. A request is identified by its
source fact and ordinal everywhere else in this contract (section 7.4);
the cause now uses the same identity.

*Two distinct requests with identical message bytes.* Scope S writes
S.5 and later S.6. Each sends, at ordinal 0, a `tell` to creator C. The
two messages have the same bytes and so the same digest, m. C's handler
creates one lane, at creation ordinal 0.

| | First request | Second request |
|---|---|---|
| Incoming delivery | From S.5, ordinal 0, message m | From S.6, ordinal 0, message m |
| Delivery cause | Digest of `{ from: S.5, n: 0, message: m }`: c1 | Digest of `{ from: S.6, n: 0, message: m }`: c2. It differs, because the source fact differs. |
| Creator's deciding entry | C.20, `applied`. Sends at ordinal 0 a `create`. | C.21, `applied`. Sends at ordinal 0 a `create`. |
| Seed | `{ lane, definition, creator: C, cause: c1, ordinal: 0 }` | `{ lane, definition, creator: C, cause: c2, ordinal: 0 }` |
| Child | X1. Its genesis names source C.20, ordinal 0. | X2, another scope ID. Its genesis names source C.21, ordinal 0. |
| Child's result | `of` C.20 ordinal 0. C records it and confirms X1. | `of` C.21 ordinal 0. C records it and confirms X2. |
| Result to S | C.20 sends the result `of` S.5 ordinal 0. | C.21 sends the result `of` S.6 ordinal 0. |

Each request has its own child and its own correlated result. With the
message digest alone as the cause, the two seeds were equal and the
second request had no child of its own.

*An exact retry.* The delivery from S.5, ordinal 0, reaches C more than
once.

| What happens | Delivery cause | Result |
|---|---|---|
| The first arrival. C's commit stops because its head moved, and the turn runs again. | c1 both times: the source fact, ordinal and message are the same. | The same seed. The deciding entry takes whatever sequence number the commit allocates; the seed does not contain it. |
| C seals C.20. The same envelope arrives again. | Not built again. | No new entry. Transport answers with C.20's fact. No second seed exists. |
| S's storage is restored from retained bytes and S sends S.5's duty again. | c1: the restore keeps S's incarnation and S.5's hash. | As the row above. |
| C delivers C.20's `create` to the child twice. | Not built again. | The child finds its genesis and answers with its fact. |

### 7.3 Updating a relationship, in order

Pull request #43 "closes" issue #42.

1. The integrator signs an intent to the pull request lane: kind
   `link`, naming the issue's `ScopeRef`.
2. The lane commits entry P.5. Its effects open a `link` item. Its
   sends contain `relate: { to: issue, name: "closes", item: self, state: "set" }`.
   P.5 does not contain its own fact reference.
3. The envelope carries the fact reference of P.5.
4. The issue lane keys its copy by the owner's scope, the owner's
   incarnation, the relationship name and the owner's item. Its
   revision is the `seq` of the owner's entry.

A revision is compared only with revisions of the same owner scope and
incarnation. Sequence numbers of different owners are never compared.
The receiver applies a message only if its revision is higher than the
one it holds for that key. A late "set" cannot undo a newer "removed".

**What a revision means on the wire.** One owner entry sends at most
one relationship update for each key (section 6.4). So a key and a
revision together name at most one message, and the owner's history
gives every update of one key a different revision. The state that a
receiver holds for a key is then the update with the highest revision
that it has received, whatever the order of arrival. Two updates of one
key with equal revisions cannot come from a valid owner entry. A
receiver that reads a source entry with two `relate` sends for one key
answers `source-unverified` and records nothing (section 7.4).

The check compares keys after resolution, so an alias does not pass it.
An act that would send "set" and "removed" for one link in one entry,
naming the link once by a field and once by a slot, is refused
`duplicate-relation` and writes no entry. The owner makes the two
changes in two entries, which have two revisions.

**Copies are bounded.** The receiver keeps one copy for each key: its
state, its revision and its detail, recorded by a `relation` effect. A
`relate` handler declares `copies`, the most keys it keeps (section
6.4). The first update for a key beyond that number is decided
`refused`, `type-full`. An update for a key that is already held is
never refused for that reason. A handler acts on local items that it
names in `also`; it needs no item to hold the copy. R2's `change` item,
the issue lane's copy of a `closes` link, is this copy.

A message that changes the receiver's state, such as a confirmed merge
closing an issue, is applied once: the receiver records which owner
entry it consumed. That entry is never consumed again, even after a
reopen.

Both delivery orders, as an example. The pull request lane writes P.5,
which sets the link, and later P.9, which removes it. The two updates
come from distinct entries and may arrive in either order. In both
orders the issue lane ends with the copy `removed` at revision 9, and
each request gets exactly one result that names it.

*In order: P.5's message arrives first.*

| Order of arrival | Issue lane entry | Result sent | In the pull request lane |
|---|---|---|---|
| P.5's "set", revision 5 | I.14, a delivery, `applied`: the copy is `set` at revision 5. | `of` P.5 ordinal 0, `applied`. | P.15 records it. The `applied` clause runs. |
| P.9's "removed", revision 9 | I.15, a delivery, `applied`: revision 9 is higher than 5. The copy is `removed` at revision 9. | `of` P.9 ordinal 0, `applied`. | P.16 records it. The `applied` clause runs. |

*Out of order: P.9's message arrives first.*

| Order of arrival | Issue lane entry | Result sent | In the pull request lane |
|---|---|---|---|
| P.9's "removed", revision 9 | I.14, a delivery, `applied`: the copy is `removed` at revision 9. | `of` P.9 ordinal 0, `applied`. | P.15 records it. The `applied` clause runs. |
| P.5's "set", revision 5 | I.15, a delivery, `superseded`: revision 5 is not higher than 9. Nothing changes. | `of` P.5 ordinal 0, `superseded`. | P.16 records it. The `superseded` clause runs, which by default does nothing. |
| P.5's "set" again | None. | None new. The answer names I.15. | Nothing. |

### 7.4 Delivery

**Classes of message.**

| Class | Examples | Has a result | Recorded by the receiver |
|---|---|---|---|
| Request | `create`, `tell`, `relate` | Yes, exactly one | One deciding entry. |
| Result | The answer to a request | No | One entry in the original sender. |
| Control | `confirm` | No | One entry in the child. |
| Advisory | `index`, `notify` | No | As the receiver's own definition says. Its handler sends nothing (section 6.4). |

Because a result and a control have no result, an exchange always ends:
a request, its one result, and for a creation one confirmation.

**Sending.** A send is written in the same transaction as its entry.
Delivery is at least once and may arrive out of order. No attempt
starts inside a commit: dispatch follows the commit, and an alarm that
is set with the commit makes it certain. The answer to the caller of
an act does not wait on another scope (I1 delta 104).

**What the receiver trusts at run time.** Before recording anything, the
receiver reads the source entry from the source scope. It reaches that
scope through the deployment's one scope namespace, by the scope ID in
the envelope, and checks the incarnation in the answer against the
envelope. It then checks the entry's canonical bytes against the hash,
and that the entry contains that send at that ordinal with that message
digest. For a `relate`, it also checks that no other send of that entry
has the same key, reading `self` in each as the envelope's source.

This is a bounded check, not a replay. Its trust is stated: the
receiver trusts that the object the namespace returns for that name is
running the platform's code and is the scope with that identity. It
does not derive the source's history again. An entry that fails any
check, or bytes that do not parse, are answered `source-unverified`,
and nothing is recorded. Independent replay (section 9.4) does not rest
on this trust.

**The read of the source entry. New in revision 10** (I1 deltas 99
and 103). That read is the platform's own. It is not a read of section
9.1, and it asks no reader. The source answers its own reference, the
name of its definition and the entry's canonical bytes. When the
source cannot be reached, or does not answer within the fetch time
limit, the delivery is not decided and transport answers `retry`: no
answer is not evidence about the entry. A source that answers with an
empty store, with another incarnation, with no entry at that position,
or with bytes of another hash gives `source-unverified`. A repeat is
looked for after the source entry is read. So a repeat that arrives
while the source cannot be read is answered `retry`, like a first
delivery. The definition name that the source gives is not covered by
the source entry's hash. Since revision 11 the entry that uses the
source entry records that name, as `under` of its `FactUse` (section
4.1), and a replay checks it (section 9.3). That decides point R1-33.

**Transport's answers. New in revision 10** (I1 delta 97). A delivery
gets one of four answers. None of them is an entry.

| Answer | When | In the sender's attempt log |
|---|---|---|
| `recorded`, with a fact | The delivery is an entry of the receiver: its first decision, or a repeat, which is answered with the entry that recorded it. | The acknowledgment. It is bookkeeping ("Advisory messages", below). |
| `retry`, with a reason | Nothing was recorded now, and a later attempt may differ: an Unavailable reason of section 4.2; `scope-full` (section 17.3); a source entry, or a creator's definition bytes, that could not be read; and, since revision 11, `unsupported-definition`, for a creation whose definition the receiving runtime cannot pin (section 7.2; I1 delta 117). | `retry` |
| A routing refusal: `wrong-incarnation` or `not-found` | The resolver of the name refused the message before the scope judged anything. | The refusal |
| `source-unverified` | The source was read, and the source entry or the message fails a check against it: the checks above, and those of a result and of a confirmation (below, and section 7.2). Nothing is recorded. | `retry`. It is not a routing refusal, so it never counts toward `undelivered`. |

I1 also answers `retry` when the deciding entry would pass the entry
size. That loses nothing, and for a message whose size cannot change
it never ends. The rule for that case is open: point R1-34.

**The resolver. New in revision 10** (I1 delta 98). The resolver of a
name is the object at that name. It answers from the scope's record
alone, before the scope judges anything.

- `not-found`: a reference of another kind; a reference to an empty
  store; and any message to a scope whose genesis was refused, except
  a repeat of its creation request. Such a scope admits nothing, ever
  (section 7.2). So `not-found` is true of the message: nothing was
  recorded and nothing will be. The request then ends `undelivered`.
  It is not retried without end.
- `wrong-incarnation`: a reference that names another incarnation
  than the one the store holds.
- A seed that is addressed to an empty store passes only with a
  `create`.

The scope's own judge makes the address check again, in the order
below, so that a verifier can make it too.

**What the receiver does with a verified request.**
