| Case | Entry in the receiver | Result message |
|---|---|---|
| First time, and its guards pass | A delivery entry, `applied`. | `applied`. |
| First time, and its guards refuse | A delivery entry, `refused`, with the reason. It applies no effect of its handler. Where a capability declares a count of decisions for a bound request, the entry holds that one `record` effect (section 6.11). | `refused`. |
| First time, and it is a relationship update whose revision is not higher than the one held | A delivery entry, `superseded`. Nothing else changes. | `superseded`. |
| First time, and its handler's sends would contain two `relate` sends for one key | A delivery entry, `refused`, with the reason `duplicate-relation`. No effect and no send but the result. | `refused`. |
| It cannot decide yet: a dependency is unavailable, the scope is busy, or it is provisional. A provisional scope still admits its creator's confirmation and a repeat of its creation request. Or the entry that would decide it is new work, and the scope has no capacity for that entry (section 17.3). That includes an entry that would record a refusal. | None. | None. Transport answers "retry". The sender keeps the duty. |
| A repeat of a request already decided | None. | None new. Transport answers with the deciding entry's fact; the first result is already in the outbox. |

**The order of a delivery's checks.** The address the send was made to,
which arrives with the message: another scope ID or kind is answered
`not-found`, and another incarnation `wrong-incarnation`. Then the
shape; the source entry; a repeat, found by the source scope, its
incarnation, the source entry's position and the send's ordinal, with
the entry's hash beside them; a due transition; the scope's status;
and then the checks of the message's class. Another hash at a consumed
position is `source-unverified`. A `create` that reaches an existing
scope from another source entry is `source-unverified`. A handler is
found by the message's class and name and the sender's kind, and the
validator refuses two handlers for one of those. A delivery judges
time when its handler or clause has a `before` or `after` guard or
sets a value from the commit time; every other delivery may be written
clamped when nothing is due (section 5.3).

**Made exact in revision 14, from the later I2 source choices.** Each
point names the entries of the I2 deltas note that it answers (section
15.6m). Each is a rule of this contract from this revision, for the
reason that the point gives. None changes an entry that the I2 source at
`58465dbf` writes, unless the point says so.

- **DR3, DR7.** A repeat reads no dependency but its source entry. The
  order above puts the repeat before the checks of the message's class.
  Exactly: the receiver reads and checks the source entry, as for any
  delivery. It then asks its own history whether it holds a decision for
  that source scope, incarnation, position and ordinal. If it does, it
  fetches no other foreign entry and no text, and the answer is the
  entry that recorded the decision, or `source-unverified` for another
  hash at that position. A founding that reaches a scope which has its
  genesis is the same case: no fact that the founding's fields name is
  fetched, and the answer is the receipt for the same founding, or
  `source-unverified` for another. A first delivery and a first founding
  are not changed. The reason: a recorded decision is never removed, so
  the answer needs nothing that may since be gone, such as a text that
  both scopes have redacted. A repeat that waited on such a text would
  never end.
- **The handler, restated.** A handler is found by the message's class
  and name, by the sender's kind, and, where the handler states
  `from.under`, by the name of the definition that the sender pins
  (section 6.4, point DR14). The sentence above names the first three.

So every verified request gets exactly one deciding entry, and that
entry sends exactly one result. The result names the request by its
source fact and ordinal. The deciding fact is the envelope's `from` of
the result; the result's own bytes do not contain it.

**What the sender does with a result.** A result is admitted only when
all of these hold:

- its `of` names one of this scope's own request sends, by entry and
  ordinal;
- the envelope's source scope is that request's target, with the
  incarnation the request named, or, for a creation, the scope whose ID
  is the seed's digest;
- the source entry, read and checked as above, is the entry that
  decided that request: a delivery or a genesis whose own source is this
  scope's request.

A result that fails any of these is answered `source-unverified` and
nothing is recorded. An arbitrary message that merely names an owned
send is not a result.

A request has one recorded result. The result's outcome must equal the
decision of its source entry. A later result from another deciding
entry is recorded only as a `conflict`, on a creation. Any other is
answered with the entry that recorded the first, and adds nothing. A
result that arrives after an `undelivered` diagnosis is answered with
the diagnosis and adds nothing; it shows that the trust stated below
failed for that send, and how that incident is kept is R3's. A clause
reads its subjects as they are when the result is recorded. If its
effects cannot apply then, the result is still recorded and nothing
changes.

An admitted result is recorded as one delivery entry, which runs the
matching clause of the send: `applied`, `refused` or `superseded`; or
`conflict`, when an applied creation result carries an incarnation
other than the one this scope already holds for that seed. A repeat of
a result is answered with that entry. Results for different requests
may arrive in any order.

**When a request cannot be delivered.** Two different things must not be
confused: that delivery is impossible now, and that the request never
took effect.

A sender records, durably and before each attempt, that the attempt is
starting, and afterwards how it was answered: no answer; a retryable
answer; or a routing refusal, `wrong-incarnation` or `not-found`, from
the object at that name. This attempt log follows the ledger rule that a
duty is written before the effect. When the sender gives up
retransmitting, it writes a `diagnosis` entry that carries the log.

| The attempt log shows | Finding | What the entry does |
|---|---|---|
| Every attempt was answered by a routing refusal. No attempt went unanswered. | `undelivered` | On the trust stated below, the addressed incarnation received nothing: each attempt was refused by the resolver of that name and recorded nothing. This is terminal. The send's `undelivered` clause runs. |
| At least one attempt had no answer, a retryable answer, or no recorded completion, and the name now refuses | `delivery-unavailable` | The request may have taken effect in the addressed incarnation before it was lost. Nothing is terminal. No clause runs. Retransmission stops. The item stays in its pending state. The correlation, any outstanding duty, any pin and any fence that waits on this request stay as they are. Admins are told. |

The number of attempts is a retry policy. It is never the proof. Only
the content of the log is.

**What the attempt log is trusted for.** The `undelivered` finding rests
on a trust in the sender and the platform. That trust requires all of
these:

- Each recorded attempt covers exactly one dispatch. There is no retry
  and no forwarded send outside the log.
- A routing refusal counts only when it comes from the resolver of the
  addressed name, before the dispatch reached any target. A refusal
  from an intermediary that may already have forwarded the message does
  not count.
- An attempt whose completion was not recorded, for example across a
  restart, is unanswered. The finding is then `delivery-unavailable`.
- A late result is matched to the original send.

The policy of three refusals is not evidence about any dispatch that
the log does not account for. A replay reports the log as trusted. It
does not claim that the log proves the remote did not execute.

**Which sends a sender gives up. New in revision 10** (I1 deltas 105
to 108). Only a request is diagnosed.

- A sender stops sending a request again when its log holds the
  number of routing refusals that section 7.5 gives, consecutive or
  not. It then offers the diagnosis in a turn of its own scope. A
  diagnosis that is not written then, as when the scope is busy, is
  offered again. The finding follows from the whole log, as the table
  above says.
- A result, a control and an advisory are never given up. Each is sent
  again until transport acknowledges it (section 7.2).
- The time that a dispatch waits for its answer, and the delays
  between attempts, are a retry policy. I1's three values are
  temporary, and the numbers are R4's.
- After an `undelivered` diagnosis the request is not sent again.
  That is the end.
- **After `delivery-unavailable`. Restated in revision 11.** This
  decides the first part of point R1-36, and it changes revision 10
  in one place. The diagnosis stops retransmission. It ends nothing:
  the request is still pending, and the only entry that can settle it
  is its result.
  - *The finding never changes.* The log of the request holds an
    attempt that was not answered by a routing refusal, and a log
    only grows. So no later log can show that every attempt was
    refused, and the finding can never become `undelivered`. A second
    diagnosis could only say `delivery-unavailable` again. It is
    never written, and nothing is reserved for one. The `undelivered`
    clause of that send can no longer run.
  - *Sending it again is always safe.* A new dispatch is the same
    send: the same source fact, ordinal and message. A receiver that
    had decided the request answers the repeat from its deciding
    entry. One that had not decides it once. The sender must already
    be able to record a late result at any time, so a new dispatch
    brings no state that a late result could not bring. Nothing was
    released on the diagnosis ("What a finding may not do", below),
    so nothing has to be taken back.
  - *So a new dispatch needs no entry.* It is transport's
    bookkeeping, like every other attempt. No judgment reads it, and
    no input of section 4.1 starts it. Revision 10 asked for an
    operator's recorded act that reserved a further diagnosis. That
    is withdrawn. No further diagnosis exists to reserve, and an act
    that no judgment reads would be an entry with nothing to judge.
  - *When it resumes.* By one of two things, and by nothing else in
    this contract. A retry policy may send a diagnosed request again
    at a slower pace. Whether it does, and how often, is R4's, and
    the policy may be never. Or an operator instructs the deployment
    to send it again. That procedure is R3's and the installation
    design's. Each attempt is written to the request's log before it
    is made, as before. Attempts after the diagnosis are in no
    entry, so no bound of an entry applies to them. They are
    bookkeeping, and how many of them transport keeps is part of the
    retry policy.
  - *When neither happens.* A restored receiver that had decided the
    request sends its result again without being asked, because that
    result is a send of its deciding entry. A restored receiver that
    had not recorded the request is reached only by a new dispatch.
    Until one is made the request stays pending, and it is shown as
    outstanding with its diagnosis (section 9.1). That is a limit of
    liveness. Nothing is released on it. I1 never sends a diagnosed
    request again (its delta 108). That is inside this rule, with
    that limit.
- A request that transport has acknowledged, and whose result never
  comes, stays pending. An acknowledged send is never diagnosed. The
  outbox read shows it as acknowledged with no result (section 9.1).
  Who watches for that, and who is told, is R3's and the installation
  design's: the second part of point R1-36. It is a gap of liveness.
  Nothing is released on it, and an acknowledgment is never read as a
  result.

Two compact exchanges. Both use a request to an existing scope by its
full reference: a `tell` from the issue lane to concern lane 42a, for
which the issue lane holds a confirmed reference. Neither uses a
creation. A creation is addressed by a seed and names no incarnation,
so no object refuses it as `wrong-incarnation`; section 7.2 gives the
repeated creation.

*Applied, result lost, storage lost.* The issue lane sends the `tell`.
The first attempt is unanswered; the concern lane had in fact applied
it, and its result was lost. The concern lane's storage is then lost.
The second attempt is answered `not-found` by the resolver of that
name, whose store is empty.

| Entry in the issue lane | Content |
|---|---|
| I.30 | An act that sends the `tell` to concern 42a by its full reference. The item that waits on it is pending. |
| I.31 | A diagnosis of I.30's send: `delivery-unavailable`, with the log "no answer; not-found". The item stays pending and is shown as "outcome unknown". No clause runs. |

Later, one of three things:

- The original history is restored with its incarnation. The concern
  lane sends the result of its deciding entry again, or a new
  dispatch reaches it and it answers from that entry ("Which sends a
  sender gives up", above). The result is recorded and runs
  `applied`.
- A late result arrives from the original incarnation's outbox. It is
  verified against that incarnation's history. If that history can be
  read, it is recorded and runs `applied`. If it cannot, the result is
  `source-unverified` and the finding stands.
- Neither. An admin records a decision on the concern, with a reason:
  an explicit act, `resolve-concern` in R2's definition. It marks the
  local item. It does not claim the remote effect did not happen, and
  it releases nothing that waited on it.

*Never delivered, routing refused.* The issue lane sends the `tell` by
a full reference. The object at that name holds another incarnation
than the one the reference names. Every attempt is answered
`wrong-incarnation` by the resolver of that name, and none goes
unanswered.

| Entry in the issue lane | Content |
|---|---|
| I.30 | The act with the request. |
| I.31 | A diagnosis: `undelivered`, with the log of three attempts, each "wrong-incarnation". The `undelivered` clause runs. |

**What a finding may not do.** No clause, and no later act that rests
on `delivery-unavailable`, may release a publication slot or a resource
reservation, or start a substitute outside effect. For effects outside
the service R3's rule holds: a later attempt never settles an earlier
unknown one. A scope with a request in `delivery-unavailable` is not
settled, and it blocks a reset of the deployment (section 9.2). This
rule applies to the affected operation and its resources. Unrelated
lanes proceed.

A receiver that is only slow or unavailable is retried. The duty stays
outstanding and is shown as such.

**Advisory messages.** Transport's acknowledgment marks the duty done.
That mark is bookkeeping. It lives outside the history. No guard reads
it, and no capacity amount counts it (sections 5.1 and 17.1). The same
is true of transport's acknowledgment of a request, a result or a
control. A request that transport has acknowledged is still pending
until its result, or an `undelivered` diagnosis, is an entry. An
acknowledgment is never a result, and it settles nothing about an
effect outside the service. A sender's log may mark an attempt as
acknowledged. That mark is bookkeeping too. A send that was
acknowledged is never diagnosed, so no `diagnosis` entry carries the
mark, and `Attempt` in section 4.1 does not have it (I1 delta 105).

So an authoritative state, such as "refused child", "superseded link",
"outcome unknown" or "owner must act", is a retained entry. It never
rests on an error string or a transport reply.

### 7.5 Bounds

| Bound | Proposed value |
|---|---|
| Entry size | 256 KiB |
| Foreign entries used by one entry | 128. Revision 7 said 64. A `propose-manifest` with s selections and d decisions uses 2s + d + 3: each acceptance and its report, each decision, the goal, the plan and a presented check entry. At 32 and 32 that is 99. A proposal; R4 measures the fetches. This decides R2's point R2-19. |
| Sends from one entry | By kind, and at most 104 in all. The table below. Revision 7 said 32. |
| Depth of the decomposition chain | Withdrawn in revision 13. Revisions 7 to 12 said 4. No rule of this contract reads the number (below; point R1-50). |
| Delivery batch | 64 |
| Time limit for one fetch before the turn | 10 seconds |
| Time limit for preparation | 10 seconds |
| Time limit for the commit transaction | None. A commit's work is bounded by counts: the records a guard may read (R4's bound R4-B2), and the bounds on effects and sends. A count is the same on every host and in replay; a time is not. A commit that the host stops writes nothing, and its input is answered `unavailable`. |
| Restarts of one turn | 6 |
| Timed attempts in one turn: every selection of section 5.2's step 3, whether it writes an entry, stops or is dropped. Turns started by an alarm are included. | 64. A proposal. The number is owed to R4's proof plan, for measurement. |
| Attempts answered by a routing refusal, consecutive or not, before a sender stops and writes a diagnosis (section 7.4) | 3. A retry policy, not a proof. |

**Sends from one entry, by kind. This decides R2's proposal R2-13 and
R3's point O4.** Every send of an entry is counted: those a definition
declares, those the platform adds, and attention. Each value is a
labelled proposal, and R4 measures the largest entry (its row F23)
before any is accepted.

| Kind of send | At most | Why it is bounded |
|---|---|---|
| Declared forms that are not a fan-out: `create`, `tell`, `relate`, `index` | 7 beside a fan-out, and 8 with none | An act or handler has at most 8 send forms, and each makes at most one send. |
| One fan-out: a `relate` with `each` | 32 | The validator refuses a fan-out over a type whose `max` is above 32, or over a final state (section 6.6). |
| The platform's result | 1 | Only the entry that decides a request sends one: a delivery of a request, or a child's genesis. |
| The platform's control | 1 | Only the entry that records a creation's applied result sends one. That entry is a delivery of a result. It decides no request, so it sends no result, and its clause holds effects and no sends. |
| Attention: `notify` | 64 | The validator bounds the members that one act, handler or timed rule can tell (section 6.6). A handler of class `advisory` tells nobody (section 6.4). |

| Entry | Declared | Fan-out | Platform | Attention | At most |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| An act | 7 | 32 | 0 | 64 | 103 |
| A delivery of a request | 7 | 32 | 1 result | 64 | 104 |
| A child's genesis | 7 | 32 | 1 result | 64 | 104 |
| A delivery of a result | 0 | 0 | 1 control | 0 | 1 |
| A timed entry | 0 | 0 | 0 | 64 | 64 |
| A delivery of a control or an advisory; a diagnosis; a preparation; a settlement; a checkpoint | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| An outcome | As its owner declares, inside the limits of an act's row | | | | 103 |

So no entry has more than 104 sends: 7 and 32 declared, 1 from the
platform and 64 of attention. With no fan-out an entry has at most 8
declared sends, and its total is lower. A platform definition's code
owes the same limits. A provisional scope's genesis seals its sends and
holds all but its result (section 7.2).

**The validator counts the whole entry. Stated in revision 13** (I2
delta DH21). For each act and each handler the validator adds the most
sends that its entry can have: one for each send form, a fan-out at its
type's `max`, each member that its attention can tell, and the
platform's one result for a handler of a request and for the genesis
act. It refuses a definition in which that sum passes the bound of 104.
At the proposed values the bounds by kind already keep every entry
within 104, so the check refuses nothing today. It decides when the
values are configured apart.

**The depth of the decomposition chain is withdrawn. Decided in revision
13** (I2 deltas DH21 and DI15). This decides point R1-50 for this
contract.

- Revisions 7 to 12 gave 4 in the first table, and no section stated a
  rule that reads it. No source reads it either: the I2 source holds
  the number as a configured value, with a comment that says so.
- No rule of this contract needs it. A chain of lanes grows by one
  admitted input for each level. Each lane admits that input under its
  own grant and its own budget, and each creation reserves its own
  closure (section 17.2). So a long chain can exhaust nothing that a
  short one cannot, and no argument of sections 5, 7 or 17 rests on a
  number of levels.
- A rule would need a scope to know its own depth. No form carries one:
  a seed names its creator and no depth, and no effect adds 1 to a
  value. The smallest form would be one more member that the platform
  puts in the body of a `create` of a lane, beside `directory`, with one
  more refusal. That changes the bytes of every creation message. It is
  not added for a number that nothing here reads.
- So the bound is withdrawn. This contract does not claim that a chain
  of lanes is bounded, and no creation is refused for its depth.
- The lane design states four levels of sub-issues as a product
  difference, and names this contract's bound for it (its point R2-4).
  From this revision that bound does not exist. Whether four levels are
  enforced, or are a statement about the first pages, is the lane
  design's to decide. If it asks for enforcement, point R1-50 names the
  form.
- The source owes the removal of the configured value: section 11.11,
  row 20.


The row for the delivery of an advisory rests on a rule of the
grammar. A handler of class `advisory` declares no sends and no
attention, and a definition in which one does is refused
`advisory-sends` (section 6.4). Revision 8 had the row without the
rule.

The entry that R2 counts fits. Revision 12 counts it again, from the
row of the lane design's adopted revision 14 (its sections 4.2 and
13.5). The change lane's deciding entry for a final `published` update
sends 32 `relate` updates by one fan-out, one `unpin`, one index row
and the platform's one result: 35. Revisions 8 to 11 counted 34, from
the companion file's row, which has no index row. The index row is a
declared send that is not a fan-out, so it is one of the 7. The row
writes its forms in this order, so by section 6.6 the fan-out has the
ordinals 0 to 31, the `unpin` 32, the index row 33 and the result 34.
When the lane staged the manifest itself, the `unpin` is not made and
takes no ordinal. That entry has 34 sends, with the index row at 32
and the result at 33. No link is cut and the result is not left out.
The bound of 104 does not change. What a merge reserves does not
change either: an index row is an advisory, so the requests are still
33 (section 17.2).

Whether an entry at these limits fits the entry size of 256 KiB is not
measured. Each `relate` send carries references, a name, a state and
at most 32 fields, and no text that a person wrote.

A child's seed names its creator, and the creator's entry must exist
before the child, so a child cannot be its own ancestor. Object links
may form cycles; they carry no authority and no guard follows them.

## 8. Audit of local guard dependencies

### 8.1 What was audited

Before this note was written, the reads made by the earlier admission
path were listed: 154 rows, kept beside this note as
`notes/2026-10-04-scope-and-replay-contract/admission-read-inventory.md`.
Its title carries the label "S1" from the request that first asked for
it; R1 uses it. The audit read the admission, authority, roster,
obligation, model and request modules in full and others in part. Its
section 6 lists what it did not open, including the policy port and the
Artifacts adapter. So the lists below are complete for what was read.

The purpose is not to keep that code. It is to make sure no guard the
earlier model relied on is lost, or left unsound, when one Room becomes
many scopes.

### 8.2 Guards that depend on an absence or a range

| # | Earlier guard | New owner | How it stays sound |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Whole-head check | Every scope | Kept, per scope (D5-4). |
| 2 | No earlier act with this idempotency key | Every scope | An index over the history (section 4.2). |
| 3 | Due expiries applied first | Scope with holds | The ordered drain of step 3 and the stop of step 6.3, section 5.2. |
| 4 | Signing key never revoked | Membership; each scope by grant | R3's freshness rule. A scope judges the grant it holds and never scans the roster. |
| 5 | Join key unused; invitation unused | Membership | Local to membership. |
| 6 | Delegation live and covering | Membership issues; each scope checks | A grant with a `principal`. R3. |
| 7 | Kind declared | Every scope | The pinned definition. A point read. |
| 8 | Roster uniqueness and no reuse of a handle | Membership | Local to membership. |
| 9 | No overlapping held extent in another lane | Not provided | Section 8.5. |
| 10 | Lane has no holder | Lane | `none` over this lane's hold items, with step 6.3. |
| 11 | Latest generation | Lane | Expected revisions. |
| 12 | No landing in flight on the lane | Pull request lane; destination | `none` over merge-intent items; the destination's slot. R3. |
| 13 | No open review obligation; no open blocking obligation | Pull request lane | `none`, `some` and `count` over review and check items of the manifest version. Evidence validity after a revocation is R3's. |
| 14 | Sole active admin | Membership | If a rule needs it for a present review qualification, membership issues a grant or commitment that says so, under R3's contract. A lane cannot count admins. |
| 15 | Last admin | Membership | Local to membership. |
| 16 | Compromised revocation: all evidence by the key, every unlanded proposal, every active landing | Membership sends; each lane applies | Delivery to scopes that hold a grant from that key. Each lane judges its own evidence again on receipt. Order against a reservation is R3's race. |
| 17 | Check binding: the active landings and snapshots for a commit | Pull request lane | A check names a manifest version by fact reference and the tree by ID. |
| 18 | Reviews carried at propose; earlier heads | Pull request lane | Earlier manifest versions are local items. Any carry is a rule over local items. |
| 19 | Rule inputs: actor's teams; counts of admins and members | Each scope | Teams arrive in the grant. Roster-wide counts are not available outside membership. |
| 20 | Land-rule input at land and at reservation | Pull request lane; destination | Eligibility is judged in the lane and frozen in a commitment. R3. |
| 21 | Sealed obligation effects, before and after | Lane | Effects are derived by the fold from local items. |
| 22 | Historical opening kinds | None | A scope has one definition. |
| 23 | Reservation slot free; publication number | Destination | Local to the destination. |
| 24 | Request nonce unseen | Each scope that takes signed requests | Local, with a time bound. R3 decides whether such requests remain. |
| 25 | Workspace request kinds | Lane | The hold capability of the pinned definition. |
| 26 | Rate-limit windows | The front of directory and membership | In memory. It decides only whether to serve. |
| 27 | Operation ID unused; attention numbering | Each scope | Allocated in the commit. |
| 28 | Notify directory: all members and teams | Lane sends; inbox resolves | A lane notifies party slots. It decides who is told, not what took effect. |

### 8.3 State read during evaluation and reused at commit

The inventory lists 21 such reads. They were safe only because of the
whole-head check. Where they are local they stay safe, because the check
stays and the commit derives guards and effects again. Three groups
needed more:

| Group | Earlier behavior | Rule here |
|---|---|---|
| Mutable state read before the snapshot and never again: lane existence, earlier heads, the recorded main, the proposed configuration | A change between the read and the snapshot was not noticed. | Only immutable inputs and configuration may be read before the snapshot (section 5.1). |
| State that changed with no entry: previews, check snapshots, a landing's integration and readiness, the recorded main | The head did not move when they changed. | Every such change is an entry, or no guard may read it. |
| The clock | An entry could be stamped earlier than it took effect; expiry of other lanes was not tested at the boundary. | One reading in the commit; newly due transitions applied first; effects derived from it. |

### 8.4 Writers that were not acts, and values built from positions

The earlier Room sealed reservation, landing outcomes, land evaluation,
check carry, policy activation and obligation recomputation outside its
admission queue, some with a narrower check than the head check. Here
every writer uses section 5.

Lane, delegation, invitation and policy identifiers were entry IDs of
the one Room log, and operation IDs were "head plus one" computed during
evaluation. Here a scope's ID comes from its seed; an item's ID is a
`seq` that is meaningful only inside its scope; an operation ID is
allocated in the commit; and outside a scope a position appears only
inside a full fact reference.

### 8.5 Two findings that change behavior

**No exclusive resource extent across lanes.** The earlier overlap guard
scanned every held lane. It was the one guard that needed the whole
repository in one queue. The choice here is deliberate: independent
lanes do not wait on each other, and in exchange two lanes may work on
the same paths at once.

What still holds: each lane's workspace is its own fork, so two lanes
never share a physical workspace; a hold fences its own holder and
epoch; and a real conflict is found when contributions are assembled,
where it is reported against the exact versions.

What does not hold: nothing stops overlapping work from starting. The
directory's index can show overlap as information. That index is a
copy and may be stale. It is never write authority, and no guard reads
it.

R2 must show, for the demonstration, independent forks, same-path
conflict reporting at assembly, and no shared workspace. An application
that needs exclusivity would ask a registry scope for a commitment.

**No roster-wide counts in a lane's rules.** A rule that needs "the only
active admin" gets it as a grant or commitment from membership, under
R3. A rule that needs another count is a finding.

## 9. Reading, retention and replay

### 9.1 Reads

```ts
type Read<T> =
  | { ok: true; at: { seq: number; hash: Digest }; value: T; complete: boolean; next?: Cursor }
  | { ok: false; reason: "not-found" | "wrong-incarnation" | "forbidden" | "scope-provisional"
        | "unsupported-definition" | "history-unavailable" | "too-large" | "unavailable";
      detail?: FactRef | ScopeRef };
```

- Every list is a page with a stated maximum and a cursor. `complete:
  false` says more exists or part could not be produced.
- A summary lists **live** items only. It gives retained final items as
  exact counts, for each item type and state, from the index of section
  6.5. It does not list them. They are read by pages.
- A reader may conclude "no such item", or a complete count, only from
  an exact count of that index at `at`, or from every page read at one
  `at`. A response with `complete: false`, a scan that stopped, or
  pages read at different positions establish neither.
- A read of state is a statement about `at`. That is the "last
  confirmed position" a page shows for a lane.
- A watcher follows one scope by `seq`. A page over several scopes holds
  one cursor each. Sorting scopes by wall-clock time is presentation.
- Repository lists come from the directory's index. Each row carries
  the fact it was built from and is marked as a projection.

| Read | Bound |
|---|---|
| Scope summary: live items with their states and parties; and an exact count of items for each type and state, retained final items included | One response. Each type's `max` bounds its live items. The counts are bounded by the definition's types and states. |
| Retained final items of one type | A page of 100, with a cursor. Their total is not bounded by `max`; the bound is owed to R4. |
| History page | 200 entries or 1 MiB. |
| One entry by `seq` | 256 KiB. |
| Comments page | 100. |
| Directory index page | 100 rows. |
| Outbox status | 100 duties. Each row gives the duty's ID, its target and class, and, once one exists, the entry that recorded its result or its diagnosis, with the outcome and the reason. Since revision 11 a row may also show transport's bookkeeping for the send: whether it is held, its attempts and its acknowledgment. Those are marked as bookkeeping, and no judgment reads them (section 7.4). |
| Outbox status of one send, by its duty ID. New in revision 11 (I1 delta 134). | One row of the outbox status. |
| History as stored. New in revision 11 (I1 delta 119). | The bounds of a history page. Each entry is given as its canonical bytes, with the hash that the service holds for it, and with the scope's reference and its definition as the service states them. A reader hashes the bytes itself before it reads the content. |
| One retained input, by its kind and its digest. New in revision 11 (I1 delta 119). | One input. The bound must be no smaller than the largest bound in section 17.1's table of bytes. An input that cannot be read cannot be replayed, and its replay is `incomplete`. I1 holds 1 MiB as a temporary value. A text that a tombstone removed is answered `not-found`, with the tombstone's fact as `detail`. |
| Relationship copies of one name | A page of 100. |
| Capability records of one kind | A page of 100, and exact counts for each kind and state in the summary. |
| Settlement of one signed intent | One receipt, or `not-found` with the position and what "Settlement, exactly" lists. |
| Preparation status of one signed intent | The scope's preparation entries for that intent: at most one for each capability step. |
| Hold status | One answer for one hold. "A read that reads the clock", below. |

Each read is bounded. A whole replay is many reads and is not bounded
by this section; its total work is R4's to budget. A bound is on what
a read takes into memory, and not only on what it returns. A read
asks the store for a size first, and answers `too-large` before it
loads bytes past the bound (I1 delta 148). Section 9.6 says what a
transport may hand to its caller as the answer of a read. The two
reads that a verifier uses, the history as stored and one retained
input, are reads like any other. Each is behind the check of its
reader, under its own name. A retained input may be a copy of another
scope's entry. Whether a reader of this scope may read it is R3's to
decide, with what authenticates a reader (section 15.6e, entry 111).

File, comparison and commit reads for a pull request follow the bounds
of the proposal-reads design N1, addressed by manifest version. R2
states them.

**Settlement, exactly. This answers R2 section 10.1.1.** The caller
presents the exact signed intent to the scope it is addressed to. The
scope checks the signature and the address, and reads its idempotency
index, which is exact at the head.

```ts
interface Head { seq: number; hash: Digest }
type Settlement =
  | { found: true;  at: Head; receipt: Receipt }
  | { found: false; at: Head;                       // `not-found`: no entry for this intent through `at`
      terminal: TerminalBasis | null;               // why none can follow, or null
      preparation: readonly PreparationStatus[];
      retryAfter?: number }                         // seconds, when a recorded time may make it terminal
  | { ok: false; reason: "bad-intent" | "misaddressed" | "wrong-incarnation" | "forbidden"
        | "scope-provisional" | "history-unavailable" | "unavailable" };
interface PreparationStatus {
  entry: FactRef; capability: CapabilityName; step: string;
  operations: readonly { operation: OperationId; kind: string; state: "settled" | "pending" | "unknown" }[];
  records: readonly { kind: string; key: readonly FieldValue[]; state: string }[];
}
```

- **`not-found` is stated at a position.** It says that this scope's
  history, through the head `at`, holds no entry for this intent. The
  index is complete at that head, so this is complete evidence of
  absence at that position. It says nothing about a later position.
- **When absence is terminal.** Only when a fact that the history
  already records makes every later admission impossible. There are
  four such facts.

  | `terminal` | The recorded fact | Why nothing later undoes it |
  |---|---|---|
  | `expired` | The head entry's time is at or past the intent's `notAfter`. | An entry's time is never earlier than the one before. An act is judged against the time of its own entry and is never written clamped (section 4.2). So every later act entry has a time at or past `notAfter`. |
  | `revision-moved` | An item that the intent's `expected` names has a higher revision now. | A revision only rises. |
  | `key-used` | A sealed entry holds the same idempotency key and actor with another intent digest. | The key stays with the first for the life of the scope. |
  | `scope-refused` | The scope's genesis was refused. | Such a scope admits nothing, ever. |

- **The clock alone is not such a fact.** A reading that no entry
  holds is not recorded, and section 5.3 lets a later reading be
  lower. So a scope that has written nothing since the intent was
  signed does not answer "none can follow" from its clock. It can make
  the absence terminal by recording the time: when the intent is not
  found, no other basis holds, and the scope's clock reads at or past
  `notAfter`, the scope may write a checkpoint entry, through an
  ordinary turn with its drain. If that entry's time is the reading,
  not clamped, the head's time is then at or past `notAfter`, and the
  read is answered `expired` from the new head. The caller chose
  nothing in that entry and gained no write. The scope writes at most
  one such checkpoint in a stated interval, and none when it has no
  capacity for one (section 17.2: the checkpoint is new work while
  another duty is pending); it then answers `terminal: null` with
  `retryAfter`. Proposed interval: 60 seconds, not measured.
- **A refusal is never a settlement answer.** The scope keeps no
  refusals. A refusal that a caller saw was true of one head.
- **Preparation.** With `not-found` the scope reports its own
  preparation entries for that intent (section 5.5): each operation as
  `settled`, `pending` while an attempt has no outcome, or `unknown`
  while an attempt's latest outcome is unknown; and each record with
  its state. An empty list says that this scope prepared nothing. It
  does not say that no other scope did.
- **Preparation in another scope.** An intent that names a hold in
  another lane was prepared there. The same read, "preparation status",
  is offered by every scope: a caller presents the exact signed intent
  and gets that scope's `PreparationStatus` list. It admits nothing.
- **A scope asks too.** A scope that holds provisional records for an
  intent addressed elsewhere asks that scope for settlement, with the
  signed intent it retained. A receipt, or a terminal `not-found`, is
  recorded as a `settlement` entry and moves the records on (section
  5.5). A `not-found` that is not terminal records nothing.

**A read that reads the clock. This answers part of R3's points O8 and
O10.** Hold status answers whether one hold is held now: its state is
not final, its end time is later than the scope's clock reading, and
that reading is not earlier than the previous entry's time. It answers
"not held" otherwise, whether or not the timed entry is written yet.
The answer carries the head and the hold's epoch.

- This read is not a statement about a position only: it also depends
  on the answering scope's clock. So it is never a judgment input. No
  scope's entry retains it as authority, and no guard reads it. An
  agent runtime uses it to fence itself (R3 section 5.2).
- A session read, a send on a stream and this read are answers and not
  entries. Section 5.3 rules on entries. R3's rule that these three
  stay closed while the clock is behind is outside section 5.3 and
  does not conflict with it.

### 9.2 Retention

A scope retains, for as long as its history is retained:

- its entries;
- its definition's bytes, by digest;
- the bytes of each other declared definition of its named closure,
  by digest, from its genesis; and, in a platform scope, of each
  definition that an input names for a creation, with that
  definition's closure (section 7.2);
- the bytes of every foreign entry in a `uses`, by content digest.
  The definition name that was read with it is in the `FactUse`
  itself (section 4.1);
- every delivered message;
- each rule evaluation's inputs and result;
- each outcome's evidence;
- the bytes of each detached text, by digest, until a `redact` effect
  removes them (section 6.6);
- the bytes of each snapshot that an ancestry record names, by digest
  (section 16.4);
- the signed intent of each preparation entry.

A retained input is kept under its digest and that digest's byte
domain. One digest value under two domains is two inputs.

**The kinds `value` and `snapshot`. New in revision 19** (I3 deltas EM4
and EL7). Section 9.6 names four kinds of retained input that are kept
apart from their entry: `definition`, `entry`, `rule` and `text`. Two
more are named here.

- `value`: a value beside an intent (section 6.2). Its bytes are the
  value's canonical JSON. It is kept under its domain and its digest.
  The record states the domain in a member `domain`, because the kind
  alone does not give it. Each other kind has one domain, so no other
  kind states the member. A value in `artroom-definition-1` is a
  definition, and is kept under the kind `definition`: one domain and
  one digest are one input. A read of one value asks by the kind, the
  domain and the digest.
- `snapshot`: the snapshot of staged refs that an ancestry record names
  (section 16.4), under its digest in `artroom-snapshot-1`. The name is
  as the I3 source has it. How the bytes reach the scope is the
  capability's.
- A replay that lacks the bytes of either is `incomplete`, as for every
  retained input. By its deltas note, the I3 source at `4f771d90` keeps
  no value, and its replay answers `mismatch` for an entry whose rule
  read one. That is not this rule. Row I3-33 of section 11.13 owes the
  change.

**A retained text, exactly. New in revision 13** (I2 delta DJ7). The
kind is `text`. The bytes are the text as one JSON string in canonical
form, and the digest is in the domain `artroom-text-1`. A scope keeps a
text with every entry whose input names it in a declared detached field,
applied or refused (section 6.2). It holds the text until an entry
redacts that digest (section 6.6). A read of the retained input returns
the bytes, and the reader checks the digest again. Two limits follow.
Both are stated, and neither is repaired here.

- A text that no slot holds is removed by no form. A `redact` effect
  names a slot. A text that a refused delivery names, or that a field
  carries and no effect copies into a slot, is in no slot. The body that
  `add-concern` sends to the concern's lane is such a text in the parent
  lane. One thing follows from the rule that a redaction is by digest:
  an act that carries the same text into a slot, and then a redaction of
  that slot, remove it. That is a consequence. It is not a form that was
  designed for the purpose. Point R1-51.
- How long a text is kept before a redaction is allowed, what a backup
  or an export still holds, and every number, are R4's, as section 6.10
  says.

These are retained inputs, not a cache. If one is missing, a replay of
that scope answers `incomplete` and makes no claim of full replay.
Retained bytes that no longer hash to the digest they are kept under
are treated as missing: the replay answers `incomplete` and lists the
reference under `dependencies.missing`. A detached text that a
tombstone entry removed is not missing. It is reported as redacted.

A retained copy of one foreign entry lets this scope's own judgment be
derived again. It does not prove that the source admitted that entry:
that needs the source's history up to it, or an anchor (section 9.4).
So a full replay of one scope depends on the histories of the scopes it
used, for as long as it is to be replayable. How long each source is
kept, and how a source is exported before it is retired so that its
consumers stay replayable, is a retention dependency between scopes
that R4 must specify. Where a source is gone and no anchor is given,
the report is `incomplete`.

The folded state that a checkpoint digests is one value: the scope's
record with its head; its items; the counts that are not zero; its
relationship copies; its capability records; the accepted keys; the
requests it sent, with their results; the deliveries it consumed; its
held duties; its operations with their attempts; and its index of
preparation entries. Each list is in the order of its key. The digest
is in the domain `artroom-state-1`. What is due and what is reserved
are derived from that value and are not part of it. Since revision 13
the value also holds, for each slot that holds a detached text, the
digests that the slot has held and that no entry has redacted (section
6.6; I2 delta DJ8). The I2 source has that member, so its state
digests differ from those of I1's source.

A checkpoint entry names a `through` sequence and a digest of the folded
state. It lets a reader start there when it trusts it. It is not proof
of the prefix. A sealed segment, the entries between two checkpoints in
canonical JSON lines with the retained inputs they name, is the export
form.

In the first version a scope keeps everything in its own storage and
nothing is evicted.

**Budgets must leave room to settle.** A scope that reaches its budget
refuses new acts with `scope-full`. It must still be able to record a
hold's end, a revocation, a cleanup, a confirmed outside result and an
unknown duty. So the budget reserves capacity for timed, delivery,
outcome and checkpoint entries. Section 17 says how: every pending duty
reserves, when it is created, what its settlement needs, in entries,
items, records, pending requests and bytes, and the bytes include the
inputs that the settlement newly retains. The reservation is of the
duty's whole closure, and one closing checkpoint is reserved for the
scope (section 17.2). A reserve of one fixed size
does not do this (section 17.3a). The numbers,
backpressure on senders, continuation of a bounded export, and what a
full lane does next are R4's. This contract depends on them.

**Reset.** A deployment may be reset before production. It may not be
reset while any outside effect or credential is unsettled, or while any
request stands at `delivery-unavailable`. Delivered duties are not
enough: the settlement R3 defines must be complete.

### 9.3 What each kind of entry means in replay

| Input | The verifier derives or checks | It cannot check |
|---|---|---|
| Genesis | The scope ID is the seed's digest. For a founding register, the one scope with no creator: the installing intent's signature, and that its digest is the seed's cause. For a child: the source entry exists in the creator's history and contains this seed at this ordinal with this message; and the cause matches the source entry by the kind of that entry, as section 7.2's table of causes says: an act's intent digest, a delivery's delivery cause digest, built from that delivery's source fact, ordinal and message digest, a genesis's seed digest, or, for a source entry that is an outcome, the intent digest of the act that opened its operation, each in its own byte domain. That the input's `kind` is the genesis act of the pinned definition; another value is a `mismatch`, `genesis-kind` (section 4.1; added before the review of revision 12). The genesis act's guards and effects. That the pinned definition passes validation, so its genesis act opens no timed item (section 6.4); a history whose genesis opens one is invalid, `genesis-timed`. That the scope retains every definition of its named closure, each under its digest (section 7.2). That no entry but the confirmation follows a provisional genesis, and none follows a refused one. | That the incarnation was minted once. That a held duty was not dispatched before the confirmation. |
| Act | The signature; `notAfter` against the entry's time; that the entry is not clamped; that no earlier entry holds the same key and actor; expected revisions; each local fact against this scope's own entry; the one grant judged, against the observation it retains (section 16.1); every guard and effect again, in the order of section 4.2; each rule from its text in the pinned definition and its retained inputs; each presented fact; the sends, their order and their bounds. | That the read behind an observation was made, and when: reported as `trusted: observation-read` (section 16.1). |
| Delivery of a request | The source entry exists and contains that send with that message digest. The message's fields against the handler's declared types. Each part that a guard reads from the source entry or from a fetched fact, from the retained bytes. The handler's guards and effects, the item it opens if any, and the capability effects. For a refused request that a capability's count of decisions binds: that the entry holds that one `record` effect and no other (section 6.11). The decision: `applied`, `refused`, or `superseded` when a held revision is not lower. For a `relate`, that the source entry has no other `relate` send with the same key. The one result it sends. | When it was delivered. |
| Delivery of a result | That its `of` is a send of this scope; that its source is the entry that decided that request, in the scope and incarnation the request addressed; the clause that ran, including `conflict` against a held incarnation. | When it was delivered. |
| Delivery of a confirmation | That the scope was provisional; that the source is its creator's entry recording this genesis's result; that the scope is active from that entry and from no earlier one; that a repeat added nothing. | Nothing further. |
| Delivery of an advisory | That the source entry contains that send with that message digest; the effects the receiver's own definition gives it, such as an index row or an attention item. An advisory sets nothing that a guard of another scope reads. That the entry sends nothing. | When it was delivered. |
| Diagnosis | That it names a send of this scope with no recorded result; that the finding follows from the log it carries: `undelivered` only when every attempt was a routing refusal; that no clause ran for `delivery-unavailable`. | That the log is what happened, that it covers every dispatch, or that the remote did not execute. The log is the sender's own record and is reported as trusted. |
| Timed | The item held that deadline under that rule; the entry's time is not before it and is not clamped; no transition earlier in the order of section 5.2 was due at that time; the rule's effects. | That the clock was right. |
| Outcome | From revision 16: that the input's `owner` and `kind` are those of the `operation` effect that opened the operation. The operation and attempt were opened by an earlier entry. At most two outcome entries name one attempt, and a second follows only an `unknown`. `unknown` has the basis `none`, and no other result has it. The evidence is well formed for its owner. `selected` is true exactly when the result is `confirmed`, no earlier outcome of the operation is selected, and the owner's local guard holds. The next attempt is opened exactly when section 4.3 allows it. The record effects that the owner derives from the evidence. For a Git publication, that the commit is reachable in the repository as read now. For an ancestry check, the row of section 16.4. | That the outside effect happened when stated. That an `unknown` one did not happen. That an answer was that attempt's own: the report names the owner's authentication as trusted. |
| Preparation. New in revision 8. | The signature; `notAfter` against the entry's time; that the entry is not clamped; the grant and its observation; the capability's guards for the step, from local state; that no earlier preparation entry has the same intent digest, capability and step; the operations and records it derives. That it opens no item and sends nothing. | That the outside effects it opened were dispatched only after it was sealed. |
| Settlement. New in revision 8. | For another scope's answer: by replaying that scope through `at`, that an entry for the intent exists and is `found`; or that none exists through `at` and the stated basis holds at `at`. For this scope's own history: the same, from its own entries. The record effects that follow. | Nothing further, when the other scope's history is replayed. With an anchor instead, the answer is reported as anchored. |
| Checkpoint | The state digest equals the fold through that sequence. | Nothing further. |

Checks that revision 8 adds for the forms of sections 6 and 16:

| Subject | The verifier derives or checks | It cannot check |
|---|---|---|
| A timed rule | That the rule is a key of the pinned definition's `timed`, and that the definition passes the validation of section 6.4. | Nothing further. |
| A capability guard or effect | The guard's result and each `record` effect, from the capability's stated rule, the arguments, the folded records and the entries in `uses`. A capability version it does not implement gives `unsupported-definition`. | Nothing further. |
| A mark of a platform definition. New in revision 15. | The rule's result at its place, again, from the rule of the pinned version and from what section 6.1 lists as given: the fold before the entry, the recorded input, the entry's time, the retained inputs and the scope's own earlier entries. For an act entry with an empty `authority`: that the act's `grant` is a mark, and that its rule passes the signing key. A version of which the verifier lacks the data, or the rule of one mark, gives `unsupported-definition` at the genesis. | That the rules which it ran are the rules of that name and version: reported as `trusted: platform-code`, with the name and the version. |
| An observation | Section 16.1's table: the value against membership's history at the recorded head; `fresh` or `reused`; the run; the window against the entry's time. Since revision 14, for the observation of a grant and for each record of `observed`: the value against the history of the scope that it is `of`, which is membership or the rules scope; that the entry holds exactly the observations that its judgment reads; that a read is retained once in an entry; and the order of heads of section 16.1, "How one observation follows another". | That the read was made, that it began at the stated time, and that no restart came between two entries of one run. |
| An ancestry record | Section 16.4's table: the snapshot's digest and count; the walk from the commit by its parents; the stops; the start and its basis; `published`, from the recorded head; the list F; the row. It reads commits by ID and never reads the refs or the branch as they are now. | That the host returned that list and that head when the staging lane read them: `trusted: staged-ref-read`. |
| A presented entry of another lane | That it is retained in `uses`; that its bytes hash to its reference; the parts that the guards read. With the other lane's history, that the lane admitted it. | Without that history or an anchor: whether the other lane admitted it. The report is then `missing-dependency` for that fact. |
| A fetched entry's definition name. New in revision 11. | When the source is replayed: that the `under` of each `FactUse` is the name of the definition that the source's genesis pins (section 6.1). Another name is a `mismatch`. | With an anchor in place of the source's history: the name. It is reported under `anchor`. |
| The kind of a fetched genesis entry. Added to revision 12 before its review. | The using entry's guard, again, from the retained bytes of the genesis entry, which hold the kind (section 6.2). When the source is replayed: the check of the Genesis row above, in the source's own replay. A kind that is not the genesis act of the definition which the source pins is a `mismatch`, `genesis-kind`, at the source's genesis. | With an anchor in place of the source's history: that the recorded kind is the genesis act of the source's definition. It is taken on trust with the anchor, as the whole entry is. |
| A detached text | That the retained bytes hash to the digest in the signed intent. For a text that a tombstone removed: the tombstone's grant, and that every digest it lists was held by that slot. Since revision 13: a tombstone answers for every earlier entry of its scope that names a digest which it lists, whatever field or slot named it, and for no later entry (section 6.6). Also that no pending request of the scope carried a listed text at the tombstone's position, and that no entry made a send of a text that the scope did not hold. The text is reported as "redacted, not derived again" and is listed in the report. | Anything that needs the removed bytes. |
| Capacity | The amounts used and reserved in each dimension at each entry, from the history, the retained inputs and the pinned definition (section 17.1). That every entry which draws on a reservation is a settling entry of a duty that was pending, and that it drew no more than that duty had reserved. No amount is read from transport's acknowledgments, which a verifier does not hold. | That a refusal `scope-full` matched the deployment's budget: the budget is configuration, reported as trusted. The bytes used at a position where a text that was later redacted was still held: its size went with its bytes. |

Changed in revision 20, in two rows of this table. The row "An
observation" says that the entry holds exactly the observations that
its judgment reads. From this revision it holds exactly those of the
subjects that its rows of `observes` give, and the verifier derives
that list (section 16.1, "The subjects that an entry observes"). The
row "Capacity" stands, and under a definition that states `holds` the
amounts include what each item still holds (section 17.2a).

Four checks apply to every entry, whatever its input. Before an entry
that is not timed, no deadline at or before the entry's time is
unapplied (section 5.2). The entry's sends contain no two `relate`
sends for one key (section 6.4). Each range guard is derived over every
item it covers, live and retained final, in the folded state (section
6.5). A guard that the runtime completed by witnesses has the same
result there. The fourth is new in revision 11 (I1 delta 149): no
entry is larger than the entry size of the bounds that the replay was
given (section 7.5). A larger entry is a `mismatch` at that entry,
before it is derived or folded. The runtime seals no such entry under
those bounds, also when its derivation would agree. This check is
apart from the traversal's byte limit, which gives `incomplete`
(section 9.4). Integrity mode reads no bounds and does not make it.

**How a judgment is derived again. New in revision 11** (I1 deltas
122 and 123). A verifier runs the judgment of each entry as the
runtime's commit does (section 5.2, step 6.4), with these readings.

| What the commit read | What the verifier uses |
|---|---|
| The clock | The entry's recorded time. For a clamped entry the reading was not recorded. The verifier judges with the clock behind, as of the recorded time. An entry that judges time cannot then be derived, which is a `mismatch` (section 5.3). |
| Local state | The fold of the entries before it, from the genesis. |
| Each foreign entry | The retained copy that the entry's `uses` names, after its bytes are checked against the `content` digest. |
| A delivery's address | The address that the retained source entry's send has at that ordinal. |
| The origin of a result or of a diagnosis | This scope's own entry, which is already checked. |
| Each rule result | The rule's text, evaluated again over the retained input, whose bytes must hash to the recorded digest. The judgment then checks that the digest is of what the rule reads in that commit (section 6.5). |
| The bounds of sections 6.1 and 7.5 | Those that the caller gives. They are configuration, and they are reported under `bounds` (section 9.5). The work limit of one guard is not applied. |
| The grant | The observation that the entry retains (section 16.1). I1 takes each recorded grant as current, because the membership contract is not built. That is I1's stated omission, and its report says so under `trusts`. |

The verifier compares what it derives with what the entry records:
the input, `uses`, `prepared`, `effects` and `sends`, and then the
whole entry. A judgment that would write nothing, or that fails, is a
`mismatch` at that entry.

Two things follow for a provisional scope. No timed entry comes before
the confirmation, because none but the confirmation follows a
provisional genesis. And the first check holds for the confirmation's
entry, because no item holds a deadline before it.

The turn's budget leaves nothing in the history. No entry records a
dropped selection or a `busy` outcome, so replay neither sees nor
checks them. Timed entries that a turn committed before it ended
`busy` are ordinary entries. They are kept (section 5.2) and replay
checks them like any other. The checks above hold however a turn ended.

**Made exact in revision 13, from the I2 source choices.** Each point
names the entries of the I2 deltas note that it answers (section 15.6l).
Each is a rule of this contract from this revision, for the reason that
the point gives. None changes an entry that the I2 source at `744f2447`
writes, unless the point says so.

- **DJ10.** How a verifier matches a text to its tombstone. It asks for
  each text that an entry's input names (section 6.2), and checks it
  against its digest. One that is not found, or whose bytes are not that
  text, is owed. A later entry of the same scope answers for it when a
  `redact` effect of that entry lists its digest. The report's
  `redacted` then holds one row for that effect, with the tombstone, the
  item and the slot. The judge derives the list of each `redact` effect
  again from the folded state, and that is the check that every digest
  it lists was held by that slot. A scope that still owes a text is read
  on to its head, because a source scope is otherwise read only as far
  as a reference needs. A text that is still owed then makes the result
  `incomplete`, at the entry that names it. A tombstone that is earlier
  than the entry which names a text answers nothing for it: that entry
  kept the bytes again. The report lists, under `trusts`, that the bytes
  of a redacted text were the text that its digest names and were within
  their field's bound. The report of an integrity run has an empty
  `redacted`.

**Made exact in revision 14.** Two points. The first answers the I3
deltas note, entry E13 (section 15.6n).

- **E13.** A verifier that does not derive a capability step answers
  `unsupported-definition` at the first entry of that step: a
  `preparation` entry, or an outcome entry of an operation that such an
  entry opened. It is never `consistent`, and its coverage ends before
  that entry. The answer at the genesis stays for a form that the pinned
  definition's own bytes use (sections 6.1 and 9.4). The two differ
  because a step is no form of the definition's bytes: whether a history
  holds a preparation of a step is not a function of the definition, and
  a definition that uses only the item form of `hold@1` passes at its
  genesis in a verifier that has no code for a step. A runtime that has
  no code for a step writes no preparation entry for it, because only
  the capability's code writes one (section 5.5).
- **An input that retains observations.** For an `act`, a delivery of a
  result and an `outcome`, the verifier takes `observed` from the
  recorded input, as it takes a grant's observation, and makes the
  checks of section 16.1 for each record. An input of another type that
  holds the member is no entry. An entry that holds an observation which
  its judgment does not read, or lacks one that it reads, is a
  `mismatch`.

**Made exact in revision 15.** Two points, for platform code (section
6.1).

- **A history under a platform definition.** A verifier derives each
  entry of it with the data and the rules of the pinned version, in the
  order of section 4.2, and compares what it derives with what the entry
  records, as for any entry. It gives a rule only what section 6.1
  lists. All of that is in the history, in the retained inputs or in the
  caller's bounds. So the same version derives the same bytes. A
  verifier that lacks the version, or the rule of one mark of its data,
  answers `unsupported-definition` at the genesis, and its coverage ends
  before it. That differs from a capability step (point E13, above),
  because every mark is in the data: whether a history can hold an entry
  of a rule is a function of the definition. It is never `consistent`.
- **What it trusts.** A platform definition is pinned by a name and a
  version, and no digest names its rules. So a verifier cannot show that
  the rules which it holds are the ones that the runtime ran. It shows
  that they derive the same bytes. The report says so under `trusts`,
  with the label `platform-code` and the name and version. An entry that
  the rules of the verifier do not derive is a `mismatch`, as for any
  entry: the report does not say which of the two has the fault.
- **Where a version's scopes record a reference. Confirmed in revision
  20** (I3 delta EU6; the authority note's ask 5). A version of a
  platform definition has code that says where its scopes record their
  membership reference and their rules reference: in the genesis, or as
  a fixed ID whose incarnation the first retained observation gives
  (section 16.1). That code is of the version, beside its rules. A
  verifier needs it as it needs the rules, and reports it under the
  same label, `platform-code`, with the name and the version. So is the
  code that gives the value of an observation (section 15.6s, entry
  EM25).

### 9.4 Proof of a foreign fact

An entry whose bytes hash to the hash in a reference is consistent. That
alone does not show that the source scope admitted it. To rely on a
foreign fact, a verifier does one of two things:

- **Replay the source** up to that `seq`, under the source's own
  genesis, definition and authority, recursively; or
- **Use an anchor**: a head or receipt for the source scope that the
  caller supplies and says it trusts, or one found in the repository
  (section 9.5).

**What a verifier must bring.** A history that is consistent with
itself shows nothing about which service wrote it. A verifier needs
two things that it did not get from the service it is checking: the
**expected scope ID**, so that it knows which scope it means to
verify, and a **known head or anchor** for that scope. With both, the
seed check ties the history to that ID, and the head ties the history
to one that the caller already trusts. Without the first, the report
is about whatever scope was served. Without the second, the report
lists the service's own answer under `trusts`, and says nothing about
freshness or equivocation (section 9.5). The word "verified" is not
used for either case.

**A known head, exactly. New in revision 11** (I1 delta 120). With a
known head, the verifier checks the whole history that the service
serves, through the service's own head, and not only up to the known
head. A served history that ends before the known head is a
`mismatch` at the service's head: the caller knows of an entry that
the service no longer shows. Another entry at the known position is a
`mismatch` at that entry. With no known head, the report lists
`service-head` under `trusts`. The scope ID is checked as the digest
of the genesis's seed in both modes.

**What an anchor covers. New in revision 11** (I1 delta 124). An
anchor covers the entry that it names, by scope, position and hash.
By itself it shows nothing about an earlier entry of that scope. An
earlier entry is covered only when the verifier also holds the
entries from it to the anchor and has checked each `prev`. I1 does
not use an anchor that way. For a fact with no anchor of its own, the
source is replayed from its genesis up to that entry. The hash of the
source's entry at that position is compared with the reference before
the entry's content is read, so a changed source entry is reported at
the entry that used it. The source's incarnation and kind must be the
reference's. A reference to an entry of a scope that is itself being
checked, at a position that the check has not reached, is a circle.
A circle cannot exist in a valid history (section 3), so it is a
`mismatch`.

**An exported source.** A source that was exported before it was
retired is replayed from its sealed segments (section 9.2). A set of
segments that covers the source from its genesis through the entry
needed, with the retained inputs they name, is replayed as that
source's history. A set that does not reach back to the genesis, or
lacks a retained input, gives `incomplete`. Segments show what a
history contained. They do not show that it is the history the service
showed its other readers: without a head from elsewhere that is the
last limit of section 9.5.

An anchor is trusted by the caller who supplies it and by nobody else.
A wrong anchor gives a wrong report for that caller. Bytes that do not
parse, or do not hash to the value named, are rejected before anything
in them is read.

Traversal is bounded. A verifier is given limits on scopes, entries,
bytes and depth. It checks each entry's canonical bytes and hash before
it reads the content. It verifies each scope once, as far as the highest
`seq` needed, however many references name it. A circle of facts cannot
exist (section 3). Two scopes may refer to each other at different
positions; the verifier advances each prefix as needed. A source it
cannot read is `missing-dependency`. A limit reached is `incomplete`,
with what was covered.

**What depth counts, in both phases. New in revision 14** (I2 deltas DR4
and DR10). The paragraph above names a limit on depth and does not say
what it counts. The builder decided it for the I2 source, and it is
stated here.

- *Depth.* The target is at depth 0. The depth of any other scope is the
  least number of foreign facts on a chain from the target to it, among
  the chains that the traversal followed. A source that an entry of a
  scope at depth d uses is at depth d + 1, or less when a shorter chain
  reaches it.
- *The limit.* A fact whose source would lie past the limit is not
  followed. The result is `incomplete`, named at the entry that used the
  fact. An anchored fact is not followed, and adds no depth.
- *Two phases.* A traversal first replays the target, and each source as
  far as a reference needs. It then settles the texts that are owed
  (section 9.3, point DJ10): a scope that owes a text is read on to its
  head, because its tombstone may be later than the entry that a
  reference needed.
- *The count goes through the settlement.* A scope is read on at the
  depth at which the traversal reached it. A fact that one of its later
  entries uses is one step further from the target, and the limit
  applies there as in the first phase. A limit on depth, on scopes, on
  entries or on bytes that is reached in the settlement gives
  `incomplete`. It never leaves the result `consistent`.
- *The settlement is closed.* Reading a scope on may prove a fact of a
  scope that was not read before, or read an earlier scope further, and
  either may owe a text. So the settlement goes on until no scope that
  was read owes one. A text that is still owed after its scope was read
  to its head is `incomplete`, at the entry that names it. The
  settlement ends: a round that does not stop the traversal has checked
  at least one more entry, and the entries and the scopes are inside
  their limits.
- *Why.* A limit that held in one phase only would let a chain pass the
  caller's bound in the other, and the report would still say
  `consistent`. Witness 18.37.

The number is R4's. The I2 source's default of 16 is a temporary value.

**What a check can rest on, and what each reads. New in revision 12.**
The commission asks that trust, a known head, an anchor and a whole
replay be kept apart by what they cost. They differ in what is read,
in what is shown and in what is taken on trust. None is a cheaper form
of another. No number is given here. The cost of each is R4's to
measure (its section 8.3), and I1's limits are temporary values.

| What the check rests on | What is read | What it shows | What it takes on trust | What its work grows with |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| The service's answer alone: a receipt that is followed (section 9.6) | One entry of the target | That the service serves an entry with that scope, incarnation, position and hash | That the entry is of the scope's history, and how it was judged | Nothing. It is one bounded read. |
| The target's own chain: integrity mode (section 9.5) | Every entry of the target, as stored | The chain, the hashes and the signatures, and that the scope ID is the digest of the seed | Every judgment. Also `service-head`, when no known head is given. | The entries of the target |
| A known head ("A known head, exactly", above) | Nothing more | Beside either mode: that the history which is served reaches the entry that the caller knows, and holds that entry there | That the caller's head is right | Nothing. It adds a comparison and no read. |
| An anchor for one foreign fact ("What an anchor covers", above) | Nothing of the source | Nothing by itself. It stands in for the replay of the source up to that one entry. | That the source admitted the entry, and the definition name that the using entry records: `anchor` | Nothing. It removes the replay of one source, for one entry. |
| A whole replay (section 9.3) | Every entry of the target and its retained inputs. For each foreign fact with no anchor: the source, from its genesis through that entry, and so on for what the source used. | Every judgment of the target, derived again | The labels of section 9.5 that its entries rest on | The entries and the retained inputs of the target and of every scope that it reaches. Nothing here bounds that. A limit that is reached gives `incomplete`. |

- A known head and an anchor are different things. A known head is
  about the target, and it is checked against the whole history that
  is served. An anchor is about a source, and it is used in place of a
  history.
- Neither makes a judgment more true. A known head guards against a
  history that was cut short, or changed at that position. An anchor
  moves a trust from the service to the caller.
- A checkpoint entry is one more thing to rest on only for a reader
  that trusts it (section 9.2). I1 starts every replay at the genesis,
  so it has no such case.
- Following a receipt is the only one of these that a client does on
  the path of an act. The others are a verifier's.

**The result for each kind of failure. New in revision 11** (I1
deltas 125 to 127, 146 and 147).

| What is found | Result | Named at |
|---|---|---|
| A source history that cannot be read, or that ends before the entry named | `missing-dependency` | The entry that used it |
| A source with another entry at that position, or of another incarnation or kind | `mismatch` | The entry that used it |
| A failure inside a source's own replay | That failure's own result | The source's entry |
| A retained input that is missing, or whose bytes are not what its digest names | `incomplete` | The entry that names it |
| A platform definition that the verifier does not implement, a capability form that the pinned definition uses and the verifier does not derive (section 6.1), or a declaration that fails validation under the bounds given | `unsupported-definition` | The genesis. One exception: a genesis that opens a timed item is a `mismatch`, `genesis-timed` (section 9.3). |
| A genesis whose `kind` is not the genesis act of the definition that it pins. Added to revision 12 before its review. | `mismatch`, `genesis-kind` | The genesis |
| A limit of the traversal reached | `incomplete`, with the coverage so far | None. For the limit on depth, since revision 14: the entry that used the fact which was not followed. |
| A `preparation` entry, or an outcome entry of its operation, for a capability step that the verifier does not derive. New in revision 14. | `unsupported-definition` | That entry (section 9.3, point E13) |
| An entry whose `observed` is not exactly what its judgment reads, or whose observation has a lower head than an earlier one of the same subject. New in revision 14. | `mismatch`; for the head, `observation-older` | That entry (section 16.1) |
| A target that cannot be read at all: no reply, a read past its deadline, or a limit that stops its first read | No report. The call fails. | None |

Changed in revision 20, in one row of this table. "Not exactly what its
judgment reads" is now: not exactly the observations of the subjects
that the entry's rows of `observes` give (section 16.1, "The subjects
that an entry observes").

A report states coverage, and with nothing read there is none to
state. So a target that cannot be read is an error of the call, and
not a result. I1's check stops at the first finding, and its report
names that one. That is accepted for I1. A verifier may go on and
report more.

**A named mismatch. New in revision 13.** Two results of
the table have a name beside `mismatch`: `genesis-kind` and
`genesis-timed`. Revision 14 adds a third of this contract's own,
`observation-older`, beside the three that the authority note names
for an observation (section 16.1). The I2 source at `744f2447` puts `genesis-timed` in the
words beside the report, and a later entry of the I2 note, DP3, says the
same of `genesis-kind` (section 11.11). The report carries the name, as the member `name`
(section 9.5). A mismatch to which this contract gives no name has no
such member. A sentence beside the report may say more. It is not part
of the report.

**Every reply is untrusted. New in revision 11** (I1 delta 146). A
verifier counts its limits on the raw bytes of each reply as they
arrive, before anything in the reply is parsed or kept. It stops
reading a reply that passes what is left of its byte limit, or the
bound of that read, and it uses nothing of that reply. A page of the
history is used only if it holds the entries from the position asked,
in order. Coverage lists a scope's entries only when they were
checked to their end, with every fact that they used shown. The
limits are on scopes, entries, bytes and depth. I1's defaults for
