them, its bounds on one page and on one retained input, and its
deadline for one read are temporary values, and each number is R4's
(I1 deltas 126, 146 and 147). I1 starts every replay at the genesis.
It uses no checkpoint as a start, and it builds and reads no sealed
segment (its delta 129). Those are I1's stated limits. Since revision 12
the reader of a reply is one rule for a client and for a verifier
(section 9.6, "The reader of a reply").

### 9.5 Reports, and what replay does not show

A report always states its mode and its coverage.

```ts
interface Report {
  mode: "integrity" | "replay";
  target: FactRef;                          // the head verified through
  coverage: readonly { scope: ScopeRef; from: number; through: number }[];
  anchors: readonly FactRef[];              // heads taken on trust, or none
  dependencies: { verified: number; anchored: number; missing: readonly FactRef[] };
  trusts: readonly string[];                // labels of the table below, and free text such as "delivery times"
  redacted: readonly { tombstone: FactRef; item: number; slot: string }[];   // new in revision 8
  result: "consistent" | "mismatch" | "missing-dependency" | "unsupported-definition" | "incomplete";
  at?: FactRef;                             // the entry a mismatch names
  name?: "genesis-kind" | "genesis-timed";  // the name of a named mismatch; new in revision 13
                                            // revision 21: or "observation-older" | "run-returned" | "observation-not-moved" | "observation-reused" (below)
}
```

`name` is new in revision 13. It is there exactly when
the result is `mismatch` and the failure is one that section 9.4 names.
Revision 11 said that the type does not change, and that a sentence
beside the report is allowed (section 15.6g, row 128). The sentence is
still allowed. The name moves into the report, so that two reports can
be compared without reading words: that is why revision 8 fixed the
labels below. The I2 source puts the name at the start of the sentence:
section 11.11, row 13.

Reconciled in revision 21. The listing gave `name` two values, and said
that it is there exactly when the failure is one that section 9.4 names.
Section 16.1 names four more mismatches, of the order of observations:
`observation-older`, `run-returned`, `observation-not-moved` and
`observation-reused`. A report's `name` is one of the six. It is there
exactly when the result is `mismatch` and the failure is one that
section 9.4 or section 16.1 names. A mismatch of `observed` against the
rows of `observes`, and every other mismatch, has no name, as before.
Row I3-57.

Revision 8 fixes these `trusts` labels, so that two reports can be
compared. A report lists each one that any entry it covers rests on.

| Label | Says that the report took on trust |
|---|---|
| `service-clock` | That each entry's time was a true reading. |
| `observation-read` | That a read of membership or of the rules was made as recorded (section 16.1). |
| `staged-ref-read` | That the Git host returned the recorded snapshot and head (section 16.4). |
| `host-read` | That a read of the outside system, used as an outcome's evidence, returned what was recorded. |
| `own-answer` | That an outcome's answer was that attempt's own, as its owner authenticated it. |
| `attempt-log` | That a sender's attempt log is what happened (section 7.4). |
| `budget` | The deployment's capacity configuration (section 17). |
| `bounds` | The bounds of sections 6.1 and 7.5 that the replay was given. New in revision 11. |
| `service-head` | That the head which the service gave for the target is the scope's head. No known head or receipt was given to check it against (section 9.4). New in revision 11. |
| `anchor` | A head or a receipt that the caller supplied. For an anchored entry, also the definition name that the using entry records (section 9.3). |

- **Integrity** mode checks the chain, the hashes and the actors'
  signatures. Its report says, in words, that no judgment was derived
  again. Plan 016 set that disclosure rule and it is kept. Exactly,
  and new in revision 11 (I1 delta 121), it checks this of the
  target and of no other scope: each entry's bytes hash to the hash
  that the source gives for it; the bytes are canonical JSON in the
  shape of an entry; `seq` and `prev` form one chain; the scope and
  the incarnation are the same throughout; no entry's time is
  earlier than the one before, and a clamped entry has the time of
  the entry before it (section 5.3); the scope ID is the digest of
  the genesis's seed; and the signature of each act and of a
  founding intent holds. A preparation entry carries a signed intent
  too, and owes the same check; I1 has no such entry. It reads no
  definition, no retained input and no source history.
- **Replay** mode derives every guard, effect and send again.
- The word "verified" is not used alone. A result is "consistent" for a
  stated mode, target, coverage and set of trusts.
- **What `target` names when the result is not `consistent`. New in
  revision 11** (I1 delta 128). `target` is the subject that the
  report is about: the head that the check was aiming for. That is
  the known head when one was given, and the service's head
  otherwise. `coverage` says how far the checks reached, and `at`
  names the entry of a mismatch. A verifier may give one sentence
  beside the report, on what it found. Those words are not part of
  the report, and nothing compares them.

**The subject of a replay and its closure. New in revision 9.** This
answers R4's point R4-10, which asks this note to accept or change the
proposal of R4's section 9.5. It is accepted, in this note's types.

- A report's `target` is its exact **subject**: one scope and
  incarnation, through one sequence number and entry hash, such as a
  checkpoint's `through` or the end of a sealed segment.
- The subject's **closure** is the retained inputs that its entries
  name, and nothing else. They are those of section 9.2: the pinned
  definition's bytes; each other declared definition of its named
  closure, and, in a platform scope, each definition that an input
  names for a creation; each foreign entry in a `uses`; each delivered
  message; each rule evaluation's inputs and result; each outcome's
  evidence; each detached text that no tombstone removed; each
  snapshot that an ancestry record names; and the signed intent of
  each preparation entry.
- A report in mode `replay` with the result `consistent` claims that
  every judgment of the subject was derived again from that closure.
- An input that only a later entry names is not in the closure of an
  earlier subject, and never supplies an input that is missing from
  it. The report for the earlier subject stays `incomplete`. A report
  over the longer subject is another report, with its own `target`.
- An input is read by its digest and by the byte domain or kind under
  which its entry names it (section 9.2). Bytes kept under one kind
  are never offered as another.

R4's table in its section 9.5 is the witness, at its boundary B9.

What no mode shows from histories alone:

- that the service's clock was right;
- that a delivery was made when stated;
- that an outside write happened, beyond what can be read from the
  outside system now;
- that the service showed every reader the same history.

The last is equivocation. A verifier that holds a head from elsewhere,
such as a receipt it kept or an anchor in the repository, checks the
history against it. A verifier with no such head is trusting the
service's answer, and its report says so under `trusts`.

**A proposed anchor.** A publication could write a small receipt in the
repository that names the pull request lane's merge fact, which would
anchor the histories that decided a merged result. This note first
proposed writing it in the same push as the branch. The R3 draft
answers the four questions that raised and proposes a second write
after the outcome is confirmed, by its own compare-and-swap, because an
atomic update of two refs is not established for the host. That
proposal is R3's and is not adopted here. Under it the receipt may lag
the branch, and a verifier that finds none reports that. Histories that
led to no publication would stay unanchored.

No replay of any earlier Artroom format exists.

### 9.6 Answers across a transport

New in revision 11 (I1 deltas 130, 133 to 136, 138, 139, 143, 144 and
152). A client reaches a scope through a transport: the service's
routes over HTTP, or a binding to the service. Revision 10 gave each
answer a type. It did not say what a transport may hand to its caller
as that answer. This section is that rule. It gives a client no
authority, and it changes no judgment.

**One result type for each operation.** The operations are the
contract's. The routes, the status codes and the names of the calls
are I1's (section 15.6e, entry 111).

| Operation | Its result type | What a value has |
|---|---|---|
| Submit an act | The four answers of section 4.2 | `accepted`, with a receipt. `refused`, with a reason of section 4.2 and `judgedAt`, the head that it was judged at. `unavailable`, with a reason of the Unavailable class. `mismatch`, with `idempotency-mismatch`. |
| Found a scope with no creator | Three answers | `accepted`, with a receipt. `refused`, with a reason. `unavailable`, with a reason. It has no `mismatch` and no `judgedAt`. |
| Settlement of one signed intent | `Settlement` (section 9.1) | A receipt, with the head. Or `not-found` at a head, with `terminal` and `preparation`. Or a reason of that type. |
| Every read of section 9.1 | `Read<T>`, with the value T of that read | With `ok: true`: `at`, which is a position and a hash; `complete`; the value; and `next` only as a cursor. With `ok: false`: a reason of the `Read` type, and `detail` only as a scope reference or a fact reference. |

A receipt has a whole fact reference, the definition, the intent's
digest or null, the list of effects, the list of duty IDs and `epoch:
0`. A fact reference is whole when it has a scope reference, with its
scope ID, incarnation and kind, and a position and a hash.

**The values of the reads.** I1 moved the shapes that its reads
return into one declared interface. The service implements it, and a
client's transport is a value of it (its delta 130). The shapes are
accepted as the values of these reads. They stay proposals until R2's
pages use them (section 15.6c, entry 92; point R1-41).

```ts
type Status = "provisional" | "active" | "refused";
type Party = MemberRef | readonly MemberRef[] | null;
interface Item { id: number; type: string; state: string; revision: number;
                 opened: Digest | null;              // the hash of the entry that opened it
                 parties: Record<string, Party>;
                 refs: Record<string, FieldValue | null>;
                 values: Record<string, FieldValue | null>;
                 attributed: readonly MemberRef[];   // section 6.7
                 epoch?: number }                    // a hold item, in I1: section 6.8 makes `epoch` a declared slot
interface Summary { scope: ScopeRef; status: Status; definition: Digest | PlatformDefinition; time: Timestamp;
                    items: readonly Item[];          // the live items
                    counts: readonly (readonly [type: string, state: string, n: number])[] }
interface Sealed { entry: Entry; hash: Digest }      // the hash is beside the entry, never inside it
interface Dispatched { at: Timestamp; answer: Attempt["answer"] | "acknowledged" }   // bookkeeping (section 7.4)
interface Duty { duty: DutyId; to: ScopeRef | Seed; class: Message["class"];
                 held: boolean; attempts: readonly Dispatched[]; acknowledged: FactRef | null;   // bookkeeping
                 result: { seq: number; clause: "applied" | "refused" | "superseded" | "conflict" } | null;
                 diagnosis: { seq: number; finding: "undelivered" | "delivery-unavailable" } | null }
interface LogPage { scope: ScopeRef; definition: Digest | PlatformDefinition;
                    entries: readonly { seq: number; hash: Digest; bytes: string }[] }
interface RetainedInput { kind: string; digest: Digest; bytes: string;
                          domain?: string }   // revision 19: stated exactly when `kind` is "value" (section 9.2)
```

- `Duty` is one row of the outbox status. `held`, `attempts` and
  `acknowledged` are transport's bookkeeping. They are shown and
  never judged. `result` and `diagnosis` are read from the history.
- `RetainedInput.kind` is one of the kinds of section 9.2 that are
  kept apart from their entry. I1 has three, `definition`, `entry`
  and `rule`, because it has no detached text and no snapshot yet.
  Revision 13 states the fourth, `text` (section 9.2), and the I2
  source has it.
  Revision 19 names two more, `value` and `snapshot`, and the member
  `domain` of a `value` (section 9.2).
  I1 also returns, with a foreign entry, the definition name that
  its fetcher kept. Under section 4.1 that name is in the using
  entry, and the read need not carry it.
- I1's settlement returns a `Read` of a receipt. The contract's type
  is `Settlement`, which also states the position of a `not-found`,
  whether it is terminal, and the preparation (section 9.1). That is
  the one result type here that the source has to change (section
  11.9). The checks of points 2 and 3 below are a separate matter: the
  source at `97518f68` did not make all of them (section 11.9).

**What a transport hands to its caller.** A reply is an **answer** of
an operation only when it is a value of that operation's result type.
A transport checks all of this before it returns a reply.

1. The discriminant is one that the type names: `answer`, with one of
   its values; `ok`, with `true` or `false`; or, in a `Settlement`,
   `found`, with `true` or `false`.
2. A reason is one that the contract names for that answer. A reason
   that the client does not know is not an answer: the client cannot
   act on it.
3. Every member that the type requires is there and is of its kind,
   to the depth of the contract's own types: the members of a
   receipt, a fact reference, an entry, an item, a summary, a duty, a
   log page and a retained input. A name from a closed set, such as a
   scope kind, a status, a message class or a clause, is one of that
   set. Since revision 12 (I1 deltas 154 and 156): a fixed record has
   exactly the members of its variant, and one with a member that the
   variant does not name is no value of the type. A member that the
   contract types as an identifier or as a fixed text has that form:
   a digest, a scope ID, an incarnation, a key ID, a signature, a
   duty ID, a timestamp, and a position or a count as a whole number
   that is not negative.
4. The check stops at what the contract's types leave to a
   definition: what an effect, an input's fields or a slot holds. A
   caller that reads those reads the scope's definition first
   (below). Since revision 12 the list of what stays opaque is exact
   (I1 delta 154): the body of a request or an advisory; the evidence
   of an outcome; a grant's `within` and `fresh`; the value of each
   field of an intent and of an `index` effect; whether a slot's
   value is of the type that its definition declares; and the stored
   text of an entry in a log page and of a retained input, which a
   reader hashes and parses itself. A slot's value is still checked
   to be a value of some field type (section 6.2).

A reply that fails any of these is **no answer**. So is a reply that
cannot be read, and so is no reply at all.

**The reader of a reply. New in revision 12** (I1 deltas 155 and 157).
Every reply is untrusted, and so is the party that sends it. A
transport that reads a reply as bytes is given two limits before it
sends the request: the most bytes that it will take in, and one
deadline for the whole exchange, which is the request and its whole
reply. A transport that receives a reply as values, over a binding,
has no bytes to count. It owes the deadline all the same: a caller is
never left to wait without end.

1. *The byte limit.* Bytes are counted as they arrive, before anything
   is decoded. At the part of the body that takes the count past the
   limit, the reader stops and asks the body to end. Nothing of that
   reply is joined, decoded or parsed.
2. *A reply that begins after the deadline.* Nothing of its body is
   read.
3. *A read that is pending at the deadline.* The exchange ends at the
   deadline, and does not wait for that read. What the read returns
   later is not kept, and no further read is made.
4. *Nothing is used after the deadline.* The reader looks at the
   deadline after each read, and before it keeps what was read. What
   it held is dropped. Nothing is joined, decoded or parsed.
5. *An empty part of a body.* It carries nothing. It is not kept, and
   it uses none of the byte limit. So only the deadline ends a body
   that sends nothing but empty parts. A reader must let its deadline
   be seen: a body that answers every read at once must not keep the
   deadline from passing.
6. *What the caller gets.* No answer, by the rule below. For a
   founding and for an act, the outcome of the submitted intent is
   unknown. A transport never says that nothing was recorded.

*What this does not promise.* The reader stops what it holds itself.
It cannot stop the other party. A service, or a layer under the
transport, that ignores the request to end may keep its own buffers
and its connection. No bound on a host's memory or on its work follows
from this rule. The two numbers are R4's. I1 holds 4 MiB and 30
seconds as temporary values, and a caller may give others. I1's
transport over a binding has no deadline yet (section 11.10, row 9). A
caller's own signal to cancel is not asked by this contract (point
R1-47). The same reader serves a verifier's reads, and section 9.4
says what a failed read gives there. Witness 18.25.

**What no answer means.** Nothing. It is not a refusal. It is not an
acceptance. It is not evidence that nothing was recorded: the act may
be an entry. The caller does what it does when a reply is lost
(section 12). It sends the same signed intent again, or it asks for
settlement. A client's transport does not send again by itself (I1
delta 133), and no client treats a missing or malformed reply as a
decision.

**What the shape check does not show.** That the answer is true of
this scope's history. A well-formed receipt may name an entry that
the scope does not hold. So a caller that relies on a receipt
**follows** it (I1 deltas 134 and 144). It reads the entry at the
receipt's position and checks it against the whole fact reference:
the entry's scope, kind and position; then its incarnation; then its
hash, which the caller computes from the entry itself. It does not
use the hash that the service sent beside the entry. This is the rule
of section 6.5, that a fact reference is verified whole, applied by a
client. A receipt that fails it is not of this history. Following a
receipt is not a replay. It shows that the service serves an entry
with that hash, and nothing about how the entry was judged (section
9.4).

**A scope's definition.** The summary names the definition's digest.
The client reads the declaration as a retained input, and checks it
against that digest in the domain `artroom-definition-1` (I1 delta
135). A platform definition has no declaration to read.

**What the service answers.** A request that reaches an operation
gets one value of that operation's result type, and nothing else.
Over HTTP the body is that value. The status code repeats it in the
transport's terms, and it is not the answer (I1 deltas 111 and 136).
A request that reaches no operation is refused by the transport in
its own terms, with a reply that is a value of no result type. That
covers a body that is not a JSON object, a body past the bound on a
request, and a path that names no route or is not well-formed (I1
deltas 111, 138 and 139). Such a
request is judged by no scope and records nothing. An act that is
sent to a name which is not a scope ID is one of these: no scope
exists to judge it, and no head to name. It is not answered
`unavailable`, because the same request can never be judged. A read
of such a name is answered `not-found`, which is true of it. A
service bounds a request body in bytes, and counts them while it
reads: a body that declares more is not read, and one that sends
more is cut off (I1 delta 138). The bound must be no smaller than the
largest input that an operation takes, with its detached texts and,
for a founding, the declarations of its closure. I1 holds 1 MiB as a
temporary value, and the number is R4's.

## 10. The three witnesses, in these primitives

The definitions used are illustrations. R2 writes the real lane forms.
Entry names are a scope letter and a `seq`.

### 10.1 An issue exists before any hold

| Entry | In | Input | Guards and results |
|---|---|---|---|
| D.17 | Directory | Act `open-issue`, signed by the requester. | Grant `open-issue`. Allocates #42. Sends the creation request at ordinal 0, with the opener. |
| I.0 | Issue lane | Genesis: the seed, the incarnation, the kind of its genesis act, source D.17 ordinal 0, the creation message. | The genesis act opens one item, `intent`, item 0, in state `open`, with four conditions and fixed party `requester` from the opener. Sends the result `applied`. Provisional. |
| D.18 | Directory | Delivery of that result, from I.0. | #42 is created. Sends `confirm`. |
| I.1 | Issue lane | Delivery of `confirm`, from D.18. | Active. |
| I.2 | Issue lane | Act `offer`, signed by the requester, with a current grant, naming the coordinator. | `state: [open]` of `also.intent`. Opens one item, `commitment`, item 2, in state `offered`. |

Each entry opens at most one item, so item 0 is the intent and item 2
is the commitment. No hold exists in the issue lane and no lease exists
anywhere. Later, in a concern lane, an act `take-hold` opens one hold
item and a `timed` entry ends it. The `commitment` item is unchanged:
the concern shows who is responsible and that there is no current hold.

### 10.2 An exact selected contribution

| Entry | In | Input | Guards and results |
|---|---|---|---|
| A.9 | Concern 42a | Act `report`, signed by agent E, naming commitment item 4. | Grant `report`; `signer: [performer]` of `also.commitment`; `state: [accepted]` of `also.commitment`. Opens one item, `report`, item 9, with the commit and tree. `attribute`, taken of `also.commitment`, fills its `authors` list. |
| A.11 | Concern 42a | Act `accept-report` on item 9, signed by the concern's requester. | `signer: [requester]`; `state: [reported]`; `notIn: [authors]`. |
| P.3 | Pull request lane | Act `propose-manifest`, signed by the coordinator. Fields name the facts A.9 and A.11. | `fact` on each: A.9 is a `report`; A.11 is an `accept-report` whose item is 9. `uses` records both with their content digests. Opens item `manifest`. Its `authors` list is the union of A.9's authors and the coordinator. |
| A.14 | Concern 42a | Act `report`: a second version. | As A.9. |

In concern 42b the report is made by agent V after a handover from
agent U. The attribution is taken of the commitment that the report
names. That commitment's `performer` slot held U and then V, and holds
under it were held by U and then V. So the report's `authors` holds V,
U, and each agent's principal if it acts for one. Taking the
attribution of the new report item alone would miss U. A reviewer who
is any of those fails `notIn: [authors]` in the pull request lane.

P.3 names A.9 and A.11 by `seq` and hash. A.14 changes nothing in the
pull request lane, because no guard there reads the concern's present
state. To use the newer report, the integrator opens a new manifest
item.

### 10.3 Replay from the merged result back to the goal

Entries in this example: G.8, the destination's `outcome` entry that
records the publication as confirmed; P.12, the pull request lane's
delivery entry that records G.8's result; I.20, the issue lane's
delivery entry that closes the issue.

1. The verifier replays the destination scope through G.8. It checks
   that the operation was opened by an earlier entry for a commitment
   whose subject is a merge-intent fact in the pull request lane, and
   that the commit is reachable in the repository as read now.
2. It replays the pull request lane through P.12. P.12's input is a
   delivery whose `from` is G.8. P.12's sends contain a relationship
   update to the issue: name `closes`, state `set`, with the detail that
   the change is merged at that commit.
3. For the manifest entry, it follows each `uses` reference to a
   concern lane and replays that lane up to that `seq`.
4. For each concern lane it checks the genesis: the seed's creator is
   the issue lane, and the source entry, the split, contains that
   creation.
5. It replays the issue lane through I.20. I.20's input is a delivery
   whose `from` is P.12, at the ordinal of that update. The copy it
   updates is keyed by the pull request lane's scope and incarnation,
   the name `closes` and the link item, at revision 12.

The issue cannot close before the effect is confirmed, because the only
message that closes it is sent by P.12, and P.12 exists only as the
delivery of G.8. No entry in this chain contains its own hash.

A forged delivery fails at step 4 or 5: the source entry does not
contain the send. A forged selection fails at step 3: the hash does not
match, or the source's replay does not produce that entry. A missing
lane gives `missing-dependency`.

## 12. Recovery examples

| Case | What happens |
|---|---|
| A submission's reply is lost | The client sends the same signed intent, or asks for settlement. The scope finds the entry and returns the same receipt. |
| A retry after a refusal | It is judged again. If the state now allows it and `notAfter` has not passed, it is accepted. Otherwise it is refused again. |
| A dependency was unavailable | Nothing was recorded and no key was consumed. The same intent may be sent again until `notAfter`. |
| An accepted act's signer is later revoked | Settlement with the exact signed intent still returns the receipt. No new act is admitted. |
| A creation is delivered twice | The child finds its genesis and answers with its fact. Its one result is already in its outbox. |
| A confirmation is delivered twice | The child answers with the entry that recorded the first. |
| A request's first and only attempts are all answered `wrong-incarnation` | The sender writes a diagnosis, `undelivered`, with the log. That clause runs. |
| A request went unanswered once, and the name now answers `wrong-incarnation` | The sender writes a diagnosis, `delivery-unavailable`. No clause runs. The item stays pending and is shown as unknown. Nothing that waited on it is released. A late result settles it. A restored history brings one: the receiver sends its result again, or a new dispatch reaches it (section 7.4). |
| A provisional child's storage is lost before its creator holds an applied result | The repeated creation reaches an empty store, which writes a new provisional genesis with a new incarnation. Its result is the first the creator records, and the creator confirms it. The lost one was never confirmed and had sent nothing but its result. |
| A child's storage is lost after its creator holds an applied result or has confirmed | The creator sends no creation again. If one is delivered all the same, it makes a provisional scope with a new incarnation. The creator holds the old one, records `incarnation-conflict` and never confirms. The replacement sends nothing but its result. |
| Two requests with the same message bytes each ask a handler to create a lane | Their delivery causes differ, because their source facts differ. Two seeds, two children, two results, each naming its own request. |
| One entry would send "set" and "removed" for one relationship key | Refused `duplicate-relation`. Nothing is written. The owner sends them from two entries. |
| A child's storage is restored from retained bytes | Same incarnation. The scope continues. |
| A "set link" arrives after a later "remove link" | Its revision is not higher than the one held for that owner and key. The receiver records one `superseded` entry and sends that result. The link stays removed. |
| A merge result arrives twice, with a reopen between | The issue lane recorded which owner entry closed it. The repeat is answered with that entry. The issue stays reopened. |
| A hold's deadline passes during preparation | The act's commit finds the transition due and stops. The drain applies it as a timed entry, and the act is judged again on the new head. |
| Two holds have the same deadline | The drain writes two timed entries, the lower item ID first. Then the waiting input is judged. |
| A timed selection is dropped again and again, because the commit's clock reads earlier than the deadline | Each selection is charged to the turn's budget of timed attempts. When it is spent the turn writes nothing more and a waiting act is answered `busy`. The transition stays due and a later turn applies it. |
| An alarm's turn meets more due transitions than its budget | It writes timed entries until the budget is spent, and they are kept. The rest stay due. The alarm is set again and the next turn drains them first. |
| A definition's genesis act would open a hold, or an item with a deadline | The validator refuses the definition `genesis-timed`. No scope pins it. A hold or a job is opened by a later act of the active scope. |
| The scope restarts between two due transitions | The next turn derives what is due from the items and drains it before any other input. |
| The clock goes backwards | Acts that judge time are answered `clock-behind`. While a transition is due, by the reading or by the previous entry's time, nothing is written and every input is answered `clock-behind`. Otherwise a delivery that judges no time may be recorded as clamped. |
| A guard asks for "none" over a final state and the scan cannot finish | The input is not judged: `guard-incomplete` for an act, a retry for a delivery. A partial scan never establishes "none". |
| A guard asks for "some" and its scan finds one matching item before a work limit | The evaluation is completed by that witness. The guard holds and the input is judged. |
| A new definition is activated while a lane is open | The lane keeps its definition. New lanes use the new one. |
| A verifier lacks a platform definition's version | `unsupported-definition` for that scope. |
| A scope reaches its budget | New work is refused `scope-full`. Each settling entry still fits, from the reservation its duty made: a timed entry, a result, an outcome, the first answer of a pending job, the closing checkpoint (section 17). |
| A deployment is reset before production | Allowed only after outside effects and credentials are settled. Old references then answer `not-found` or `wrong-incarnation`. |
| An accepted intent is sent again after its `notAfter` | The idempotency index is read first. The scope returns the first receipt. |
| An attempt's answer arrives after the attempt was recorded `unknown` | One more outcome entry records it. The `unknown` entry stays. A later attempt is not changed by it. |
| Two attempts of a selecting operation are both answered `confirmed` | The outcome entry recorded first selects. The other records `selected: false`, and its result is cleaned up by an operation of its own. |
| An act's commit is staged, and the act is then refused or expires | The preparation's records and duties stay. The owning scope asks the addressed scope for settlement. On a receipt it confirms its pin; on a terminal `not-found` it releases it; on anything else it changes nothing. |
| A device asks whether its act was admitted, and the lane has written nothing since | `not-found` at the head, not terminal. Once the lane's clock is past `notAfter`, the lane records a checkpoint and answers terminal `expired`. |
| A pending job's answer arrives when the lane is at its capacity | It records, and opens its result item, from the job's own reservation. A second answer on that job, and a new job, are refused `scope-full`. |
| A request reaches a scope that is at its capacity and settles nothing there | It is not decided. Transport answers "retry", and the sender keeps the duty. |
| Transport acknowledges a send | Nothing that is judged changes. No amount of section 17 counts an acknowledgment, so the same input gets the same answer before it and after it. A request stays pending until its result is an entry. |
| A settling entry must retain foreign entries that the scope did not hold | Their bytes were reserved when the duty began, each at the bound on one entry. The entry fits from that reservation, whatever room is free. |
| A scope with a fixed reserve has admitted more duties than the reserve can settle | That state must not be reachable. Under section 17 the act that would create the duty with no room is refused `scope-full`. A fixed reserve is acceptable only inside the static rule of section 17.3a. |
| A handler refuses a request after it has read a foreign entry | The deciding entry is written `refused` and keeps that entry in `uses`. It is new work, and it is charged for what it keeps. With no room for it, nothing is written, the fetched bytes are discarded and the request is retried (section 17.3). |
| A timed rule leaves its item in a state of another timed rule | Both timed entries were reserved when the first deadline was created, by its chain (section 17.2). |
| A late result's clause puts an item back under a timed rule | The entry of the new deadline was reserved with the request (section 17.2). |
| A checkpoint is asked for while a hold is pending and no entry is free | It is not written. The reserved entry is the closing checkpoint's, which is written when no other duty is pending (section 17.2). |
| A creation reaches an empty store whose creator does not serve the definition's bytes in time | Nothing is written, and the creation is retried. No answer shows nothing about the definition (section 7.2). |
| The exact retry of an accepted act arrives after a fact that it names can no longer be fetched | The key is on a sealed entry, so nothing is fetched. The scope returns the first receipt (section 5.2, step 1). |
| A replay finds a detached text's bytes gone | With a tombstone entry: "redacted, not derived again". With none: `incomplete`. |
| A replay finds that the staged refs differ from an ancestry record's snapshot | No fault. It judges from the snapshot and reports `staged-ref-read`. |
| The founding register's store is empty or holds another incarnation | Nothing is founded. An empty register never mints an incarnation in answer to a founding (R3 section 3.8). |
| A founding lacks a declaration that its definition's closure names | Unavailable `dependency-unavailable`. Nothing is written. The same signed intent is sent again with the declaration (section 7.2). |
| A bound license request must be refused at a lane with no free room | The refusal is written from the entry that the receiver pin reserved for that number, and `decided` moves. A second request with that number is new work (section 6.11; R3's rule, stated in the authority note's adopted revision 13). |
| A second incarnation's result reaches a creator that is at its capacity | It is not recorded. Transport answers `retry`, and the result is offered again. No second incarnation is confirmed, whether or not the `conflict` is recorded (section 17.2). |
| A request with a `delivery-unavailable` diagnosis is sent again | It is one more attempt, and no entry. A receiver that had decided it answers from its deciding entry. One that had not decides it once. The result settles the request (section 7.4). |
| A client reads a reply that is not a value of its operation's result type | No answer. The client sends the same signed intent again, or asks for settlement. It does not take the reply as a refusal (section 9.6). |
| A receipt names a true position and hash, and another incarnation | Following it fails. The receipt is not of this history (section 9.6). |
| A reply is longer than the transport's byte limit, or no whole reply comes within its deadline | No answer. Nothing of the reply is decoded. For an act the outcome is unknown: the client sends the same signed intent again, or asks for settlement (section 9.6). |
| A read answers after the deadline of its exchange | What it returns is not kept, and no further read is made (section 9.6). |
| The first authentic answer arrives on a job that timed out, and no retry superseded the job | It decides the job, from the job's own reservation, and its entry replaces the timed entry as `decidedBy`. While a merge is in progress it is refused, and may be sent again (section 6.10). |
| A definition has an item type, a field or a state named `__proto__` or `constructor` | It is a name like any other. The scope reads what the record itself holds (section 6.1). |
| A delivery names a detached text, and its sender cannot be read | Not decided. Transport answers `retry`, with `dependency-unavailable`. The sender still holds the text, because the request is pending, so the read succeeds when the sender can be read (sections 6.2 and 6.6; new in revision 13). |
| An act would redact a text that a pending request of the scope carries | Refused `text-in-use`. Nothing is written. The same act is admitted once the request has its result, or an `undelivered` diagnosis (section 6.6; new in revision 13). |
| A result arrives after the slot through which its origin entry selected an item could have changed | That cannot be: the validator refuses a clause on a name that is selected through a slot which is not fixed. The clause selects the origin's items again (section 6.6; new in revision 13). |

## 15. Dispositions

Every point that is addressed to this contract has one disposition
here. There are three kinds.

- **Adopted.** A form or a rule of this note, with the section that
  defines it. "Base" means that revision 7 defined it and its adoption
  decided it. Every other "adopted" in sections 15.1 to 15.6f is a
  disposition of revisions 8 to 10, and the adoption of revision 10
  decided it. The same holds for "accepted" and "changed" there. The
  dispositions of sections 15.3a, 15.6g and 15.6h, and every row that
  is marked "revision 11", were proposals of revision 11, and its
  adoption decided them. The dispositions of sections 15.3b, 15.6i,
  15.6j, 15.9 and 15.10, and every row that is marked "revision 12",
  were proposals of revision 12, and its adoption decided them. The
  dispositions of sections 15.3c, 15.6k and 15.6l, and every row that
  is marked "revision 13", are proposals of revision 13. They take
  effect only if that revision is reviewed and adopted. Revision 13 is
  adopted since, and its adoption decided them. The dispositions of
  sections 15.3d, 15.6m and 15.6n, and every row that is marked
  "revision 14", are proposals of revision 14. They take effect only
  if that revision is reviewed and adopted.
  Dated in revision 19, 2026-10-05: revisions 14 to 18 are adopted since
  (the opening, "The standing in force, for revision 19"), and the
  adoption of each decided its dispositions: those of sections 15.3d,
  15.3e and 15.6m to 15.6r, and of each row that is marked with one of
  those revisions. The dispositions of sections 15.3f and 15.6s, and
  every row that is marked "revision 19", are proposals of revision 19.
  Dated in revision 20, 2026-10-06: revision 19 is adopted since (the
  opening, "The standing in force, for revision 20"), and its adoption
  decided them. The dispositions of sections 15.3g and 15.6t, and every
  row that is marked "revision 20", are proposals of revision 20.
- **Expressible.** No form is added. The row gives the mapping onto
  forms that exist, and the companion file shows it in a definition.
- **Owned gap.** Not expressible, or not decided, here. The row names
  the owner and why.

A sentence that says a guard exists is not counted as expressible. Each
"expressible" row names the act where the mapping is written out.

### 15.3c What the authority note's revision 15 asks for a form

New in revision 13. The input is "Authority, effects and publication",
revision 15, at `8dfda899`. It was proposed and under review when it
was read, after its revision 14, at `b3e55edb`, received the verdict
`14ad7c42`, which requested changes. Corrected after the review
`a7f1c108`: its revision 16, at `7bc60cf6`, is now adopted (act
`d6e7e878`). Revision 16 was not read here, and that reading is owed
to this note's next revision. Read here: its section 12.1 as far
as the table of messages, its section 12.1.8 in full, and its sections
13.6 and 13.7 (the opening has the limits). Section 12.1 writes seven
platform definitions in this contract's forms. Section 12.1.8 lists 25
places where it could not: 12 forms of this contract that the source
lacked, P1 to P12, and 13 things that have no form in this contract,
P13 to P25. Its section 13.6 asks this note for the thirteen forms, "or
a statement for each that it stays platform code".

This section decides this contract's part of each, and nothing else. It
decides no rule of a lifecycle, a license, an activation, a platform
definition, a task or a capability. It does not touch that note's
repairs of restore-before-ready and of an administrator's stop, or its
binding of a stream to a device. "Stays platform code" means that this
contract gives the thing no form that a declared definition can write.
The rule is then code of the platform definition's version, whose
meaning is fixed for that version (section 6.1). Every entry that such
code writes still has this contract's forms, and a verifier derives it
again with the same code.

| That `artroom-check-configuration-1` has a bound on one value | Section 6.2. The number is R4's. |
| The I3 deltas E3, E4, E6, E10, E11 and E12 | Each is that note's (section 15.6n). |

### 15.3e Platform code, and what the authority note's revision 19 asks

New in revision 15. Two inputs. The first is the I3 deltas note's entry
EC6, which asks four questions of this contract and of the authority
note. The second is the authority note's revision 19, at `c3f2f103`,
which is filed and under review and is not adopted.
Dated in revision 19, 2026-10-05: that was so for revision 15. That
note's revision 24, which holds this content, is adopted (the opening,
"The standing in force, for revision 19").
Its section 13.9
asks four things of this contract's next revision. The authority note's
revision 20 is the platform side of the first input: it states the rule
as its own, and lists every cell of its section 12.1 that begins "Code"
as a mark. This section decides this contract's side, and nothing of a
platform definition.

**The four questions of EC6.**

| # | The question | Answer | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Whether a rule replaces the one guard or effect that its cell marks, runs after the data row and adds to it, or replaces the derivation of the whole row | None of the three, exactly. A rule is one form of its row. It stands at a place, and is run where a written form of that kind would be derived. It replaces no written form. A place that only code can fill holds the mark, and no data form. | Section 6.1 |
| 2 | What the data holds at a marked place, and whether the validator and the judges skip a marked form | The mark, `{ code, row }`, and nothing else. No data form is written and then skipped. The validator reads the mark and derives nothing. The judge runs the rule. The inbox's effect on `source`, which validates and which the commit refuses, is not written: an effect mark stands in its place. | Section 6.1; section 15.6o, entry E10 |
| 3 | Where a rule runs in the order of the checks | At the check of its place: a field's type at 7, a name of `also` at 8, the grant at 9, a guard at 10, an effect and a slot's type at 11, a send at 12. A rule at `grant` stands in place of the grant check. | Section 4.2 |
| 4 | The order of several rules of one entry | The order of the checks, and inside one written list the order of the list. It is in the data. | Section 6.1 |

**What was weighed, and not taken.**

| Candidate | Why it is not taken |
|---|---|
| A rule replaces the derivation of the whole row | The data of every row with a rule would then be a description that no judge reads. It could say one thing while the code does another, and no check would show it. |
| A rule is one more step after the row: it is given the state and the input, and returns a refusal, or effects and sends that are added after the written ones | It is the nearest to what the I3 source holds. Three rows do not fit it. A join's checks have a stated order in which a secret check stands between two written guards (the authority note's section 3.6). A request that a rule sends has no clause to run when its result arrives. A required slot that only the rule sets is unset when the written effects are checked. It also still needs a mark for the grant and for a type, so it has places as well. |
| The marks stay in a table beside the data, bound to the version | The data alone would not say which rows are code. A platform definition has no digest, so nothing would bind the table to the data but the version's name, which already names both. |

**The forms P13 to P25, by place.** Sections 15.3c and 15.3d stand: four
have an adopted form, and nine stay platform code. This table says where
the code of each stands under section 6.1. It decides no rule.

| # | Stays platform code, in | The place of its mark |
|---|---|---|
| P13 | An act that no grant judges | Place 1, `grant` |
| P14 | The signing key as a value | No place of its own. A rule reads the key from the intent's `actor`: at place 1, in a guard at place 4, or as the value of an effect at place 5. |
| P15 | Selecting a local item by a value that it holds | Place 2, a name of `also`. Place 5 as well, where the row opens the item when none is selected. |
| P16 | An operation that a platform entry opens, and what its outcomes derive and send | Place 5, for the `operation` and `attempt` effects. Place 7, for each outcome entry. Place 6, for a request that an outcome's row cannot write. |
| P17 | A counter | Place 5: one `value` effect, or two |
| P18 | A digest computed in a guard | Place 4. Place 2, where the digest selects the item, as an invitation's secret does. |
| P19 | The part that stays code: which entry reads which observation, and what it concludes | Places 4, 5 and 7. The rule reads `observed` from the entry's input. |
| P20 | The part that stays code: which membership scope a scope names, and when its incarnation is fixed | No mark. It derives nothing of an entry. Guard 1 of section 16.1 reads the reference from the genesis, and the incarnation from the first entry of the history that retains an observation. |
| P21 | A `create` whose definition an input names; each check of a value's content | Place 6, for the `create`. Place 4, for a check of the bytes beside the intent. |
| P22 | A `fact` type that names more than one definition | Place 3, a slot or a field typed by code. Place 5 only, where the forms can write the slot's type and no operand builds the value. |

Counts, by a script: 8 rows. By reading them: 4 are decided, rows 1 to
4; 1 is confirmed, row 5; 2 are answered, rows 6 and 8; and 1 is
carried, row 7.

**No effect of a refused deciding entry. Decided in revision 20.** That
note asks for one more place of a mark: an effect of a refused delivery,
limited to one `value` effect on the item that the binding read. It is
not added, for three reasons.

- A refused request applies no effect of its handler (section 7.4). A
  reader takes `refused` to mean that nothing of the handler happened.
  The one exception is the count of a capability record (section 6.11),
  which is a record of the capability and no slot of an item. A place
  for a platform rule would put a second exception into the items that
  a definition's own guards read.
- What it would buy is small. That note says so: at a destination with
  no free room, the answer to a `withdraw` that must be refused waits,
  the publication goes on, and nothing unsafe follows.
- The count that is needed has a form already. An applied `withdraw`
  takes its publication out of the state `queued`, so a handler that
  declares `settles` on that state has its entry reserved by row 3 of
  section 17.2, while the publication is `queued`. No mark counts it.

So in a platform definition a bound request that is refused is new
work. It is decided when room is free. With none it is not decided, and
transport answers "retry". The five conditions of section 17.3 stand for
a capability. For a platform definition, condition 3 can be met only by
an entry that applies an effect, so no declaration of a platform
definition covers a refusal. Section 17.3 is dated where it says
otherwise.

**A rightful `withdraw` draws on what its publication holds. Changed in
revision 21**, as the planner decided (act `1f8aba72`). The planner took
the answer above until this revision, and not for good: a member's
`withdraw` of their own pending publication settles it, and takes its
room from what the publication held. Only a malformed `withdraw` is new
work.

- *What stands.* A refused deciding entry holds no effect of a platform
  definition, and no place of a mark is added. Row 2 of the table above
  and its first two reasons stand.
- *What is replaced.* The conclusion: "in a platform definition a bound
  request that is refused is new work". From this revision the deciding
  entry of a bound request is a settling entry whatever it decides, and
  its room comes from the item that the request is bound to.
- *The form.* Section 17.2a, "A request that is bound to a holder". The
  item's `holds` states `decisions`, by message name. The handler states
  `bound`. The fold counts each bound deciding entry by the entry
  itself: it is a delivery of that message, and the binding held on the
  state before it. That is how condition 3 of section 17.3 is met with
  no effect.
- *What stays new work.* A `withdraw` that is not bound: one whose
  fields are not values of their types, one that names no publication,
  one whose sender is not the lane that owns the publication, one for a
  publication that is final, and a second `withdraw` after the one that
  the count allows. Each is decided when room is free. With none it is
  not decided, and transport answers "retry". A repeat of a decided
  request is answered from its deciding entry, and uses nothing (section
  7.4).
- *What the authority note owes.* The `decisions` of a publication and
  the `bound` of its `withdraw`, in this form. Its slot
  `withdrawDecided` is then no count of this contract: whether it stays
  is that note's.

Changed in revision 22 (the verdict `dc1da38a`, its first finding). As
revision 21 wrote the form, the `bound` of a `withdraw` could not be
stated: the publication is found by that note's mark `publication-of`,
and revision 21 let no mark be the source of a binding. A mark at place
2 may now be that source, as a binding selector that is given only the
items of its type and the message's fields (section 17.2a, "The source
of `bound.of`"). "One that names no publication", above, is the
`withdraw` that arrives before its `reserve`: the selector gives none,
the request is new work, and the adopted row applies it and opens the
publication as final. The planner confirmed that a `withdraw` for a
final publication is new work (act `39749e26`). With `decisions` the row
of `withdraw` needs no `settles` on the state `queued`: `dec(m)`
reserves the one decision, whether it applies or refuses. So the third
reason of "No effect of a refused deciding entry", above, is history.
That matters for one more rule of this revision: a rule of a form that
declares `settles` returns no change of state (section 6.4), and that
row holds an effect mark.

Changed in revision 23 (the verdict `675776bc`; the planner's act
`2d3fa911`). "The items of its type", above, is replaced. The binding
selector is given the items that a declared index returns for the field
`operation`, at most 8, and no other item of the type. So that note's
`publication` declares the index on its slot `operation`, and its mark
`publication-of` names it. The key is the whole fact reference of the
lane's `merge` entry. Nothing else of the paragraph above changes: a
`withdraw` that arrives before its `reserve` finds no item, and is new
work.

**A list inside a record. Answered in revision 20.** The grammar of
`FieldType` lets a member of a record be any field type (section 6.2).
Revision 13 said it in words: "A member may be of any field type, also a
record or a list" (section 6.2, point DF1). So a list may be a member of
a record, and the type of the rules' extents is written as data: a list
of records, of which two members are lists of texts. Four limits hold. A
list states its `max`, within the bound of section 6.1. A detached text
is no member of a record and no element of a list. A mark is the type of
no member and of no element (section 6.1, the point on EJ5). A value
nests at most 64 containers (section 2.1). The lane forms ask one thing
more: whether an `each` may read its list from a member of an element.
By the grammar it may: the `list` of an `each` is an operand, and
`{ element }` names a member of a record element with a dot (section
6.5). Whether the validator of the I3 source takes both was not read:
row I3-49. What stays code under P28 is its other two parts, which have
no form: a rule on the characters of a text, as P27 has it, and a
`relate` whose detail is a projection of a value.

**A grant on one destination. Carried.** Point R1-66 stays open, and
this is what blocks it. An observation of a key holds one list of
`actions` and one `within` for all of them (section 16.1). A grant on
one destination needs an action that holds within one scope beside
actions that hold within the repository. So one of two things must
change: the answer depends on which scope asks, where today one answer
serves every scope of a repository; or an observation holds pairs of
actions and a filter. Neither is small, and each changes the bytes of
every grant. Which record of membership would give such a grant is that
note's missing forms 12 and 13, which are not designed. So the form
waits for them. Until then a grant on the repository stands, as that
note says.

### 15.6a Eight findings on the derivation source

An independent static review of I1's derivation package, report
`d3930ee8`, found eight defects in supported forms. Where a defect
showed that this contract's rule was unstated or open to two readings,
the rule is now stated, so that the repair has an authority. No choice
of the implementation is adopted because it exists.

| # | Finding | The contract's rule | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Only the first operand of an equality was validated | Each operand is validated by itself, with the nascent-item rule. A bare `null` is not an operand. | Section 6.5 |
| 2 | A copy into a value slot ignored the destination's bounds | A slot never holds a value outside its type. A copy needs an assignable source, or the value is checked in the commit. | Section 6.6 |
| 3 | A reference copy admitted a value slot as its source and read only reference slots | A copy preserves its source. A slot operand reads the slot of that name, whatever its kind. | Section 6.6 |
| 4 | Two fact references with one hash were deduplicated before each was checked | A fact reference is verified whole, scope, position and hash, before any deduplication. | Section 6.5 |
| 5 | An admitted timed effect could refuse, and the drain then never moved | A timed rule's effects are total. The validator refuses a rule that could be refused in its commit. | Section 6.4 |
| 6 | An effect could change a secondary subject that was already final | No effect of any kind changes an item that was final before the entry. | Section 6.6 |
| 7 | Attribution lost a holder changed in the same entry, and a later principal | An `attribute` takes the history after the entry's earlier effects. A principal joins whenever an attributed member changes the item under a grant that has one. | Section 6.7 |
| 8 | Bounded queries scanned every retained item | The index is ordered, so bounded work costs what it returns. No bound on retained items follows from this. | Section 6.5 |

Finding 7 changes the disposition of delta 39 in one respect: keeping
the history with each entry is accepted only if it meets both rules of
section 6.7. Deriving it from retained history is equally allowed.

### 15.6b Four security details

The checker's reconciliation `0d72ada6`, carried by `82edb034`, names
four details from an earlier security review of the earlier code. Most
belong to the authority design. Each has a disposition here as far as
it touches this contract. None is a reason to repair a parked package,
and nothing was run.

| Detail | What this contract fixes | Owner of the rest |
|---|---|---|
| 1. An invitation's budget was consumed before the signature was checked; one shared rate table could lock out every redemption | Nothing authoritative is consumed before a signature is checked: check 1 of section 4.2 comes before every other, and a refused or unauthenticated input writes nothing and consumes no key. A rate limit is serving protection in memory. It decides only whether to serve, and no guard reads it (section 8.2, row 26). So it can never consume a single-use invitation. | R3, built in I3: the order of the secret check, separate abuse budgets or another choice, what happens at overload, and what a valid invitation can still do. Not decided here. |
| 2. Text that a member wrote reached an agent's tools unmarked | In this contract text is data. No form turns a field's text into a grant, a guard's result or an instruction: every act needs a current grant for its own action (section 6.4), a link grants no authority (section 3), and attention carries references (section 6.6). | R3, with I5 and IA: that tool results and summaries keep authorship and the data boundary, and that prose asking for a token or a control grants nothing. Marking alone is not claimed to resist injection. |
| 3. What a person's revoked device or membership does to holds, fork credentials and duties in flight | A hold ends only by an entry: its timed end, a release, or the end of what it is under (section 6.8). A revocation is not such an entry unless R3 makes it one. A token's expiry or revocation settles no attempt and no sent write (section 4.3). | R3 states the policy for a person, apart from its rule for an agent's key: whether bounded writes to a private fork continue, and the fences on minting, staging and reporting. Built in I3. |
| 4. The runner image that ran differed from the one in its digest; credentials passed on a command line; unpinned credential-bearing tools | A job fixes the digest of its check's configuration (the companion file's `request-check`), and an outcome's evidence is typed by its owner (section 4.3). What ran, as opposed to what was declared, is evidence that R3 must type. | R3 and R4 for check evidence; I3 for runner provenance; I5, IA and operator acceptance for secret transport and pinned tools. |

The same report recalls that a verifier needs a trust anchor. Section
9.4 now says so in those words: the expected scope ID, and a known
head or anchor.

### 15.6l Every entry of the I2 deltas note, by its ID

New in revision 13. The I2 deltas note, at the fixed snapshot
`744f2447`, holds 165 entries. Each has one row here, under the ID that
its own worker gave it. No ID is changed, and the ten groups keep the
order of the note's own list. The writer read each entry whole. For 121
of them a second reader compared the entry with the source that it
names, at the snapshot (the opening says how). The other 44 are 30 of
the 31 that section 15.6k covers, whose source the first draft read,
and 14 that were read as entries and not compared with files: D2 and
D6, which only point to later entries; DK6 and DK11, which are
observations; and DM1 to DM5 and DN2 to DN6, which are arrangements of
files and of guides.

A row has one of four dispositions.

- **Accepted, and stated.** The contract adopts the rule. The row names
  the section that states it. A row that says "point" names a point of
  the passage "Made exact in revision 13" in that section, and the
  point gives the reason. A row that names section 15.6k has its rule
  in the section that the row there names.
- **Accepted.** A source choice inside an adopted rule. It is how the
  source does something that the contract already allows, and no rule
  changes. The row names the rule.
- **Changed.** The rule of this contract differs from what the source
  built. The row states the difference, and names the row of section
  11.11 that the source owes.
- **Not this note's.** The row names the owner that exists, and the
  question, or says that nothing is asked.

No entry is left open whole. Two rows leave one part open, each with a
point and an owner: DJ7 (R1-51) and DI17 (R1-45).

Three things are kept apart in every row. A *rule* is what this
contract states. A *source mechanic* is how the I2 source does it, and
it is the builder's, whatever the row says of the rule. An
*observation* is what the producer saw in a test, a control or a
measurement; it is cited as the producer's, and it is evidence of
nothing here. A *stand-in* is a scripted capability or a scripted peer,
and a result with one proves nothing about what it stands for.
"Accepted" never means that the source was reviewed, and no row is
accepted because it was built.

Totals, by a script over the first cell of each row below: 104 accepted
and stated, 14 accepted, 10 changed, 37 not this note's. The table after
the ten groups has them by group.

### 15.6n The I3 deltas E1 to E13

New in revision 14. The I3 delivery records, in
`notes/2026-10-05-i3-contract-deltas.md`, the places where its types
found the notes silent or apart. The file was read whole at `79ed2923`,
the head of `request/i3-authority-effects`. It holds 13 entries, E1 to
E13, and each names an owner. This section answers the entries that ask
this contract a question which sections 4.1 to 16.1 of this revision do
not already answer. It decides nothing of the authority note's side. No
source of I3 was read, and nothing here accepts any.

| Entry | The question for this contract | Answer | The rule, and why |
|---|---|---|---|
| E1 | The source's `Input` has no `settlement`, and its `FactUse` has no `under` | Accepted, as a report | Both are forms of this contract, and both stay owed: `under` is row 4 of section 11.10, and the `settlement` input is a row of section 11.8 whose first user is I3. No row is added. |
| E2 | Whether the pairing of an outcome's result with the basis of its evidence is in the type | Accepted | It is a check, and not a type. `unknown` has the basis `none`, and no other result has it (section 9.3). The judge derives no outcome with another pairing, and a verifier refuses one as a `mismatch`. `Evidence` stays one record, and a union of three records by basis is a narrower way to write it. Each body is its owner's. |
| E8 | What an entry means whose grant holds no freshness proof | Accepted, with the rule stated | `Grant.fresh` is an `ObservationUse` (section 16.1). A grant without one is no grant, and bytes that hold one are no entry. A fixture that builds `fresh` as `null` is a labelled stand-in, and a result with it proves nothing about authority. The guard of the fixed record owes the member from the delivery step that builds the authority port. That is the row "Retained judgment inputs; `FreshnessProof`" of section 11.8, and no row is added. |
| E9 | Whether the validator may take an option that lets a platform definition's data state a name that begins `platform:` | Accepted, inside one condition | It is a source choice inside the rule of section 6.1. A platform definition is code with one fixed meaning, and how much of it the source holds as data is the source's. The condition: the option is reachable from no input. A definition that a founding, a creation, an `activate` or any other input names is validated without it, so a declared definition still never states such a name. With the authority note's successor. |
| E10 | The form of a notice's `source`, a record of four values, where a fact reference has three members | Left open, with the question | A fact reference has one form: `{ at, seq, hash }` (section 3). A slot whose type is a record of four values does not hold one, and the commit's refusal is right (section 6.6). P22 stays platform code (section 15.3c). The question is the authority note's successor's: is the notice's `source` typed by the inbox's code, or is it a record type whose members are those of a fact reference? |

| EY3 | Whether the body of a creation that a genesis sends holds the member `directory` | Confirmed | It does not, as built. The platform puts `directory` in a `create` of a lane. A child whose seed names a directory as its creator reads its directory from the seed (section 6.6, point DH13). So the three creations of a directory's genesis need no member, and the row of the authority note that gives them one is its owner's to amend. |
| EY4 | Whether the evidence check is given the state, and where the body of an `unknown` outcome comes from | Confirmed | The evidence check is a rule like every other, and is given the six things. The body of an outcome that is not known is derived by the rule of the kind, or given by the port, and is judged like every body. Section 6.1, "Place 7, completed" and "The body of an outcome that is not known". As built. |
| EY5 | What the creator does with a rule that returns a creation which names no opening entry | Confirmed | A fault of the rule. Nothing is written. Section 6.1, "A creation that no child could verify". As built. |
| EY6 | Whether the rule of an outcome's send is given `selected` | Decided | Yes, with whether the entry opens a further attempt, as part of what the judge resolved. Section 6.1. Row I3-47. The built reading, which derives it again in the rule, gives the same value today and is to be replaced. |
| EY7 | The form of a request that names no incarnation | Decided | `of` is an `ObservedScope`, which may leave out `inc` only while the asking scope records no incarnation. The answer always states it. Section 16.1, "The first read of a scope names no incarnation". As built. The citation of row I3-18 in the authority note's revision 25 is not the rule. |
| EZ1 | The form and the bounds of what a runner returns | Not this contract's | Owner: the authority note, with R2 and R4. One rule of this contract bears on it. Whatever an entry retains has a stated bound, or the definition is refused `reserve-unbounded` (section 17.2). So a report that an outcome keeps needs a bound from its owner before a scope runs under the definition. The three numbers of the I3 source are its own. |
| EZ4 | The bound on one retained input, and whether the scope refuses at the commit what no reader could read | Decided | A scope stores no retained input that is larger than the bound on one retained read (section 9.1). Bytes over it are not stored. For a snapshot the check is then `too-large` (section 16.4), and its owner states that bound in bytes within this one (point R1-28). For any other kind an answer with such bytes is no answer. The reason: an input that no verifier can read makes its entry `incomplete` for ever. The number is R4's. Row I3-48. |
| EZ5 | Whether a retained input whose bytes are not canonical is a mismatch for a verifier | Decided | It is not that input. A digest is over a domain tag, a newline and the canonical JSON of one value (section 2.1), and the bytes of a retained input are those canonical bytes. Bytes that parse to the same value in another order or spacing are not what the digest names. A scope does not keep them, and a verifier does not take them: it then lacks the input, which is `incomplete` by the table of section 9.4. As built in the driver. The verifier of the I3 source takes such bytes: row I3-48. |
| FB2 | The member `extents` of a `RulesContent`, and the size of `content` | Decided | A digest, with the list as a retained value. 48,931 bytes, as a sum. Section 16.1. Row I3-43. |
| FB3 | Whether one type with an optional member is the "two fixed records" | Decided | One type may write them. The record check must require the member exactly when the data of the observation's `definition` states the value, and refuse it otherwise. Section 16.1. Row I3-43. |
| FA3 | An exemption, `covered`, in place of the reservation by a publication | Decided | The flag is replaced by a reservation that an item holds. A held kind is in no closure because its holder counts it. Section 17.2a. Row I3-44. |
| FA4 | Whether a reference may name the item that its own entry opens | Confirmed | It may, where the item is of the slot's type. The entry records `"self"`. Section 6.1. As built. |
| FA5 | A read of the operations of one publication | Decided | The folded state holds, for each operation, the holder that it is `for`. So the operations of one item are read by the item, with no search of entries. Section 17.2a, "What holds the count". Row I3-44. |
| FA6 | Whether an effect may change a `published` publication, for the receipt's records | Answered | The rule stands and is not relaxed: no effect changes an item that was final before the entry (section 6.6). A final state is what a reader, a copy and now a release rely on (section 17.2a). So the rows are the authority note's to change: the receipt's records stand on an item that is not final, or `published` is not final while a receipt is owed. An item that the publishing entry opens for them counts in `items` of the publication's `holds`. |
| FA7 | An answer of a port that is not known and still holds a body | Answered | This contract does not limit the body of an `unknown` outcome to what the state gives. It is recorded input, and the evidence check judges it. Section 6.1. How the driver carries it is the builder's. |
| FC1 | The six things that no text states for the reservation by a publication | Decided, for rows 1 to 3 | Row 1: the folded state holds the counts. Row 2: the form is `holds`, with `adds`. Row 3: the release, by what the open operations can reach. Section 17.2a. Rows 4 to 6 are counts that the authority note owes in that form: the reads, a `resend` and the receipt. |
| FC2 | A request that an outcome entry sends is reserved by nobody; no platform data declares a reservation | Decided, for the first. Not this contract's, for the second. | A request of an outcome's send mark is counted with its operation, or with the holder that the operation is for (sections 17.2 and 17.2a). The rows of membership, the register and the directory need no new form: `settles` exists for platform data too, and the authority note owes the declarations (its row P11). |
| FC3 | What the `uses` of an outcome holds | Decided | A copy of the `uses` of its one origin, and nothing else. Not the entries that a rule read, and not whatever a caller gave. Section 6.1, "The origin of an outcome". Row I3-41. |
| FC4 | The window of a record of `observed` in an outcome and in a delivery of a result | Decided | Each row of `observes` states its window and its use. Ten seconds and `fresh` is right for the two rows that the authority note states, and is confirmed for them. A constant by kind of input is a stand-in. Section 16.1. Row I3-39. |
| FC6 | The form by which a scope knows what to read before a turn | Decided | The rows of `observes`, the order of four parts before the turn, and the list derived again in the commit. Section 16.1. Rows I3-39 and I3-40. The answer of a rules scope to a read waits on the authority note (I3 deltas FB10 and EQ8). |
| FC7 | The form of the route that reads a value | Answered | A read of one value asks by the kind, the domain and the digest (section 9.2). That is the operation, and it is this contract's. The route, its status codes and its name are the transport's, as for every read (section 9.6). The bytes of a value count in used bytes once it is kept (section 17.1), and no source counts bytes yet. |

Counts, by a script over the rows: 21 rows. 11 decided, 4 confirmed, 3
answered, 2 decided in part and 1 that is not this contract's. The
script reads the third cell. The 2 decided in part are FC1 and FC2.

### 15.7 Boundaries that touch this contract

| Boundary | The rule here | The rest belongs to |
|---|---|---|
| The freshness of a grant | An observation with its read and use, inside its restrictions: section 16.1. | R3: the windows. R4: their cost. |
| One scope's decision reaching another | Only as a message of a sealed entry, judged by the receiver's handler, which may read parts of that verified source entry; or as an entry that the receiver's input names by hash and retains. Never as a read of present state: sections 5.1 and 16.3. | None |
| A task scope's decision reaching a lane | `export-license` asks; the lane's deciding entry is the license, and the task scope retains it. `export-settled` tells, and the lane's handler reads the task scope's final entry: sections 6.11 and 16.3. | R3 and IA: the task definition and the release's states. |
| Publication progress | A relationship that the destination owns, with one result for the change lane's `reserve`. That class is right for it: an older update cannot replace a newer one (section 7.3). | R3 |
| A read that depends on a clock | Allowed as an answer, never as a judgment input: section 9.1. | R3: the fence. |
| A read session and a stream | Not entries. Outside section 5.3. A deployment secret that checks a session is not a scope signing a fact (section 6.9). | R3 |
| A control of a hosted agent | An act of the task scope: a signed intent, an entry when admitted, and settlement like any act. That it was applied is a later outcome. | R3 and IA |
| A request that makes a lane mint a credential | An outside effect of that lane. It is an operation, opened by an entry before anything is sent (section 4.3). A `preparation` entry can carry a signed request addressed to the lane. | R3 states the step and its guards. |
| The dispatch of a job to the checker service | Not a send form. A send outside the application is not a form in the first version (section 6.6). | R3 (its section 3.11) |
| Which definition a name stands for | A definition states its name; a reader checks it against the bytes that the source's seed pins: section 6.1. | R3: that the repository's rules scope activated that definition. Point R1-22. |
