rows that give one subject did not say which is absent: "Rows that give
one subject", above.

**The order of the reads, and the judge of a destination. Decided in
revision 21** (the verdict `0cf59056`, an item that does not block;
point R1-69). The authority note's adopted section 6.5 was read whole
for this. It has the destination G read four things before the turn of a
reservation, each resting on the one before: the `merge` entry of the
lane P and the entries that its eligibility statement names; the branch
rules; for each check that the observed rules require, two entries; and
the keys behind what counts. It computes the number of entries to fetch,
2 + v + 2c for v live verdicts and c required checks, "from the
`reserve` message and from the rules that it observed, before it fetches
anything", and ends the publication `not-reserved`, with
`evidence-too-large`, when that is over the bound. Revision 20 put every
entry before every observation, and let nothing rest on an observation.
This is the order from this revision, with the bound of each step.

| Step | What the scope does | From what | Its bound |
|---|---|---|---|
| Part 1 | It checks the shape of the input, and for an act its signature. | The input | The size of an input |
| Part 2 | It has the entries at hand. For an act and for a delivery: it fetches each entry that the input names, which are the facts and the source entry. A clause reads, beyond its source entry, only what its origin retained. For an outcome: the entries that its origin retained, and nothing is fetched. | The input and the pinned definition | The bound on the foreign entries of one entry, and the time limit for one fetch (section 7.5) |
| Parts 3 and 4, the first step | It derives the subjects of the rows that do not state `second`, and reads one observation for each: the signer's first, then the rows in their order. | The state at the head, the input, and the entries of part 2 | The `max` of each row, and the ceiling on the observations of one entry (checks 2 and 6) |
| Parts 3 and 4, the second step, in an outcome only | It derives the subjects of the rows that state `second`, and reads one observation for each. | The same, and the observations of the first step | The same ceiling, which check 6 counts over all the rows of the form |

It is one pass. Each step is done once, in this order, and none goes
back to an earlier one. A turn that the commit stops starts again,
inside the bound on restarts. The entries of part 2 stay at hand over
those restarts, because an entry cannot change. An observation ages, and
is read again.

What the destination's rule `judge` can do in this order, against that
section.

| What the authority note's section 6.5 states | In this order |
|---|---|
| G reads P's `merge` entry and the entries that its statement names | Part 2. Each is at hand from the origin of the outcome: the entry of G that recorded the `reserve` message, which fetched every fact that the message names when it was admitted. |
| G observes the branch rules | The first step: a row `of: "rules"`, with `retains` for the extents. |
| G observes the merger's key | The first step: a row `of: "key"`, `from: "rule"`. The rule names the key from the `merge` entry at hand. |
| G counts under the rules that it observed: which checks are required, with which configuration and which checker | The rule of the outcome, in the commit, over the entries at hand and the observation of the rules. It reads the entries that the rules require and no other. |
| G observes each key behind a counted verdict or result | The second step: a row that states `second`. The rule names the keys behind the entries that the observed rules count. |
| G reads the branch's head from the host | The evidence of the outcome, as that note has it. It is no read of the turn. |
| G computes 2 + v + 2c from the message and the observed rules, before it fetches anything; over the bound, nothing is fetched and the publication ends `not-reserved` | It does not fit. Below. |

- *What does not fit, and why.* A fetch that an observation selects is a
  fetch before the turn of an outcome. An outcome cannot be refused. So
  the room for every entry that it might fetch would have to be reserved
  when its operation is opened: the most entries of the fetch, each at
  the entry size, for each outcome entry of the operation. At the
  proposed bounds that is 128 entries of 256 KiB, which is 32 MiB for
  one outcome entry, by a script and as a product of two bounds. At the
  origin the same entries are fetched by an entry that can be refused,
  and are admitted at their real size. So this contract adds no row for
  a fetch, and an outcome still fetches nothing (section 6.1, "The
  origin of an outcome").
- *What the authority note must change.* Three things, in its sections
  6.5 and 12.1.5. Each is owed by that note, and none is claimed as
  agreed.
  1. The `reserve` message gives a written type of fact to every entry
     that the statement names. Revision 20 asks this already (section
     6.1, "What an entry of another scope must be to be at hand"). Each
     is then fetched when the `reserve` is delivered, read or not, for a
     required check or not.
  2. The count is of the facts that the message names: 2 + v + 2j, for j
     listed jobs, and not 2 + v + 2c. It is made when the `reserve` is
     delivered, with no observation. A message that names more than the
     bound is decided `refused`, `bad-field`, and nothing is fetched
     (section 6.4, point DH4). No publication is opened for it. So the
     end `not-reserved` with `evidence-too-large` has no case left for a
     count of entries, and neither has the evidence `{ over: "entries"
     }`. The reason `evidence-too-large` stays for a row of observations
     that is over ("Past the bound", above).
  3. The entries of a job that the observed rules do not require are
     fetched and retained by the origin. The rule checks nothing of
     them, as that note says of a job that is not required.
- *What does not change for P.* The way forward is the same: a new
  manifest version, or fewer live verdicts. P learns it from the result
  of its `reserve`, and not from an update of a publication.
- *The other way, not taken.* A row of an outcome's kind that states a
  fetch, with a `max`, reserved as above. It would keep that note's text
  as it is, at the cost of that reservation for every `judge`. Whether
  it is wanted is the planner's to say: the corrections file lists the
  question. Until then the three changes stand as what is owed.
  Decided in revision 22: the planner answered (act `39749e26`). The
  three changes of that note's section 6.5 stand, and an outcome fetches
  nothing. They are decided, and they are still owed: the adopted
  authority note has its section 6.5 as it was, until its next revision.
- *Point R1-69.* Decided in part, by the second step. Its part for an
  act and for a clause stays as revision 20 left it.

**An observation of the holders of one action. New in revision 20** (the
authority note's missing form 11). That note asks for one more kind of
observation of membership: the action, the head, and the members who
hold it, to a stated bound.

```ts
/** The members who hold one action, at one head of membership. Revision 20. */
interface HoldersObservation {
  subject: "holders";
  of: ScopeRef;                                   // the membership scope, with its incarnation
  head: Head;                                     // the membership head that was read
  action: string;
  count: number;                                  // the members who hold the action at that head
  holders: readonly MemberId[];                   // the first of them, in byte order of member ID
  definition: PlatformDefinition;
  at: Timestamp;
}
```

- *Who holds an action.* An active member who has an active key, and
  for whose key an `Observation` at that head would list the action in
  `actions`. That is the meaning that the authority note gives. This
  contract fixes the record.
- *The request.* `{ of, holders, most }`: the action, and how many IDs
  the answer may list. `holders` of the answer has `count` IDs, or
  `most` when `count` is higher. `most` is the row's, and is at most the
  bound on the elements of a list.
- *It is a fixed record*, with exactly these members, as the other kinds
  are. It has the four common members, so "Three kinds, one envelope",
  above, now holds for four kinds. Its subject, for the order of heads,
  is the action, of the observed scope.
- *The count permits nothing.* The record says how many hold the action
  and who the first are. No rule of this contract lets anything take
  effect because the count is 1, or is any number. A definition that
  wants a behaviour for a repository with one controller declares it in
  its own data, as the rules declare `singleControllerException`, and
  its rule reads the declaration and the observation together.
- *Replay.* The verifier derives `count` and `holders` from membership's
  history at `head`, by the role table of the observed version. Code of
  that version gives it, and it is reported under `platform-code`
  (section 9.3).
- *Its size.* At most the bound on the elements of a list in member
  IDs, and one text for the action. The largest is R4's to count.
- *The controller of an authoring agent* (that note's missing form 15).
  No kind is added. A `MemberObservation` carries `controller`. So the
  form is one row of `observes` on the kind whose rule judges the
  authors: `of: "member"`, `from: "rule"`, with a `max`. The rule names
  the authors from an entry at hand. The row, its `max` and its window
  are that note's, inside the ceiling on the observations of one entry.

**The extents, in an observation of the rules. New in revision 20** (the
authority note's ask 1 and its missing form 2; I3 delta FB2). That note
gives the rules a list of 1 to 8 extents, and counts the largest list at
101,553 bytes with plain letters and 330,929 bytes by its bounds alone.
The entry size is 256 KiB, which is 262,144 bytes. So the list cannot be
a member of `content` by its bounds: one observation would pass the size
of the entry that holds it.

- *The member.* A `RulesContent` that was asked as "rules" has the
  member `extents: Digest`, under a rules definition whose item `rules`
  states a slot of that name. It is the digest of the list as that slot
  holds it, in a byte domain that the rules definition declares
  (section 2.1, "A domain that an owner declares"). Before a first value
  is set, it is the digest of what the definition gives as the value
  then. Under a rules definition whose data states no such slot, the
  record has no such member.
- *The bytes.* The canonical JSON of the list is a retained input of
  the kind `value`, with that domain (section 9.2). The rules scope
  gives the bytes beside its answer. The asking scope checks them
  against the digest and against the bound that the owner of the domain
  states for one value, and keeps them when an entry of it names the
  digest. One list is kept once, however many entries name it (section
  17.1).
  From revision 21 the bound that the asking scope checks is the `max`
  that its own row states for the domain, under `retains` ("A value that
  a row may retain", above). It is in the asking scope's pinned data, so
  neither the scope nor its validator needs the data of the rules
  definition.
- *What a rule that reads the observation gets.* The observation, with
  the digest, in `observed`. And the list itself, as a retained value of
  its entry. Item 4 of what a rule is given names each value beside the
  intent (section 6.1). From this revision it also holds each value
  that an observation of the entry names. The rule reads the extents
  from those bytes. The authority note's rule `judge` is the first such
  rule.
  Without the bytes the scope has no observation: an answer whose bytes
  are missing, or do not hash to the digest, is no answer.
- *What a reader gets.* The entry, with the digest. And the bytes, by a
  read of one retained value: the kind `value`, the domain and the
  digest (section 9.2). A replay without them is `incomplete`.
- *Replay.* The verifier derives the digest from the history of the
  rules scope at `head`, as it derives the rest of `content`, and checks
  the retained bytes against it.
- *The size of `content`, and the bound. This decides point R1-61.* The
  member adds 84 bytes: its name in quotes, a colon, a digest in quotes
  and a comma. With the 48,847 bytes of revision 19 the largest
  `content` is 48,931 bytes. That is a sum, and no script counted the
  types again. The bound on `content` is that size by the declared
  types. No smaller number is set, and no guard on the canonical size
  of the fields of `publish` is asked: the type check of each field is
  the guard, and the largest value that passes it is inside the entry
  size. The bound on one value of the extents is its owner's to state,
  as the largest list that its types allow. Every number is R4's to
  measure.
  *Qualified in revision 21* (the verdict `0cf59056`, an item that does
  not block). The sentences above on the bound and on a guard are about
  the compact record `RulesContent` only. Each of its members is bounded
  by its type, and the whole record is inside the entry size. They are
  not about the act `publish`. Its field `extents` is the list itself,
  as that note's row states it, and by its bounds the list alone can
  pass the entry size. So the type check of each field does not show
  that every `publish` fits. A `publish` whose entry would pass the
  entry size is refused `entry-too-large`, by check 13 of section 4.2,
  as any act is. No guard is added, because that refusal exists.
- *Two fixed records, in one type* (I3 delta FB3). The I3 source has one
  type for `RulesContent`, in which `singleControllerException` is
  optional. That is a fair way to write two fixed records. The check of
  the record is what must be exact, and by the word of the deltas note
  it is not: it takes the member where it is present. The rule is that
  the member is present exactly when the data of the observation's
  `definition` states the value, and absent otherwise. The same holds
  for `extents`. Row I3-43.

**The first read of a scope names no incarnation. New in revision 20**
(I3 delta EY7; the authority note's section 12.1, "Where the rules scope
and the destination record their membership reference"). That note has a
scope that is created beside its membership scope hold the membership
scope's ID as a fixed value, and take the incarnation from the first
observation that an entry of it retains. A request had no form for that.

- *The form.* The `of` of an `ObservationRequest` is an `ObservedScope`:
  a `ScopeRef`, or `{ scope, kind }` with no `inc`. The second is used
  only while the asking scope records no incarnation for that scope:
  no entry of it retains an observation of it. As built.
- *The answer.* Its `of` is a `ScopeRef`, always, with the incarnation
  of the scope that answered.
- *Guard 1, then.* While the scope records no incarnation, guard 1
  compares the scope ID and the kind. Every observation that one entry
  retains of one scope states one incarnation. The first entry that
  retains one fixes it, and from then on guard 1 is as it was.
- *What this does not give.* Nothing binds the incarnation before that
  first entry. Which check a replay makes of it against the directory's
  history is the authority note's rule, and is not built (I3 delta
  EY8). A scope whose entries retain observations of more than one
  incarnation of one scope ID has a history that guard 1 does not allow.
- *A citation.* The authority note's revision 25 cites row I3-18 of
  section 11.13 for this. That row is about the scope part of a read
  route (section 3.1). It is not the rule for a request of an
  observation. This passage is.
- The request is in no entry, so no entry's bytes change.

### 16.2 A fetched entry of another scope

Revision 7 already defines this input: a fact field's entry, fetched by
hash and listed in `uses` (sections 6.5 and 9.2). It is stated here so
that the two kinds that follow can refer to it.

| Aspect | For a fetched entry |
|---|---|
| Typed domain | `Entry`, with its `FactRef`. |
| Source and cause | The scope that the reference names, reached through the one scope namespace. The cause is a fact field, a presented fact, or a delivery's source. |
| Immutable bytes and digests | The entry's canonical bytes hash to the reference's `hash`. `uses` holds the reference and the SHA-256 of those bytes. Since revision 11 it also holds `under`, the definition name that was read with the entry (section 4.1). |
| Completeness | One whole entry. |
| Trust label | At run time: that the object the namespace returns is that scope and runs the platform's code (section 7.4). In replay: none, when the source is replayed; `anchor`, when a caller's anchor is used. |
| One-commit, restart and clock | None. An entry is immutable. It says what was true at its position, and nothing about now. |
| Guard path | A `fact` guard and the parts of section 6.5. |
| Replay path | The retained bytes for this scope's judgment, and the source's history or an anchor for the claim that the source admitted the entry (section 9.4). |

### 16.3 Another lane's check entry, with its attribution list

A manifest whose commit was built under a hold in an issue lane L
relies on what L recorded for it. L's check entry (section 6.11) is
presented beside the `propose-manifest` intent to the change lane P.
R2 and R3 call it the pin entry. This answers R3's point O2 and gap
G18.

| Aspect | For a presented check entry |
|---|---|
| Typed domain | An entry of L whose input is the outcome of an operation `check` of `hold@1`, and whose effects hold one `check` record: the intent digest, the commit, the consumer, the source's lane, hold and instance, the root, the attribution list, and the ancestry record. |
| Source and cause | L's sealed history. Its cause is L's `preparation` entry for this exact intent, which names the intent's digest. The record names P, with P's incarnation, as the consumer. |
| Immutable bytes and digests | As section 16.2. The attribution list and the ancestry record are inside the entry's bytes. The snapshot of staged refs is under its own digest, in L's retained inputs. |
| Completeness | The attribution list is the whole set that L derived in that commit, by section 6.7, from complete evidence. P copies it whole. P adds its own sources by union and removes nothing. |
| Trust label | For the entry: as section 16.2. For what its ancestry record rests on: `staged-ref-read` (section 16.4). |
| One-commit, restart and clock | It is made for one intent digest, so it serves the one entry that can admit that intent. P judges no time on it. Nothing of it is held in memory, so a restart changes nothing. |
| Guard path | P's guards read it as `presented`: a `fact` guard for its kind and definition; `carried` parts for the intent digest, the commit, the consumer, the hold and the instance, each compared with the intent; the attribution list as a source of `attribute`; and the capability guard `ancestry` for the row over F. |
| Replay path | The bytes in P's `uses`, for P's judgment. L's history, for the claim that L admitted the entry and derived that list. Without L's history or an anchor the report is `missing-dependency` for that fact. |

- **What it says about L's present state: nothing.** It says that, at
  that entry, L held a `live` root for the commit and recorded a
  `provisional` pin for P's intent. P does not judge whether the root
  is live now.
- **What keeps that safe is L's own commitment.** A root with a pin
  that is `provisional` or `held` is never retired (R3 section 6.2).
  L releases a provisional pin only by an `unpin` from P, or by a
  `settlement` entry that records P's own answer: an entry exists for
  the intent, or none exists and none can follow (section 9.1). After
  a terminal `not-found`, P can never admit the intent. So between L's
  check entry and P's admission, L's own history keeps the root. This
  is the pattern of point R1-5: a decision about another scope's state
  is made through that scope's commitment, and in no other way.
- **Loss is not release.** If P cannot be reached, or P's storage is
  lost, L records nothing and the pin stays.
- **The same pattern carries a task scope's decision to a lane.** An
  export is dispatched by a task scope T only on a license entry of
  the lane L that owns the receiving hold. T names that entry as a
  fact, fetches it, and retains it in the entry that records the
  dispatch. T uses it only inside R3's license window, on T's own
  clock, and only in the run that asked for it (R3 section 4.2). L
  learns T's final decision from T's `export-settled` message, whose
  handler reads T's sealed source entry through the capability guard
  `settled`. Neither scope reads the other's present state.

### 16.4 An ancestry record

R3 proposes a check, by the `git-read` capability, of a commit's
ancestry against the refs staged in the canonical repository (R3
section 6.2; R2 point R2-18). The record below is R3's `AncestryCheck`,
restated. R3 owns the walk and its bounds. This section fixes the
record as a retained input. It answers R3's point O9 and gap G19.

```ts
interface AncestryCheck {
  commit: CommitId;                              // the commit judged: the start
  root: { number: number; state: "live" };       // the staging lane's root for it, as its records held it at the check
  head: CommitId;                                // the destination branch's head, as read for this check
  snapshot: { digest: Digest; count: number };   // the staged refs as returned, in the domain `artroom-snapshot-1`
  start:
    | { foreign: null }
    | { foreign: string; published: true }
    | { foreign: string; basis: { kind: "own-check"; checked: FactRef }
                               | { kind: "input"; input: FactRef }
                               | { kind: "row" } };
  stops: readonly (
    | { kind: "own-root"; commit: CommitId; root: number; state: "live" | "retiring" | "retired"; checked: FactRef }
    | { kind: "selected-report"; commit: CommitId; input: FactRef })[];
  F: readonly (
    | { commit: CommitId; ref: string }
    | { commit: CommitId; ref: string; start: true }
    | { commit: CommitId; via: CommitId })[];
  visited: number;
}
```

| Part | Is | A retained input because |
|---|---|---|
| `head` | The branch's head at the read. | The branch moves. "Published" is judged against this value and never against the branch as it is later. |
| `snapshot` | The digest and the count of the list of staged refs, each with its target, as the host returned it. The list's bytes are kept under that digest. | The refs change: a staging adds one and a retirement removes one. |
| `start` | The judgment of the commit itself: no foreign ref targets it; or one does and the commit is published; or one does and one basis answers for it. | It is derived from the snapshot, the head and the staging lane's own history. |
| `stops` | Where the walk stopped apart from the branch: an own root with its prior check, or a selected report. | Each names an earlier entry of the staging lane as its evidence. |
| `F`, with what is carried | The staged commits the walk met; the start, on the basis `row`; and the commits carried from the prior check of an own-root stop. | It is the result that the act's row judges. |
| The published-history boundary | Not a member. It is the set of commits reachable from `head`. | It is derived from `head` and from commits, which are named by their content. |

| Aspect | For an ancestry record |
|---|---|
| Typed domain | `AncestryCheck`, as the evidence of the outcome entry of an operation `check`, and as a member of the `check` record that entry holds. |
| Source and cause | One read of the canonical repository by the staging lane, under a credential whose duty the lane recorded first (section 5.5). The cause is the preparation of one intent. |
| Immutable bytes and digests | The record is in the entry. The snapshot's bytes are a retained input of the staging lane under `snapshot.digest`, stored before the entry that names the digest. Commits are named by ID. |
| Completeness | The snapshot is the whole list the host returned to that read. A list that was cut short, or a walk that passed a bound, gives no judgment: the record's state is `too-large` and the act is refused `ancestry-too-large`. |
| Trust label | `staged-ref-read`: that the host returned exactly that list and that head when the lane read them, and that the lane kept what was returned. It rests on R3's host property H2. The host keeps no history of its refs, so no later read confirms or denies a snapshot. |
| One-commit, restart and clock | A record is made for one intent and one root, and serves the act with that intent digest only. A reuse of a root makes the walk again. No window bounds it: it goes stale by state, not by time. The guards below catch that. A restart changes nothing, because the record is in an entry. |
| Guard path | The capability guard `ancestry` (section 6.11), in the commit of the act. When the record is this scope's own, it is read from this scope's `check` record, and R3's guards 2 to 6 are judged again against local state. When it is carried by another lane's check entry, it is read as `carried`, and only the commit and the row are judged. |
| Replay path | The record, the snapshot's bytes, commits read by ID, and the staging lane's history. The verifier derives the walk from the commit's parents, each stop, the sorting of the refs on the start, `published` from `head`, F with what is carried, and the row. |

Rules that hold for every use and every replay:

1. **No walk of the refs as they are now replaces the snapshot.** A
   replay never reads the staged refs or the branch again. A
   difference between the snapshot and the present refs is expected
   and is no fault.
2. **No new own root certifies foreign work.** The start is never a
   stop. A root is a stop only on a **prior check**: an earlier entry
   of the staging lane that admitted an act for that commit under that
   commitment and retains its record, or a check entry whose pin was
   later confirmed. The entry being judged is never its own basis. An
   own ref on the start never answers for a foreign ref on it. A root
   is not a stop because the lane's records hold it, because it is
   `live`, or because its pin is `provisional`. So an unpublished own
   ancestor whose root is staged, and whose own act was refused or
   never admitted, is listed in F like any other staged commit: whose
   ref it is makes no difference. This is R3's rule (R3 section 6.2,
   "The walk"), and R4's key L7 and row F30 state it at R4 revision 8.
3. **A stop carries what lay under it.** Every commit in the F of an
   own-root stop's prior check is carried, except one that is
   reachable from this record's `head`. A carried commit comes from
   the earlier record. This record's snapshot is not read for it. In
   F, a commit that the walk found has a `ref`, and a carried commit
   has the `via` of its stop, so the two are told apart.
4. **Published history is never listed.** A commit reachable from the
   recorded `head` is a stop at the branch, as the start, as an
   ancestor and as a carried commit. A commit published after the read
   is not published for this record. That fails closed: a basis is
   asked.
5. **What the record does not see** is R3's to state and R3 states
   it: content copied without its commits, a ref the host did not
   return, a ref created after the read, and a commit whose every root
   is retired.

A replay answers `incomplete` for a check when the snapshot's bytes are
missing or a commit that the walk needs can no longer be read, and
`missing-dependency` when it needs another lane's history and cannot
read it. It makes no claim in either case.

### 16.5 The kinds, side by side

| Kind | Serves | After a restart | Clock that bounds it | Trust label | What it says about now |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Observation, ten-second kind | One commit | Read again | The observing scope's | `observation-read` | Nothing. A grace window. |
| Observation, other kinds | The commits of one run inside the window, each at a later reading | Read again | The observing scope's | `observation-read` | Nothing. A grace window. |
| Observation in `observed`: of another key, of a member or of the rules. New in revision 14. | As the kind that the entry's specification states. A ten-second kind serves one commit. | Read again | The observing scope's | `observation-read` | Nothing. A grace window. |
| Fetched entry | Any commit that names it | Unchanged | None | Namespace at run time; none or `anchor` in replay | Nothing |
| Presented check entry | The one entry that admits its intent | Presented again | None | As a fetched entry; `staged-ref-read` for its record | Nothing. The other lane's pin keeps the root. |
| Ancestry record | The act with its intent digest | Unchanged | None | `staged-ref-read` | Nothing. Stale by state is refused. |
| License entry of a lane, at a task scope | One dispatch, inside the license window | Asked for again | The task scope's | As a fetched entry | Nothing. The hold was held at that entry. |

Operational assumptions stay separately owed and are not established
here: R3's host properties H1, H2 and H4, and its clock assumptions H5
and H6. No measurement by R4 turns one into a guarantee. Where one
fails, each conclusion above that names it is not safe.

## 17. Capacity accounting

Section 9.2 says that a full scope refuses new acts and must still
settle what it owes. R4's proof plan and the planner's correction
`8070b3f7` ask how: a pending job's first authentic result, or an
essential settlement, must stay recordable when the scope is at its
capacity for new acts or new items, also when that result opens an
item. A reserve of bytes alone does not answer that, because a result
needs an entry and an item as well. A class of input that may always
exceed the budget does not answer it either, because nothing would
bound it. This section gives a finite accounting. Every number is R4's
and none is proposed here.

Revision 9 corrects and completes it, after the review `bfe096fe` and
the planner's requests `a89dcea1`, `873621d2` and `1f52493c`.

- No amount is read from transport's acknowledgments (section 17.1).
- A reservation covers the bytes of the inputs that its settling
  entry newly retains, and not only that entry's own bytes (section
  17.2).
- Both amounts are derived from the folded state inside the commit
  (section 17.1).
- A reserve of one fixed size is not this accounting. Section 17.3a
  says why, and what a static rule would have to guarantee if one is
  used as a temporary step.

Revision 10 corrects two statements and decides two seams, after the
review `114e2cc5` and the planner's follow-through `cc570904`.

- Fetched inputs are discarded only when no entry is written. An
  entry that records a refusal is charged for what it retains
  (sections 17.2 and 17.3).
- A reservation is of a duty's whole closure. A deadline reserves its
  chain of timed rules, and a request reserves what its clauses can
  start (section 17.2).
- The closing checkpoint has an exact rule (section 17.2).
- The reserve of the static rule follows the chains (section 17.3a).

Revision 11 states five more things, after the I1 entries 140 to 142,
the I1 delivery note, and the review `74b21dc8` of R3's revision 10.

- A runtime may reserve more than a duty's closure, and never less
  (section 17.2).
- The budget decides only whether new work is written (section 17.3).
- A refusal uses a reserved entry only by its owner's declaration,
  inside five conditions (section 17.3).
- A creation reserves nothing for a `conflict`, and no request
  reserves a second diagnosis (section 17.2).
- An item that holds two deadlines reserves the longer chain, and a
  scope retains its definitions at its genesis (sections 17.1 and
  17.2).

Revision 12 changes no rule of this section. It says that the index
row of the entry which records `published` changes no reservation
(section 17.2). It sets the rule beside what the source counts
(section 17.5).

Revision 13 makes three points exact (sections 17.2 and 17.3). It was
corrected after the review `a7f1c108` in one count: the foreign entries
of a byte reservation are counted by what a form declares, and not by

Revision 20 adds one form and makes two counts exact, after the I3

- A request that an outcome's send mark makes is counted with its

- Of foreign entries an outcome newly retains none (section 17.2).

- A value that an observation names is reserved for every form that

### 17.1 What is counted

A scope has a **budget** in five dimensions. Each is a deployment value
(section 5.1, configuration).

| Dimension | Counts |
|---|---|
| Entries | The entries of the history. |
| Items | The scope's items in every state, live and retained final together. This is R4's bound R4-B1, and it is checked when an item is opened, never when one reaches a final state. |
| Records | Capability records and relationship copies, in every state. |
| Bytes | The canonical bytes of each entry, and the bytes of each retained input that an entry names (section 9.2). A retained input is counted once for each byte domain and digest under which it is kept, however many entries name it. |
| Pending requests | The requests that the scope's entries sent, for which its history holds no result and no `undelivered` diagnosis. Revision 8 called this dimension outstanding sends, and also counted the sends that transport had not acknowledged. That part is withdrawn. |

For each dimension the scope keeps two amounts.

- **Used.** What the history holds.
- **Reserved.** The sum of the reservations of its **pending duties**.

The invariant is: used plus reserved is never more than the budget.

**A list, in these counts. Stated in revision 19.** A list value is one
value of one slot or of one field. Its length moves no count of entries,
items, records or pending requests. It moves bytes only. Used counts the
canonical bytes of each entry as it was written, with the list at the
length that it has. Reserved counts each entry form at its static size,
with each list at the `max` that its type states (section 6.1, "The
bound on the elements of a list"). So a reservation is the same whether
a list holds 2 elements or its `max`, and no amount reads the length of
a first value.

**Derived in the commit.** Both amounts are functions of the folded
state of section 9.2, the retained inputs and the pinned definition.
For one thing they also read this scope's own history, which is local
state under the same head check: the origin entry of a pending
request says which send form made it, as it does when a clause runs
(section 6.6). That sentence is new in revision 11.
The scope computes them inside the commit transaction, on the head
that the head check covers. Neither is a counter kept beside the
state, a high-water mark, or a value read before the snapshot. So the
amounts that admit an entry are those of the head it is written on,
and a verifier derives the same amounts from the same history.

**What the fold holds for an item that reserves. New in revision 20.**
Under a definition whose data states `holds`, the folded state has
three things more: what each such item still holds, as counts; the
item that each operation is for; and the account of each pending
request. Each is derived from the entries alone, and a checkpoint's
state digest covers it. So both amounts are still functions of the
folded state, and no counter is kept beside it. Section 17.2a has the
rule.

**Nothing outside the history is counted.** Whether transport has
acknowledged a send is bookkeeping (sections 5.1 and 7.4). No entry
records it and no retained input holds it. So neither amount reads it,
in any dimension, and the rule of admission cannot depend on it. Two
scopes with the same history, the same retained inputs, the same
definition, the same budget and the same rule of reservation (section
17.2, "More, and never less") give the same answer to the same
input, whatever transport has acknowledged. Witness 18.14.

- A request is pending until its result, or an `undelivered`
  diagnosis, is an entry. Transport's acknowledgment of the request
  does not end that. It is never a result, and it resolves nothing
  about an effect outside the service (section 4.3).
- A result, a control and an advisory are in no dimension as sends.
  Each is part of the entry that sent it. Its bytes are in that
  entry's bytes, and section 7.5 bounds how many one entry holds.
  Nothing in the history says whether one is still to be delivered,
  so nothing here counts that.
- What transport still has to deliver is bounded all the same. Every
  send is a send of an entry, and the entries and their bytes are
  inside the budget.
- **Transport backpressure** is a limit on dispatch: how many sends
  transport has out at once, and how fast it retries. It delays
  delivery. It never refuses an input `scope-full`, never stops a
  settling input, and never drops, resets or marks a send done. It is
  outside both amounts, and R4 sets it (section 17.5).

**Bytes, exactly.** These are the retained inputs that are kept apart
from their entry, with the bound on one of each.

| Retained input | Kept under | Bytes of one, at most | Who states the bound |
|---|---|---|---|
| A foreign entry in a `uses` | The `content` digest of its `FactUse` | The entry size of section 7.5. One entry is read by the bounded read of section 9.1. Bytes past that bound are not an entry and are not used. | This note; the number, R4 |
| A detached text | Its digest, in `artroom-text-1` | The field's `max`, which is at most 64 KiB (section 6.1) | The definition |
| A definition's bytes | Its digest, in `artroom-definition-1` | The bound on a definition's bytes (section 6.1). The scope's own is retained once, at genesis. So is each other definition of its named closure, and the bound on a closure bounds how many there are (sections 6.1 and 7.2). In a platform scope, a definition that an input names is retained once, with its closure, by the first entry that names it. | This note; the numbers, R4 |
| A value beside an intent, in a domain that its owner declares. New in revision 14. | Its digest, in that domain (section 6.2) | The bound that the owner of the domain states for one value. A check's configuration, in `artroom-check-configuration-1`, is the first. A definition that travels in this way has the bound of the row above. | The owner of the domain; the number, R4 (point R1-28) |
| A rule evaluation's inputs | The `input` digest of its `Prepared` record | The pinned profile's limit on a rule's input. I1's value is temporary (delta 77). | The profile; the number, R4 |
| A snapshot of staged refs | Its digest, in `artroom-snapshot-1` | The bound past which the check is `too-large` (section 16.4). It is not stated in bytes. | R3: point R1-28 |
| Evidence that an outcome keeps under a digest, apart from its entry | The digest and the domain that the effect's owner declares | What that owner declares | R3 or the capability: point R1-28 |

One more row, from revision 21. Revision 20 made the extents of the
rules a retained value, and gave it no row here.

| Retained input | Kept under | Bytes of one, at most | Who states the bound |
|---|---|---|---|
| A value that an observation names. Counted from revision 21. | Its digest, in the domain that the observed definition declares for it (section 16.1) | The `max` that the observing scope's row of `observes` states for that domain, under `retains`. It is at most the bound on one retained read (section 9.1). | The definition of the observing scope; the number, R4 |

A delivered message, a rule's result, evidence that is inside its
outcome entry, an observation and the signed intent of a preparation
entry are part of their entry, and are counted in its bytes. Since
revision 14 that holds for every record of `observed` too (section
16.1).

- **Counted once.** Two entries that use one foreign entry retain its
  bytes once, and Used counts them once. One digest value under two
  domains is two inputs (section 9.2) and is counted as two.
- **A redaction.** A `redact` effect removes bytes (section 6.6). From
  that entry on, Used does not count them.
- **Storage that is derived.** Indexes, the folded state and the
  outbox with its marks are functions of the history, or bookkeeping
  about it. They are in no dimension. The budget bounds the history,
  and so bounds them. Sizing them is the deployment's, and R4
  measures it.
  Confirmed in revision 23: the index that an item type declares is such
  storage (section 17.2a). A checkpoint holds no row of it, and it is
  rebuilt from the items.

### 17.2 Pending duties, and what each reserves

A pending duty is something the scope has started and must be able to
finish. It exists from the entry that creates it until the entry that
settles it. What is pending is derived from the scope's items, records,
sends and operations, as what is due is derived from its items. No list
is kept anywhere else.

The table gives each duty's reservation in entries, items, records and
pending requests. Its bytes follow by one rule for every row: "Bytes
of a reservation", below.

| # | Pending duty | Pending while | It reserves |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A request the scope sent | No result and no `undelivered` diagnosis is recorded for it | 2 entries: one for a diagnosis, and one for the result, which may arrive after a `delivery-unavailable` diagnosis. And what its clauses can start: "A request's clauses", below. After a `delivery-unavailable` diagnosis: 1 entry, for the result, and what the clauses that can still run can start. No second diagnosis is reserved, because none is written (section 7.4). The request itself is 1 pending request. That one is used, not reserved, from the entry that sent it. |
| 2 | A deadline | A live item holds it under a timed rule | 1 entry, and 1 for each further rule of its chain: "A chain of timed rules", below. An item that holds deadlines under two rules reserves the longer chain, and not the sum. A rule's attention is advisory and is part of its entry. |
| 3 | An item awaiting its settlement | The item is in a state that a `settles` declaration lists (section 6.4) | For the settling act or handler: 1 entry; 1 item, when it opens one; the records it changes; and 1 pending request for each request among its sends, at their bounds. Where several forms settle one state, the largest of each amount. |
| 4 | A relationship copy awaiting its settlement | The copy is in a state that a `settles: { copy }` declaration lists | As row 3. |
| 5 | An operation | It is not settled (section 4.3) | For each attempt that may still be opened or answered, 2 entries: its first outcome and its late answer. And the records and operations that its outcomes derive, such as a cleanup, each by this row. The owner declares them, and the bound on attempts makes the sum finite. |
| 6 | A capability record awaiting its messages | The record is in a state that the capability declares pending | What the capability declares. For a `pin`: 3 entries, for a `pin-confirm`, an `unpin` and a `settlement`. For a `receiver-pin`: 1 entry for each license number above `decided`, up to 3 (section 6.11; the rule is R3's, stated in the authority note's adopted revision 13). The one `export-settled` is reserved by the `export` item that is `authorized`, by row 3, and not a second time here; revision 10 named it in both rows. The results that those entries send are part of the entries. |
| 7 | A provisional scope's confirmation | The scope is provisional | 1 entry. Each request among its held genesis sends is a duty of row 1 from the genesis entry. |
| 8 | The closing checkpoint | From the genesis on, except while the head entry is a checkpoint and no other duty is pending | 1 entry, once for the scope: "The closing checkpoint", below. An export of a full scope ends on it. |

- **A reservation covers what its settling entry starts.** When a
  settling entry itself creates pending duties, their reservations are
  part of the first duty's reservation, and so on for what those
  start. The **closure** of a duty is the duty, and every duty that a
  settling entry of the closure can create. A duty reserves for its
  whole closure: the sum along each path, and, where a settling entry
  has alternatives, such as which clause runs or which state a rule
  leaves, the largest of them. The entry that records a
  merge as published sends up to 33 requests, and each is a duty of
  row 1. So a merge that is asked for reserves that entry, 33 pending
  requests and 66 more entries. Since revision 12 that entry is
  counted with its index row, as 35 sends (section 7.5). An index row
  is an advisory, and is in no dimension as a send (section 17.1), so
  none of these amounts changes. The 33 is the static bound: 32 links
  and one `unpin`. A merge with fewer links, or with a manifest that
  its own lane staged, reserves the same, and what the entry does not
  use is released when it is written. The validator computes each
  reservation from the definition, at the static bounds of sections
  6.1, 6.6 and 7.5. It refuses a definition, as `reserve-unbounded`,
  when a closure is not finite: because settling forms create each
  other's pending states in a cycle, because timed rules lead to one
  another in a cycle, or because a form may retain an
  input that has no stated bound. Revision 9 had this rule and did
  not write out two of its cases. The next two points do. One finite
  closure covers both; no second kind of timer and no further refusal
  is added.
  Changed in revision 20: an operation of a kind that an item holds is
  in no closure, because its holder counts it (section 17.2a). So kinds
  that open each other in a cycle refuse a definition only where no
  item holds them.
- **A chain of timed rules. New in revision 10.** A timed rule takes
  its item out of its own `states` (section 6.4). It may leave the
  item in a state of another timed rule of the same type. Rule r
  **leads to** rule s when an effect of r can set a state that the
  `states` of s list. The **chain** of r is the longest sequence of
  rules that starts with r and in which each leads to the next. A
  deadline under r reserves 1 entry for each rule of that chain,
  whether or not a later rule's deadline slot holds a time yet. The
  timed entry of r is a settling entry and is never refused, so the
  room for what it starts must exist before it is written. The bytes
  are the static bound of each of those entries (section 6.4). A
  definition has at most 8 timed rules, so a chain has at most 8.
  When the rules of one type lead to one another in a cycle, no chain
  is finite, and the drain of such an item need never end. The
  validator refuses that definition `reserve-unbounded`. In both lane
  definitions every chain is 1. The witness is the table of section
  17.3a. An act that puts an item back under a timed rule is new
  work, and the admission check counts the deadline that it creates.
  **An item with two deadlines. New in revision 11** (I1 delta 142).
  Two timed rules may apply in one state of an item, each with its
  own deadline slot. The two deadlines are not two paths. When the
  entry of one rule is written, the other deadline either no longer
  holds, because the item left that rule's states, or it is under a
  rule that the first one leads to, and that rule is already in the
  first one's chain. So the item reserves the longest chain among
  the rules under which it holds a deadline, and not the sum. I1
  reserves, for an item in a live state, the longest chain from that
  state, whether or not a deadline slot holds a time. That is never
  less.
- **A request's clauses. New in revision 10.** A request is settled in
  one of three ways: by its result, whose entry runs one clause; by an
  `undelivered` diagnosis, whose entry runs that clause; or by a
  `delivery-unavailable` diagnosis, which runs none, and then a late
  result, which runs one (section 7.4). So one clause of the send
  runs, in a settling entry. A clause has effects and no sends
  (section 7.5). Its effects can still create a duty:
  - a deadline, when an effect can set a state that the `states` of a
    timed rule list, or can set that rule's deadline slot. That
    includes a state that the item was in before. A clause that sets
    `asked` again, after a timed rule moved the item to `paused`,
    creates a new deadline;
  - a duty of row 3, when an effect can set a state that a `settles`
    lists;
  - a duty of row 6, when a capability effect can leave a record in a
    state that its capability declares pending.

  The reservation of a request is its 2 entries, and the largest, over
  its clauses `applied`, `refused`, `superseded` and `undelivered`, of
  the closures of the duties that the clause can create. The validator
  derives that from the definition. Each request reserves it for
  itself: two requests whose clauses can each set one item's timer
  again reserve two timed entries ("Nothing shared is assumed",
  below). When the clause that runs creates less, the rest is
  released.

  That is the rule: the reservation covers the closure. This contract
  does not instead refuse every definition whose clause can create a
  duty. The companion file has one: the `applied` clause of the
  `create` of `add-concern` leaves the concern `created`, which a
  `settles` lists. The named refusal is `reserve-unbounded`, for a
  definition in which the closure is not finite. A runtime that
  reserves less than the closure, such as two entries for a request
  and nothing for its clauses, is a temporary step. It is inside this
  contract only for definitions in which no clause can create a duty.
  It refuses, as `unsupported-definition`, to found or create a scope
  under any other definition, before any duty is admitted (sections
  6.1 and 17.3a). The fifth witness of section 17.4 is the planner's
  case.
  - *A `conflict` is not reserved. Decided in revision 11* (the I1
    delivery note, section 7). A creation request reserves for its
    clauses `applied`, `refused`, `superseded` and `undelivered`,
    like any other request. It does not reserve for `conflict`.
    There are three reasons. First, a `conflict` is not a way in
    which the request settles. The creation's first result settled
    it, and its duty ended there (section 7.4). Second, nothing
    bounds how many may come. Each loss of a child's storage that is
    followed by a delivered creation makes one more incarnation, and
    each sends one result. Third, a reservation for an entry that
    may never come would never be released, and a scope that had
    ever created a child could then never reach its closing
    checkpoint. So a `conflict` result is new work, and the duties
    that its clause creates are counted when it is admitted. At
    capacity it is not recorded, and transport answers `retry`.
    Nothing is lost by the wait. A result is never given up (section
    7.4), and the creator confirms no second incarnation whether or
    not the entry is written. That a full creator records the
    incident late is the gap of liveness of section 17.5.
  - *No second diagnosis exists. Restated in revision 11.* Row 1
    reserves one diagnosis. After a `delivery-unavailable` diagnosis
    the finding cannot change, and a new dispatch is bookkeeping
    (section 7.4). So nothing more is reserved. The part of the
    reservation that was for the `undelivered` clause may be
    released, because that clause can no longer run. Revision 10
    reserved a further diagnosis with an operator's act. That is
    withdrawn.
- **More, and never less. New in revision 11** (I1 delta 141; the I1
  delivery note, section 7). The reservations of this section are the
  least that a runtime may hold. They are the amounts that a verifier
  derives. A runtime may hold more for a pending duty, in any
  dimension, when three things are true of its rule.
  1. The amount is a function of what section 17.1 names: the folded
     state, the origin entry of a pending request, the retained
     inputs and the pinned definition. It is derived in the commit,
     and it reads nothing else.
  2. It is finite, and it is released when the duty ends.
  3. It is used only in the check of new work. A settling entry is
     admitted as section 17.3 says, whatever the runtime holds.

  A runtime never holds less. What "never less than a request's own
  closure" means is exact. Take a request q that was sent by the
  send form f. Its own reservation, R(q), is its 2 entries, or 1
  after a `delivery-unavailable` diagnosis, and the largest closure
  that one clause of f can start, over the clauses that can still
  run. R(q) has an amount in each dimension. A runtime's rule is
  sound for q when, at every head at which q is pending, and in
  every dimension that the runtime counts, what it holds for q is at
  least R(q). I1 holds, for every request, the largest amount over
  all the request send forms of the definition, because its folded
  state does not say which form a request came from. That amount is
  at least R(q) for each q. So it is sound in the one dimension that
  I1 counts, which is entries. It may refuse new work that would
  have fitted. It never admits a duty that cannot settle.
  - Which form made a request is read from the request's origin
    entry, which the scope holds and which a clause reads in any case
    (section 6.6). A runtime that wants the exact amount may keep
    that as an index, which is derived storage. The folded state of
    section 9.2 does not change.
  - Holding more changes only whether new work is written. It
    changes nothing that a written entry holds (section 17.3, "The
    budget decides only whether"). So a history that a runtime with
    a larger reservation wrote passes a verifier that derives the
    least amounts.
  - The rule by which a runtime reserves is part of its capacity
    configuration. A report names it with the budget, under `budget`
    (section 9.5).
  - A dimension that a runtime does not count at all is not a larger
    reservation. It is a missing one, and it stays owed (section
    15.6f, row 7).
- **The closing checkpoint. New in revision 10.** Revision 9 reserved
  "one closing checkpoint" and did not say which checkpoint uses the
  reservation, or what follows. This is the rule.
  - *What it reserves.* 1 entry, and the bytes of one checkpoint
    entry. A checkpoint entry has a fixed size and retains nothing
    new. The size is R4's to measure; until then the entry size of
    section 7.5 stands in for it. There is one reservation for the
    scope, not one for each duty.
  - *When it is pending.* From the genesis entry on, except while the
    head entry is a checkpoint and no other duty is pending. That is
    derived from the head and from the pending duties, like every
    other amount (section 17.1). No flag is kept.
  - *Which checkpoint uses it.* A checkpoint that is written when no
    other duty is pending, on a head that is not a checkpoint, is the
    **closing checkpoint**. It is a settling entry and draws on the
    reservation. After it Reserved is zero, and the history ends on a
    checkpoint.
  - *Which checkpoint does not.* A checkpoint that is written while
    another duty is pending is new work, and it leaves the reservation
    as it is. Each pending duty's settling entry will move the head
    on, and the scope must still be able to end on a checkpoint. So
    such a checkpoint needs a free entry, and with none it is not
    written. A checkpoint on a head that is already a checkpoint is
    new work too.
  - *What arms it again.* The next entry that is not a checkpoint.
    After a closing checkpoint no duty is pending, so that entry
    settles nothing: it is new work. The admission check counts the
    reservation again, and the entry is admitted only if it, its
    duties and one closing checkpoint fit. So at every head Used plus
    Reserved is within the budget, and Reserved holds a checkpoint
    unless the history already ends on one with nothing pending.
  - *What a count must not do.* Owe one checkpoint at every head and
    also let every checkpoint into that entry. A checkpoint beside a
    pending hold then takes the entry that the closing checkpoint
    needs. The fourth witness of section 17.4 is that case.
- **Bytes of a reservation. New in revision 9.** Revision 8 reserved
  the bytes of the settling entry only. A settling entry may also
  retain inputs that the scope did not hold, and those can be many
  times larger than the entry. A handler whose message declares a list
  of 32 facts writes a small entry and retains 32 foreign entries,
  whether or not a guard reads them. So the
  byte reservation of a settling entry is the sum of three amounts.
  1. *Its own bytes.* The static size bound of the entry form: its
     declared fields at their maxima, its derived effects and sends at
     theirs, and a fixed allowance for the envelope. The allowance is
     R4's to measure. Until it is, the entry size of section 7.5
     stands in for this whole amount. That is a labelled stand-in and
     not a budget.
  2. *The inputs it may newly retain.* For each row of section 17.1's
     table, the most that the form can retain, times the bound on one.
     The validator derives the counts from the form, by the table
     below.
  3. *The duties it starts.* The byte reservation of each pending duty
     that the entry creates, by this same rule.

  | Retained input | How many one settling form may newly retain |
  |---|---|
  | Foreign entries | One for each fact that a declared field of the act or of the message can name, whether or not a guard or a part reads it (section 6.4, point DH4). A field counts by its type, at the declared maxima of section 6.2: a `fact` counts 1; a `list` counts its `max` times the count of its element type; a `record` counts the sum of the counts of its members, required or not; every other type counts none. One more for each fact that the act's `presents` declares. One more, once, for the source entry, when the form is a handler or the entry is a delivery. For a result clause, none: it reads only entries that the origin entry retained (section 6.6). In all, at most the bound on foreign entries of section 7.5. Corrected after the review `a7f1c108`: "Every fetched fact is counted", below. |
  | Definitions | None. A scope holds its named closure from its genesis (section 7.2). In a platform scope whose code takes a definition's name from an input: that definition and its closure, at the bound on a closure. |
  | Detached texts | One for each detached field of the act or of the message, at that field's `max`. |
  | Values beside an intent. New in revision 14. | One for each place of the act that names one, at the bound of its domain. For a place that names a definition: that definition and its closure, at the bound on a closure. None for a handler, because no value travels beside a message (section 6.2). None for an act of a declared definition, which has no such place. |
  | Rule inputs | One for each `rule` guard of the form. |
  | A snapshot, or other evidence under a digest | What the capability version, or the effect's owner, declares for that guard, effect or outcome, with the bound on each. |

  For the entries that the platform builds: a timed entry and a
  checkpoint retain nothing new. A diagnosis retains nothing new, and
  a delivery of a result only its source entry: a clause reads what
  the origin entry retained (section 6.6). Revision 9 reserved for
  facts that a clause might fetch. A delivery of a control retains
  its source entry. A
  settlement entry retains at most the two entries that its `at` and
  `found` name. An outcome retains what its owner declares. Since
  revision 14: the observations that an outcome, a delivery of a result
  or an act retains are inside the entry. They are part of amount 1,
  the entry's own bytes, at the most that the definition states for
  that entry, and they are no input of amount 2 (section 16.1).
  Made exact in revision 20: of foreign entries an outcome newly
  retains none. Its `uses` is a copy of the `uses` of its origin, which
  the scope holds (section 6.1, "The origin of an outcome"). What its
  owner declares is evidence under a digest, and each value that an
  observation of the entry names, at the bound of its domain.
  Changed in revision 21, in three sentences of this point. "A delivery
  of a result only its source entry": and each value that a row of its
  clause states under `retains`. "They are no input of amount 2": the
  records are none, and a value that one of them names is one. "Each
  value that an observation of the entry names, at the bound of its
  domain": at the `max` of the row. One rule states all three, for every
  form: "A value that an observation names", below. With it the table
  above has one more row.
- **Every fetched fact is counted. Corrected after the review
  `a7f1c108`.** Revisions 9 to 13 counted, in the row "Foreign entries"
  above, one for each fact field and each presented fact "that a `fact`
  guard reads, or that a part reads which needs the entry's bytes".
  Revision 13 also made exact that every foreign fact that a declared
  field names is fetched before the turn and recorded in `uses`,
  whether or not a guard or a part reads it (section 6.4, point DH4).
  The two did not agree. A settling form could declare a list of
  facts, read none of them, and count none, although its settling
  entry retains every one. So the count was not a maximum. The count
  is now by declaration. This is the formula, for a settling form f.
  - n(t) is the most facts that one value of the field type t can
    name. For `fact` it is 1. For `{ type: "list", of: u, max: m }` it
    is m times n(u). For a `record` it is the sum of n over its
    members, each counted whether it is required or not. For every
    other type it is 0.
  - D(f) is the sum of n(t) over the declared fields of f: the
    `fields` of an act, or of a handler's message. Every field is
    counted, required or optional, read or not.
  - P(f) is the number of facts that the `presents` of f declares, at
    most 4 as proposed (section 6.4). It is 0 for a handler.
  - S(f) is 1 when f is a handler, or the entry is a delivery, for the
    source entry. It is 0 for an act. The source entry is counted
    once.
  - B is the bound on the foreign entries of one entry (section 7.5).
  - The count of foreign entries is F(f): the smaller of B and
    D(f) + P(f) + S(f). The bytes reserved for them are F(f) times the
    bound on one foreign entry (section 17.1).

  Why F(f) is a maximum. The foreign entries that an entry retains are
  those that it names in `uses`. No part causes a fetch (section 6.5,
  point D20), and a clause fetches none (section 6.6). So `uses` holds
  only the source entry and the foreign facts that the input names in a
  declared field or presents. An input cannot name a fact anywhere
  else: a field that the form does not declare, a member that a record
  does not declare, and a presented name that the act does not declare
  are each refused (sections 6.2 and 6.4). A list holds at most its
  `max`. An input that names more foreign entries than B is refused
  before any is fetched (section 4.2, `entry-too-large`; section 6.4,
  point DH4), and a refusal is not the settling entry of this duty
  (section 17.3). Each retained entry is at most the bound on one.

  The count assumes nothing about the values. An optional field may be
  absent. A fact may be local, and a local fact is not fetched (section
  6.2). A field may name the source entry again, or an entry that the
  scope already keeps. Each of those adds no bytes when the settling
  entry is written, and that part of the reservation is released with
  the duty, as the next point says. The count does not leave such a
  field out, because the form does not say which value will arrive.
  The companion file's `result` handler declares five fact fields and
  reads inside none: it counts 6, and not 1.

  No mechanism is added. The maxima are the declared ones of section
  6.2 and the bound of section 7.5, and the validator already derives
  the counts from the form. The source counts no bytes at all (section
  17.5), so this changes no row of what the source must change. Bytes
  in source stay with the capacity follow-through `cc570904`, and every
  number with the proof plan.
- **Nothing shared is assumed.** A reservation is made as if none of
  those inputs were retained yet. When the settling entry finds one
  already kept under the same domain and digest, it adds no bytes for
  it, and that part of the reservation is released with the duty. Two
  pending duties that will retain the same input each reserve it.
  That reserves more than is needed, and it is finite.
- **Bytes that exist before the entry that names them.** Some bytes
  are in the scope before the entry that will name them is sealed.
  They are never an uncharged cache, and no judgment rests on them
  before that entry.

  | Bytes | Where they are until that entry is sealed | When it is sealed |
  |---|---|---|
  | Entries fetched before the turn, detached text and, since revision 14, values received with an input, and the definitions read for a genesis (sections 5.2, step 1, 6.2 and 7.2) | In the turn's working memory. They are not durable, and a restart loses them. A turn holds at most the foreign entries, the texts, the values and the definitions of one input. This is a temporary allocation of the platform, in neither amount. | Those that the written entry names are written with it, in its transaction, and are then Used. That holds for every entry that is written, and so for one that records a refusal: it keeps what was read before the refusal (section 6.5). The charge follows the entry's kind (section 17.3). For new work the admission check counts them. For a settling entry they are drawn from its duty's reservation. They are discarded, with nothing charged, only when the turn writes no entry: an act that is refused, an input that is not judged, or new work that does not fit. Revision 10 added here: "A fetched input that the written entry does not name is discarded too." Since revision 14 that sentence covers less. A written entry names every foreign entry that was fetched for its input (section 6.5), so a turn that writes discards no fetched entry. What is still discarded is a text or a value that came beside an input and that no place of the input names: it was never kept (section 6.2). Revision 9 said that they are discarded whenever the input is refused. That was wrong for a refusal that is written. |
  | A snapshot of staged refs, stored before the outcome entry of its `check` (section 6.11) | Durable. Its room is the byte reservation of that operation, which row 5 made when the operation was opened. Reserved does not change when the bytes are stored. | They are Used, and that part of the reservation ends. If no outcome entry names them, they are not a retained input: nothing reads them, and the scope discards them. |
  | The attempt log of a request (section 7.4) | Durable. Its room is the diagnosis entry that row 1 reserved. | The diagnosis entry carries the log, so the log is part of that entry's bytes. A log must therefore fit that entry. The retry policy that keeps it inside the bound is R4's (point R1-32). |

  So a durable byte that a judgment may come to rest on is always in
  one of two places: in Used, under an entry that names it; or inside
  the reservation of the pending duty whose settling entry will name
  it.
- **A reservation is released** when its duty ends without using all
  of it: a job that is superseded, a request whose result arrived and
  needed no diagnosis, a clause that created less than was reserved
  for it, a deadline that no longer holds, an input that
  was already retained.
- **A request that an outcome sends. New in revision 20** (I3 delta
  FC2). Row 5 counts the records and the operations that the outcomes
  of an operation derive, and names no request. Since revision 17 the
  mark of a kind may hold one `send`, whose rule returns no request or
  one in each outcome entry. That request is a duty of row 1, and the
  outcome entry that sends it cannot be refused. So the reservation of
  an operation counts it when the operation is opened: 1 pending
  request, its 2 entries, and what one clause of the `send` can start.
  It counts that once where the send mark states `once: true`: at most
  one outcome entry of one operation then makes the request, and a
  second is a fault of the rule. Otherwise it counts it once for each
  outcome entry that the operation can have, which is 2 for each
  attempt. What is not used is released when the operation is settled.
  A kind whose request is made on its selecting outcome, and on no
  other, states `once`. Under `holds` the request is counted by the
  item instead (section 17.2a).
- **The closure of an operation. Made exact in revision 21** (the
  verdict `0cf59056`, its first finding). Row 5 reserves 2 entries for
  each attempt, "and the records and operations that its outcomes
  derive". It did not say how often one operation's outcomes may open a
  kind, or what else a rule may start. This is the count, for one
  operation of a kind k of `outcomes` that no item holds.
  - n(k) is 2 times `attempts(k)`: the outcome entries that the
    operation can have, a first outcome and a late answer for each
    attempt.
  - One outcome entry may start what the mark of k states, and no more
    ("What a mark may start", below): one operation of each kind in
    `most.operations`, one item of the type `most.opens`, and changes of
    state. The request of its `send` is the point above.
  - C(k), the **closure** of the operation, is n(k) times the sum of
    these: the outcome entry itself; C(j) for each kind j in
    `most.operations`; what the item reserves; and what the changes of
    state start. To that is added the request of the `send`, once or
    n(k) times, as the point above says.
  - C(k) is an amount in each of the five dimensions. An outcome entry
    is 1 entry, and in bytes the three amounts of "Bytes of a
    reservation". In items, records and pending requests C(k) holds only
    what the entry starts.
  - Every kind j of that sum is one that no item holds. The validator
    refuses the mark of such a kind that lists a held kind (section
    17.2a, check 5). So C(k) is computed from the data alone.
  - C(k) is finite exactly when no kind reaches itself. Otherwise the
    definition is refused `reserve-unbounded`, as before.
  - *How it moves.* When an outcome entry opens an operation of the kind
    j, C(j) moves from the first operation's reservation to the new
    operation's own. Used plus reserved does not grow. What the outcome
    entries did not start is released when the operation is settled.
  - *The verdict's kinds.* U has 3 attempts and opens nothing: C(U) is 6
    entries. K has 1 attempt and lists U: one operation of K counts 2
    times (1 + 6), which is 14 entries. A script made the sum.
  - A late answer is an outcome entry, and its rule runs. So it is
    counted like a first outcome. That is never less.
    Decided in revision 22 (the planner's act `39749e26`): this full
    count is the default, and it stays. A kind may later state that only
    its first outcome opens. That would be a member of the data, which
    the validator reads and to which the judge holds the rule. It is
    never inferred from what a rule did. No such member is in this
    revision.
- **What a mark may start. New in revision 21.** A rule's result is not
  in the data. So the validator counts a mark by what its `most` allows,
  wherever the mark stands: at place 5 of an act, of a handler or of a
  clause of a result, and at place 7.
  - *An operation.* One of each kind in `most.operations`. A kind that
    no item holds counts its closure C. A held kind counts nothing here:
    the holder that the effect is `for` counts it (section 17.2a).
  - *An item.* One item of the type `most.opens`: 1 item, and what an
    item of that type reserves in its initial state. That is the chain
    of a deadline there (row 2), and what it awaits there as a
    settlement (row 3).
  - *A change of state.* A rule may set the state, or a deadline slot,
    of an item that it names, and the data does not say of which. So
    each of the `most.effects` effects counts as a change of state of
    one more item, at the largest, over the item types of the definition
    and their states, of what an item in that state reserves: the chain
    of a deadline, and what it awaits. Under a definition with no timed
    rule and no `settles` that is nothing. It is the worst case, and
    never less than what the rule does. A form by which a mark names the
    states that its rule may set would count less. No row asks for it,
    and it is its owner's to ask.
    Decided in revision 22: the planner accepted the count at the worst
    case (act `39749e26`). A mark that names the states that its rule
    may set may come later, as a smaller count, and no form of it is in
    this revision. Read with revision 22: "what an item in that state
    reserves" is the sum of rule 6 of "A marker duty", below, with no
    mark completed.
  - *A clause.* "A request's clauses", above, lists three duties that a
    clause's effects can create. A clause that holds an effect mark can
    create these too, and the reservation of its request counts them.
    This answers the open row of section 15.6s on what a mark in a
    result clause can open, and what revision 19 left owed for it.
  - *A settling form.* Point DI18, below, counts "what its own effects
    can start". A mark of the form counts there as this point says.
    Changed in revision 22: with one exception. A rule of a form that
    declares `settles` returns no change of state, so a mark of such a
    form counts none: its operations and its item only (section 6.4, "A
    rule of a form that declares `settles` sets no state"). Without that
    the worst case of the point above held the form's own duty, and no
    such form had a finite closure.
  - *A timed rule.* No mark stands in one (section 6.1). So a timed
    entry starts nothing by a rule, and opens no operation of a kind of
    `outcomes`.
- **A value that an observation names. New in revision 21** (the verdict
  `0cf59056`, its second finding). The table of "Bytes of a reservation"
  counted a value for the places of an act and for an outcome, and none
  for a delivery of a result, although a clause may state a row whose
  observation names one. The rule is one, and it is read from the
  declaration: **every form that states a row of `observes` with
  `retains` counts, in what its entry may newly retain, one value for
  each record of `retains`, at that record's `max`.**

  | Retained input | How many one form may newly retain |
  |---|---|
  | Values that an observation names. New in revision 21. | One for each record of `retains`, of each row of `observes` that the form states, at the record's `max` (section 16.1, "A value that a row may retain"). None for a form that states no such row. |

  Where the amount is reserved follows the form, as for every other
  input of amount 2.

  | The form that states the row | Its entry | Where the bytes are reserved |
  |---|---|---|
  | An act that settles nothing | New work | Nowhere. Its admission counts what the entry newly retains, at its real size. |
  | An act that declares `settles` | Settling, when it settles | Row 3 or row 4: in what the item or the copy reserves while it awaits. |
  | A kind of `outcomes` | An outcome entry | Row 5: when the operation is opened, for each of its outcome entries. Under `holds`: in `one(k)`, when the holder is taken. |
  | A clause `applied`, `refused` or `superseded` | A delivery of a result | Row 1: when the entry that sends the request is admitted. The request reserves the largest, over the clauses that can still run, of the whole byte amount of the clause's entry. Where an outcome sends the request: with its operation, or in `req` of its holder. |
  | A clause `conflict` | New work | Nowhere. Its admission counts it. |

  - *Nothing shared is assumed*, as for every input. A value that is
    kept already, under the same domain and digest, adds no bytes when
    the entry is written, and that part of the reservation is released
    with the duty.
  - *Missing bytes give no observation.* An answer without the bytes, or
    with bytes over the `max`, is no answer (section 16.1). Nothing of
    it is stored, so nothing is charged.
  - *One rule.* No other kind of observation names a value today. One
    that does later states `retains` on its row, and is counted by this
    sentence.
  - The row "Values beside an intent" stands as it is: no value travels
    beside a message. A value that an observation names does not travel
    with the input. The scope reads it.
- **A marker duty. New in revision 22** (the verdict `dc1da38a`, its
  second finding; section 6.4, "`settles` by a mark"). Row 3 of the
  table above is one row for two kinds of duty. An item whose state a
  `settles` of the first form lists has a **state duty**, as before. An
  item with marks has a **marker duty** for each. This point says what a
  marker duty is, what it reserves and why its count ends. It replaces
  three sentences of revision 21 that did not agree (section 6.4,
  "Several marks on one item").
  1. *Its identity.* A marker duty is a pair, written (item, slot): one
     item, and one slot of it that a `settles` of the third form names
     for the item's type. At any head one item has at most one marker
     duty for one slot, however many forms can settle it.
  2. *When it is pending.* While the slot is `false` and the item's
     state is in the `in` of at least one form that settles that slot.
     Both are read from the folded state.
  3. *When it begins, and what reserves it.* A mark is `false` from the
     entry that opens its item. So "pending" does not wait for an entry
     that touches the mark. The duty begins with the entry that leaves
     the item in a listed state with the slot `false`: the opening
     entry, where the initial state is listed, and otherwise the entry
     that sets a listed state. That entry reserves the duty, once. Where
     the entry is new work, its admission counts it (section 17.3).
     Where the entry is settling, the closure of the duty that it
     settles counted it (rule 7, and point DI18). An entry that finds
     the duty pending and leaves it pending reserves no second one. The
     duty goes on, with the amount of the state that the item is then
     in.
  4. *When it ends.* It is **completed** when the slot is `true`,
     whichever entry set it. A mark is set once (section 6.4), so a
     completed duty is never pending again for that item. It also ends
     when the item leaves the listed states with the slot `false`. What
     it reserved is then released. It begins again if a later entry puts
     the item back into a listed state, and that entry reserves it, as
     rule 3 says.
