  5. *Alternatives are of one duty.* The **alternatives** of (item, s),
     in the state x, are the forms whose `settles` names s for the
     item's type and whose `in` lists x. The duty reserves the largest,
     in each dimension, over those forms. No other form is compared with
     them: not a form that settles another mark, and not a form that
     settles by state.
  6. *Distinct duties are summed.* What one item reserves is a sum of
     three things: the chain of its deadline (row 2); its state duty,
     where a form `{ of, in }` lists its state, with the largest over
     the forms that settle that state, as before; and each of its marker
     duties that is pending. So an item with two marks that are both
     `false` in a listed state reserves two settlements, and a third
     where a form settles its state.
  7. *What one marker duty reserves.* Take the duty (item, s), the
     item's state x, and the set D of the item's marks that are `true`.
     For each alternative f it is: 1 entry; the records that f changes;
     for each request among its sends, what row 1 reserves; what its
     effects can start on its other subjects and in an item that it
     opens, as point DI18 counts them; and, for the settled item, one of
     two amounts. Where no written effect of f sets the item's state:
     nothing. The entry leaves the item's other duties as they are, and
     each of them is reserved for itself. Where a written effect of f
     can set its state to y: what the item reserves in y by rule 6, with
     s and the marks of D taken as completed. That is the chain in y,
     the state duty in y, and each marker duty (item, t) whose forms
     list y, for every mark t that is not s and not in D, each by this
     rule with s added to D. Where f can set several states, the largest
     of them counts. A deadline slot that f sets counts its chain, as
     point DI18 says. The duty reserves the largest over its
     alternatives.
  8. *A completed mark is in no later closure.* Each step of rule 7 by a
     mark adds that mark to D, and nothing takes a mark out, because a
     mark only becomes `true`. The same set is used where the item's
     state duty counts a state that its form can set: a mark that is
     `true` is not counted there either. So a path of settlements of one
     item passes each (item, slot) at most once. This is why the count
     ends for an item with several marks. The item has a fixed number of
     marks. Between two steps by a mark the path goes by states and by
     timed rules only, and that part is finite or the definition is
     refused, as before.
  9. *The check for a cycle.* For states and for timed rules it is as it
     was: forms `{ of, in }` that create each other's listed states in a
     cycle, and timed rules that lead to one another in a cycle, refuse
     the definition `reserve-unbounded`. A step by a mark of the settled
     item is no edge of a cycle, by rule 8. So two forms that each set
     one mark and move the item between two states validate: the path is
     the first mark, then the second, and it ends. For any other item no
     mark is taken as completed. An item that the entry opens, and
     another subject whose state an effect sets, are counted in that
     state with every mark `false`. That is never less. So a form by a
     mark whose effects can leave another item of its own type in a
     state of its own `in` reaches its own duty by type. Its closure is
     not finite, and the definition is refused `reserve-unbounded`.
  10. *In the fold, and at admission.* Both amounts stay functions of
      the folded state (section 17.1). The state holds each item's state
      and slots. From them and from the pinned definition the scope
      derives which duties are pending, the set D, and each amount. New
      work is admitted only if used plus reserved is within the budget
      after it, and "reserved" then holds every marker duty that the
      entry leaves pending. An entry that settles (item, s) is admitted
      against that one duty's reservation, and draws on no other duty of
      the item. When a mark becomes `true`, by any entry, the amounts of
      the item's other duties are derived with it in D. They fall or
      stay, and what falls is released.
  11. *An item that is not named.* Where this section counts "what an
      item in a state reserves" for an item that the data does not name,
      it is the sum of rule 6 with no mark completed. That is so for the
      item that a mark opens, for a change of state by a rule ("What a
      mark may start", above), and for `itm` and `one(k)` of section
      17.2a.

  *Why the guarantee of section 17.3 follows.* Take an entry of the form
  f that settles (item, s) in the state x. Before it the item reserves,
  by rule 6, the amount of (item, s) and of each other pending duty. The
  amount of (item, s) is at least the entry, what it sends and starts
  elsewhere, and, where it sets the state y, everything that the item
  reserves in y with s completed. After the entry the item reserves
  exactly that last amount, or, where the state did not change, its
  other duties as they were. So reserved falls by at least what the
  entry uses and starts, and used plus reserved does not grow.

  *The case that the form exists for, checked.* The planner's purpose is
  that the first notice that a key behind a publication is compromised
  can be recorded at a destination with no free room (act `1f8aba72`).
  The authority note's adopted rows were read for this: its section 5.8,
  which reserves "1 for the first `compromised` notice that names a key
  behind it"; and in its section 12.1.5 the row `compromised`, the slot
  `aborting` and the rule `abort-if-behind`. In this form:
  - the mark is the slot `aborting` of a publication, which that note
    states as a truth value, required, with `default: false`;
  - the handler names the publication by a written rule: `via` the slot
    `slot` of the branch, which is the one item of its type. No selector
    is needed;
  - `in` lists `reserved`, `publishing` and `unresolved`. None is final;
  - the duty (publication, `aborting`) begins with the outcome of
    `judge` that sets `reserved`. Its room is in what the publication
    holds from its taking entry, which is the delivery of `reserve`:
    `one(judge)` counts a change of state by the rule of `judge` at the
    worst case, and that worst case holds this duty. It becomes the
    publication's own duty when the state is set;
  - it reserves 1 entry. The rule `abort-if-behind` sets the mark,
    empties one slot and opens two operations of held kinds, which draw
    on the counts of the publication while it is not final. It returns
    no change of state, as "What a mark may start" now asks of a rule of
    a settling form;
  - it is released when the mark is set, or when the publication is
    `published` or `aborted`.

  So the first notice that sets the mark is a settling entry, and it is
  written with no free room. A notice that names a key which is not
  behind the publication sets no mark, and is new work. So is a second
  notice. The purpose holds, on what the authority note owes: the row in
  this form, with the name of `also`, and counts of `revoke` and of
  `read` that cover the two operations of the notice.

  Witness 18.54.

**Made exact in revision 13, from the I2 source choices.** Each point
names the entries of the I2 deltas note that it answers (section 15.6l).
Each is a rule of this contract from this revision, for the reason that
the point gives. None changes an entry that the I2 source at `744f2447`
writes, unless the point says so.

- **DI18.** What a settling form reserves in entries, made exact. For a
  form that declares `settles`: 1 entry; what its own effects can start,
  by subject; and, for each request among its sends, at the bounds, 2
  entries and the most that one clause of that send can start. A fan-out
  counts at its type's `max`. "What a list of effects can start" is, for
  each subject, the largest, over the states that the list can set, of
  the chain of a deadline in that state and of what an item in that
  state reserves for its settlement; or the chain of a deadline slot
  that the list sets. An item that the form opens counts in its initial
  state. A state of the settled subject that the form's own `settles`
  lists is not counted: an entry that leaves the subject there settles
  nothing. Where several forms settle one state, the largest counts. At
  the proposed bounds this gives 67 entries for a merge that is asked
  for in the `change` definition, which is the number that this section
  states. This point is in entries only. The other four dimensions
  follow rows 3 and 4 as they are written, and the source does not count
  them (section 17.5; the capacity follow-through `cc570904`).
- **DI19.** An item in a state from which a timed rule leads to a state
  that awaits a settlement reserves that settlement already. The reason:
  a timed entry is a settling entry and is never refused, so the room
  for what it leaves pending must exist before it is due.

Changed in revision 22, in points DI18 and DI19 (the verdict `dc1da38a`,
its second finding). They are read with "A marker duty", above. In DI18,
"what an item in that state reserves for its settlement" is the sum of
rule 6: its state duty, and each marker duty whose forms list the state.
"Where several forms settle one state, the largest counts" stands for a
state duty. For a marker duty it is rule 5: the largest over the forms
that settle that one mark. For the subject that a form of the third kind
settles, rule 7 stands in place of the sentence "A state of the settled
subject that the form's own `settles` lists is not counted": the form's
own mark and the marks that are `true` are completed, and a state is
counted only where a written effect of the form sets it. Point DI19
holds for a marker duty too: a state that a timed rule leads to counts
each marker duty whose forms list it, for the marks of the item that are
not `true`.

### 17.2a A reservation that an item holds

New in revision 20 (I3 deltas FA3, FA5, FC1 and FC2; the capacity
follow-through `cc570904`; the authority note's section 5.8 and its row
P11, "No form says it"). Section 17.2 reserves for one duty and for what
that duty starts, by a closure that the validator computes by kind. That
does not work where the kinds of one definition open each other in a
circle. In the authority note's destination an outcome of a `judge`
opens a push, and an outcome of that push opens the next `judge`, for
another publication. By kind the closure is not finite, and section 17.2
refuses the definition `reserve-unbounded`. The I3 source took five
kinds out of the check with a flag, `covered`, which reserves nothing,
and counted 71 entries of each publication that no admission reserved.
That is an exemption, and this section replaces it with a reservation
that is counted, checked and released.

The thing that is finite is not a kind. It is one item: one publication
has one push, a stated number of attempts and a stated number of
tokens. So the reservation is taken for the item, once, by the entry
that opens it, and each operation says which item it is for.

```ts
/** On an item type, and on an act. In platform data only. Revision 20 (section 6.1). */
interface Held { operations?: Record<string, number>;   // by kind of `outcomes`: the most that are opened for one item
                 requests?: number;                     // the most requests that are sent for one item
                 items?: number }                       // the most items that are opened for one item
// ItemType.holds?: Held      what one item of the type reserves, from the entry that opens it
// ActType.adds?: Held        what an act adds to the reservation of the item that it is on
// Effect, section 4.1:       { effect: "operation"; ...; for?: Local }
// Revision 21:
// Held.decisions?: Record<string, number>                        by message name: the most bound requests that are decided for one item
// ReceiveType.bound?: { of: Subject; where: readonly Where[] }   on a `tell` handler ("A request that is bound to a holder", below)
// Revision 22: the name of `also` that `bound.of` names may be bound by a mark at place 2, a binding selector ("The source of `bound.of`", below).
// Revision 23: ItemType.indexes?: readonly string[], and on a binding selector `index: string; key: string` ("An index that an item type declares", below).
```

**The words.**

- A **holder** is an item of a type that states `holds`.
- A **held kind** is a kind of `outcomes` that the `holds` or the `adds`
  of some form of the definition lists.
- The **account** of an entry is at most one holder: the item on whose
  reservation the entry draws. The table below gives it.
- What a holder **still holds** is three counts, as `Held` has them:
  what is left of each kind, of its requests and of its items.

| The entry | Its account | What it does to the counts |
|---|---|---|
| The entry that opens a holder: the **taking** entry | That item | Sets them to the type's `holds`. Then it draws, as the rows below say, for what it opens and sends itself. |
| An act whose form states `adds`, on a holder: an **adding** entry | That item | Adds the act's `adds`. Then it draws for what it opens and sends. |
| An outcome entry | The holder that its operation is `for`. None, where the operation states no `for`. | Draws for what it opens and sends. |
| A delivery of a result, and a diagnosis | The account of the entry that sent the request | Draws for what its clause opens. A clause sends nothing. |
| Every other entry | None | Nothing |

**A draw.** An entry draws 1 from a count for each of these.

- An `operation` effect whose `for` names the holder: 1 from the count
  of its kind.
- A request among its sends, where the entry has an account: 1 from
  `requests` of that account.
- The opening of an item by an entry that has an account, other than
  the holder itself: 1 from `items` of that account.

**`for`.** An `operation` effect of a held kind states `for`: the local
ID of a holder, or `"self"` in the taking entry. An `operation` effect
of a kind that is not held states none. A rule gives it with the
operation. So one entry may open operations for two holders. In the
authority note's rows, the outcome that publishes one publication opens
the next `judge` for another, and that `judge` draws on the other's
reservation. This changes
one sentence of revision 19, which said that an `operation` effect
gains no member (section 6.1, the point on ER6): it gains this one, and
only under a definition that states `holds`.

**What the validator checks.** With its platform option:

1. `holds` stands on an item type, and `adds` on an act whose `on` is a
   type that states `holds`. Each key of `operations` is a key of
   `outcomes`. Each count is a whole number, at least 1, and at most a
   ceiling that R4 sets. Until it does, the bound on the elements of a
   list stands in for it (section 6.1).
2. An item type that states `holds` is opened only by a form whose
   entry is new work, and so is asked whether it fits: an act, a handler
   of a request, or the genesis act. Its type is the `opens` of no mark
   of `outcomes` or of a clause, and of no handler of an advisory.
3. It computes the amounts of each `holds` and each `adds`, by the
   table "What a holder reserves", below. No total is written in the
   data, so a total cannot be stated lower than its counts.
4. A held kind is in no closure. Where the closure of a duty would
   count an operation of a held kind, it counts nothing: the holder
   counts it. The closure of every kind that is not held, and of every
   other duty, must be finite as before, or the definition is refused
   `reserve-unbounded`.
5. Each kind that the mark of a held kind lists in `most.operations` is
   a held kind, or has a finite closure.

A definition that fails 1, 2 or 5 does not validate.

Changed in revision 21, in checks 4 and 5 (the verdict `0cf59056`, its
first finding). Check 5 let the mark of a held kind list a kind that no
item holds, and nothing reserved that kind for the holder. The two
checks are now these. "What a holder reserves, in full", below, has the
amounts.

4. A held kind is in no closure by kind: its holder counts it. A kind
   that no item holds has the closure of section 17.2, "The closure of
   an operation", and that closure must be finite.
5. The mark of a held kind may list held kinds, and kinds that no item
   holds. The mark of a kind that no item holds lists no held kind. So
   from a kind that no item holds no held kind is reached, and its
   closure is a number that the validator computes from the data.

A definition that fails check 4 or check 5 is refused
`reserve-unbounded`: no reservation by kind can be computed for it. A
definition that fails check 1 or check 2 does not validate, as before.
The reason for the second sentence of check 5: an operation of a kind
that no item holds states no `for`. Nothing in the data would say for
which holder its outcomes open a held kind, and a holder that is final
could have released the count before the draw. An effect mark of an act,
of a handler or of a clause may still list a held kind, and its entry
draws on the holder that the effect is `for` ("A draw", above).

**Check 5, by every edge of a closure. Made exact in revision 22** (the
verdict `dc1da38a`, a clarification). Revision 21 stated "from a kind
that no item holds no held kind is reached" as what follows, and checked
only the mark of the kind. It is the condition that the validator
checks, and it is not only about that mark. For a kind u that no item
holds, the closure C(u) counts entries that the platform builds, that
cannot be refused, and that have no account. None of them may open an
operation of a held kind. These are the edges of a closure, each with
what the validator does there.

| # | The edge | The entry that would open | A held kind there |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The `most.operations` of the mark of u | An outcome entry of u. It has no account: u states no `for`. | Refused, as in revision 21 |
| 2 | The `most.operations` of an effect mark in a clause of the `send` of u: `applied`, `refused`, `superseded`, `undelivered` or `conflict` | A delivery of a result of that request, or its diagnosis. Its account is that of the entry that sent the request, which has none. | Refused. Stated in revision 22. |
| 3 | A kind j that no item holds, reached by edge 1 or by edge 2 | The outcome entries of j, and the results of its `send` | Refused, by edges 1 and 2 again, for every such kind |
| 4 | The item of `most.opens`, of the mark of u or of a clause's mark | None. The opening draws on no count. | A type that states `holds` is refused there by check 2 |
| 5 | A deadline of an item that the closure opens, or leaves in a state | A timed entry | None is possible: no mark stands in a timed rule |
| 6 | A settlement, by state or by a mark, of an item that the closure opens or leaves in a state: the effect marks of the settling form, and the clauses of the requests that it sends | An act or a delivery of that form. It is judged as any entry of its form, and its request has the account of that entry. | Not refused by this check. The opening draws on the holder that the effect is `for`, as for any act or delivery (section 17.3, "The induction, by edge") |

A definition with a held kind at edge 1, 2 or 3 is refused
`reserve-unbounded`.

- *The reason, which is one.* The rule of release keeps the counts of a
  final holder for the operations that are `for` it, and for the pending
  requests of its account ("Release", below). An outcome entry of u is
  neither. A request that such an entry sends has no account. So nothing
  would keep a holder's count until the clause of that request runs. The
  holder could become final and release the count, and the clause, whose
  entry cannot be refused, would then draw past it.
- *The path of the verdict, refused.* A kind `u` that no item holds
  states a `send`. The clause `applied` of that send holds an effect
  mark whose `most.operations` lists `v`. The item type `job` holds `v`.
  That is edge 2. The validator refuses the definition,
  `reserve-unbounded`.
- *What is not refused, and stays visible.* A held kind may open a kind
  that no item holds, and the closure of that kind is inside `one(k)`.
  An act, a handler and a clause of a request that an act or a handler
  sent may list a held kind. An entry with an account may open a held
  kind for another holder. Each of those draws on the holder that the
  effect is `for`, and a draw past a count is a fault ("Past a count",
  below).
- *Check 2, read with revision 22.* A handler that states `bound` may
  hold an effect mark whose `most.opens` is a type that states `holds`.
  Its rule opens the item only in a delivery that is not bound, which is
  new work ("The source of `bound.of`", below).

**What a holder reserves.** These are the amounts of what it still
holds. `attempts(k)` is the most attempts of the kind k, as its row in
`outcomes` states it.

Replaced. Marked in revision 22: the table that follows is revision
20's, and is kept as history. It counts the attempts of a held kind and
no more. It is not the amount. The amount is "What a holder reserves, in
full", below, which replaced it in revision 21.

| Dimension | What is counted, for the counts c by kind, q requests and i items |
|---|---|
| Entries | For each kind k: c(k) times 2 times `attempts(k)`, which is the first outcome and the late answer of each attempt (section 17.2, row 5). For the requests: q times 2, a diagnosis and a result, and q times the most entries that one clause of a send of the account can start (section 17.2, "A request's clauses"). |
| Items | i. And for each request, the items that one clause can open. |
| Records | None from a rule, which returns no `record` effect (section 6.1). For each request, the records that one written clause can change, as row 1 counts them. |
| Bytes | For each entry that is counted above, the three amounts of section 17.2, "Bytes of a reservation": its own static size, which for an outcome counts the `most` of its kind and the rows of its `observes` at their `max` (section 16.1); what it may newly retain, which for an outcome is what its owner declares under a digest, and one value for each observation that names one, at the bound of its domain; and nothing for the duties that it starts, which are counted in this table. An outcome newly retains no foreign entry: its `uses` is a copy (section 6.1). |
| Pending requests | q. Each is reserved until it is sent, and is used from the entry that sends it. |

**What a holder reserves, in full. Changed in revision 21** (the verdict
`0cf59056`, its first finding). The table above counts, for a held kind,
its own attempts and no more. A held kind may list a kind that no item
holds. An operation of that kind states no `for` and draws on no count.
So nothing reserved it, and used plus reserved grew when it was opened.
This passage replaces the table above. The words:

- n(k) is 2 times `attempts(k)`.
- C(j) is the closure of one operation of a kind j that no item holds
  (section 17.2, "The closure of an operation"). It is an amount in each
  of the five dimensions. By check 5 it reaches no held kind.
- `one(k)`, for a held kind k, is what one operation of k reserves. For
  each of its n(k) outcome entries: the entry itself; C(j) for each kind
  j in the `most.operations` of k's mark that no item holds; and what
  its effects can start by a change of state (section 17.2, "What a mark
  may start"). It counts nothing for a held kind that the mark lists,
  for the item of `most.opens` or for the request of the `send`: each of
  those draws on a count.
- The **forms of the account** are the forms whose entries can have the
  holder as their account: each form that opens the holder's type, each
  act that states `adds` on it, each handler that states `bound` to it,
  and each held kind that its `holds` or such an `adds` lists.
- `req` is what one request of the account reserves: 1 pending request;
  2 entries, a diagnosis and a result; and the largest, over the request
  sends of the forms of the account and over the clauses of each that
  are reserved, of what the clause's entry may newly retain and of what
  the clause can start. A held kind that a clause's mark lists counts
  nothing there, and an item that a clause opens draws on `items`.
- `itm` is what one item of the account reserves: 1 item, and the
  largest, over the item types that the forms of the account and their
  clauses may open, of what an item of the type reserves in its initial
  state.
- `dec(m)` is what one bound decision of the message m reserves ("A
  request that is bound to a holder", below).

A holder that still holds c(k) of each kind, q requests, i items and
d(m) decisions reserves, in each dimension: the sum over k of c(k) times
`one(k)`; q times `req`; i times `itm`; and the sum over m of d(m) times
`dec(m)`.

| Dimension | In `one(k)` | In `req` | In `itm` | In `dec(m)` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Entries | n(k); and n(k) times the entries of each C(j) and of what the changes of state start | 2; and the entries that one clause can start | The chain of a deadline in the initial state, and the entries of what the item awaits there | 1; and the entries that the handler's effects can start when it applies |
| Items | n(k) times the items of each C(j). Revision 22: and of what the changes of state start. | None: an item that a clause opens draws on i | 1 | None: a bound handler opens no item |
| Records | n(k) times the records of each C(j). None from a rule of k, which returns no `record` effect (section 6.1). Revision 22: and n(k) times the records of what the changes of state start. | The records that one clause can change | The records of what the item awaits | The records that the handler changes |
| Bytes | For each entry that the first row counts, the three amounts of section 17.2, "Bytes of a reservation": its static size, with the rows of `observes` at their `max`; what it may newly retain, which for an outcome is its owner's evidence under a digest and each value of `retains`; and nothing for the duties that it starts, which this table counts. An outcome newly retains no foreign entry. | The same, for the diagnosis and for the result. The result's entry may newly retain its source entry, and each value that a row of its clause states under `retains`. | The same, for each entry that the first row counts | Its static size, with the result that it sends; and what it may newly retain: the source entry, each fact that a declared field names, and each detached text |
| Pending requests | n(k) times the pending requests of each C(j). Revision 22: and of what the changes of state start. | 1. It is reserved until the request is sent, and used from then. | Those of what the item awaits | None: a request that the entry sends draws on q |

Changed in revision 22, in three cells of the column `one(k)` (the
verdict `dc1da38a`, a clarification). The definition of `one(k)`, above,
counts what the effects of an outcome entry can start by a change of
state, and that is an amount in every dimension. The cells for items,
records and pending requests named only C(j). Each now names the changes
of state too: a settlement that a change of state starts may open an
item, change a record or send a request. "What an item in a state
reserves" is there the sum of rule 6 of section 17.2, "A marker duty",
with no mark completed.

**The moves, by entry. Revision 21.** "How the two amounts move", below,
stands, and is read with these amounts.

- The taking entry is admitted with the whole sum reserved.
- An entry that opens an operation of a held kind k for the holder: c(k)
  falls by 1, and `one(k)` moves from the holder to the operation, as
  its duty of row 5.
- An outcome entry of that operation uses 1 entry and its bytes, out of
  `one(k)`. When it opens an operation of a kind j that no item holds,
  C(j) moves from the first operation's duty to the new operation's own.
  When it opens an operation of a held kind, sends a request or opens an
  item, the count that it draws on falls, and `one`, `req` or `itm`
  moves from that holder to the new duty.
- So at every entry of the account, and at every outcome entry of a kind
  that no item holds below it, reserved falls by at least what the entry
  uses and starts. Used plus reserved does not grow.
- *Release.* What an operation did not use is released when it is
  settled: the outcome entries that were not written, and the C(j) of
  each kind that they did not open. What a holder still holds is
  released by the rule "Release", below.

Witness 18.49.

**How the two amounts move.** The taking entry is new work. It is
admitted only if, after it, used plus reserved is within the budget in
every dimension, with the whole of the table above reserved (section
17.3). When it does not fit, nothing is written: an act is refused
`scope-full`, and a request is not decided, transport answers "retry",
and the sender keeps the duty. An adding entry is new work in the same
way, for its addition. A genesis that opens a holder is a creation, and
a creation that does not fit is a request that is not decided.

After that, nothing of the account is asked whether it fits. When an
entry opens an operation for the holder, the count of that kind falls
by 1, and the operation is a duty of row 5 that reserves the same 2
entries for each attempt. When an entry sends a request of the account,
`requests` falls by 1, and the request is a duty of row 1 that reserves
the same. So at each entry of the account, reserved falls by what the
entry uses, and used plus reserved does not grow. That is the
guarantee of section 17.3 for a settling entry, with the holder as the
duty.

An operation of a held kind reserves, by row 5, its own attempts and
nothing for what its outcomes open: those openings draw on the holder.
That is the checked form of what the flag `covered` said.

Corrected in revision 21. "Nothing for what its outcomes open" holds for
a held kind that an outcome opens, for the item that it opens and for
the request that it sends: each draws on a count. It was wrong for a
kind that no item holds, which draws on none. One operation of a held
kind reserves `one(k)`, and that includes the closure of each such kind
("What a holder reserves, in full", above).
Marked in revision 22: in the two paragraphs before this one, "reserves
the same 2 entries for each attempt" and "a duty of row 1 that reserves
the same" are the smaller amounts of revision 20. They are replaced: the
operation reserves `one(k)`, and the request `req`.

**What holds the count.** The folded state. For each holder it has
what the holder still holds, as three counts. For each operation it has
the holder that the operation is `for`, so the operations of one item
are read by the item: an index of the fold, as the index of accepted
keys is. For each pending request it has the account of the entry that
sent it. All three are derived from the entries alone: from the `open`
effect of the taking entry and the pinned `holds`; from the kind of an
adding act and the pinned `adds`; from each `operation` effect with its
`for`; and from each send. They add no member to an entry beside `for`.
A checkpoint's state digest covers them by the rule that covers the
index of accepted keys (section 9.2). So both amounts stay functions of
the folded state (section 17.1), a reader that starts at a checkpoint
has the counts, and a verifier derives them from the history.
Read with revision 23: this index, of operations by the item that each
is `for`, is not the index that an item type declares. "An index that an
item type declares", below, sets the two side by side.

This answers two things that the I3 source could not build. What a
publication has left is a value of the state, and falls as its entries
are written (entry FC1, row 1). And the operations of one item can be
read without a search of the scope's entries (entry FA5): a rule is
given the folded state, and the index is part of it.

**Past a count.** A rule that opens an operation of a held kind with no
`for`; for an item that is not a holder, or whose type does not list
the kind; or when the count of that kind is 0, has a fault. So has a
rule whose entry would send a request, or open an item, when that count
of its account is 0. The input is not judged and nothing is written
(section 6.1, "A fault of a rule is no judgment"). An outcome then
stays offered, and the fault is reported to operators.

So a definition whose rules can open more than its data states is never
under-reserved without a sign. The validator refuses what the data
shows: a kind in a circle that no item holds. The rest it cannot show,
because how often a rule opens a kind for one item is in the rule's
code. There the count is kept at run time, and the entry that would
pass it is not written. The witness of a definition shows that each
count is enough for its longest path, and that is its owner's to state
and the proof plan's to measure.

**A draw past a count, as the planner decided.** The planner confirmed
the rule above (act `1f8aba72`): a draw past a count that the definition
states is a fault, the outcome stays offered, and no end state is
forced. It is written here in revision 21, with the two things that the
planner added.

- *It shows as a state that a member can see at the lane.* A fault
  writes no entry. So no slot, no state of an item, no result and no
  update can hold it, and this contract adds none: an entry that
  recorded the fault would need room that nothing reserved. The state is
  derived by the runtime. An input is offered for an operation or a
  request of a holder, and a fault of a rule stops it. It is shown by a
  read. Two rows are owed, and no form of this contract carries the
  state. The authority note owes the read of an item of a platform scope
  that says so, with the name of the rule and the time since which the
  input is offered. The lane forms owe what a member is shown at the
  lane for a publication whose destination reports it. Until both exist
  the fault is reported to operators only, as before.
  Confirmed in revision 22: the planner accepted this split of owners
  (act `39749e26`). The read and the report of the fault are the
  authority note's, and what a member is shown at the lane is the lane
  forms'.
- *The way out.* One of two, and neither happens by itself. The first is
  an operator's act: an act whose form states `adds`, on that holder. It
  is new work, it is admitted with room for what it adds, and it raises
  the count. The outcome is offered again and is then judged. The act
  and its grant are the authority note's row. The second is a revision
  of the definition: a version whose rules stay inside the counts, or
  whose data states higher ones. How a scope comes under a later version
  is that note's, and this contract adds no form for it.
- *What this covers, and what it does not.* A draw past a count, and no
  other case. An operation of a kind that no item holds draws on no
  count. It is covered by a reservation, and by no fault ("What a holder
  reserves, in full", above).

**Release.** What a holder still holds is released by this rule. No
flag is kept: it is derived from the state.

- While the holder is not final, it holds every count.
- When the holder is final, it holds the count of a kind only while
  that kind can still be reached. It is reached from the kind of an
  operation that is `for` the holder and is not settled, and from each
  kind that a clause of a pending request of its account may open, in
  one step or in several of the relation "the mark of kind j lists kind
  k in `most.operations`". It holds `requests` and `items` only while
  such an operation exists, or a request of its account is pending.
- So when the holder is final, every operation for it is settled and no
  request of its account is pending, it holds nothing. Nothing can then
  draw on it: no entry has it as its account, and an act on a final
  item is refused `final` (section 6.6), so nothing adds to it.
- Added in revision 21. A holder holds its `decisions` while it is not
  final, and none of them once it is final: a request for a final item
  is not bound. A kind that no item holds needs no line of this rule.
  Its closure is inside what an open operation of a held kind reserves,
  or is the duty of its own operation, and it never draws on a holder.

The rule covers each end that the authority note describes. A
publication that is withdrawn while queued, or is not reserved, is
final at once, and what it took for a push is released when its `judge`
is settled. One that is aborted is final when the read shows it, and
holds on only for the kinds that its open operations can reach. One
that is published still has its receipt to write, and holds the counts
that the open operations of the receipt can reach.

**An attempt that stays `unknown`** (point R1-38; that note's ask 8). An
operation with an `unknown` attempt is not settled (section 4.3). Under
this rule it keeps two things, and no more: the 1 entry of row 5 for
its late answer, and, of what its final holder still holds, the counts
of the kinds that an outcome of its kind can reach. A mint whose answer
is lost keeps the count of revocations. A push whose answer is lost
keeps what the mark of a push lists. So the release does not wait for
point R1-38 to be decided, and a lost answer cannot hold a whole
reservation unless the data lets that kind reach every other. How much
it holds is in the data: a definition that wants less for a late answer
than for a first outcome states two kinds. If a later revision lets a
decisive read settle an attempt, that part is released too. R1-38 stays
open, and it still blocks a reset.

Made exact in revision 21. "The 1 entry of row 5 for its late answer" is
that outcome entry with what it may start for a kind that no item holds:
the part of `one(k)` for one outcome entry ("What a holder reserves, in
full", above). The counts that it keeps are of held kinds, as the
sentence says.

**What an outcome sends, and who reserves it** (entry FC2). Under
`holds`, a request that an outcome entry sends is one of its account's
`requests`, and its 2 entries and its clause are in the table above.
For an operation of a kind that no item holds, section 17.2 now counts
it with the operation ("A request that an outcome sends"). So no
request of an outcome is reserved by nobody.

**What this form does not cover.** An act or a delivery on a holder that
is no outcome and no result is not of the account. It is new work,
unless its form declares `settles` and the entry settles its subject by
state (section 17.3). So the first notice that a key behind a
publication is compromised, which sets a mark and changes no state, has
no reserved entry here: point R1-68. A bound request that is refused is
new work too (section 15.3g, ask 2).

Changed in revision 21. Both sentences are answered. An entry that sets
a mark is settling under the third form of `settles`, and row 3 of
section 17.2 reserves it (section 6.4, "`settles` by a mark"): point
R1-68 is decided. A request that is bound to the holder is settled from
the holder's `decisions`, whatever it decides ("A request that is bound
to a holder", below). What is still not of the account, and is new work:
an act or a delivery on a holder whose form declares no `settles` and no
`bound`, and a request that is not bound.

**What a verifier does.** It derives the counts, the accounts and each
`for` again, and both amounts with them. An entry whose `for` its rule
does not give, or that draws past a count, is a `mismatch`. It needs
the budget only to check that a taking entry and an adding entry
fitted, as for any new work (section 17.3).

**The numbers are the authority note's.** Its section 5.8 has two rows
for a publication, of 4 and of 68 entries. They are that note's
numbers, for the proof plan to measure, and this contract adopts none.
As an instance of the arithmetic only: with 1 `judge` of 1 attempt, 1
push and 1 receipt of 3 attempts each, 6 mints of 1 attempt, 6
revocations of 3 attempts, 2 reads of 1 attempt, and 3 requests whose
clauses are empty, the table above gives 66 entries for 17 operations
and 6 for the requests, 72 in all. A script added them.
The two rows of that note also give 72, and they are not the same 72:
they count 1 entry for a `judge` and for each read, where row 5 counts
2, and they hold 3 entries for a `withdraw`, an abort and a notice,
which are no operations. So that note owes its rows again, in this
form. By the I3 deltas note (entry FC1, rows 4 to 6), its rows are also
no upper bound of what the built rules open: the rule as built opens
more than one read for a publication, a `resend` has no row, and the
rule `receipt` is not written. Each of those is a count of `holds`, or
an `adds` of an act, that the note must state.
Marked in revision 22: the sum of 72 above is by the table that revision
21 replaced, which counts attempts only. By "What a holder reserves, in
full", each operation also counts what the mark of its kind may start, a
`withdraw` is counted by `dec(m)`, and a first notice by a marker duty.
So the 72 is an instance of the older arithmetic, and it is at most the
amount.

**A request that is bound to a holder. New in revision 21**, as the
planner decided (act `1f8aba72`; section 15.3g). A member's `withdraw`
of their own pending publication must be decided at a destination with
no free room, whatever the decision is. Revision 20 could not reserve a
refusal, because a refused deciding entry applies no effect that could
move a count. The count is moved by the fold instead, from the entry
itself.

- *The form.* A `holds` or an `adds` may state `decisions`: for the
  message name of a `tell` handler, the most bound requests that are
  decided for one item. A `tell` handler may state `bound: { of, where
  }`: the item that a delivery is bound to, and the conditions of the
  binding.
- *When a delivery is bound.* When all of this holds, on the state
  before its entry. Its handler states `bound`. Its fields are values of
  their declared types. The subject `of` resolves to an item whose type
  lists the handler's message in `decisions`. That item is not final.
  Each `where` holds. And the item's count for the message is above 0.
- *What a `where` may read.* The sender, the message's own fields and
  the slots of that item, by `equals` and `differs`. It reads nothing
  else. That is condition 4 of section 17.3.
- *What follows.* The deciding entry of a bound delivery is a settling
  entry, whether it decides `applied`, `refused` or `superseded`. Its
  account is that item. It draws 1 from the count of its message, and
  `dec(m)` is its room. A request among its sends draws on `requests`,
  as for any entry with an account.
- *It decides nothing.* Whether a delivery is bound changes one thing:
  against which room its entry is admitted. The handler's guards decide
  the request in the same way, bound or not, and no guard, effect or
  rule reads the count to decide (section 17.3, "The budget decides only
  whether"). A count that is not used permits nothing.
- *How the count moves.* The fold derives the draw from the entry: its
  input is a delivery of that message, and the binding held on the state
  before it. No effect records it. So a refused deciding entry still
  holds no effect of its handler (section 15.3g), and the count is still
  a function of the entries alone.
- *What the validator checks.* `bound` stands on a handler of the class
  `tell` whose `opens` is null. Its `of` is a name of `also` that a
  written rule binds, and no mark. Each `where` reads only the three
  things. Each key of `decisions` is the message of such a handler,
  whose `of` names this item type. Each count is a whole number, at
  least 1, within the ceiling of check 1.
  Changed in revision 22: "that a written rule binds, and no mark" is
  replaced. The name may be bound by a written rule, or by a mark that
  is a binding selector ("The source of `bound.of`", below).
- *The five conditions of section 17.3*, each met. An admitted duty made
  the reservation: the taking entry, or an adding entry. The requests
  are bounded and counted: by `decisions`, in the folded state. Each
  covered decision moves the count in its own entry: the fold derives it
  from that entry. The binding reads only the verified envelope, the
  message's own fields and local state. A repeat uses nothing: it is
  answered from the first deciding entry (section 7.4).
- *What is not bound, and is new work.* A request whose fields are not
  values of their types. One that names no item, or an item of another
  type. One for which a `where` fails, as when the sender is not the
  owner. One for a final item. And one that arrives when the count is 0:
  a second request, where the count is 1. Each is decided when room is
  free, and waits with none.
  Stated in revision 22, case by case: the table of "The source of
  `bound.of`", below. Confirmed by the planner (act `39749e26`): a
  request for a final item is new work.
- *Replay.* The verifier derives whether each delivery was bound, the
  draw and both amounts, from the history. A draw that does not follow
  is a `mismatch`.

**An index that an item type declares. New in revision 23** (the verdict
`675776bc`; the planner's act `2d3fa911`, answer 3). Revision 22 let a
binding selector read every item of its type, and asked for no index.
That scan was finite: section 17.1 counts live and retained final items
against the budget of items, and the selector read each at most once.
The owner requires another access all the same: a binding selector names
an indexed slot, or the validator refuses it. The contract now requires
that. This passage states the index. "The source of `bound.of`", below,
states the selector that uses it.

- *The form.* An item type of platform data may state `indexes`: a list
  of names of its own slots. Each is an **indexed slot**. The list holds
  at least 1 name and at most 4, and no name twice. The member is
  platform data, as `holds` is. The validator reads it only with its
  platform option, and refuses it in a declared definition as it refuses
  any member that it does not know (section 6.1).
- *Which slots.* A slot of `refs` or of `values`, and no party slot. It
  is `fixed` and `required`, both. Its type is one of seven: `fact`,
  `item`, `scope`, `member`, `digest`, `commit` and `tree`. Each is an
  identity with one canonical value. A `text`, an `int`, a `bool`, a
  `time`, an `enum`, a `record`, a `list` and a type that is a mark are
  not indexed. No adopted row asks for one of them.
- *Why fixed and required.* A fixed slot is set by the entry that opens
  the item and never again. A required slot holds a value after that
  entry, or the input is refused `required-unset` (section 6.3). So each
  item has exactly one key for each indexed slot, from its opening and
  for as long as it is kept. No row of the index moves, and none is
  removed. And "no value" is never a key: no item is indexed under none,
  and none finds no item.
- *When two keys are equal.* By the equality of section 6.2: the
  canonical JSON of the two values is equal, after a local fact is put
  in normal form. That is also the rule of the index on the slots of a
  `where` (section 6.5). For a fact of another scope the key is the
  whole `FactRef`: `at`, with its scope, its incarnation and its kind,
  then the position and the hash. Two such keys are equal exactly when
  their texts are the same bytes, as "A fact reference as text" has the
  text (section 3). No part matches alone: not the scope and the
  position with another hash, and not the same hash under another
  incarnation. A local fact is its position, after the check of section
  6.2. An `item` is its local ID.
- *What it holds.* For each indexed slot of each type, one row for each
  item of the type that the folded state holds, live and final: the key
  and the item's ID. The rows of one key are in order of item ID. An
  item's ID is the position of the entry that opened it (section 4.1),
  so that is the order in which the items were opened.
- *When it is written.* In the transaction of the entry that opens the
  item, with the item. No later entry writes a row, because the slot is
  fixed. A change of state moves none: the state is no part of a key. An
  item that reaches a final state keeps its rows for as long as it is
  retained, which is as long as the history is kept (section 6.3). No
  row is evicted to meet a bound.
- *It is complete at every head.* At each head the index holds a row for
  every item of the type that the folded state at that head holds. So a
  lookup on the state before an entry finds an item that an earlier
  entry of the same turn opened. Each item that it returns is read as
  that state holds it: where a timed entry of the same turn changed the
  item's state, the changed state is read. The index is local state
  under the head check. A runtime whose index does not hold every item
  of a type answers no lookup from it. The delivery is then not judged
  and is retried, and nothing is written. That is the rule of section
  6.5 for an index that was added to a scope which already held items.
- *The lookup, and no other query.* There is one. For a type, an indexed
  slot and a key, it gives the rows of that key in order of item ID, up
  to 9. Nine is one more than the 8 items that a selector may be given,
  so that "more than 8" is known from one read. The index answers no
  range, no prefix, no part of a key, no two slots together and no
  count.
- *It is derived state, and a checkpoint holds no row of it.* The index
  is a function of the items of the folded state: of each item's type,
  its ID and the value of a fixed slot. The value that a checkpoint
  digests holds the scope's items (section 9.2), and a final item is an
  item that the scope keeps (section 6.3). So the digest covers the
  state from which the index is rebuilt, and the index is no member of
  that value. Nothing of section 9.2 changes. In this it differs from
  the three things of "What holds the count", above, which the digest
  covers themselves. "Storage that is derived" holds for it as written
  (section 17.1): it is in no dimension. It has at most 4 rows for each
  item, so the budget of items bounds it.
- *Replay.* A verifier builds the index by folding the entries, or from
  the items of a checkpoint that it trusts. It makes the same lookup on
  the state before the entry, and gets the same items in the same
  order. A runtime and a verifier that differ in a lookup differ in the
  items of the folded state.
- *The work of one lookup.* One read of the index, of at most 9 rows,
  and one read of each item that is given, at most 8. It does not grow
  with the items that the scope retains. It is a count of records read,
  the same in a runtime and in a replay, as section 7.5 asks of the work
  of a commit. It is in no dimension of the budget. The numbers 4, 8 and
  9 are this note's proposals. Whether a lookup is charged, and to what,
  is charged work, and that is R4's, with the capacity follow-through
  `cc570904`.
- *The two other indexes.* "What holds the count", above, has the
  operations of one item, read by the item. That is another relation,
  from a holder to the operations that are `for` it. It is part of the
  folded state that every other rule is given, and a binding selector is
  not given it. The index on the slots of a `where` (section 6.5) is of
  the same kind as this one: the items of a type by the value of a slot.
  A declared index meets the conditions of that section by its form. So
  a runtime may keep one table for both, and may answer an `equals` of a
  `where` on an indexed slot from it. The difference is in what else is
  allowed. A guard may read every page in place of an index. A binding
  selector may not: it has the lookup, and nothing else.
- *What the validator checks.* Check 6, with its platform option.
  `indexes` stands on an item type. It is a list of 1 to 4 names, none
  twice. Each is a slot of `refs` or of `values` of that type, `fixed`
  and `required`, of one of the seven types. A definition that fails it
  does not validate, as for check 1: `unsupported-definition`. An index
  that no selector names validates. It is storage that nothing reads,
  and no judgment rests on it.

**The source of `bound.of`: a binding selector. Changed in revision 22**
(the verdict `dc1da38a`, its first finding). Revision 21 asked that
`bound.of` be a name of `also` that a written rule binds. The case that
the form was written for cannot be stated so. The authority note's
adopted rows were read for this: its section 5.8, "The exception for one
`withdraw`, stated exactly"; and in its sections 12.1.5 and 12.1.8 the
item type `publication`, the rows `reserve` and `withdraw`, and row 34
of its table of rules. A destination holds many publications. A
`withdraw` has one field, `operation`: the fact of the lane's `merge`
entry, which is an entry of another scope. The publication that it is
for is the one whose slot `operation` holds that fact. No written rule
finds it. `by` names a local item, or the item that a local fact opened.
`via` reads a slot of a subject that is bound already, and the
publication that a `withdraw` is for need not be the one that the
branch's `slot` or `judging` names. `one` needs a type that is not
`many`. That note finds the publication by the mark `publication-of`, at
place 2. So revision 21 refused the one row that its form was for.

- *The choice.* A mark at place 2 may bind the name that `bound.of`
  names, under the restrictions below. Its rule is then a **binding
  selector**. No way of naming an item is added to `AlsoRule`.
- *Why this, and not a written selector.* A fourth alternative of
  `AlsoRule`, which selects the item whose slot equals a field, would be
  a form for every definition. It would need its own rule for several
  matches, for `expected`, for an unbound name and for a clause, and an
  index that every runtime keeps. The adopted row has the mark already,
  under that note's gap P15. So this changes one sentence of the
  validator and what one kind of rule is given, and it changes no row
  that is adopted.
  Read with revision 23: one of these reasons no longer tells the two
  apart. A binding selector now needs an index that a runtime keeps, as
  a written selector would. The others stand: a written selector would
  be a form for every definition, with its own rules for `expected`, for
  an unbound name and for a clause, and the adopted row has the mark.
  And one sentence above is no longer so: the index asks one more thing
  of that note's adopted row ("What the authority note owes", below).
- *Which mark is one.* The data says it, with no new member. The name of
  `also` that a `bound.of` names is bound by a written rule, as in
  revision 21, or by a mark. A mark that binds it is the binding
  selector of that handler. A mark that binds any other name is not one,
  and is given what every rule is given.
  Changed in revision 23: which mark is one is still read from the name
  that `bound.of` names. Such a mark now states two members more,
  `index` and `key` ("What the validator checks", below).
- *What it is given. Changed in revision 23.* Two things, in place of
  the six of section 6.1. First, the items that the declared index
  returns for the key ("An index that an item type declares", above).
  They are the items of the mark's type whose indexed slot equals the
  value of the field that the mark names as `key`: live and final, as
  the folded state before the entry holds them, in order of item ID, and
  at most 8. For each its ID, its state and its slots. Second, the
  fields of the message as check 7 read them. For a field of the type
  `fact` that is the reference: its scope, its position and its hash.
  Revision 22 gave the rule every item of the type. It is given no other
  item now, and it can ask for none: a rule is a function of what it is
  given.
- *None, one, several, and more than 8. New in revision 23.* The judge
  makes the lookup, and then one of three things follows.
  - *The index returns no item.* The selector gives none, and the rule
    is not run: it could return nothing else. The name is unbound. That
    is row 2 of the table below.
  - *It returns 1 to 8 items.* The rule is run on them and on the
    fields. It returns the ID of one of them, or none. With one item it
    may still return none. With several it chooses by what it is given:
    the states, the slots and the order. This contract does not say
    which it chooses. A definition that may hold a final item and a live
    one under one key owes a rule that reads the state.
  - *It returns more than 8.* The selection is a fault. The rule is not
    run, the delivery is not judged, it is retried, and nothing is
    written (section 6.1, "A fault of a rule is no judgment"). No item
    is chosen from a part of the matches. This is the policy of "Past a
    count", above, for a bound that the contract states. It is a limit
    of liveness, and it does not end by itself: a key is fixed and a
    final item is retained, so the items of one key never become fewer.
    The way out is a revision of the definition. So a definition keeps
    the items of one key within 8, by a guard on the form that opens the
    item. The validator does not check that guard.
  - *In the adopted rows* one key finds at most one item. The authority
    note's `reserve` is refused while any publication exists for its
    operation, in any of the seven states of the type. Its `withdraw`
    opens a publication only when none exists for the operation (that
    note's section 12.1.5, the rows `reserve` and `withdraw`). So a
    withdrawn publication and a later one for the same operation do not
    both exist, and the rule for several items is not used there.
- *What a binding selector can no longer do. Stated in revision 23.*
  This is a narrower interface than revision 22 had. It is the owner's
  direction (act `2d3fa911`, answer 3), and it is stated here so that
  nothing is lost without a word. Revision 22 let the rule compute over
  every item of the type. It may now find items in one way: the value of
  one required field equals one fixed and required slot, of one of seven
  types. Among the at most 8 items that it is given it may still choose
  by any state or slot. It cannot select by a slot that changes, by a
  part of a value, by a value that it computes from a field, by a range,
  or among more than 8 items of one key. The one adopted row that binds
  a request by a mark needs none of those: `publication-of` matches the
  whole fact of the field `operation` against a fixed and required slot,
  and finds at most one item. A definition that needs another selection
  writes the value that it selects by into a fixed and required slot
  when the item is opened, and indexes that slot.
- *What it is not given.* The envelope's sender: a `where` reads that.
  The entry that a fact field names, or any other entry of `uses`. An
  observation, which a delivery of a request never holds. A value beside
  the input. The clock reading. An earlier entry of the scope. Items of
  another type, operations, requests and the counts of a holder. The
  budget and the free room. So the selection rests on nothing outside
  the scope, on nothing that was fetched for this message, and on no
  time.
  Added in revision 23: an item of its own type that the index does not
  return for the key, and the index itself.
- *What it returns.* The ID of one item among those that it was given,
  or none. Any other result is a fault: the delivery is not judged, it
  is retried, and nothing is written (section 6.1, "A fault of a rule is
  no judgment").
- *It is determinate.* The selection is a function of those two things
  and of the rule of the pinned version. A runtime and a verifier that
  hold the same state before the entry and the same message derive the
  same item. The order in which other inputs arrived, and what transport
  has acknowledged, change nothing of it.
- *Its work, and its bound. Changed in revision 23.* One lookup: at most
  9 rows of the index and at most 8 items, whatever the scope retains
  ("The work of one lookup", above). Revision 22 said: at most one read
  of each item of the type, live and final, within the budget of items
  (section 17.1). That scan was finite, and it is no longer permitted.
  The `max` of the type bounds neither count, because final items are
  retained: that is entry ER11 of the I3 deltas note.
- *An index is required. Changed in revision 23*, as the planner decided
  (act `2d3fa911`, answer 3). Revision 22 said here that an index is
  allowed and not required, that the data states none and that the
  validator checks none. All three are replaced. The type declares the
  index. The mark names it. The validator refuses a binding selector
  without one. And a runtime answers the selector from the index, and in
  no other way: it does not read every item of the type in its place. A
  verifier gives the rule the same items in the same order ("Replay",
  above).
- *What the validator checks.* In place of "a written rule binds, and no
  mark", three things. First, `bound.of` is a name of `also` of the
  handler. Second, the name is bound by `by`, by `one`, by a `via` whose
  every subject a written rule binds, or by a mark at place 2. Third,
  where a mark binds it, the mark's `item` is a type that lists the
  handler's message in `decisions`, and the mark states `code`, `row`,
  `item`, `index` and `key` and no other member: no `clock`, no `most`
  and no `refusals`. A definition that fails the second or the third is
  refused `bound-source`. So no rule that is given the clock, an
  observation or a fetched entry is the source of a binding, and none is
  reached through a slot.
  Changed in revision 23: the third thing named three members, `code`,
  `row` and `item`, and no other. It names five now. And a fourth thing
  is checked. `index` names a slot that the `indexes` of the type `item`
  lists. `key` names a field of the handler that is `required`, and
  whose declared type is the type of that slot: the same `type`, and
  beside it the same members, where the kinds of a `fact` are compared
  as a set. A definition that fails the fourth is refused
  `bound-source` too. That is three cases: a binding selector with no
  index, an index that the type does not declare, and a key that is no
  required field of the slot's type.
- *A mark at place 2 that is no binding selector. Stated in revision
  23.* It states neither `index` nor `key`: a definition in which one
  does is refused `bound-source`. It is given the six things, and the
  folded state among them, as before. The planner's words are "a binding
  selector must use an index", and this contract asks an index of no
  other rule. The adopted marks at place 2 were read for this, in the
  authority note's section 12.1.8: `invitation`, on the acts `join` and
  `enrol` (its rows 19 and g), and `publication-of`, on the handler
  `withdraw` (its row 34). `bound` stands on a `tell` handler only. So
  `invitation` can be no binding selector, and `publication-of` is the
  one.
- *What the judge does.* It reads the fields (check 7). It binds the
  names of `also` (check 8), and runs the selector there with its two
  things. It then derives whether the delivery is bound, from the
  conditions below, on the state before the entry. All of that is before
  any guard of the handler. The other marks of the handler are run as
  before, and are given what every rule is given.
  Changed in revision 23: at check 8 it makes the lookup with the value
  of the field that the mark names as `key`, and runs the rule only
  where 1 to 8 items are returned.
- *A bound delivery opens no item.* An effect mark of the handler may
  state `most.opens`: the adopted row opens the publication as final
  when the selector gives none. In a delivery that is bound, an `open`
  effect of a rule is a fault. So `dec(m)` counts no item, as its cell
  says, and check 2 holds: a holder is opened only by new work.

Each condition of the binding, in the order in which it is judged, with
the answer when it fails. "It waits" means: the entry is new work, it is
written when room is free, and with none the request is not decided,
transport answers "retry", and the sender keeps the duty.

| # | The condition, on the state before the entry | When it fails | The answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The fields are values of their declared types. A fact that a field names is fetched before the turn, as for any delivery. | A field is missing, ill-typed or not declared | Not bound. Decided `refused`, `bad-field`, as new work: it waits. While a named fact cannot be fetched the delivery is not decided and is retried, whatever room is free. |
| 2 | The source of `bound.of` selects an item | It selects none: the scope holds no item for what the message names | Not bound, and new work: it waits. What is decided is the handler's own. In the adopted row a `withdraw` that arrives before its `reserve` is `applied`, and opens the publication as final. Its admission counts the entry and the item. |
| 3 | The item is not final | It is final | Not bound, and new work: it waits. The handler's guards decide it, in the adopted row `refused`, `ended`. Confirmed by the planner (act `39749e26`). |
| 4 | Each `where` holds. In the adopted row: the sender is the scope that the operation's fact is in | One fails | Not bound, and new work: it waits. The handler's guards decide it, in the adopted row `refused`, `not-owner`. No count of the item moves. |
| 5 | The item's count for the message is above 0 | It is 0 | Not bound, and new work: it waits. A second request in another envelope is this case. |
| | All five hold | | Bound. The deciding entry is settling, and is written with no free room, whether it decides `applied`, `refused` or `superseded`. It draws 1 from the count, and `dec(m)` is its room. |

Two more conditions are of the data, and cannot fail in a commit: the
handler states `bound`, and the type of the item lists the message in
`decisions`. A fault of the selector is none of the rows: the delivery
is not judged.
Read with revision 23: in row 2, "It selects none" is one of two things.
The index returns no item for the key, or the rule chooses none of the
items that it was given. More than 8 items of one key is a fault, as a
fault of the selector is, and is none of the rows.

- *Before its opening request.* A request that arrives before the item
  exists is row 2. It is never bound, because no item holds a count for
  it. If it waited, and is delivered again after the item was opened, it
  is judged on the state then, and may be bound then.
- *A repeat.* A repeat of an envelope that was decided is answered from
  its deciding entry (section 7.4). No selector runs, nothing is drawn
  and nothing is written. An envelope that was not decided is no repeat.
  It is judged again, whole, on the state at that commit.
- *Several items at once.* Each item has its own count. The selector is
  given no item of another type, so it cannot read which publication the
  branch's `slot` or `judging` names. A request finds its own item
  whichever item those name. Two requests for two items are each bound
  to their own, in either order, and neither draws on the other.
- *Replay.* The verifier is given the same two things from the history:
  the folded state before the entry, and the recorded message. It runs
  the selector of the pinned version, and derives the item, the binding,
  the draw and both amounts. A selection that does not follow is a
  `mismatch`.
  Changed in revision 23: the first of the two things is the items that
  the index returns. The verifier derives them by folding ("An index
  that an item type declares", above).
- *What the authority note owes.* That its mark `publication-of` is
  stated as a binding selector: its row reads "the `publication` items"
  and the field, which is inside the two things. And the `where` of
  `withdraw`, in this form.
  Added in revision 23, as one more row that is owed: its item type

  the index returns for the field", in place of "the `publication`
  items". That the field's type is the slot's was not found in the rows

### 17.3 The rule of admission

Every input is one of two kinds, by what it does in the commit that
would write it.

| Kind | Which inputs | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| **Settling** | A timed entry. A delivery of a result or a control. A diagnosis. An outcome of an attempt that an entry opened. A settlement. An act or a delivery of a request whose form declares `settles`, when its subject is in a listed state at the commit and the entry takes it out of the listed states. A delivery that a pending capability record reserved; and, where its capability declares a count of decisions, whatever that delivery decides ("An entry that records a refusal", below). The closing checkpoint, as section 17.2 defines it. | It is admitted against its own duty's reservation, in every dimension, and it draws on no other. It fits, because the invariant held before it and the reservation covers the entry, what it newly retains and what it starts. What it newly retains is counted by what the form declares, and not by what a guard reads (section 17.2). |
| **New work** | Everything else: an act that settles nothing, a new job, a new request or an advisory from another scope, a preparation, a later answer on an item that is already settled, a repeated confirmation, a cleanup that no operation reserved, a `conflict` result of a creation, an entry that records a refusal (below), any other checkpoint. | It is admitted only if, after the entry, used plus reserved is within the budget in every dimension. That counts the entry, the bytes of every input it newly retains, and the reservations of every duty it creates. |

When new work does not fit:

- an act is Refused `scope-full`, and names the dimension. Nothing is
  written and no key is consumed;
- a preparation is refused the same way, so nothing outside is caused;
- a request from another scope is not decided. Transport answers
  "retry" and the sender keeps the duty (section 7.4). No entry is
  written for it, because a refusal entry and its result would
  themselves be new work;
- an advisory from another scope is not recorded, and transport does
  not mark it done. How long transport keeps offering it is part of
  backpressure, R4's. Nothing in the sender is judged on it;
- a checkpoint is not written.

So a settlement is never refused for capacity, and it can never use
more than was set aside for it when its duty began. The first
authentic result of a pending job is a settling input. A second answer
on the same job is new work. A new job is new work, and it is admitted
only with room for its own deadline and its own first result.

*The guarantee, restated after the review `a7f1c108`.* A settling entry
fits its own duty's reservation in every dimension. In entries, items,
records and pending requests that follows from the rows of section
17.2 and from the closure. In bytes it follows from the three amounts
of "Bytes of a reservation": the entry's own static bound; every input
that the entry can newly retain, each at its bound; and the duties that
it starts. For foreign entries the second amount is F(f) of section
17.2, which counts every fact that admission can fetch and retain for
the form, read or not. Revision 13 as filed counted only the facts
that a guard or a part reads, and from that count the guarantee did
not follow in bytes. The guarantee is of the rule. The source counts
entries only (section 17.5).

A form that declares `settles` is still judged in full: its grant, its
guards and its bounds. Only the capacity check differs.

**Changed in revision 21: two more settling inputs.** The row "Settling"
of the table above gains two. An act or a delivery of a request whose
form declares `settles` by a mark, when its subject awaits that
settlement at the commit and the entry sets the mark (section 6.4,
"`settles` by a mark"). And the deciding entry of a request that is
bound to a holder, whatever it decides (section 17.2a). Each is admitted
against its own duty's reservation: row 3 for the first, and the
holder's `decisions` for the second. The row "New work" loses those two
and nothing else.

**The induction, by edge. Checked in revision 21.** The guarantee of
this section is an induction: used plus reserved is within the budget
after every entry, because new work is admitted only if it is, and a
settling entry draws only on room that an earlier admission reserved.
The verdict `0cf59056` showed one edge on which it failed. This is every
edge on which one entry starts an operation, with what reserves the
second.

| The edge | Permitted | What reserves the second, and when |
|---|---|---|
| An outcome of a held kind opens a held kind | Yes | The holder that the effect is `for`, from the entry that took it. The draw moves `one(k)` from that holder to the operation. It may be another holder than the first operation's. |
| An outcome of a held kind opens a kind that no item holds | Yes, when that kind's closure is finite | `one(k)` of the first kind, which holds C(j), from the taking entry. Repaired in revision 21. C(j) moves to the new operation when it is opened. |
| An outcome of a kind that no item holds opens a held kind | No. The validator refuses the definition `reserve-unbounded` (section 17.2a, check 5). | Nothing could, by kind: the first operation states no `for`, so no holder is named for what it opens. |
| An outcome of a kind that no item holds opens another such kind | Yes, when no kind reaches itself | C(k) of the first kind, from the admission of the entry that opened the first operation (row 5). Made exact in revision 21, by outcome entry. |
| A clause of a result opens an operation, by an effect mark | Yes | A kind that no item holds: its C(j) is in the request's reservation, from the admission of the sending entry. Stated in revision 21. A held kind: the holder that the effect is `for`. |
| A timed rule opens an operation | It opens none of a kind of `outcomes`: no mark stands in a timed rule. A `hold` or a `capability` effect of a timed rule opens what its capability declares. | Row 6, and the capability's declared maximum with its opening (section 6.1) |
| An act or a delivery that is new work opens an operation | Yes | Its own admission, for a kind that no item holds. For a held kind: the holder, by the draw, or its own admission where it is the taking entry. |
| An act or a delivery that settles, by `settles` or as a bound request, opens an operation by a mark | Yes | Row 3, or `dec(m)`, which count what the mark may start. A held kind: the holder that the effect is `for`. |

The result. With the two repairs every permitted edge has a reservation
that an admission checked, in each of the five dimensions, and the one
edge that had none by kind is refused. So the induction holds for the
rule. It rests on three things that the data states and a runtime
enforces. A count of a `holds` is the most that a rule may draw, and a
draw past it is a fault and no entry. A `max` of `retains` is the most
that a value may be, and a larger one is no answer. And a mark is
counted at the worst case of its `most`. The guarantee is of the rule:
the source counts entries only (section 17.5).

**The induction, checked again in revision 22** (the verdict

and the eighth is made exact. These are the changes.

| The edge | In revision 21 | In revision 22 |
|---|---|---|
| A clause of a request that an outcome of a kind which no item holds sent opens a held kind | Not stated. The fifth row said "Yes" for every clause. | No. The validator refuses the definition `reserve-unbounded` (section 17.2a, check 5, edge 2). The request has no account, so nothing keeps the holder's count until the clause runs. |
| The same clause opens a kind that no item holds | Yes | Yes. Its C(j) is in the reservation of the request, which is in the closure of the first kind. |
| A clause of a request that an act or a handler with no account sent opens a held kind | Yes, by the fifth row | Yes, with a limit that the row did not state. The draw is on the holder that the effect is `for`. The rule of release keeps a final holder's count for a pending request only where the request is of its account, and this one is not. So the rule must open only for a holder that is not final, and a draw on a holder that has released is a fault ("Past a count"). |
| An entry that settles by a mark, or as a bound request, opens an operation by a mark | Yes, by the eighth row | Yes. What reserves the entry is now determinate: the marker duty of its item and its mark, or `dec(m)` of the holder that the source of `bound.of` finds. A rule of a form that declares `settles` returns no change of state. |

  Decided in revision 23: the planner answered (act `2d3fa911`, answer
  1). The fault stands. A holder that is final opens nothing. The clause
  has a fault, nothing is written, and the result stays offered. The
  fault is shown as a state that a member can see, by the policy of "A

  final holder. How a scope comes under a later version is the authority
