**Changed in revision 22: the duty of an entry that settles by a mark.**
"Its own duty's reservation", in the table of the two kinds, is for such
an entry the reservation of one marker duty: its subject and the mark
that its form names (section 17.2, "A marker duty"). It draws on no
other duty of the item: not on another mark's, and not on the state
duty. The admission of new work counts every marker duty that the entry
leaves pending and that was not pending before it.

**An entry that records a refusal. New in revision 10.** Three written
entries record a refusal of their input: a refused genesis, the
deciding entry of a refused request, and the entry of an advisory
whose handler refused. Each keeps, in `uses` and `prepared`, what was
read before the refusal (section 6.5). Made exact in revision 14: in
`uses` it keeps every foreign entry that was fetched for its input,
also one that no guard reached. Those bytes are written and
charged in the entry's own transaction. Which amount they are charged
to follows the entry's kind, like everything else of the entry.

- A refusal takes no item and no copy out of a pending state. So it
  ends no duty of row 3 or row 4, and it does not draw on that duty's
  reservation, which the duty still needs. It is new work. It is
  admitted only if the entry, what it retains and the reservations of
  what it starts fit in the room that is free. When they do not, no
  entry is written, a request is not decided, and transport answers
  `retry`.
- A refusal draws on a reservation only where the owner of a duty
  declares that the refusal itself uses the reservation up. **The
  five conditions. New in revision 11.** Revision 10 had this rule,
  and left the declaration and its limits to the owner. The review
  `74b21dc8` of R3's revision 10 showed that, without the
  declaration, a reserved decision could not be written at a full
  scope. A declaration is inside this contract only when all five of
  these hold.
  1. *An admitted duty made the reservation.* The entry was reserved
     by a record or an item in a pending state, before the request
     arrived. A declaration creates no room.
  2. *The requests are bounded, and counted.* The owner states the
     most requests that the duty covers. Local state holds a count
     of those that are decided: a value of the record, or a mark on
     the item.
  3. *Each covered decision moves the count, in its own entry.* So an
     entry is used once, and Reserved falls by that entry whatever
     was decided.
  4. *The binding reads only the verified envelope, the message's own
     fields and local state* (section 5.1). A request that is not
     bound is new work.
  5. *A repeat uses nothing.* It is answered with the first deciding
     entry (section 7.4).

  Under them a declaration lets nothing unbounded pass the budget: at
  most the stated number of entries, each reserved by an admitted
  duty, and each used once. Section 6.11 gives the form for a
  capability record, and what `hold@1` declares for a license
  request. R3 makes two declarations. Both are stated in the
  authority note's adopted revision 13: a license
  request that is bound to a standing receiver pin, and a
  publication's one `withdraw`. The second is in the destination's
  platform definition. Its code owes the same five conditions, and
  its mark that the `withdraw` was decided is the count of condition
  2. Where nothing is declared, the refusal is new work.
  Dated in revision 20, 2026-10-06: the second declaration covers an
  applied `withdraw` only. That note's adopted revision 26 narrowed it,
  and section 15.3g decides that no place gives a refused deciding
  entry of a platform definition an effect. So a platform definition
  meets condition 3 only by an entry that applies an effect.
- A delivery of a result whose outcome is `refused`, and a diagnosis,
  are not refusals of their input. Each is the settling entry of its
  request, by row 1.

So fetched bytes are discarded, with nothing charged, in one case
only: the turn writes no entry. Witness 18.18. Since revision 14 the
witness shows it for a declared fact that no guard read: its cases 5
and 6.

**The budget decides only whether. New in revision 11.** The budget,
and the amounts that are held against it, decide one thing: whether
an entry that is new work is written. They decide nothing about what
a written entry holds. No effect, no send, no decision and no clause
reads the budget, the free room or a reservation. An act that does
not fit is refused, which is an answer. A delivery that does not fit
is not decided. A checkpoint that does not fit is not written. A
settling entry is written whatever is free. So a verifier derives
every entry without the budget, and needs the budget only to check
that new work fitted (section 9.3). This is why an owner's retry
rule may not read the free room (R3's point O13; section 15.3a). The
entry that opens the next attempt would hold an effect that no
recorded input explains.

**Made exact in revision 13, from the I2 source choices.** Each point
names the entries of the I2 deltas note that it answers (section 15.6l).
Each is a rule of this contract from this revision, for the reason that
the point gives. None changes an entry that the I2 source at `744f2447`
writes, unless the point says so.

- **DI21.** Whether an entry is settling is derived, and no entry
  records it. For a form that declares `settles`, the judge says so: the
  subject was in a listed state before the entry, and is in none after
  its effects; or, for a copy, the copy that the scope held was in a
  listed state and the update's state is not listed. An entry of such a
  form that leaves its subject in a listed state, and a second answer
  on an item that is settled, are new work, as the table says. So is
  every refusal by a form that declares `settles`: a refusal takes no
  subject out of a listed state. *Corrected after the review
  `a7f1c108`:* this point said "every refusal" and no more. The words
  are about a declared `settles` only. They do not cover the two
  refusals that draw on a reservation by an owner's declaration, inside
  the five conditions above. One is a capability's: the first decision
  on a request that a pending capability record's count of decisions
  binds (section 6.11). The other is a platform reservation: the one
  `withdraw` of a publication, in the destination's platform
  definition. A verifier derives every entry without this word, and
  needs it
  only to check that new work fitted. The I2 source computes the word in
  its judge and checks no budget in its verifier. That is inside this
  rule, since a verifier may check less and says what it trusted
  (section 9.5).
  Dated in revision 20, 2026-10-06: of the two refusals that this
  point names, the `withdraw` of a publication is no longer one. The
  platform reservation covers an applied `withdraw` only (section
  15.3g).

### 17.3a A reserve of one fixed size, and a static rule as a temporary step

I1's first runtime held two temporary values (its delta 81, as first
written): a bound on a scope's entries, and a settlement reserve of
one fixed size. An act was refused `scope-full` when its entry would
be at or past the bound less the reserve. A timed entry or a
checkpoint was written up to the bound. Past the bound nothing was
written. I1 has since removed the fixed reserve, and counts the
entries that the admitted duties still need (the deltas note, section
15; section 15.6f here). This section keeps the reasoning, and the
conditions under which a static rule may be used.

That is one high-water mark. It does not count the duties that the
admitted acts created. So it does not guarantee that each of them can
settle: the third table of section 17.4 is the planner's case, in
which a third hold's end cannot be written. A scope in that state is
stuck, because no ordinary input may pass the due expiry (section
5.2). The mark is not the rule of this section, and it is not accepted
as one (section 15.6c, entry 81). Raising the number without a
derivation does not repair it. Nor does dropping the third duty,
skipping its expiry, or evicting history: section 6.3 forbids all
three.

A static rule may stand in for the accounting of sections 17.1 to 17.3
as a temporary step. It is acceptable only if it states and checks all
of this.

1. **Its domain.** The definitions and configurations that it
   supports, stated so that a scope can check, when it is founded,
   that it is inside the domain. A scope outside it is not founded
   under the rule. It is not admitted and left to fail later.
2. **A static bound on what is pending at once.** For every row of
   section 17.2 that a scope in the domain can create, the most
   duties of that row that can be pending together, from the
   definition's own bounds. For deadlines that is, for each timed
   item type, `max` live items, each with the longest chain of that
   type's timed rules (section 17.2). Revision 9 counted one entry
   for each item, which is too few when one rule leads to another.
   For row 3 it is the sum of `max` over
   the item types that a `settles` names. No static bound of a
   definition limits how many requests a scope has sent and not seen
   answered, how many operations are unsettled, or how many
   capability records are pending. So the domain excludes the forms
   that create those duties, or the static rule is not available.
3. **A reserve in every dimension.** At least the sum, over those
   rows, of that count times the row's reservation, and one closing
   checkpoint. That is entries, items, records, pending requests and
   bytes, and the bytes include what a settling entry newly retains.
4. **Admission against it.** New work is refused when its entry would
   pass the budget less the reserve, in any dimension. A settling
   entry is written up to the budget.
5. **The guarantee.** Every duty that an admitted entry created can be
   settled, in any order and however many are pending together. So
   the state in which a settling entry cannot be written is not
   reachable. A rule that guarantees less is not this rule.
6. **Its label.** It is temporary. The per-duty accounting stays the
   contract, a verifier derives the per-duty amounts whatever the
   runtime used, and the report names the configuration as trusted.

**The rule for a definition with timed rules only.** Take a definition
that declares no send, no `settles` and no capability that opens an
operation, and whose timed rules lead to one another in no cycle. Its
only duties are deadlines, with their chains, and the closing
checkpoint. For a timed item type T, write L(T) for the longest chain
among the rules on T. The static rule is then all of this.

- A reserve of entries that is not smaller than the sum, over the
  timed item types, of `max` times L(T), plus one for the closing
  checkpoint.
- A reserve of bytes that is not smaller than the static bound of
  each of those timed entries (section 6.4), plus the size of one
  checkpoint entry. A timed entry and a checkpoint retain nothing
  new.
- No reserve of items or pending requests. A timed entry and a
  checkpoint open no item and send no request.
- No reserve of records, unless a capability declares that its timed
  effect creates or changes one. What `hold@1` declares at a hold's
  end is R3's to add. Stated in the authority note's adopted
  revision 13 (its section 5.8): the entry that ends a
  hold creates no record, changes the hold's `instance` and each live
  `token`, and opens that token's revocation. An opened operation is
  a duty that no static bound limits. So a scope whose holds have a
  fork or a token is outside this rule's domain, and a fixture whose
  holds have neither is inside it.

A scope whose definition or reserve does not meet that is outside the
domain. When every chain is 1, as for a hold's end, the entries are
the sum of `max`, plus one. Revision 9 gave that sum for every
definition in this domain. The review `114e2cc5` showed that it is too
small when one rule leads to another.

*The witness: rule A, then rule B, then a final state.* X11 is made up
for this table. Its one timed item type, `step`, has `max` 1, the live
states `first` and `second`, and the final state `done`. Rule A
applies in `first` and sets `second`. Rule B applies in `second` and
sets `done`. Both read one deadline slot, which the opening act sets
from a field, to a time that has passed. A leads to B, so L is 2. The
budget of 10 entries is made up.

| | Revision 9's reserve: the sum of `max`, plus one | This revision's: `max` times L, plus one |
|---|---|---|
| The reserve of entries | 1 + 1 = 2 | 1 x 2 + 1 = 3 |
| New work is written while the entries used, after it, are at most | 8 | 7 |
| The founding, other acts, and last the act that opens the `step`, which is the last new work that fits | 8 used | 7 used |
| Timed, rule A: `first` to `second` | 9 used | 8 used |
| Timed, rule B: `second` to `done` | 10 used | 9 used |
| The closing checkpoint | No entry is left. The scope cannot end on a checkpoint. | 10 used. Written. |

Both timed entries must be written. Each takes the item out of a state
in which it was due, and no ordinary input may pass either. Under
section 17.2 the same scope reserves 2 entries when the `step` is
opened, by the chain of rule A, and 1 for the closing checkpoint. An
act that would leave fewer than 3 entries for them is refused
`scope-full`.

I1's present count is not this static rule. It counts duties in the
commit, in the entries dimension only (section 15.6f).

### 17.4 Witnesses at capacity

**A pending job.** The numbers in these examples are made up to show
the accounting. They are not proposals. P is a change lane with a
budget of 1,000 entries
and 300 items. Job 20 is `requested`, with a deadline. It reserves 1
entry for the deadline's timed entry, and 1 entry and 1 item for its
first answer. The closing checkpoint reserves 1 entry. Pending
requests and records are left out: they are counted the same way.
Bytes are in the second table.

| Step | Input | Kind | Used entries, items | Reserved entries, items | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | The state before | | 994, 298 | 3, 1 | Free: 3 entries and 1 item. |
| 1 | A `comment` | New work: 1 entry, 1 item | 995, 299 | 3, 1 | Admitted. Free: 2 entries and no item. |
| 2 | A second `comment` | New work: 1 entry, 1 item | 995, 299 | 3, 1 | Refused `scope-full`, items. The one item left is job 20's. |
| 3 | `request-check` for another check | New work: 1 entry, 1 item, and a new job's reservation of 2 entries and 1 item | 995, 299 | 3, 1 | Refused `scope-full`. A job is not admitted without room for its own answer. |
| 4 | `check` on job 20, passed: the first authentic answer | Settling: job 20 is `requested`, and the entry makes it `passed` | 996, 300 | 1, 0 | Admitted. It opens its result item from job 20's reservation. The deadline no longer holds, so its entry is released. Free: 3 entries and no item. |
| 5 | A second `check` on job 20, as a new signed intent | New work: job 20 is `passed`, which no `settles` lists | 996, 300 | 1, 0 | Refused `scope-full`, items. It would be history only. |

In another order, the deadline passes before step 4. The timed entry
draws its 1 entry, and job 20 becomes `timed-out`. That state is listed
by the `settles` of `check`, so the answer's reservation stays, and the
late answer still records and opens its item (R2's point R2-11).

When a retry supersedes job 20 instead, the new `request-check` is new
work, and job 20's reservation is released in the same entry. A later
answer on job 20 is then history only, and new work.

**Retained inputs with the deciding entry. New in revision 9.** X10 is
a definition made up for this table. Its item type `claim` has a state
`waiting`. Its act `prove` declares `settles: { of: "on", in:
["waiting"] }`. It has a field `proofs`, a list of at most 24 facts,
and an `each` guard with a `fact` guard on each. It has a second
field, `annexes`, a list of at most 8 facts, which no guard and no
part reads. The second field was added after the review `a7f1c108`.
Until then `proofs` was a list of at most 32, and the totals below are
the same. The table counts bytes
only, in KiB, with section 7.5's proposed entry size, 256 KiB, as the
bound on one entry. The budget, 100,000 KiB, and every size are made
up. A claim that is `waiting` reserves (1 + 24 + 8) x 256 = 8,448 KiB:
its own entry at the stand-in, and 32 foreign entries, which are the
24 of `proofs` and the 8 of `annexes`. Both lists are counted because
the form declares them (section 17.2). The closing
checkpoint reserves 256.

| Step | Input | Kind | Bytes it adds | Used | Reserved | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | The state before, with claim 12 `waiting` | | | 91,000 | 8,704 | Free: 296. |
| 1 | An act whose entry is 40 KiB and which reads foreign entry Q, of 200 KiB | New work | 240 | 91,240 | 8,704 | Admitted. Free: 56. |
| 2 | Another act of 40 KiB that reads Q | New work | 40. Q is already kept under its digest. | 91,280 | 8,704 | Admitted. Free: 16. |
| 3 | An act of 40 KiB that reads another foreign entry, of 200 KiB | New work | 240 | 91,280 | 8,704 | Refused `scope-full`, bytes. A refused act writes no entry, so the fetched bytes are discarded and nothing is charged. |
| 4 | `prove` on claim 12, with 24 proofs and 8 annexes, none of which the scope holds. Each is an entry of 70 KiB, most of it one text of 64 KiB. The act's own entry is 12 KiB. | Settling | 2,252: 12 and 32 x 70 | 93,532 | 256 | Admitted, from claim 12's reservation. The other 6,196 of it is released. Free: 6,212. |

Step 4 adds 2,252 KiB when 16 are free, and fits. Under revision 8's
rule the claim would have reserved 256 KiB, the stand-in for one
entry, and step 4 would have had no room for what it must retain.

A count of the facts that a guard reads would have reserved
(1 + 24) x 256 = 6,400 KiB for the claim, and nothing for the 8
annexes. Admission fetches and retains them all the same (section 6.4,
point DH4). At the bound they are 8 x 256 = 2,048 KiB. A `prove` whose
own entry and 32 foreign entries are each at the bound needs
33 x 256 = 8,448 KiB, and 6,400 would not hold it. The count by
declaration reserves all 8,448.

**Three holds, twelve entries: the planner's case (`1f52493c`).** The
planner read this from I1's source at `4b91a2e4` and ran nothing.
Neither did this note. A scope is founded with a bound of 12 entries
and a fixed reserve of 2. Its genesis is entry 0. Each hold takes
three accepted acts. They are written here as `offer`, `accept` and
`take-hold`; the fixture's own acts are as the planner read them.

Under the fixed reserve, an act is refused from entry 10:

| Entries | Input | The fixed-reserve rule | Written |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | The founding | | Yes. |
| 1 to 3 | The three acts of hold 1 | Each is below entry 10. | Yes. Hold 1 is held. |
| 4 to 6 | The three acts of hold 2 | The same. | Yes. Hold 2 is held. |
| 7 to 9 | The three acts of hold 3 | The same. | Yes. Hold 3 is held. Three deadlines are pending and 2 entries are left. |
| 10 | Timed: hold 1 ends | A timed entry is written up to the bound. | Yes. |
| 11 | Timed: hold 2 ends | The same. | Yes. The history has 12 entries. |
| None | Timed: hold 3 ends | Entry 12 would pass the bound. | No. Hold 3 stays due. No later turn can write its end, and no other input may be written ahead of it. |

Under this section, with the same budget of 12 entries and no other
dimension counted:

| Step | Input | Kind | Used | Reserved | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | The founding | | 1 | 1 | The closing checkpoint reserves 1. |
| 1 | `offer` and `accept` for hold 1 | New work, 1 entry each | 3 | 1 | Admitted. |
| 2 | `take-hold` 1 | New work: 1 entry, and a deadline that reserves 1 | 4 | 2 | Admitted. |
| 3 | The three acts of hold 2 | New work, as steps 1 and 2 | 7 | 3 | Admitted. |
| 4 | `offer` and `accept` for hold 3 | New work, 1 entry each | 9 | 3 | Admitted. Used and reserved are 12. |
| 5 | `take-hold` 3 | New work: 1 entry, and a deadline that reserves 1. That would be 10 and 4. | 9 | 3 | Refused `scope-full`, entries. The third deadline is never admitted, so none is left that cannot settle. |
| 6 | Timed: hold 1 ends | Settling | 10 | 2 | Written, against its own reservation. |
| 7 | Timed: hold 2 ends | Settling | 11 | 1 | Written. |
| 8 | The closing checkpoint | Settling | 12 | 0 | Written. |

Every admitted duty settled, nothing was skipped or evicted, and the
refusal came at the act that would have created a duty with no room.
Under the static rule of section 17.3a the same fixture needs a
reserve of the hold type's `max` times its chain, which is 1, plus
one. If that `max` is 4, as the planner reads the fixture, the reserve
is 5, a reserve of 2 is outside the rule's domain, and with 5 the
first act of hold 3 is refused. I1 reports that it has since repaired
this case by counting duties, and that its third `take-hold` is now
refused as in step 5 (the deltas note, section 15). That report is
I1's. Nothing was run here.

**A checkpoint beside a pending hold: six entries (the planner's first
seam, `cc570904`).** The planner reports this from the static review
`41484d04` of I1's source. This note read neither and ran nothing. A
scope has a bound of 6 entries. Its count owes one checkpoint at every
head, and lets every checkpoint into the entry that is owed for one.

| Entries | Input | That count | Written |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | The founding | 1 written, 1 owed: the checkpoint. | Yes. |
| 1 to 3 | The three acts of one hold | 4 written, 2 owed: the hold's end and the checkpoint. | Yes. |
| 4 | A checkpoint | It is let into the entry that is owed for a checkpoint. One is still owed afterwards: 5 written, 2 owed, which is 7 of 6. | Yes. |
| 5 | Timed: the hold ends | Its duty was counted when it was admitted. | Yes. The history has 6 entries. |
| None | The closing checkpoint | Entry 6 would pass the bound. | No. The scope cannot end on a checkpoint. |

Under this section, with the same budget of 6 entries and no other
dimension counted:

| Step | Input | Kind | Used | Reserved | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | The founding | | 1 | 1 | The closing checkpoint is reserved: the head is not a checkpoint. |
| 1 | The three acts of the hold | New work; the last creates a deadline that reserves 1 | 4 | 2 | Admitted. Used and reserved are 6. |
| 2 | A checkpoint | New work: the hold's deadline is pending, so this is not the closing checkpoint. It would be 5 and 2. | 4 | 2 | Not written. |
| 3 | Timed: the hold ends | Settling | 5 | 1 | Written. |
| 4 | A checkpoint | Settling: no other duty is pending and the head is not a checkpoint. It is the closing checkpoint. | 6 | 0 | Written. The history ends on it. |

With a budget of 7 the checkpoint of step 2 is admitted into the one
free entry, and leaves 5 used and 2 reserved. The hold's end then
leaves 6 and 1, and the closing checkpoint 7 and 0.

**A late result sets a timer again (the planner's second seam,
`cc570904`).** The planner reports this too from the static review
`41484d04`. X12 is made up for these tables. Its item type `ask` has
`max` 1, the live states `asked` and `paused`, and a deadline slot.
One timed rule applies in `asked` and sets `paused`; its chain is 1.
The act `ask` opens the item and sends two requests. Each request's
`applied` clause sets the state `asked`. The act sets the deadline
from a field, to a time that has passed, so an item that is `asked` is
due at once.

First, a count that owes 2 entries for each request and 1 timed entry
for the item, and nothing for what a clause starts, with a bound of 8
entries:

| Entries | Input | That count | Written |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | The founding | 1 written, 1 owed: the checkpoint. | Yes. |
| 1 | `ask` | 2 written, 6 owed: 1 timed entry, 2 for each request, and the checkpoint. That is 8 of 8. | Yes. |
| 2 | Timed: `asked` to `paused` | Counted with the item. | Yes. |
| 3 and 4 | A diagnosis of each request, `delivery-unavailable` | Counted with the requests. | Yes. |
| 5 | The late result of the first request. Its clause sets `asked`, and the deadline holds again. | Counted with its request. Nothing was counted for the deadline that it creates. | Yes. |
| 6 | Timed: `asked` to `paused` | Not checked: it settles. | Yes. |
| 7 | The late result of the second request. Its clause sets `asked` again. | Counted with its request. | Yes. The history has 8 entries. |
| None | Timed: the third end | Entry 8 would pass the bound. | No. The item stays due, no other input may pass it, and the scope cannot end on a checkpoint. |

Under this section, with a budget of 10 entries and no other dimension
counted:

| Step | Input | Kind | Used | Reserved | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | The founding | | 1 | 1 | The closing checkpoint. |
| 1 | `ask` | New work: 1 entry; a deadline that reserves 1; and two requests that reserve 3 each, which are 2 entries and 1 for the deadline that the clause can create | 2 | 8 | Admitted. With a budget of 8 it is refused `scope-full`, entries, and no duty is created that cannot settle. |
| 2 | Timed: `asked` to `paused` | Settling | 3 | 7 | Written. It comes first: the item was due at once. |
| 3 | A diagnosis of each request, `delivery-unavailable` | Settling | 5 | 5 | Written. Each request keeps 2: its result, and the deadline. |
| 4 | The late result of the first request. Its clause sets `asked`. | Settling | 6 | 4 | Written. The new deadline takes the 1 that this request reserved for it. |
| 5 | Timed: `asked` to `paused` | Settling | 7 | 3 | Written. |
| 6 | The late result of the second request. Its clause sets `asked`. | Settling | 8 | 2 | Written. |
| 7 | Timed: `asked` to `paused` | Settling | 9 | 1 | Written. |
| 8 | The closing checkpoint | Settling | 10 | 0 | Written. |

In every row Used plus Reserved is 10. In another order, a result
arrives while the item is still `asked`. Its clause then changes
nothing, and the 1 that its request reserved for a deadline is
released. Loss of an answer was never read as proof: each

### 17.5 What this does not decide

- Every number: the five budgets, the allowance in the byte bound, the
  bound on each retained input of section 17.1, and the interval of
  section 9.1's checkpoint. They are R4's, by the method of its
  section 8.4, with R3 for the inputs that it owns. I1's temporary
  values are not adopted.
- What a full lane does next: whether it continues in a successor
  lane, and how a bounded export proceeds (R4 point R4-4). Until that
  is decided, a full scope keeps refusing new work, and a request to
  it from another scope stays outstanding at its sender and is shown
  as such. That is a gap of liveness, with R4 as its owner. It is not
  a gap of safety: nothing is dropped, reset or evicted.
- Backpressure, which is two things. A bound on a sender's pending
  requests is the fifth dimension, and R4 sets it. A limit on what
  transport has out at once is transport's, outside the accounting
  (section 17.1). R4 sets that too, and reaching it must not drop or
  reset a send (point R1-31).
- The reservations of platform definitions: the destination's
  publications, membership's notices and a task scope's releases. R3
  declares them in the same form, with the byte bound of each input
  that they retain (point R1-28).
  Stated in revision 20: for the operations, the requests and the
  items that are opened or sent for one item, as for one publication,
  the form is section 17.2a. R3 owes the counts in it.
- A scope cannot check its budget in replay unless the budget is
  given. A verifier reports the budget as trusted (section 9.5).
- Whether a deployment may change the budget of a scope that exists.
  The amounts are derived from the budget in force at each commit. A
  higher budget makes room and breaks no rule here. A lower one can
  leave an admitted duty with no room, which is a fault of the host,
  like a lowered entry size (section 6.4). R4 decides, with what a
  full lane does next.
- A delivery whose entry would pass the entry size (point R1-34), and
  the size of one checkpoint entry.
- The bound on a definition's named closure (point R1-37), and the
  policy by which a diagnosed request is sent again (section 7.4).
  Both are R4's.
- When a full creator records a `conflict` (section 17.2). It waits
  for room, like any new work. That is part of what a full lane does
  next.

**The rule and the source, kept apart. New in revision 12.** The
commission asks that the budget of admission and of settlement in five
dimensions be stated beside what I1 implements, so that neither is
read as the other. A scope has one budget, with an amount in each
dimension. Admission and settlement are its two uses: new work is
admitted against what is free, and a settling entry draws on what its
duty reserved (section 17.3).

| Dimension | Admission of new work, by this section | Settlement, by this section | The source at `a3e5a77e`, in `packages/derive/src/reserve.ts` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Entries | Refused `scope-full` unless the entry, and the entries that its duties reserve, fit | Each duty's entries are reserved when it is created, for its whole closure, with one closing checkpoint for the scope | Counted, by duty, in the commit. One amount for every request of a definition, which is never less. A timed entry, a diagnosis, an outcome, a delivery of a control, and a delivery of a result other than `conflict` are not asked. Everything else is new work. |
| Items | Refused unless the item that the entry opens, and each item that its duties reserve, fit the bound R4-B1 | An item is reserved for a settling entry that opens one | Not counted. The live items of a type are bounded by its `max`. |
| Records | Refused unless the records fit | The records that a settling entry changes are reserved | Not counted. The source has no capability record. |
| Bytes | Refused unless the entry's bytes, the inputs that it newly retains, and the bytes that its duties reserve, fit | A settling entry's own bytes, the inputs that it may newly retain, and the duties that it starts are reserved | Not counted. One entry is bounded by the entry size, and its foreign entries by their bound. The source has no budget of bytes. |
| Pending requests | Refused unless the requests that the entry sends, and those that its duties reserve, fit | A request that a settling entry sends is reserved with the duty | Not counted. A pending request is counted for the entries that it reserves, and for nothing else. |

- What the source's count guarantees is exact, and it is of one
  dimension: no admitted duty lacks an entry to settle in.
- In the other four the source refuses nothing, so it guarantees
  nothing. A settling entry is not refused there either, because no
  budget exists that could refuse it. That is not the rule of this
  section met. It is the rule absent. A limit of the host on storage
  would then be reached with no reservation behind it. A settling
  entry that the host cannot store is a fault of the host (section
  4.2).
- So "the source has the capacity rule" is true of entries only. Each
  of the other four is owed (section 11.9; the I1 delivery note,
  section 6). Owner: the builder, in I1 or the delivery that follows
  it. R4's revision 9 says the same. It adds that two witnesses of
  this contract have no candidate witness yet: a pending job at
  capacity, which needs items, and retained inputs with the deciding
  entry, which needs bytes (its section 5.1).
- No number moves. The source's bound on entries is a temporary value.
  The five budgets are R4's.

## 18. Witnesses for the forms of revisions 8 to 23

One compact witness for each new form, in the style of the tables
above. Each names the boundary of R4's section 2 that owns its
evidence: B1, a pure function; B2, one scope on real storage; B3,
several scopes; B4, a local Git server; B9, independent replay. None
is a sweep over fields or guards. Nothing here was run. R4 folds these
into its plan; no gate and no quota is added.

### 18.5 Absence at a position, and terminal absence

An intent with `notAfter` T is addressed to lane P. P's head is P.40,
whose time is earlier than T.

| Step | P's clock | Settlement answers | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Before T | `not-found` at P.40, `terminal: null` | A copy can still be admitted. |
| 2 | Past T; P has written nothing | P writes P.41, a checkpoint, with its time the reading. Then `not-found` at P.41, `terminal: "expired"`. | P.41's time is at or past T, and no later act entry can have an earlier time. |
| 3 | Past T, a second request within the interval, for another intent whose `notAfter` is later than P.41's time | `not-found` at P.41, `terminal: null`, with `retryAfter` | One checkpoint for each interval. |
| 4 | P's clock reads earlier than P.40's time | `not-found` at P.40, `terminal: null` | A checkpoint would be clamped. A clamped time proves nothing. |
| 5 | Any; item 9, which the intent expects at revision 4, is at revision 5 | `not-found`, `terminal: "revision-moved"` | A revision only rises. |

Owner: B2. R4's row F22 is its neighbour.

### 18.6 The largest fan-out

Pull request P has 32 links that are `set`, and a manifest that an
issue lane staged. G's final update arrives.

|---|---|
| `relate`, `closes`, `merged`: one for each `set` link, by the fan-out, in order of link item ID | 32, ordinals 0 to 31 |
| `tell`, `unpin`, made because the manifest's `staging` is set | 1, ordinal 32 |
| `index`: the row for the directory, which shows the merge | 1, ordinal 33 |
| The platform's result to G | 1, ordinal 34 |
| Attention | 0 |
| Total | 35, inside the row for a delivery of a request: 7, 32, 1 and 64 |

With 33 links the lane would already have refused the 33rd `link`,
`type-full`. With the manifest staged by P itself, the `unpin` is not
made and takes no ordinal: the index row is ordinal 32, the result is
ordinal 33, and the entry has 34 sends. Of the 35 sends, 33 are
requests that get a result: the 32 updates and the `unpin`. The index
row is an advisory, and the result is a result. Owner: B2, built at
the limit by a fixture. R4's row F23.

Changed in revision 12. Revisions 8 to 11 had 34 sends here, with the
result at ordinal 33, and 33 for a manifest that P staged. They
counted the companion file's `publication` row, which has no `index`
send. The row counted now is that of the lane design's adopted
revision 14 (its section 13.5).

### 18.16 A job, and what decided it

P is a change lane. Manifest 7 is current, and the rules require the
check `combined`. The last column is the record that a `merge` entry
written at that point would carry for the job, by `collect`.

| Entry | Input | The job | Its `decidedBy` | Its record in a statement |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P.20 | `request-check`, `combined` | Job 20, `requested` | Empty | `{ job: P.20, name, state: "requested" }`. No `decidedBy`: nothing has answered. |
| P.21 | Timed, `job-deadline` | Job 20, `timed-out` | P.21 | `state: "timed-out"`, `decidedBy: P.21`. That entry's kind is `timed:job-deadline`. It is not a result. |
| P.22 | `check` on job 20, passed: the first answer | Job 20, `passed` | P.22 | `state: "passed"`, `decidedBy: P.22`. |
| P.23 | A second `check` on job 20, failed, as a new signed intent | Job 20, `passed` | P.22, unchanged | The same. Result 23 is history. |
| P.24 | `request-check`, `combined`, naming job 20 as `earlier` | Job 20, `superseded`; job 24, `requested` | Job 20 keeps P.22. Job 24: empty. | Job 20 is not listed: it is not live. Job 24: `{ job: P.24, name, state: "requested" }`. |
| P.25 | A late `check` that names job 20 | Unchanged | Unchanged | Unchanged. Result 25 is history of job 20. Its effect names job 20, so it cannot become job 24's `decidedBy`. |

- **Derivable.** The fold sets `decidedBy` in the entry that changes
  the job's state, and in no other. A verifier derives it again.
- **Checkable from the named entry.** For a record with a
  `decidedBy`, the named entry is an entry of P; its own effects give
  that job that state, which the part `{ set }` of section 6.5 reads;
  and, for a `check` or a `check-error`, its field `job` names that
  job. So no entry can be offered as the decision of another job.
- **Superseded history stays attributable.** A superseded job keeps
  its `decidedBy` and its result items, and the `request-check` entry
  that superseded it names it in its field `earlier`.
- **While a merge is in progress. New in revision 12.** Had a `merge`
  been `intended` when the answer of P.22 arrived, the act would have
  been refused `merge-in-progress`, with no entry. Job 20 would stay
  `timed-out`, with P.21 as its `decidedBy`, and with its reservation.
  The same signed answer could be sent again. An entry that already
  carried job 20's record keeps its bytes, whatever is decided later
  (section 6.10).
- What the destination does with the named entries at reservation is
  R3's: its key, its configuration and its result, under rules that
  the destination observed itself (R3 section 6.5; point R1-30).

Owner: B2 for the lane; B3 for a destination that reads the named
entries. R4's check results table (R4 section 9.5) is its neighbour.

### 18.17 A merge closes an issue

I is an issue lane and P a change lane. G.8 is the destination's
outcome entry that confirms the publication. P.12 is P's delivery
entry that records it and sends the `closes` update `merged`. I.20 is
I's deciding entry for that update.

| Case | The issue before I.20 | I.20 | The issue after | The result that I.20 sends to P |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `open`. It has no current plan, or the update names its current plan. | `applied`. The copy is `merged`. The three closing effects apply. | `closed`; `closeReason` is `completed`; `closedBy` is I.20. | `of` P.12 at that send's ordinal, `applied`. |
| 2 | `open`. Its current plan is another one. | `applied`. The copy is `merged`. The closing effects are not applied. | `open`; `closedBy` is empty. | `applied`. The result says that the update was applied. It does not say that the issue closed. |
| 3 | `closed` by `close-any` at I.18. | `applied`. The copy is `merged`. | `closed`; `closedBy` stays I.18. | `applied`. |
| 4 | As case 1; then `reopen-any` at I.22; then P.12's update arrives again. | No new entry. The repeat is answered with I.20. | `open`; `closedBy` is empty, as I.22 left it. | None new. |

| Definition | The closing effect on `closedBy` | Validation |
|---|---|---|
| As revision 8 wrote it | From `{ source: "ref" }`, which is P.12, an entry under `change` | Refused: the slot holds entries under `issue` (section 6.6). |
| As revision 9 writes it | From `self`, which is I.20, a delivery of `closes` under `issue` | Passes: the slot's kinds include `closes`. |

Three things stay apart. The publication is G.8, and P.12 records it.
The closure is I.20. A reader of I.20 finds P.12 as its `from`, and
P.12's bytes in its `uses`. The requester's judgment is a later
`judge`, which sets `satisfied` and `judgedAt`; I.20 sets neither.
Owner: B3. R4's key L11.

### 18.18 A written refusal keeps what it read

L is an issue lane with the companion file's `unpin` handler. Its
message declares two fact fields: `manifest`, which is required, and
`merge`, which is optional. Its guards read the `manifest` fact first,
and then refuse `not-the-owner` when that manifest is not an entry of
the sender. No guard reads `merge` before that. L holds pin (P, d),
`provisional`. The table counts bytes only, in KiB. The budget, 10,000,
and every size are made up. The pin reserves 2,304, which is 3 entries
and 6 foreign entries at a stand-in of 256 each (the companion file's
reservations table). Three of the 6 are for `unpin`: its source entry,
the manifest and the merge. The closing checkpoint reserves 256. So
Reserved is 2,560 before each case.

Revision 14 states what each message holds. In cases 2 to 4 the message
leaves the optional `merge` out: its `because` is `superseded`. So each
names two foreign entries, and 6 + 20 + 90 = 116. Cases 5 and 6 are new:
the message names a `merge`, of 40 KiB, and 6 + 20 + 90 + 40 = 156.

| Case | Input | Kind | Used before | Free before | Bytes it adds | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | An act that names a foreign entry of 150 KiB, and whose guard fails | No entry: a refused act is an answer | 7,000 | 440 | 0 | Refused `guard-failed`. The fetched entry is discarded. Nothing is charged. |
| 2 | An `unpin` from lane X, which is not the pin's consumer, with no `merge`. Its entry is 6 KiB. Its source entry, of 20 KiB, and the manifest, of 90 KiB, were fetched. | New work: a refusal ends no duty | 7,000 | 440 | 116 | L.60, a deciding entry `refused`, `not-the-owner`. Its `uses` holds both entries. Used is 7,116. The pin's reservation is untouched. The result `refused` goes to X. |
| 3 | The same `unpin`, in a scope with less room | New work | 7,340 | 100 | 0 | 116 does not fit in 100. No entry is written and the request is not decided. Transport answers `retry`. The fetched entries are discarded. Nothing is charged. |
| 4 | An `unpin` from P for a superseded manifest, with no `merge`, in the scope of case 3. Its entry is 6 KiB, its source entry 20 KiB and the manifest 90 KiB. | Settling: the pin's record reserved it | 7,340 | 100 | 116 | Written, from the pin's reservation, with 100 free. The pin is `released`, and the other 2,188 of its reservation are released. Used is 7,456, and Reserved is 256. |
| 5 | The `unpin` of case 2, from X, with `because` `published` and a `merge` fact of 40 KiB. The source entry, the manifest and the merge were fetched. | New work | 7,000 | 440 | 156 | A deciding entry `refused`, `not-the-owner`. The refusal came before any guard read `merge`. Its `uses` holds all three entries all the same, and all three are charged. Used is 7,156. |
| 6 | The `unpin` of case 5, in the scope of case 3 | New work | 7,340 | 100 | 0 | 156 does not fit in 100. No entry is written, and the request is not decided. All three fetched entries are discarded. Nothing is charged. |

Cases 1, 3 and 6 write no entry, and only they discard. Case 2 is the
review's case: under revision 9's sentence its inputs would have been
discarded, and the written refusal would have rested on bytes that the
scope did not keep. Case 5 replaces a sentence of revisions 10 to 13,
which said that a fetched `merge` fact "would not be in `uses`, because
the refusal came before any guard read it; it would be discarded". That
was against point DH4 of section 6.4 and against section 17.3. A written
entry keeps every entry that was fetched for its input (section 6.5),
and a fetched declared fact is never dropped from a written refusal. The
numbers were added up by a script. Owner: B2 for the entry and its
`uses`; B9 for a replay of L.60, and of the entry of case 5, from what L
retained.

### 18.19 A child reads its definition from its creator

Rewritten in revision 11, for the named closure (section 7.2). C is a
lane under a declared definition whose digest is x. Its act `split`
sends a `create` with `definition: "self"`. Its act `spawn` sends a
`create` under another declared definition, whose digest is y. The
definition y has a `create` of its own, under z, and z has none. So
the named closure of x is x, y and z.

| Case | What happens | Written |
|---|---|---|
| C is created by its creator B, which holds x, y and z | C's object reads x from B, checks it against x and validates it. It then reads y and z from B, each by its digest, and checks and validates each. Its genesis C.0 is written, with the three definitions retained in its transaction. | C.0, provisional |
| The same, and B answers that it holds no bytes under z | That is a fault at B: B's own genesis needed z. The creation is not decided. Transport answers `retry`, `dependency-unavailable`, and B keeps the duty. | Nothing in C |
| C.9 is a `split`. Its `create` carries a seed that names x. | The child K reads x from C, and then y and z. K.0 is written, and K retains all three. | K.0 |
| C.12 is a `spawn`. Its `create` carries a seed that names y. | The child M reads y from C, and then z. M.0 is written, and M retains y and z. C.12 newly retains no definition: C has held y since C.0. | M.0 |
| As the `split`, and C does not answer the read within the time limit | The creation is not decided. Transport answers `retry`, and C keeps the duty. No answer shows nothing about the definition. | Nothing in K |
| As the `split`, and the bytes that C serves do not hash to x | They are not the definition. As the row above. | Nothing in K |
| A scope with no creator is founded under x, with the declarations of y and z beside the signed intent | Each is checked against its digest and validated. The genesis is written, and the scope retains x, y and z. | The genesis |
| The same founding, with y supplied and z not | The closure is not whole. The founding is answered `dependency-unavailable`. The same signed intent may be sent again with z. | Nothing |

### 18.22 A reply that is not an answer

New in revision 11 (section 9.6). A client submits a signed act and
reads the reply. Its transport returns a reply only when it is a
value of the operation's result type.

|---|---|---|
| `{ answer: "accepted", receipt }`, with every member of a receipt | Returns it | The service says that the act is an entry. Following the receipt checks that the service serves that entry. |
| `{ answer: "accepted" }`, with no receipt | No answer | Nothing. The act may be an entry. The caller sends the same signed intent again, or asks for settlement. |
| `{ answer: "accepted", receipt }`, whose fact has no incarnation | No answer | The same. |
| `{ answer: "refused", reason: "guard-failed" }`, with no `judgedAt` | No answer | The same. It is not taken as a refusal. |
| `{ answer: "refused", reason: "tired", judgedAt }` | No answer: the contract names no such reason | The same. |
| `{ ok: "yes" }`, in answer to a read | No answer | Nothing about the scope's state. |
| A summary whose `status` is a word outside the three | No answer | The same. |
| No reply, or bytes that are not JSON | No answer | The same. |
| The transport's own refusal of a request that reached no operation | No answer of the operation | That this request was not judged. The caller corrects the request. |

| Following a receipt whose fact is F | Result |
|---|---|
| The entry that is served at F's position has F's scope, kind, incarnation and hash | The receipt is of this history, as the service serves it. |
| It has F's position and hash, and another incarnation | Not of this history. The hash alone is not the reference (section 6.5). |
| Its bytes do not hash to F's hash | Not of this history. |

Owner: B1 for the table of replies; B2 for the real service's replies
passed through the same check. No sweep over fields is asked.

New in revision 11 (section 17.2). X13 is made up for this table. It

entries, and a request of form b reserves 2. Runtime E holds exactly

definition's forms, as I1 does. The budget of 13 entries is made up,

| 4 | In M, the act of step 2, sent again | | | 9, 4 | Admitted: 9 and 4 are 13 |

form a would hold less than that request's closure. The fifth witness
of section 17.4 shows what follows.

deadline slot is `hard`. A leads to B. So the chain of A is 2, and
the chain of B is 1.

| The item | It holds a deadline under | Reserved, by section 17.2 | Timed entries that can still be written |
|---|---|---|---|
| `open`, with `soft` and `hard` set | A and B | 2: the longer chain. The sum would be 3. | At most 2: A, and then B. Or 1: B alone, after which the item is `closed` and holds no deadline. |
| `late`, with `hard` set | B | 1 | 1 |
| `open`, with only `hard` set | B | 1. I1 holds 2, the longest chain from `open`. That is more, and never less. | 1 |

### 18.25 A reply that is too long, or too late

New in revision 12 (section 9.6, "The reader of a reply"). A client's
transport sends one request. Its byte limit is L, and its deadline is
D. Each row is an order of events, and the witness sets that order
itself. It holds a clock that moves only when the witness moves it,
and a body whose reads answer only when the witness lets them. No row
waits on real time, and none states a duration. In every row the other
party ignores the request to end, so that the row shows what the
reader holds, and not what the other party does.

| Case | The order of events | What the transport does | What the caller gets |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The parts of the body add up to no more than L, and the body ends before D | Joins them, and reads the reply as section 9.6 says | The answer, or no answer by its shape |
| 2 | A part arrives that takes the count past L | Asks the body to end. Joins nothing. | No answer. For an act, the outcome is unknown. |
| 3 | D passes before any reply begins. The reply then begins. | Makes no read of the body | No answer |
| 4 | One read is pending when D passes. It then answers with a whole, well-formed answer that is shorter than L. | Ends at D, and does not wait. Does not keep what the read returned. Makes no further read. | No answer. The well-formed bytes are never parsed. |
| 5 | A part was read and kept. D passes. The next read then answers. | Drops the part that it kept, and keeps nothing of the next | No answer |
| 6 | The body answers every read at once with an empty part, without end | Keeps none of them, and counts none against L. Lets D pass, and ends there. | No answer |
| 7 | Empty parts come between parts that hold bytes. The body ends before D, inside L. | Passes over the empty parts | The answer, as case 1 |
| 8 | Any of cases 2 to 6, for a read and not for an act | The same | No answer. Nothing was read, and the read may be made again. |

Each row tells a wrong reader from a right one. A reader that kept the
late part would return an answer in case 4, and one that read on would
make a second read there. A reader that counted empty parts, or that
never looked at its deadline while reads answered at once, would not
end case 6 at D. A transport that said "not recorded" in case 2 would
tell its caller something that it does not know. The same rows hold
for a verifier's source, with "a failed read" in place of "no answer",
and with nothing decoded after D.

Owner: B1, as one table with a controlled source and a controlled
timer. R4's keys O2 and O12 are its neighbours. I1's present witnesses
of these cases wait for short real times. Replacing those waits with a
controlled timer is I1's existing follow-through, and the review of
its source says so (`5019cff4`). No new suite is asked, and no count.

### 18.43 An outcome's request, its clause and the cause of what it creates

New in revision 17 (sections 6.1 and 7.2). R is a made-up value of
platform data for a register. Its `outcomes` holds the kind
`create-repository`, with the mark `selected`, `attempts: 3`, and a
`send` whose mark is `create-directory` and whose clause `applied` holds
one effect mark, `claim-active`. R.5 is an act, `found`, that opens the
operation 5:0 of that kind. R.8 is its first `confirmed` outcome.

| Case | The entry | What is derived |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | R.8 | The rule `selected` gives the effects. The rule `create-directory` gives one `create`, at ordinal 0. Its seed's cause is the digest of the intent of R.5, in `artroom-intent-1`: the fourth cause. |
| 2 | The directory's genesis, from that `create` | It checks that R.8 is an outcome, that its operation was opened by an act with that intent digest, and that R.8's sends hold this seed at ordinal 0. |
| 3 | R.11, the delivery of the result `applied` | The clause is found in `outcomes` by the kind of R.8, which its input holds. The rule `claim-active` gives the effects on the claim, which it finds by the operation. No name of `also` is bound. |
| 4 | R.9, a second `confirmed` outcome of the same operation | The rule `create-directory` gives no request: the claim has a repository. The entry has no send. |
| 5 | An outcome of an operation that a delivery opened, whose rule gives a `create` | A fault: no cause is stated for it. Nothing is written. |
| 6 | The data of R, with a second send mark under that kind, or a written send | Refused by the validator: an outcome's mark holds at most one `send`, and it is a mark. |
| 7 | A rule `selected` that returns 5 effects where its mark states `most: { effects: 4 }` | A fault. Nothing is written. |

Owner: B1, at the judge and the validator, with stand-in rules. Case 2:
B3. The rules are stand-ins, so this shows where a request, a clause and
a cause stand. It proves nothing about a rule of the register.

### 18.44 A list of 64, and what each count reads

New in revision 19 (sections 6.1 and 17.1). M is a made-up value of
platform data. One item type of M has five value slots, each of the type
`{ type: "list", of: { type: "text", max: 64 }, max: 64 }`, and one act
of M has a field of that type. Every size is made up.

| Case | The input | Judged | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The data of M, in a runtime whose configured bound on a list is 64 | Each `max` is at most the bound. | It validates. |
| 2 | The same data, in a runtime whose configured bound is 32 | A `max` passes the bound. | It does not validate there. No scope is founded or created under it: `unsupported-definition`. |
| 3 | The data of M with one list type that states `max: 65`, at the bound 64 | The `max` passes the bound. | It does not validate. |
| 4 | An entry that sets one of the slots to a list of 34 texts | 34 is at most the slot's `max`. | Written. Used bytes grow by the entry as it was written, with 34 texts. |
| 5 | An act whose field holds a list of 65 texts | The value is longer than its type's `max`, at check 7. | Refused `bad-field`. Nothing is written. |
| 6 | A reservation for an entry form that copies one such list | The static size counts the list at 64 elements, each at the largest that a text of 64 bytes can be. | The same amount whether the list holds 2 texts, 34 or 64. |
| 7 | A pinned lane definition, each of whose lists states a `max` of at most 32, at the bound 64 | Nothing of it changed. | It validates, with the same bytes, the same digest and the same static sizes as at the bound 32. |
| 8 | An act of a declared definition with three list fields of 64 facts each, and a `fact` guard on each element | The input names 192 foreign entries, which is more than the bound of section 7.5. | Refused `entry-too-large`, before any is fetched (section 17.2). |

Owner: B1 for cases 1 to 3, 5, 7 and 8; B2 for cases 4 and 6, on real
storage. The number 64 is a proposal, and this shows which number each
check reads. It measures nothing.

New in revision 19 (sections 6.1, 6.2, 7.2 and 9.2). D is a made-up

### 18.46 The subjects of an entry, read before the turn

New in revision 20 (sections 6.1 and 16.1). M is a made-up value of
platform data. Its act `set-checks` has a list field `checks`, of
records with a member `checker` of the type `member`, and one row of
`observes`: `{ of: "member", from: { each: { field: "checks" }, as:

"reuse" }`. Its kind `weigh` of `outcomes` states `origin: "rule"` and
three rows: `{ of: "rules", window: 10, use: "once", without: "wait" }`;

"wait" }`; and `{ of: "holders", action: "x.do", most: 2, window: 10,
use: "once", without: "write" }`. G is a scope under M. G.20 is an entry
of G whose `uses` names two entries of a lane, each signed by another
key. Every rule is a stand-in, and every number is made up.

| Case | The input | Judged | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The data of M, with the platform option | Each row passes the seven checks. | It validates. |
| 2 | The data of M, where the row of `set-checks` states `from: "rule"` | A row of an act states an operand. | It does not validate. |
| 3 | The data of M as a declared definition, without the option | The member `observes` is unknown there. | Refused by the validator. No pinned lane definition states the member. |
| 4 | `set-checks` with three checks, whose checkers are two members | The list gives three subjects, and two are one. | Written. `observed` holds two records, one for each member, in ascending order of `read.n`. |
| 5 | `set-checks` with five checks, of five members | The row is over: 5 is more than its `max` of 4. | Refused `entry-too-large`. Nothing is written, and no member is read for the row. |
| 6 | `set-checks` whose first checker is a member of another repository | It names no subject of this scope. | Refused `bad-field`. |
| 7 | An outcome of `weigh`, where the rule names G.20 as its origin and the two keys that signed the entries in G.20's `uses` | The subjects are the rules, two keys and the holders of `x.do`. Each has an observation that began less than 10 seconds before the commit. | Written. `uses` is a copy of G.20's. `observed` holds four records, each `fresh`. |
| 8 | The same, where the commit's reading is 10 seconds after the read of one key began | An age that equals the window is outside it. | Not written. The observation is discarded and read again, and the outcome stays offered. |
| 9 | The same, where the rule names four keys | The row of keys is over. | Written. `observed` holds the rules and the holders, and no key. The rule is told that the row is over. |
| 10 | The same as case 7, where membership cannot be reached for the holders | That row states `without: "write"`. | Written, with three records. The rule is told that the row is absent. |
| 11 | The same, where the rules scope cannot be reached | That row states `without: "wait"`. | Not written. The outcome stays offered, and its operation keeps its reservation. |
| 12 | Between the derivation before the turn and the commit, another entry changes the state so that the rule names a third key | The commit's list holds a subject with no observation at hand. | The commit stops. The key is read, and the turn starts again. |
| 13 | A replay of the entry of case 7 | It derives the origin, the list of four subjects, the guards with the window of each row, and each value. | `consistent`, with `observation-read` and `platform-code` under `trusts`. |
| 14 | The entry of case 7 with a fifth record, of a key that the rule did not name | `observed` holds a record that no row gives. | `mismatch`. |
| 15 | The entry of case 7 with `uses` in another order than G.20's | The `uses` is no copy of the origin's. | `mismatch`. |
| 16 | A rule of an entry whose form states no row reads an observation | No subject is on the list. | A fault. Nothing is written. |

Owner: B1 for cases 1 to 6 and 16, at the validator and the judge; B2
for cases 7 to 12, on real storage with a controlled clock; B9 for
cases 13 to 15. The rules are stand-ins, so this shows where a subject
comes from and what an entry retains. It proves nothing about a rule of
a destination or of a rules scope.

### 18.47 A reservation that an item holds, taken once and drawn down

New in revision 20 (sections 4.1 and 17.2a). M is a made-up value of
platform data. Its item type `job` states `holds: { operations: { step:
2, tidy: 1 }, requests: 1 }`. Its kinds `step` and `tidy` have 1 attempt
each. The mark of `step` lists `step` and `tidy` in `most.operations`,
and holds a `send` with empty clauses. The handler `start` of a request
opens a `job`. The act `again`, on a `job`, states `adds: {
operations: { step: 1 } }`. G is a scope under M with a budget of
entries. Every rule is a stand-in, and every number is made up.

| Case | The input | Judged | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The data of M, with the platform option | The kinds open each other in a circle, and each is a held kind. | It validates. The amounts of `holds` are 6 entries for three operations and 2 for the request: 8 entries, and 1 pending request. |
| 2 | The data of M without the members `holds` and `adds` | The closure of `step` holds `step`. | Refused by the validator, `reserve-unbounded`. |
| 3 | The data of M, where `holds` lists a kind that `outcomes` does not have | Check 1 fails. | It does not validate. |
| 4 | A `start` to G, whose free room is 9 entries, when its rule opens one `step` for the item that it opens | The entry is new work: 1 entry and the 8 of the item. | Written. The `operation` effect states `for: "self"`. The item still holds 1 `step`, 1 `tidy` and 1 request, and the open operation reserves 2 entries by row 5. |
| 5 | The same `start`, when the free room is 8 entries | The entry and the item's 8 do not fit. | Not decided. Transport answers "retry". Nothing is written. |
| 6 | The first outcome of that `step`, at a scope with no free room, when its rule opens the second `step` and sends the request | A settling entry of the account. Each draw is within a count. | Written. Used plus reserved does not grow. The item still holds 1 `tidy`. |
| 7 | An outcome of the second `step` whose rule opens a third `step` for the item | The count of `step` is 0. | A fault. Nothing is written, the outcome stays offered, and the fault is reported. |
| 8 | An outcome whose rule opens a `tidy` with no `for` | A held kind states `for`. | A fault. Nothing is written. |
| 9 | An outcome of a `step` of one job whose rule opens a `step` for another job that is not final | The effect states `for` the other item. | Written. The draw is on the other job, and this job's counts do not move. |
| 10 | `again` on a job that is not final, with free room for 3 entries: its own, and the 2 of its addition | An adding entry: new work, for its addition. | Written. The count of `step` rises by 1. With less room it is refused `scope-full`, with the dimension. |
| 11 | `again` on a job that is final | An act on a final item. | Refused `final`. |
| 12 | The job becomes final while one `step` is open and its attempt is `unknown` | The mark of `step` reaches `step` and `tidy`. | The job still holds what is left of both, and of its request. The operation keeps 1 entry for its late answer. |
| 13 | The job is final, every operation for it is settled and its request has its result | Nothing can be reached. | The job holds nothing. The entries that it did not use are free. |
| 14 | A checkpoint, and a reader that starts at it | The state that the checkpoint digests holds each job's three counts and the holder of each operation. | The reader derives the same amounts as one that read from the genesis. |
| 15 | A replay of the history of cases 4, 6 and 9 | It derives each `for`, each draw and both amounts. | `consistent`. With the `for` of case 9 changed to this job: `mismatch`. |

Owner: B1 for cases 1 to 3, 7 and 8, at the validator and the judge; B2
for cases 4 to 6 and 9 to 14, on real storage; B9 for case 15. Every
count is made up. This shows that the reservation is finite where the
kinds are in a circle, that it is checked where it is taken, and that
it is released. It measures no number of the authority note.

Read with revisions 21 and 22: M is read as holding no timed rule and no
`settles`, and no kind that no item holds. So a change of state starts
nothing, `one(k)` of each kind is its 2 entries, and the amounts of the
cases stand.

New in revision 20 (sections 3 and 16.1). F is the fact of an entry of a
lane at position 41. U is a made-up value of platform data for a rules
scope, whose item `rules` states a slot `extents` and declares the byte
domain `x-extents-1` for it, with a bound of 400,000 bytes on one value.
D is a scope that observes a scope under U. Every number is made up.

| Case | The input | Judged | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The text of F | The canonical JSON of the reference. | One line: `at` with `inc`, `kind` and `scope`, then `hash`, then `seq` as `41`. It holds no space and no line feed. |

| 3 | The name of a ref for F, after the prefix `refs/artroom/receipts/` | The 64 hexadecimal characters of F's `hash`. | A name of 86 bytes, with no colon. |
| 4 | A commit whose message holds a line with the text of F, under the ref of case 3 | A reader compares the last part of the name with `hash` in the line. | They are equal. No entry and no host was read. |

The entry that retains it holds the digest, and the list is one retained input of the kind `value`. The entry is far below the entry size. |
| 7 | The same answer, with no bytes beside it, or with bytes that do not hash to the digest | The answer is not whole. | No observation. The row's `without` says what follows. |
| 8 | A second entry of D that retains a later observation with the same `extents` | One domain and one digest are one input. | Nothing more is kept, and used bytes do not grow for the list. |
| 9 | An observation under U whose `content` has no member `extents` | The data of its `definition` states the slot. | The record check refuses it. It is no observation. |

### 18.49 A held kind opens a kind that no item holds, at capacity

New in revision 21 (sections 17.2 and 17.2a; the verdict `0cf59056`, its
first finding). M is a made-up value of platform data. Its item type
`job` states `holds: { operations: { k: 1 } }`. Its kind `k` has 1
attempt, and its mark lists `u` in `most.operations`. Its kind `u` has 3
attempts, lists no kind, and no item holds it. M has no timed rule and
no `settles`, so a change of state starts nothing. The handler `start`
of a request opens a `job`, and its rule opens one `k` for it. M0 is M
with one change: the mark of `k` lists no kind. That is the control. G
is a scope under M, and G0 a scope under M0, each with a budget of
entries. Every rule is a stand-in, and every number is made up.

| Case | The input | Judged | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The data of M, with the platform option | `k` is held. `u` is not, its closure is finite, and it reaches no held kind. | It validates. C(u) is 6 entries. `one(k)` is 2 times (1 + 6), which is 14 entries, and a `job` reserves 14. |
| 2 | The data of M0 | The mark of `k` lists no kind. | It validates. `one(k)` is 2 entries, and a `job` reserves 2. |
| 3 | A `start` to G, whose free room is 15 entries | New work: 1 entry and the 14 of the item. | Written. The job holds no count of `k`, and the open operation of `k` reserves 14. |
| 4 | The same `start`, when the free room is 14 entries | The entry and the item's 14 do not fit. | Not decided. Transport answers "retry". By the count of revision 20 it needed 3 and was written: that is the verdict's case. |
| 5 | After case 3, at G with no free room: the first outcome of `k`, confirmed, whose rule opens one `u` with no `for` | A settling entry. It uses 1 entry of the 14, and C(u), 6 entries, moves to the operation of `u`. `k` is settled. | Written. The 7 entries of the outcome entry that was not written are released. Used plus reserved for the job was 14, and is 1 and 6. It did not grow. |
| 6 | Each outcome of the three attempts of that `u`, with no room beside what case 5 left | Settling entries of the operation of `u`, which reserved 6. | Written, each of them. At most 6 entries. |
| 7 | A `start` to G0, whose free room is 3 entries | New work: 1 entry and the 2 of the item. | Written. The control: with no child, the count of revision 20 was right. |
| 8 | At G0, the first outcome of `k`, whose rule opens a `u` | The mark of `k` does not list the kind. | A fault. Nothing is written, and nothing was under-reserved. |
| 9 | The data of M, where the mark of `u` lists `k` | A kind that no item holds lists a held kind. | Refused by the validator, `reserve-unbounded` (check 5). |
| 10 | The data of M, where the mark of `u` lists `u` | The closure of `u` holds `u`. | Refused by the validator, `reserve-unbounded` (check 4). |
| 11 | The data of M, where `job` also holds `h: 1`, the mark of `k` also lists `h`, and `h` has 1 attempt and lists no kind | A mixed graph: `k` lists a held kind and a kind that no item holds. | It validates. A `job` reserves 14 and 2, which is 16 entries. An outcome of `k` that opens an `h` states `for`, and draws the 1. |
| 12 | A replay of the history of cases 3 and 5 | It derives the counts, C(u), `one(k)` and both amounts at each head. | `consistent`. |

Owner: B1 for cases 1, 2 and 9 to 11, at the validator; B2 for cases 3
to 8, on real storage; B9 for case 12. A script made the sums 6, 14, 15,
7 and 16. This shows the edge from a held kind to a kind that no item
holds, at capacity, with its control. Witness 18.47 shows kinds that are
all held, and does not show this edge.

Read with revision 22: one more control, by check 5 as section 17.2a now
states it. The data of M, where `u` states a `send` whose clause
`applied` holds an effect mark that lists `k`. A clause of the request
of a kind that no item holds lists a held kind. It is refused by the
validator, `reserve-unbounded` (check 5, edge 2). Owner: B1.
